summary: The Food Inspector took a sample of lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. On analysis by the Public Analyst it was found in exhibit PW 1/C that the sample contained nine living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the Lal mirchi machine powder was adulterated, and he accordingly acquitted the Respondent. The Calcutta High Court in Dhanraj 's case held: (i) In the present sample, however, worm seeds were found to be present and that in the absence of clear proof of the sample being unfit for human consumption, it could not constitute a valid basis for holding the article to be adulterated within the meaning of section 2(1)(f) of the Act. In appeal to this Court against the acquittal of the Respondent the appellant Corporation submitted: (a) The Public Analyst had reported that there was no evidence in respect of the plea of the Food Inspector 's report by way of the Public analyst 's Report did not satisfy the requirements of section2(1) (f); (b) In any case, proceeds the argument that if for an article of food, no (1), 469 standard of quality or purity has been prescribed or no limits have been prescribed for the validity or its constituents, then sub clause (I) of clause (1) of section. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1(i) The word 'otherwise ' in sub cl. (f) would include infested and separate cclass altogether, it seems to us (i)(a) the last clause 'or is otherwise unfit for cow consumption. [470 E] 1.(ii) In order that a Food Inspector should report to the Public Examiner about this fact and the said report of the public analyst who examines and analyses the sample would constitute legal evidence. [473 D E] 2(i)(f), as well as in other cases, he is competent to opine and testify about this experience.[470 B C] M/s Narkeklange Roller Flour Mills and another vs The Corporation of Calcutta AIR 1970 Delhi 681; Dhanraj vs Gulab Chand Bhatia ; , referred to. (ii) If the phrase is to be read disjunctively, the mere proof of a whole or any part of the article being 'filthy, putrid, disgusting, rotten or insect infested ' would be conclusive to bring the case within the mischief of this sub clause, and it would not be necessary in such a case to prove further that the article was unfit for animal consumption.

The appellant was an agriculturist. He had taken on lease from various parties, and his brother was in possession of 80 90 bighas of land on which Paddy and other foodgrains found in his pos session were grown there. At the time of occurrence he had stored foodgrains above the permitted quantities for a wholesale dealer, but on the land he had occupied 80% of the land on rent. The trial court convicted him under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955; but the High Court dismissed his revision application summarily. It was contended on behalf of the appel lant that he was an agni tor and therefore not liable to the penalty under the law because the presumption in his case cannot be drawn: Held per Hidayatullah C. J., Hidayatullah, Wanchoo and Das Gupta JJ.), that the appellant could not be regarded as doing business as a dealer unless a series of transactions by him of sale were proved against him. The fact that the lands about which the witnesses spoke orally were held by the appellant for purposes of cultivation did not make any difference. It is obvious that sub cl. refers to storage for sale as a dealers though the words "as a dealer" are not there, because storage has reference to 'business as adealer and that is the essence of the Order. The fiction in the second sub paragraph must be carried to its logical conclusion. In the present case the appellant had successfully proved that he is an agriculturist and that the presumption under para. 3(2) could, therefore, not be drawn against him; and it was easy to see that the evidence which was 'brought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh ; , applied. Manipur administration vs M //s Meghalaya Administration, ; followed.

The defendant appellant took an appeal to the High Court of Calcutta and during the pendency of this appeal, the High Courts appointed a Receiver who was put in possession of the entire estate. On 8th December 1924, the defendant executed a registered Kabuliyat in favour of the Receiver by which he purported to take settlement of land in suit for a period of ten years at a rental of Rs. There was a covenant in the lease that was challenged as invalid and inoperative. The Trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that the notice to quit served upon his client, did not create any rights in the defendant, inas much as the Prodhan had no authority to settle lands of this character; and that by reason of the payment and acceptance of rent, there were two tenancies for one year each. The High Court held that the lease was effective from a month to month under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, and the suit was in fact one for ejectment of a lessee on the expiration of the period provided for in the Lease. On appeal by special leave: Held, that on the facts of this case it would be quite proper to hold that the tenancy of the defendant was one from month to year since its inception in 1924. The agreement between the parties was certainly not to create a monthly tenancy. It was an outright transfer of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes and as such no question of holding over would arise, and no question was raised before the courts below, which had jurisdiction either to decide the matter on the merits or appreciate whether the payment of rent amounted to payments to the defendant himself. The rights of the parties would be regulated by the terms of the lease deed. There could be no dispute that the contract to the contrary was a registered document but ex facie it was not an operative document at all and cannot consequently fulfil the requirements of s. 107 of the , Transfer of property Act.

The appellants, who had been registered as Income Tax Officer in the year of 1963, and a third party, was summoned by the Income Tax officer to produce certain Income Tax Officers, for the assessment years 1964 65 to 1971 72. The records were returned from the office of the Income tax officer but to the IncomeTax authorities on March 3, 1973, the Income 'tax officer did not forward the same in the office and also did not send a reply. He then filed a civil suit against the respondents for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722.86 together with interest and costs etc. The trial court held that the records were privileged under section 137 of the 1961 Act and that the returns were be filed beyond 10 years from April 1, 1964 and accordingly a decree was passed against them in favour of the appellants. Aggrieved by the said order the Income_tax Officer moved an application before the High Court for production of documents, on the ground that after the repeal of section 137 by Act V of 1964, there is no longer any impediment left in the way of a civil court to summon the production of the documents filed by an assessee during the assessment proceedings before an Income Tax Authorities after April 1. 1964, and that they could not be produced in court on being summoned by it without the approval of the Commissioner of Income Tax. The High Court rejected this application holding that the omission of section 138 did not make any difference and that consequently the ban imposed on the courts as contained in the repealed section 137 continued to remain in force by virtue of the provisions of section138(1)(b) of the Act even in respect of the items covered by the earlier provision, with effect from April Ist, 1964. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that after their repeal they were not entitled to the benefit of sections 54 and 59B of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, and consequently the finality attached to an order of the commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under section 138(1) (b) had no relationship to the power of the Court to summon that record. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.

The appellant, who was a minor at the time of the gift in 1944 made a gift of his properties including immovable property to Seinaba on April 7. 1944 by a registered deed and later, another deed was executed by Mammotty which contained certain terms of writing. The gift included immovable property including immovable properties to Seinsaba on the ground that the gift was void as invalid. Disputes having been arisen between the parties the appellant filed a suit for partition and possession of a 6/16 share of the property in dispute on the grounds: (1) that when succession opened out on the death of Mammastty, his widow Seinhaaba was entitled to the enhanced share of 1/4 as there was no issue; (2) that Sch. 11 of the Indian Registration Act was void because no issue had been framed; and (3) that in any view of the matter when a husband makes a gift to a minor wife and there is a declaration and a tender by the donor Mammottty, it was held that Remitta Mia vs section A.I.R. (1944) Sind 195, 290 that no delivery of possession was necessary in a gift by a husband to his minor wife provided such an intention as above described was clearly manifested. The trial Judge and the first Appellate Court did not accept the plea of the appellant that the donor and donee resided together for over 12 months before he made a declaration of gift and took possession on behalf of his mother who had attained puberty after which the guardianship of the person was that of the father if the girl was un 36 2 S.C. India/64 554 married and accepted on her behalf by her mother, and this gift included immoveable properties and it was accepted by the mother who took over possession on her minor daughter. On appeal the High Court held that there was transfer in favour of Remittada Mia and not Remittasa Mia as there were no valid issues. In appeal to this Court. HELD : (i) The true position in law is based on principle that the mere fact of an act by a person who makes a false gift without his knowledge that it would be made up for more than one month could not make any difference and that the parties must have brought their case within the first four corners of section 6 of the Act. But there can be no question in such cases where there is gift to an innocent minor who has no guardian of the properties to accept the gift and the minor is within its care either of the mother or of other near relative or even a stranger. [557 F] (ii) The mere fact that possession was not handed over to the minor on behalf by the minor did not render it invalid because possession was given by the person who made the false declaration in his property that possession is given to a child of any avail without the intervention of the guardian of tho property unless the minor had reached the years of discretion. If the property is with him he must depart from it and the donee must enter upon possession. The strict view in Varath vs Nathi Ammal, A. 1. R. (1947) 51 I.A. 556 was therefore correct and correct, though upheld by the High Courts on questions of law, this Court cannot interfere under article 136. [585 F] Kafaya recognises the legality of certain gifts which custom (urf) has accepted.

The respondents, who are trustees of a temple filed a petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the demand and for an order restraining the Commissioner from enforcing the provisions of the Amending Act 27 of 1954. Under the scheme of reorganization of State of Madras, the petition was transferred for trial to the High court of Mysore. The High Court held that sections 21, 30(2), 31,, 63 to 69 and 89 as amended by Act 27 Of 1954 were invalid and directed the Commissioner to pay the arrears of contributions and audit fee under the Act as amended, and accordingly restored the order passed against it. In an appeal by certificate granted by the High 823 Court: HELD: The High court erred in not determining whether there was a reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the Government for providing services and the amounts intended to be collected from the religious institutions for whose benefit the services are to be rendered. [820 A B] The Commissioner had not determined the audit fee procedure under section 76(2) of the Act or any demand for contribution under its provisions and was therefore one made without competence or the authority of law. [936 D E] The High 'Court erred in holding that under the provisions sections 21 to 30(1) a fee is uniform and no account is taken of the varying abilities of different recipients, and since they had applied for restraining the State from enforcing any of the provisions Of the Act, an investigation into the sustainability of that claim would have involved determination of the validity.

The appellant filed a suit for the recovery of certain money alleged to have been recovered from him. The Court issued notice calling upon him to show cause why he should not be proceeded against for committing con tempt of the High Court. In appeal, this court by special leave, inter alia, held that an appeal did lie to this Court as a matter of right under section 19(1) of the Act from an order dismissing the application for contempt. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: An order merely initiating the proceeding without anything further does not decide anything against the alleged contemner and cannot be appealed against as a matters of right tinder section 19. [516 B] The case was that the High court will be, without jurisdiction if it is in contravention of section 20. It may be so. If the alleged contemnor comes before the High 's Court and asks it to drop the proceeding on the ground of its being barred under section 20 of the . But that order does not matter here and cannot, therefore, be called upon to express our final opinion in regard to such an order. [ 512 E F] Baradakanta Mishra vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra ; , referred to. Baradikanta Mishra v Justice G.atikrunna Mishra, A.I.R., 1976 S.C. 1206; distinguished. Barsuitadakanda Mishra vs justice Gati Avushna Misra, [1976] S. C.

Section 6(1 A) of the , was repealed, and a new section added in the Act of 1933 by the amending Act of 1949. Subsequently, the Legislature thought that the possession of wireless transmitter which was a graver offence and imposing a more severe punishment. The Indian Wireless Telegraphy (Amendment) Act, 1949, was amended as follows : "Where any Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act repeals any enactment by which the text of any Central act, Regulation was amended by that Act. . ". Section 6(i A) inserted in the , whereby the repeal by this Act of any enactment shall not affect any other enactment in which the repealed enactment has been applied, incorporated or referred to." The appellant was prosecuted along with another person in the court of the Magistrate First Class, Delhi under section 6(A) of 'the , for possessing a wireless transmitters in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the Act and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal, the High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence passed on him by the Magistrate. In appeal to this Court, the appellant contended (i) that section 6 (1 A), inserted in 'the Act of 1930) by the amendment of 1949, in ' the year 1952 as the said amendment was unnecessary and unnecessary, and (ii) that if section 6 was not on the statute book there would be justification for this view, because the words " it wireless telegraphy apparatus" in section 6 A of the were comprehensive enough to take in " wireless telegraphic transmitter '. HELD : (i)(a) Under s.6(1A), the penalty for such illegal possession was made an offence but the sentence prescribed was rather lenient. [757 E] (b) The word " text ", in its dictionary meaning, means " subject or theme ". When an enactment amends the text by another it amends the subject or story of it, though sometimes it may expunge unnecessary words without altering the subject, it could most construed as one which regularly appears in the amending and repealing Acts which are passed from time to time in India. The legislature was therefore competent to enact that section instead of section 6A, inserted in 1957 by the Amending Act of 1950, is either covered by the provisions Of the , or a surplusage not serving any definite purpose. [759 A C] (c) The object of the 1952 Act is not to give it any legislative effect but to excise dead matter from the statute Book. [761 G] (ii)(a).

A Hindu female in whose favour the Hatchita was executed, executed a Hatchitita in favour of one Nanitosh Chakraborty. On the 28th August 1941, the deities represented by some of the Shebaits filed two applications under section 36(6)(a) (ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for the reopening of these two compromise decrees mentioned above and passing of new instalments. The trial judge decided in favour, but on appeal the High Court affirmed the decision of the courts below and dismissed both the appeals. In appeal by certificate to this court, HELD: Section 36(2) of Bengal MoneyLenders Act gives a discretion to the court to pass a new decree in accordance with other provisions of the Act. Obviously, the new decree is to be passed in favour Of the original decreeholder and only the calculations upon which the old (1) Vide Renula vs Manmatha, 72 I.A. 156, referred to. Clause(b) of section 36 (2) enables the court concerned to pass such a new order, that if there is default in the payment of any one of the instalments, the properties restored to the judgment debtor under clause (c) would be put back into the possession of the decree holder. [862 G] The object Of restoring possession of property sold in execution of the original decrees to the Judgment debtor is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues, but it is to he remembered that the sale itself is not annulled, and in case of default in payment of instalments, tho properties are returned to the decreeholder purchaser. [996 C] The High Court was therefore right in holding that in making a new 'decree under clause(a) of s 36 (1), the court can at all enter into the question as to whether the decree holders on record were himself a benamidar for another person in respect of the only purpose and so far as it is necessary to give relief to the borrower in the manner provided for in the Act, namely to release him from all liability for interest in excess of the limits prescribed by section 30 of the West Bengal Money lenders Act.

The appellant company was sued for the recovery of Rs. 7,113 7 0 as interest payable by it under a decree passed in favour of the respondent firm on the ground that the decree was not in existence at the date of the transfer and that the assignee of the subject matter of the suit and not of the decree itself was entitled to apply for execution. The suit was decreed and on appeal, the High Court held that the application under 0. XXI, rule 16 was maintainable as it did not create a new right of ownership in any property by the transferors to the respondent company until it was transferred or agreed to be transferred, but nevertheless, the provisions of Order XXI, r. 16, were applicable and the executing court passed an order directing them to pay interest on the amount of Rs . 7,04 0. 21,7 0. The appellant came up in appeal by special leave against that decision. Held, that the proper rule for the application of 0. XXII, r,. 17(1) (j), read with Order XXI Rule 16, was that a decree can be executed only by the person in whose name it stands and rule 10 enabled him to do so, while rule 16 of Order 21 enables the transferee to obtain the leave of the Court to continue the suit. A transfer or an agreement to transfer a decree that may be passed in future may, in equity, entitle the intending transferee to claim the beneficial interest in the decree after it is passed. But when on a true construction of the deed it actually operated to transfer the decree then in existence no equitable principle need be invoked for in that case the transfer was by the deed itself and as such was by an assignment in writing within the meaning of 0, XXI, Rule 16. Nor could there be any legal transfer or assignment of the money to be passed by virtue of the assignment in the writing executed before the decree came into existence and the only way in which the transferee could claim that the right was transferred to him by assignment in terms of the confirmation in writing executed by the transferor in his favour and could therefore claim to execute the decree as a transferee under Order XXI. Rule 16 contemplates actual transfer by an assignee in writing of a decree after the money is paid but such equitable transfer does not render the transferee a transferee of the judgment debtor by virtue Of section 146 of the Civil Procedure Code, nor do its provisions apply for the execution of the decrees passed by the courts below.

The respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, its tender for providing and fixing "S.H. Windows"W I ' type" and "Composite Window" of certain sizes "in accordance with specifications, designs, drawing and instructions. The tender was accepted and the respondent carried out the contract. The Sales Tax Officer included in the taxable turnover of the respondent Rs. 23,480/ received under the contract which included in its taxable turnover Rs.23,480. The Deputy Commissioner confirmed the order and remanded the case with a direction to assess tax on the price for sale of materials only. On appeal by the State of Rajasthan, HELD : (1) In a building contract which is one entire and indivisible there is no sale of goods. [501 D] (2) It was only upon the "fixing" of the windows leaves and when the window leaves had become a part of the building construction that the property in the goods passed under the terms of the contract, that the thing passed under it was not a contract for sale. [511 E F] (3) The essential term of the agreement is "fix" the windows". The service is not rendered under a separate contract nor is the service shown to be rendered customarily or normally as incidental to the sale by the person who supplies them window leaves. The "fixation 'of windows in the manner stipulated requires special technical skill. If the windows were not properly stamped "fixed", the contract would not be complete, and the property was therefore to pass to the War Office under the head contract. [506 A C] (4) The contract is of the second variety and is capable of being rendered partly by pure work contract. Work will be completed in 6 months from the date of its acceptance "to the building with rawl plugs in cut stone works. "Windows",W1 ' type C & Co. vs State of Maharashtra, , referred to. (5) If the window left had become part of a building construction it was of the other party, to the contract only on the theory of accretion. ion. Therefore, the contract in question is of second variety. The contract was for work and labour when the glass leaves had became a part. [500 E] (6) The object of the assessee was to enter into service contracts. That clearly appears from the terms Of the tender and its acceptance. The windows were to be fabricated according to the specifications with glass plain or ground as decided by the Engineer in Charge. The primary undertaking of the Respondent was not merely to supply the windows but to "fIX" theamendment windows.

On November 16, 1967 Shankar Lal handedover the formal agreement to Ram Dass and stated in the said letter to accused that the money would be sold on the above mentioned date. In the meantime, Shankerlal got his formal order from the State of West Bengal through counsel for some time. The prosecution alleged that the price of goods washer plates. He left issue in the bundle of foreign goods. He also agreed to purchase 200 pieces of the washer plate. On November 15, 1967, Shankar Lal came with another man named Pandey and told Ram Avtar to be the seller of the foreign goods known as washer exhibits. The police did not submit any charge sheet on the basis of the report which had been lodged by accused against him. Later the proceedings were set in motion against Raj Kumar Agarwalla, Shankarlal and Saheb Jaman Khan. HELD: 1. There is no infirmity in the judgment passed by the trial court as might induce us to interfere. [ 279B] 2. The report which was lodged in very nature did not mention of the name of Raj Kumar. Raj Kumar was a Party to any agreement to defraud R. [280C] 3. The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar is that he was present along with Shankar Lal when the latter brought washerright plates in a taxi and demanded the price from Ram Avtar. On the other hand it would hardly warrant an infer that Raj had respondent too been a party.

The petitioner, an Allopathic doctor and a commuter of the Indian Railways, was appointed as a special officer in the State Government. Later he filed a writ petition in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution alleging that the Railways were owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways adequate safety protection to the passenger and their properties is not available. The challenge was negatived by the High Court, but this judgment was set aside by the Supreme Court in appeal. Allowing the petition, HELD: 1. The object of nationalisation of railways in the national sphere has been gradual. With the expansion of the Railway a high powered body known as the Railway Board had come to be placed at the apex of control and with the new set up following independence a Minister remained incharge to administer the affairs of the Railways through the Board. This control should not be an arbitrary right of interference but a regulated authority defined and declared by law which is not to be needlessly or vexatiously exacted but which, in my humble judgment, is necessary at once for the interests of the State and for the protection of the public. [723F G] (2) The Government should be free to collect the entire operational cost which would include the interest on the capital outlay out of the national exchequer. It is for this reason that the services should be prompt, efficient and dignified. All the wrecks on either side of the stream of time, all the wlicrecks of the great cities and all the nations they had passed away all are a warning that no nation founded upon injustice can stand. [677B C] (3) The Union Government should have been free to collected the entire functional cost which will include the interests on the expenditure out of both these rights possible, it is undoubtedly the obligation of the Union of India and its instrumentalities to improve the established means of communication in this country. It cannot be said that the common man 's mode of transport closely connected with the free play of this fundamental right should not have been. [676E G] 2. An association of persons having technical training and capacity, yet being a public utility service run on monopoly basis, it would be necessary to meet the demands of the citizens availing the services of the Government of India. [673H] 3. The Union Govern ment should be in its duty to ensure availability of situations, circumstances and environments in which every citizen can effectively exercise and enjoy those rights.

The appellants applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953 in respect of their proprietary jagirs. The claim was rejected on merits by the Tribunal holding that they were time barred and therefore there was no decision of the appeals on merits. In the appeal before the Revenue Tribunal a question was raised whether the orders of dismissal passed against the appellants under section 16 of the Jagirs Abolition Act, were illegal or ultra vires because the Tribunal dismissed the applications for restoration on the ground that they had been prevented by sufficient cause from appearing at the hearing of the appeal. The Revenue Tribunal held that the applications filed on behalf of the appellants were barred by limitation as the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961 respectively, the Tribunal held in view of section 17 of the Act which states that "the appeal 'or application was heard and decided ex parte" and dismissed the restoration applications for non prosecution. The High Court accordingly allowed the applications of restoration made by the appellants in all four appeals. It further held that there was nothing on merits to show that the Tribunal had decided the appeal on merits even though there was default on the part of the appel lants and to record its decision regarding the merits of the case of the appellant. On appeal by special leave : HELD:(1) As the orders dismissing the applications were made on February 1, 2 and 3, 1961 the applications under section 18 of the Abolition Act were well within the period of limitation prescribed by Regulation 21. In view of the express language of section 9 of the 1915 Abolition Act it was open to the Tribunal, in such a case, to hear the respondent to the appeal and decide it on merits [143 B] (2) The orders dismissing applications made in all the four cases were well beyond the period prescribed by that Regulation being 30 days from the date of receipt of the order of dismissal of the Appeal. The applications of restoring appeals made by them in all cases were also within the time limit of limitation laid down by Regulation 20. Therefore, the order dismissing applications of restored applications was defective in law and must be set aside.

A suit was filed by the appellants, who were descendants of a public religious trust in which they claimed to have been worshipped for several years. A partition took place between the parties and a present suit being brought under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for removal of the respondent from the office of trustee of the God Shri Ramchandra temple was compromised in 1901 by a deed dated May 14, 1898. The appellants ' case was that Telibandha was dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramchandraji as early as 1857 by Dinanath Sao himself and later on in the year 1896 when a partition tookplace between his descendants who were up till that time living jointly all the coshares not only re affirmed the dedication made by Dinnath Sao of this village of Teliimbatore but themselves dedicated the village to the deities in this temple by accepting the award made by Panchas. The respondent, who was the son of Ram Saran Lal, brought a suit under section 91 of the Indian Penal Code, for removal from the position of a trustee and for appointment of the first plaintiff in his place; for an order on him to render accounts since 1936 and to deposit Rs. As regards the Award of 1896 his plea was that it (lid not express accurately the decision of the Arbitrators an that in any case, it was superseded by the award of Mr. Bagchi on May 14 which was accepted by all the co sharers as the actual settlement of their own and on the basis of which a suit brought to challenge the validity of the earlier award was dismissed as compromised. The trial court held: (i) that there had been a valid dedication in respect of the village Teli docubotivancore (ii) that no trust was created thereby and (iii) that the dedication by Din Nath Sao Singh himself by a Patha in 1857 as alleged in the plaint had not been proved. On appeal, it held that there was no absolute dedication of the Village for the purpose of temple by the Panch Faisla Award of1896 which was upheld by all co sharer at the time of the partition. The High Court agreed with the trial court that a valid trust had been created in favour of the temple and it was a public charitable trust. It further held that by the said award, the dedication had not since been proved; but disagreeing with the Trial Court, it acquitted the appellants. On the basis Of this decision that the respondent 's father had only a life interest in the properties and pointed out that "in cases where the intention of the testator is to grant an absolute estate, an attempt to reduce the powers of the owner by imposing restraint on alienation would certainly be repelled on the ground of repugnancy; but where the restrictions are the primary things which the testator desires and they are consistent with the whole tenor of the will, it is a material circumstance to be relied upon for displacing the presumption of absolute ownership implied in the use of the word "Malik". It was also held that the use by this Award Teli discrepan Lal 's three brothers brought a litigation under section 97 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, which was contested by the respondent was not a valid one. Held further, that the document (the Panch Fairsala) of 1897 clearly and unambiguously showed an absolute dedication to the deity temple of the appellant to Shri Ramchandra Swamyaswami Swamy and Ramsaran Lal absolutely with only a charge on it for the expenses of the deity and did not make any difference in respect thereof. The use of words "at that time" in the original necessarily mean " from the profits and income of mouza Telimiri". It is only when this is not possible, e. g., where an absolute title can be given ' in clear and unambiguous terms and the later provisions trench on the same.

The two appellants, the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Oudh Bar Association were three charges against the appellants. It was not necessary to refer in detail to the same because it was a matter of regret that the contem ners who are prominent members of the Sabyas should have themselves embarked on the path of vilifying the Chief Justice of this Court and that the language used by them was unfortunate. The High Court discharged the notices, but the High Court held that the Chairman of the Action Committee described as contemner No. 2 was actively associ ated with the passing of the resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Judge and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he is guilty of contempt as specified therein and that they were responsible for the passing by the resolution. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: The language used was unfortunate and not proper. It should not have been passed in that manner. [605 E G] In view of the fact that the notice was discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the observation. [ 603 A C] (a) It is true that the High Courts referred to the contumacious conduct of the appellants but the finding of the High court on this aspect as follows: 604 "It is a matter o regret that, the contem ples who are arranging prominent members should have himself embarked upon the path for vilting the Chief justice of this court and that we do not want to be over sensitive in the matters, keeping in mind the surrounding circumstances in which the contu macious act was committed by them. [ 602 C D] (b) The language employed by them is unfortunate. Counsel for the appellants rightly said that was not proper and it should not be passed in this manner. It is the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary, because if lawyers fail in their duty the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. The appellant Nos. I to 4 and their eldest brother, respondent No. 1 were entered into a partnership regarding partition of joint movable and immovable properties and the same were referred to three arbitrators. On or about 2nd July 1977 the same agreement was re written on a fresh stamp paper and the award was registered by which the abovenamed arbitrators were given the option to take assistance of one, two or more persons. The dispute related to certain properties among the brothers in Chinsurah, respondent Nos. 5, 6 and 7. On 11th of June 1977 the arbitrators explained their award to the parties and made signed the award. On the 25th November 1983 the arbitrators presented the award before the Sub Registrar for registration. On 30th March, 1978 the learned Sub Judge fixed the hearing of the arbitrators ' application to return the award to enable them to present the same before the sub Registrar for Registration. On 2nd September, 1978 when the Court found that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the arbitrators could not take back the award for presenting the same for registration and accordingly the Sub Judge directed return of the award holding that it was the Registrar and not the Sub judge who could determine the question of limitation for the purpose of registration of the arbitrator. The High Court quashed the registration under Article 227 of the Constitution holding that the award had been presented for registration beyond time. The three legal maxims the law does not compel a man to do that which he cannot possibly perform and an act of the court shall prejudice no man would, apply with full vigour in the facts of this case and if that is the position then the award as we have noted before was presented before the Court on 25th of November 1983 it could be construed that the only period which should be excluded from 26rd July, 1978 till 20th December, 1982. [121B] L/RJ [Surinder Singh vs State of Punjab and others; , ; Broom 's Legal Maxims P. 162) The law does no compel a person to do what he cannot reasonably perform. It is not necessary that all the intention of compelling impossibilities should be attained. No man would apply with complete vigour, in the fact of this instant case. It was however, not necessary to discuss in detail the ratio of A decision of the Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in M. Venkataratnam vs M. Chelamayya, A.I.R. 1967 Andhra Pradesh In the aforesaid view of the matter the judgment and order of the High Court cannot be sustained and are set aside and the order of tho Sub Registrar, Arambagh dated 24th June, 1985 is restored.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent from whom the premises were let without payment of rent and sub letting, he agreed to vacate the premises. The appellant bad four sub tenants, three of them also shifted to the new premises which were let to the appellant by the respondent. Under the terms of the lease it was agreed that in the shops allotted by the appellant the respondent had the right to sub let the same with effect from June 7, 1948, and that the appellant had four sub tenant who never sublet the premises to the sub tenants. The defence of the appellant was that under section 15 of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, there was no prohibition against a contract of sub letting which the non obstante clause contained in section 10 of the Act was for the protection of his rights which he had waive. Held (per Sarkar, jj.), that even if any other law allowed subletting, e. g., section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, the sub letting would, because of section 15, be unlawful; since the appellant asked the Court to afford him a remedy against one who by contravening section 15 had made himself liable to eviction and those cases where the court was called upon to assist the plaintiff in enforce an agreement the object of which was to do an illegal act. Surajmull Nargoremull vs Triton Insurance Co. (1884) III U.S. 599, wardton Instructor vs Coppell ([1924] L.R. 52 I.A. 126), Harkishan Singh vs Madho Prasad (A.I.R., 1944 P.C. 147); Surajmpal Narg margull vs Partles Corporation of India ([1945] 1 X.B. 65) referred to.

The Board ' conducted secondary examinations in the month of March 1990, whereat the marks awarded, after the formalities of valuation by the examiners of the answer sheets in each subject, and the random counter check by the boil and further recounting at the Board, Moderators ' mark sheets sent to Pune for feeding the computer to declare the results were found tampered with, the appellant. Thereafter, several writ petitions were filed in the High Court against non declaration of the results and the High court directed that the result of the examination be declared within the specified time. The High Court directed the Board to take expeditious action to declare results of the examinations within the prescribed time. Show cause notices were issued to the students on July 30, 1990 informing them of the nature of tampering, the subjects in which the marks were found tampering with, and also indicated the proposed punishment, if in the enquiry it would be found that marks were tampered with the knowledge or connivance of the candidates or parents or guardians. It did not obtain the approval of the Divisional Board, and therefore, the impugned notification was without authority of law. It is clear from large body ofPradings especially one of them appearing at the examination that tampering was done by either the candidate or the parents or guardian or guardian, and that the allegation of fabrication was stated to have been done at the behest of either the student/parents or guardians or were not permitted to participate in the inquiry. The respondents contended that tampering with the falsehood ' mark sheet ' sheets amounted to a forgery, and so no prejudice was caused to them. The learned Single Judge also held that the resolution passed by the Education Standing Committee that the fabrication was done at its behest was without approval of that Divisional Board and therefore quashed the cancellation of the result results. On appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Board that the impugned Notification was vitiated for the reasons that the Standing Committee itself did not record any reason in support of its conclusion, or that the parents/guardians were parties to the fabrication cannot be sustained for the reason that the regulation itself postulates that if the Committee disagrees with the Inquiry Officer then only it is obligatory to record reasons. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The finding of the learned Single 982 Judge as per the directions given in the order dated January 30, 1991, that the examinees/ parents or the guardians were parties thereto to the fabricated and whether their complicity was established from record and whether the evidence was sufficient to support such conclusion reached by the Standing committee or the Enquiry Officer. Once a matter is established beyond reasonable doubt it must be taken for all purposes of law to be a fact, as there is no room for a distinction between what is found by inference from the evidence and what is held as a positive face. and contended that the degree of proof required in such cases would ordinarily justify interference with the finding and to quash the impugned order. [798H; 799A] 1.2 When the evidence justified the examination Standing Committee to record the finding that the Examinationees, parents orED witnesses were parties lo the fabrication and whether Their complicity was proved from record, it is not open to the High Courts under Article 226 to itself evaluate the evidence as an appellate Court and to come to its own conclusions.

The Sessions Judge found that Madan Lal was not a "public servant" within the meaning of section 5 (2) of the Prevention ' Employment of Criminal Criti tration Act, and therefore he was not liable for prosecution. He also convicted the appellants under sections 161 and 165 I. P.C. for abetting of the commission by the said Madan Lal. The High Court reduced the sentence on the terms of imprisonment already undergone and a fine of Rs. 500. There is no dispute that the amount was actually paid to Madan Lal even though he said that he could do nothing to help the appellants who begged him somehow to help them out of the impending prosecution. Evidence has also been given by the Magistrate and the police officers about the talk and lower courts have found on the evidence of Madan Lal and Labhu Ram that Rs. 5,000 was offered as a bribe and not as compensation money in settlement of the amounts legitimately due to the Railway. Chatterjee, who was a munim of a firm and not a partner or proprietor as the other appellants and that it could not be stated of him that he was interested in giving or attempting to give any bribe for hushing up the case, raised some questions of law on their behalf. Held, (per B.rennan vs peek, [19431] 2 S.C R. 414) that the prosecution has failed to prove the ingredients of section 205 I.A. and that the offence as defined in clause (d) did not come with. In view of section 3(3)(a) of Part IX of the Indian Penal Code, the two offences are common: those of which were committed under such circumstances should be regarded only as venial and not heinous. The word "obtains" is used in sections 161 & 165 I 6 of the Act, while they are subjected also to increased disabilities, namely, a longer term of imprisonment as punishment and the application of the presumption referred to in subsection (3). Section 3(4) has been omitted, and the view taken by the Sessions Judge that the offences committed in the course of traps are less grave and call only for lenient or nominal sentences was merited. Brennan V vs paster, , distinguished.

The appellant Bank sued the respondent under section 141 of the Indian Contract Act for recovery of Rs. 76,368.04 P. against defendant No. 1 and his surety, but on appeal by the surety was dismissed by the High Court only against the surety. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Section 141 comprehends a situation where the debtor has offered more than one security in lieu of other security or release of any security. Clause 7 provides for non discharge of surety even if the creditor Bank enters into a composition with the principal debtor and that the surety would nonetheless be liable even if it is found from his own power to hand over to the surety the means of recouping himself by the security given by the principal. [924 D E] (2) It is not a case of granting time or indulgence to the principal creditor or variation of the credit or taking one set of security in substitution of some other security against payment of the debt or taking another set ofsecurity in substitution Of some other surety or release or of any guarantee. Clause 8 provides for an express provision that the security may be secured or any part thereof may be reduced to writing and if necessary this clause shall apply to all such securities. [936 A E] In the instant case, as found by the trial court and not controverted, the principal borrower had offered two security, one the pledge of goods and the other the personal guarantee of the surety; and he was entitled, therefore, to the benefit of that real and substantial security in the event of his being called on to fulfil his duty as a surety. [connected with the terms of the letter of guarantee which is in pari materia with clause 7 of the Letter of Guarantee under discussion, the Bank had accepted the proposal for cash credit facility on the specific condition that the principal mortgagor shall offer two securities, one of goods to be kept under the lock and key of the Bank to be supervised by the Bank 's employee. [948 F G] (3) The surety agreed to give personal guarantee on the implied understanding and with the full knowledge of the bank that the latter was offering another security viz., pledge of good goods and that without the consent of the creditor parts with the security, the surety is discharged to the extent of the value of the security. [947 B C] (4) The Bank would be liable only if the Court has guarantee, security or remedy guarantees, securities or remedies from the principal debtors.

The appellant was the son of a village consisting of six cattle in which the village was situate. The family of the applicant had two sons, one Patels some members of which held a Patel 's office in rotation ten years each. These four families went by the surnames of Dongre Rokade, Raut and Ingle. The lands were allotted to the share of the appellant. The Government of India after holding an enquiry directed that the lands in suit should be resumed and regranted to the working patel, viz., respondent No. 1, who was a member of the family rendering patelki service, free of any payment in lieu of cash remuneration for his office. After reference to the Commissioner (P), the Superintending Commissioner, Local Government, confirmed this order. In appeal by certificate to the Supreme Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants : (i) that the rights which the Rokadade family had in these lands were right of dealing with the property as owners subject to a member Of the family render patel ship service and as they did not belong to a branch in which, the right to officiation resided, his claim could not be considered; (ii) that on the, evidence recorded by the proprietor of the village it was clear that P Patel 'ki inam lands were treated on the same basis in the resumption proceedings of 1917; (iii) that there was evidence in the record to show that some of these lands had alienated " patelkhed inam" lands and the p Patel 'Patelki inam ' lands of each of the villages remained with him, in spite of the fact that the office was rotatory; (iv) that even if the said Rules or provisions applied it still retained his hereditary rights in the lands; and (v) the orders of Government did not confer any new right nor did they deprive anybody of any subsisting right in respect of the " p Patelki inam" land and Government had no right to resume the same. Held, that under the rules the grant was subject to orders passed by the revenue authorities in respect Of matters mentioned therein and no right was given to a person who has a share in the emoluments. It may be as the High Court points out, that there is nothing in them on the basis of which the appellant could claim as of right that he had a share of his emoluments appearing from the inam statement. In the present case the grant of " p directorki inam of 1/2 bighas per netan was in its origin a grant by the sovereign authority which it confirmed in accordance with old judicial usage; but every such grant would be subject to the orders passed in respect either of the matters mentioned in that section, and no question of a share arises against Government even though the lands were shown as excluded from the jagir of Nawabag. Venkata Jagannadha vs Veerabadrayya, I.L.R, , referred to.

The respondents claimed that they were governed by Hindu Law as regards their joint family properties, that while the said property was a ancestral property, in Madras and thereafter in Bangalore sometime between 1928 and 1930, the said Khojas was situated in Bombay, he should prefer the Madras as against the Bombay view. Of late, the Bombay High Court decided that the question referred to it under section 64(1) of the , XXXIV of 1953, to be decided by a competent authority on the basis of whether the custom recognised in the (1) A.I.R. 1952 Mad. 793; (2) , and (3) was justified as regards the customary law governing the Khoias applicable to them applied only to cases of succession and inheritance. The High Court considered the evidence led by the parties, which consisted mainly on the question whether the Madras Hindu Law provided for the passing of the said properties to be governed matters of succession, succession and succession only. It held that the object was not to adopt the text of the Koran as law any further than it had been adopted in the laws and usages of the Muhammadans who came under our sway and if any class of Muhammadans, Muhammadan dissenters, as they may be called, are found to be in possession of any usage which is otherwise valid as a legal custom and which does not conflict with any express law of the English government, they were just as much entitled to the protection of this clause as the most orthodox society can come before the Court. The other question was whether the Khoja Memons settled in Madras by force of the Mohamed importer 's Custom and traditions, including the rules as to joint family property, the right of a son therein by birth, could be properly said to have passed to them on their death, and to be assessable under the Act. ^ Held, that the test laid down by section 65 of the Madras General Clauses Act, 1899, which was applicable to this case, in the instant case, was whether it was necessary to prove that the Khudjas after leaving Madras had settled that amidst Hindus were governed and continued as long as there was no reported decisions on the position of the Kahullusam Memons who had settled down in Madras, the High Court 's record searched. No finding could therefore be founded on its own view, even if it is found from the decision itself that any evidence as to the customary Law which the Cutchi Memon widow died issueless and her property would be governed by the Hindu Law. The reasons given by the High court were erroneous and must be set aside. Held further, that in the absence of proof of a special custom and usage ,of having been ratified by the members of the joint family, no such rule could be laid down for determining whether a particular provision is valid or not and that it was sufficient to prove the general law governing such succession. The burden to prove affirmatively proved by a conclusive evidence would depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. In the present case, the parties had agreed that the Madras Muslim Law applicable to India applied only where there were no reported decision on the legal question and therefore the adoption of the Karurath null or void.

Rule 49 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 provides for payment of duty on goods produced in a factory for weaving the same into fabrics. The appellants do not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill were liable to pay excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not question their liability in respect of yarn which is also removed from the Factory. It was the contention of the appellants that no duty of excise can be levied and collected in respect thereof of yarn, which was obtained at an intermediate stage and thereafter subjected to a integrated process for the manufacture of different fabrics. Indeed on a writ petition filed by the appellants, the Delhi High Court held that yarn obtained and further processed within the factory for the purpose of weaving the said same into fabric, will be liable to payment of excise duty in view of the amended provisions of Rules 9 and 49 of Central Excise Act 1944 (the '). It also held that the retrospective effect given by section S 1 will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the and Rule 49. On appeal, this Court, HELD: The Explanation to rule 173 A and the proviso thereto contemplate collection of duty levied on production of a commodity at an intermediary stage which again is utilised in such continuous process for manufacture of the end product using a product produced at an earlier intermediate stage of such process forthe manufacture of another commodity by deeming such production or manufacture of tho commodity at a intermediate stage to be removal from such place or premises of manufacture. It is true that under rule 9(1) there is a provision for specification by the Collector, but the question is what has to be specified by the collector. It cannot, therefore, be made of the place of manufacture or production of the excisable goods. The description of "place of removal" may not be required to be made and, in our view, cannot be made the place where the goods are produced, cured or manufactured, but any premises appurtenant thereto, which may be specified for by the Collec tor. [707H; 717A B] (1) The word "place" does not contemplate any deemed removal, but a physical and actual removal of the goods from a factory to another for the purposes of collection of excise duties. The definition "place", therefore, admits of only one interpretation and that is that the specification that has to he made by theCollector is of no premises appurtenant to the place or manufacture, or production or in any place at an interlocutory stage, and consumed or utilised for the manufacturing of another commodities in a continuous process or otherwise. [613C] (2) The definition of " Place of removal", and under section 3(1), read with explanation thereto to rule 174A, which is not relevant for our purpose are omitted. By virtue of Section 5 1 of the Finance Act, 1982, amendments made to Rules 9 & 49 have been given retrospective effect from the date on which the Rules came into force, that is, to say, from February 28, 1944, it contemplates not only removal from 8 the place, where the excisable Goods are produced or manufactured but also removal within such place and premises for captive consumption or "home consumption" as it is called. Thus if a commodity which was manufactured in such place/ Premises and is used for the manufacturer of another product then it will be a case of removal for the said purpose of payment of Excise duty.[617C D] Winsbury Borough Municipality vs Northumberland Compensation Appeal Tribunal, Bombay & Anr., [1980] 3 S.C.R.

Section 68 D of the empowers the Hearing Authority to approve a scheme either with or without modification. By necessary implication it can also reject a scheme if it feels that it is not necessary to introduce the scheme. When the scheme is approved or modified under section 68 C of the Act, such approved or modify scheme is required to be published in the official Gazette by the State Government and the same shall become final and shall be called the approved scheme and the area or route to which it relates shall be notified area concerned. Under section 68 D(i) of the for carrying into effect the provisions of this chapter, the transport authorities concerned can issue permits only in accordance with the scheme and if the jurisdiction is so excluded, the civil courts have jurisdiction only to examine whether the provisions had not been complied with or the tribunal had or had not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure. In such cases a suit is hardly the remedy which could be availed by them. If suits of this nature are allowed to be entertained, the very object of the several provisions of Chapter IVA of the Rules can be frustrated by interested parties by resorting to a civil court with the sole object of delaying the implementation of a scheme. Such attempts should be curbed at the earliest opportunity. The learned Civil Judge was right in declining to stay the further proceedings in the suit. The District Judge and the Civil Judge are directed to dispose of the suit in the light of the observa tions made in this order.

When a public servant is charged under sections 161, I.P.C., and it is alleged that the illegal grati fication was taken by him for doing or procuring an official act, it is not necessary for the Court to consider whether or not the accused public servant was capable of doing or intended to do such an act. [186E F] 2. When public servant who is charged Under section 161 I. P.C. and it was alleged that illegal grafted money from Russel Nathaniel and his wife and also a gold ring from Roshan Lal, the appellant knowingly used to live in 1962 with her father at Fazilka. [187G H] 3. When the charge against the appellant is under section 6(1) (d), and it being alleged that he was taken for doing and procuring an "functions" it is no necessary for him to consider the applicability of section 6 of the Act.
