Instead them proved facts disclose that there was a gross abuse of his official position on the part or the appellant and in the circumstances of the case, it was clear that the sentence imposed is not excessive. [185G H, 186A] 5. When PW 1 went to the house of RusselNathaniel who speaks of the manner in which he speaks of such acts as was done by him, the respondent could not say which were the documents which were sent to the D.I.G.

The appellant was charged under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and under section 161 I.P.C., for having accepted illegal gratification from his superior officers as a motive or reward for doing any official act and showing in exercise of his official functions favour to whomsoever in seeing that a speedy settlement of the claim cases preferred by him against the Bengal Nagpur Railway (later the Eastern Railway) had the power to deal finally with claims up to Rs 75 and for claims in excess of that sum to make a recommendation to his superior officer, the Assistant Commercial Superintendent. Brief facts which were required to be stated were that on or about May 12, 1952 the appellant had accepted Rs. 100 as illegal gratification by corrupt means or by otherwise abusing his position as a public servant. In his examination in chief stated " On the prayer of the police I accorded sanction for the prosecution of the appellant, who was then an Assistant Supervisor of Claim Cases of the Bengal, Nagpur Railway Police (Iater then the Eastern Railways) Garden Reach Calcutta, was prosecuted and convicted under section [161 of the Indian Penal Code and section 5 (2) read with section 5 of the Act. On appeal by special leave : Held, that the sanction accorded in this case in no way conflicts with the observations of their Lordships of the Judicial Committee. The sanction accorded was a valid sanction and it clearly states all the facts which concern the prosecution case alleged against the appellant with reference to his acceptance on May 12. 1952, in circumstances which, if established, would constitute offences under section I. P. C., and also the offence of criminal misconduct by the illegal and corrupt use of his Official position as public servant to obtain a pecuniary advantage for himself punishable under section S 5 (1) P.C. The sanctioning authority had rightly and properly applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case, and it was not necessary in the ends of justice to accord sanction to the prosecution. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, (1952) L.R. 75 I.A 30, disapproved.

B tenant 's premises are situated in an Anna Pinai Street, Madras. Originally the premises belonged to late section Manicka Chettyar, father of section M. Gopalakrislina, the present landlord. By virtue of a Deed of Settlement executed by section Manocha Chettyar on May 9, 1934 possession of the said premises was delivered to his wife Manoranjithammal as trustee and guardian an of her three minor children, section Makrishna (appellant) shall enjoy the rents and profits of the property for her life time subject to certain charges on account of his two sisters. It is further stated in the deed that after the life time of Gopalakrishna, his son and his heir of any predeceased son living at that time shall enjoy them the property subject to identical charges as absolute owners with right of sale, gift etc., There were further directions in case of other contingencies with which we are not concerned. The Rent Controller held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction of the tenants. The High Court also refused to interfere in revision. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that a single petition with regard to two different tenancies, though in the same premises, one for residential purpose and the other for nonresidential purposes was not maintainable as grounds for eviction were raised in this appeal by the tenants were irrelevant in a litigation between the landlord and tenants when a suit for eviction was instituted by the former on any of the grounds available to him under the Act. Dismissing the appeals ^ HELD: (1) The right between section M Sri Rama and the remainder man with regard for the terms of the Deed of settlement win has to be worked out in appropriate proceedings, if necessary and the general law win govern the matter if any occasion arises. [276G H] (2) When the objection on the score of the landlord being a holder of life interest and hence incapable of invoking section 14(1)(b) fails the suit must be decreed. [277D E] M/s Raval & Co. vs K. G. 276 Ramachandra and others, ; relied on. (3) In the present case, when the objection was raised by the landlord in a proceeding between the landlords and tenants, the tenant has a right to demolish his property in order to build a new structure on the site with view to improve his business or to get better returns on his investment. Such an action per se cannot be characterised as mala fide on the part of the tenant. There is no merit in this contention.

According to the definition of "intermediary" as contained in section 3(13) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, trees, before they were cut, formed parts of land '. The respondent decree holder in execution proceedings was that after the coming into force of the Act, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees of groves as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary. This Court rejected this contention and held that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6 of the said Act in the State of Uttar Pradesh, new bhumidhari rights came into existence under section 18 of the . It also held that the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force was provided in section 8(h) of that Act read with section 73 of the , so that nothing more than the compensation awarded to the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagee. HELD: The respondent 's grove is bhumidhari property. Rights in it are part of bhumidhari right. After these clear words of the enactment, it is not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut trees, which are parts of grove lands and groves and grove land. [196E F] The plea that after com pleting of section 6 in the U .P. Act read as above, nothing more except the compensation award awarded to 'intermediaries could be con cerned by this Court in view of the definition Of the intermediary 's ' grove under section 3 of the Uttar. U. P. Zamindari ( Abolition and land Reforms Act) is not attracted.

The prosecution case was sought to be proved by the ocular testimony of PW4 Biju and PW5, both aged about 13 years at the time of occurrence. The accused persons were alleged to have caught hold of Suku by the collar and inflicted injuries on their hands with a chopper. The trial Court found four eye witnesses including PWs 6 and 7 salesmen and his assistant in the arrack shop and PW8 Unni @ Velayudhan turned hostile and did not support the prosecution case. The Trial Court convicted accused 2 to 6 under Section 326 I.P.C., and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. Accused Nos. 2 to 4 were also convicted for an offence under Section 325 read with section 149 IPC, but no separate sentences were awarded on any of those counts. On appeal before the High Court, the conviction and sentence passed against them by the Trial Court was set aside. While setting aside the conviction, the High court did not hold that beside the four accused convicted by it, there were some other known or unknown persons who had also been a party to the commission of the crime. The participation of the 6th accused and the role assigned to him by the prosecution was doubted by the learned Judges of the High Courts and he was given the benefit of doubt and acquitted. Thus, only four accused could be said to have been the members of the assembly but such an assembly which consisted of less than five members was not an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 I. P.C. The conviction of accused 2 for an offences under Section 302 I.C.; and 3 for an offen cation under section 307 I. C., is, therefore, unwarranted and cannot be sustained. While convicting accused 2 and 3 to 4 for an an offence with the aid of Clause (b) and (c) of Section 299 I. The appellants would be liable for the substantive offence of murder punishable under Section 304 Part 1 I. As already noticed, though it may not be possible to attribute to him and the medical evidence also shows that the injuries inflicted by him were not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death of the deceased. The plea of alibi taken on behalf of accused No. 2 was rejected by the High Judge. The High Court acquitted two of them. While allowing appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is difficult to say that all the four appellants had shared the common intention of causing such bodily injuries on the deceased as were likely to cause the death of Suka or were sufficient in ordinary course to cause such death. [92G; 93A] 1.2 The existence of an unlawful occu nial assembly is a necessary postulate for invoking Section 149 I.I.P., and it is not possible to say to that all these four appellants have shared the t intention of committing such bodily injury on the accused as were intended to cause a death or such bodily harm as is sufficient in an ordinary course. The existence,of an unlawful com mitted assembly is not proved, the appel lant No. 1, Subran was never called upon to meet a charge under Section 149 simplicitor and, therefore the conviction of appellants 2 to 5 for anc punish ment under Section 307 I, IPC cannot be maintained.

The assessee is a non resident company, having its place of business at Coventry in the United Kingdom. It entered into an agreement with the Standard Motor Products of India Ltd., which in November, 1939 had expired in November 1970. For the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69, it was filing its returns through the Indian Company. The collaboration agreement between the assessee and the Indian company expired in the year 1965. Later it was renewed. The agreement expired in May 1971. For these assessment years, 1969 70 and 1970 71, however, the assessee filed returns in which it stated that it was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis. On a reference made at the instance of Revenue, the High Court answered the question in the negative i 'e. in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. The appellant filed these appeals by special leave before this Court contending that though the Indian Co. had credited to the assessee in its account books for the relevant years (accounting year for the Indian Firm) the assessee did not actually receive the amount nor did it take credit for the said amounts in its books at Cochventry, and that as soon as it noticed that said mistake it corrected the same and filed the return for the assessment year 1969 70 on correct basis showing that the method of accounting was mercantile, that for the A.Y. 1967 68, the assesses did not really receive the royalty amount but entered its accounts in regard to royalty and that, therefore, nothing is taxable. Allowing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The assessee has been filing its income tax returns in India through the U.K. in the shape of Calendar Journal. It does not take the stand that the said credit entry in the books of the Indian companies did not give rise to income in India nor did not it ever say that the receipt in U. K. alone constitutes income or for that matter receipt of income. It may also be noticed that in its returns relating to the assessment period 1967 68 & 1968 69 it had raised the plea that it is maintaining its books on mercantile foundation. Only in the Return relating to assessment years 1966 67 and 1967 68 it did raise the plea of that it does not actually received the amount from the Indian Companies, which was not aware of the true state of affairs relating to that assessee 's accounts. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner exercised all the powers of the assessing authority, that it had done is to direct an inquiry to find out the true State of affairs viz., whether the assessee was maintaining his accounts on local basis or on cash receipt basis in so far as the royalty money amount is concerned. [108E; 110B C D] Keshav Mills Ltd. vs CL T., Bombay, ; Keshav Mills etc. vsC.T., Bombay [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 905 and Keshav Mills, Ltd. & Anr. vs CIT, , referred to. 1.2 The High Court was right in answering the question against the Revenue. [110F G] 1.3 In the instant case, it is not suggested that the assessee has received the royalty amounts only when it receives the same in U .K., but it cannot be said that until it is so remitted to and received by the Japanese company, the Indian co was crediting the said amount to the account of the assessee towards the commission in the account books of Income Tax Department awaiting further instructions regarding its remittance. [101G] 1:4 The assessee was assessed as the statutory agent of the non resident Company. [1C D] 1 :5 Section 145(1) confers a right on the assessee to enforce a demand for payment of rent etc.

The appellant and four others were alleged to have taken part in the murder of Lahu Vithu Patil. The deceased was murdered with the knife which was used by Rama Krishna Patil accused No. 1, Bhiva Doulu Patil accused no. 2 (now appellant before us) and Deoba was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., read with section 34 for the murder 'of one Lahu Yithu Pandey on the night between May 23, and 24, 1960 at village Pasarde. Four persons Rama Krishna Hegde accused No: 1 Bhiva Bhabia Doulu v The approver was given a true version of the occurrence and was also examined by his brother and also by his own brother. The trial court convicted the appellant as above stated and sentenced him to death but on appeal the sentence was reduced to one of imprisonment for life. The appellant contended that the statement of Santu had been corroborated in material particulars and qua the appellant: Held, that there should be corroboration of the approver in material details and qua each accused. Section 133 of the evidence Act which deals with the admissibility of an accomplice is not meant merely that the accomplice is on his own admission a man of bad character who took part in it; but it has been accepted by the trial court as well as by the judge under section 133, Cr. P.C. The rule of guidance is to be found in illustration (b) to section 114 of the Evidence which is as follows: "The Court may presume that an accomplice was unworthy of credit unless he is corroborated in evidence material particulars". Both sections are part of one subject and have to be considered together, judged together, and so judged. The law may be stated in the words of Lord Reading C. J in R. vs Baskerville (1918) L.R. 76 I.A. Mad. 308 followed. Bhubonioni Sahu vs The King, [1916] 2 A.K. 603 and Suryanarayana Sahu vs State of Orissa, [1924] 2 section C.W.N. 308, relied on.

Section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act provided that "public servant" includes every officer in the service or pay of a local authority or of a corporation engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or of 'State Act or a Government company as defined in section 617 of the . The appellant was charged with offences under Sections 5(2) read with Section 5(i)(d)(e) of Indian Penal Code. He pleaded that on the morning of July 6, 1961 the Electrical Executive Engineer accompanied by his Head Clerk the appellant paid Rs. 180/ for Sri A.D. Singh, Executive Engineer ' along with his head clerk who had been previously noted down by the Magistrate, P.W. 2 was the lessee of the Mills. The Executive Engineer and the appellant then left the mill premises. At about 10 a.m. on the same day the Electricity Inspector met P.Ws. 2 and 9 in the Mill premises and handed over a petition to P. W. 11 Girjan Sinha expressing his apprehension that the Executive Engineer or his Head clerk might demand some bribe from him. It was alleged that on July 8,1961, a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, P,W. 6, Basudeo Singh, the manager of the mill should meet him at his office at Patna within two days and get the matter settled, otherwise they would be put to a big loss. Thereafter, P 2 went to the office of the Anti Corruption Department at Patna and handed back a petition for lodging a false case against the appellant under section 5(4) read 'with section 5 (1)(b) of Prevention of 1947 Act. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted the appellant with imprisonment for five years. The High Court dismissed the appeal, On appeal by special leave it was contended that upon the findings recorded by the High Court the appellant could not be deemed to be a 'public servant ' within the meaning of section 21(1) of ' the Prevention Corruption Act or section 21 of the Indian Penal code. HELD: (i) The provisions in section 1 1 5 (A) of section 7 were intended to protect public servants against mal practices and that the object of the Act was only to protect their independence, liberty and security from exploitation which the law provides for punishment in case of Corruption. [687 E] (ii) A person taking a bribe could not therefore be said to be 'a public servant within the definition of Section 21(i). The appellant could therefore be deemed as a "public" within the scope of section 2(1), on the findings reached by the Special Judge in cases under sections 161 and 409 of the I.P.C. [688 E] Therefore, the appellant was an officer of the Electricity Board constituted under the provisions of the , and that also of section 5 of the 1947 Act as it stood after the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958 came into force on February 27, 1958.

The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence imposed on the appellant in respect of contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Scheduledgrains (Declaration of Stocks) (Second) Order, 1964 and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ . In appeal by special leave it was contended that r. 141(2) which dealt with forfeiture to the Government of packages, coverings or receptacles in which any stocks of jowar were found was ultra vires, as it laid down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: Rule 141 (2) falls within section 3 because it is essential to the scheme of ' the Defence of India Rules. The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under rr. and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. The rule must necessarily provides for the issue of orders under the rules and they should also provide proof in a judicial proceeding of the same fact of 'publication. [273 E, G H; 274 B C] The order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture was allegal and liable to be set aside. On the second point it had been contended that the rule laid down in section 115(9)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was ultra rites because it lays down a Rule of evidence contra ' to the Law contained in s. 114 of Evidence Act which confers very wide powers. The fact that the rules are inconsistent with existing legislation does not matter because sections 43 of the Defence Of India Act provide that 'the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder shall have effect notwithstanding 'that they are inconsistent therewith. Therefore the order of confiscation was alleged to be illegal.

One M, a practising lawyer and after finishing his work for the day he left the Fatehgarh court along with the brother lawyers, Brijendra Singh Yadav and Om Prakash Dubey. They were proceeding on their bicycles and as they reached a spot near Barhpur Block Violet was alleged to have shouted "the Vakil has come". The deceased Kunwar Singh was a practising advocate and after ten years his work went for the night. He had left the court along alongwith his brother Advocate, Brijendra singh Yadav and another unknown person when Ramesh and an unknown person were carrying hockey sticks. All the three accused were tried by the Sessions Judge. The learned Sessions Judge convicted one of them under section 302 read with section 109 I.P.C. and sentenced him to death. The remaining three accused appealed against their conviction but the High Court confirmed the convic tion of all the three charges. Hence these appeals. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. In order to constitute abetment, the abettor must be shown to have "intentionally" aided the commission of the crime. Mere proof that the crime charged could not have been committed without the interposition of the alleged abettor is not enough compliance with the requirements of section 107.A person may, for example invite another casually or for a friendly purpose and that may facilitate the murder of the invite. But unless the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate the commission by the murder, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder. [629G; 627C] 1.2. Even assuming that the accused persons were lying in wait on the other side of the road and it was necessary to inform them so that they might accomplish their aim. In case the accused were not assisted by Smt. Vio Radilet, they would have had to act on their own, the deceased may notice their presence and may not proceed further. [625E] 1:3. There is nothing at all to show that she was aware of the nefarious design of Sia Ram and his associates. The fact that he made the guarded statement that he did not remember or that he had seen. Dubey claimed that he would be able to recognise Balister and that it was possible that he may not be able "to recognise Manphool". [627C] 2.1 There is no rule of law requiring that an oral testimony of a witness should be corroborated by evidence of identification. In fact, evidence of identifi cation is itself a weak type of evidence. But the point of the matter is that the court which acquitted Shri Ram was justifiably influenced by the consideration that though at the earliest stage he had asked that an identification parade be held, the demand was opposed and opposed by the prosecution and the parade was there fore not held, That is not the only point in favour of Shri Ram.

In 1959, two persons by name Ramachandra Budhya and Govind Dhaya were committed to trial for the murder of one Vishwanath, by other persons. In all the accused including one or more of the other accused committed this offence and that accused No. 2 was acquitted. During that the trial Deoram Maruti Patil 's uncle had died leaving behind him. This fact was exaggerated in the Grime. It is not safe to hold that each one of the four named accused who were charged under section 302 read with section 34, Penal Code were acquitted in respect of the same incident. While acquitting all the six accused under section 304, read with s 34, I.P.C., it convicted him under section 147 and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. The High Court, on appeal by special leave, held that the conviction was bad in law, as both the injured were acquitted. On appeal by the State, Held, that there were no legal bar which prevents the court from reaching such a conclusion. It would be seen from the observations of this Court that though the charge names five or more persons as composing an unlawful assembly, evidence may nevertheless show that the unlawful assembly consisted of some other persons as well who were not identified and so not named so, it cannot be said that they acted conjointly with them. Where the witnesses named only the said accused also participated in the commission of the offence, there must be some foundation in the evidence that persons other than those named had taken part in the occurrence.

The petitioner company, a manufacturer of MSCR defective sheets or coils was the petitioner in the application for grant of import licence. The foreign supplier shipped the material in three consignments and the goods arrived at Bombay port on 12th June, 1984. It may be mentioned that the rate of duty on the day was 60% plus 40% + Rs.650 per M.T. and 10% C.V.D. at Rs325 per M,T & 10 per cent C. V.D., and 10%. On 21st August, 1984, the petitioner 's clearing agent filed six bills of entry for ex bond clearance. However, on 4th April, 1988, the Income Tax Department issued a necessary no objection certificate, thus lifting the ban. Thereafter, on 14th April 8 1988, notices were served to the petitioner, calling upon it to pay the customs duty and other duties as leviable on 21st November, 1984 for presenting the goods. The notice was challenged by the peti tioner contending that he was not ready and willing rather was anxious to get the material on payment of customs duty, but due to circum stances beyond the control of the petitioner. It was contended that the duty at a particular rate prevalent at a certain date was not payable, and the liability of the company could not be released because of the prohibitory orders of the Income tax Department under section 102 of the Act. The Customs Authorities and the Central Government were right in taking the view that the rates of duty applicable to the imported goods should be determined according to the law prevalent on the date they were actually removed from the warehouse, but could not have been cleared because of prohibitory orders, arbitrary or not. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioner has no fundamental right as such to clear any goods imported without payment of duties in accordance with the law. [629B] 2. Article 32 does not give this Court an appellate jurisdiction Such as is given by articles 132 to 136. Article for enforcement of fundamental rights. If there is breach of the fundamental rights, the peti tions can certainly have recourse to Article 32 of the Constitution provided other conditions are satisfied. But, there must, in all such cases, be circumventive of what is the right claimed. [625B C] Prakash Cotton Mills (P) Ltd. vs B. Sen & Ors., ; , followed.

The question for determination in the appeal was whether a son is liable even after partition for the pre partition debts of his father which are not immoral or illegal, and for the payment of which no arrangement was made at the date of the partition. Held (per Imam and Kapur jj.), that the liability of the sons to pay the debt of the father which were not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on a pious obligation of the son which continues to exist in the life time and after the death of the mother and which does not come to an end as a result of partition of the joint family property. Though the liability for the sons under the Mitakshara law does not become any different merely because the sale is held under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code rather than the Code of Civil Procedure, which creates an absolute obligation, but where such duty exists and partition takes place after the decree and (i) (1934) L.R. 47 I.A. 1. (2) A.I.R, (1883) L Lah. 5, (1943) L L. R. 15 I. A. 178 and (3) Where the sons do not challenge the liability to pay debts of their father after partition, their share remains unaffected because except where the debt is for an illegal or immoral purpose it is open to the execution creditor to sell the whole estate in satisfaction of the judgment obtained against the father alone. The necessary corollary which flows from the pious obligation imposed on Hindu sons is that it is not ended by the partition of his family estate unless a provision has been made for the Payment of the just debts of the parents, and that there must be a change in the mode of enjoyment and what was held jointly is by the Partition held in severalty and therefore attachment of the whole coparcenary property would not be affected by the change in mode of disposal, because the liability under the doctrine of pious obligation continued to remain intact. The test which is to see whether partition takes out place during the lifetime of the testator or after the partition was passed clearly postulates that all such events are happening when the testator died and the time taken for execution would have ended from the death. No question of inconvenience will arise as to how the interest of the children in joint family properties can be attached and sold, whether it is a case dealing with legal rights or property should depend on their facts. As the decision applies to this case the liability that of the decree holder is not an avyavaharika debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals". The Privy Council was dealing with the father 's power of disposal of property before and after partition which power vests in the Official Assignee on his bankruptcy, the question of the right of the manager to dispose of the property by sale will not arise. The liability of a father is an avoyment life estate and is a question of fact in each case dependent upon what was the estate put up for sale, what the court intended to sell and what the purchaser was intending to buy and what he purported to buy. Held further that the obligation imposed by the Mitakshara Law would be sufficient to sustain the sale and defeat the sons ' suit in the same way and on the same grounds as in the case of execution proceedings.

The petitioners, who are both guardians of law and who constitute two important segments of society on whom the stability of the country depends, filed affidavits before the Committee, which recommended their transfer to Delhi Administration as also filed affidavits, sworn by various witnesses, that if three persons referred to above to whom notices under section 8 B have been issued are to be examined even according to the Committee at the end of the inquiry there is no justifiable reason to deny the same treatment to the petitioners in case they held the Committee in great respect and that they never intended to show any kind of discourtsey to the committee, and, therefore, rejected their petitions. The petitioners have contended before this Court that if a party has the right of cross examination or not, it would be governed by section 8B of the Act. It is further submitted that there was nothing in section 8C of the , which required application of mind to the Commission or the Committee to take into consideration all the aspects of the case and that the Committee should not have passed orders confirming the proceedings on the complaints filed on behalf of the Committee for an offence punishable under section 178 I.P.C., in view of the fact that the petitioners did not either wish to delay the proceedings or to show disrespect to the Com missioner for using one or two strong words against the Committee. It was further contended that there were no sufficient reasons to deny their right in seeking to delay any proceedings or show disrespect, and that even if three of the persons referred above to the respondents in this case held the committee and the High Court set aside the orders of the committee as also the criminal proceedings. In support of the aforesaid order it was contended on behalf, inter alia, that they did not wish to put forth any kind to pressurise the Committee but only wanted to protect their own interest by making the submission which they made before the Commission as per legal advice given to them; and that only wanted the petitioners to protect his own interests by making out the submission made which they were made before them, in the absence of any justifiable reason. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The orders of this Committee directing the filing of complaints and the criminal proceeding initiated against the petitioners before the Metropolitan Magistrate pursuant to the complaint filed on their behalf should be quashed and the proceedings should be accordingly quashed. [582C D] 2.1 As a result of the order passed by the Committee on 29th June, 1988 after it was asked by this Court by its order dated 6th August, 1988 to reconsider the whole question relating to the order in which the witnesses had to be examine at the beginning of the enquiry, there is nothing justifiable reason for denying the same. On behalf of both the petitioners it was submitted that they were not bound to delay proceedings or say disrespect to them, and even wanted to safeguard their own interests.

Section 3 of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules, 1959 provided that "the tax payable under the Act on fares by the owner of a motor cycle rickshaw shall be paid to the State Government in lump sum. Section 6 required the owner to keep accounts and to submit periodic returns and provides for levy of penal ties in case of failure, which penalties are laid down in section 8. The petitioners who were seven in number challenged the Act, the Rules and the notification from many angles, in their petition under article 32 of the Constitution, on the ground that they infringed their fundamental rights guaranteed by articles 301 and 304 as being unreasonable restriction upon inter State trade, commerce and intercourse to article 19 as involving an unreasonable restriction on the business of the petitioners and also to article 14 as discrimination between operators of public motor vehicles using roads has been pointed out, and they contended (i) that the Act was within the competence of the Legislature in view of section 9 (2) of those Rules which authorised the imposition of tax by means of stamps to be affixed to the tickets, and (ii) that under r. 8 and r. 7 the notification alone laid down what lump sum payment had to be provided for by the rules. Held: (i)(a) The levy of tax cannot be said to offend article 301 and does not contravene articles 301 or 304 of the Constitu tion. (b) The word "shall" in r. 2(1) (b), is a mandatory provision and must be read harmoniously with the prescribing of the lump sum rates, and if the two Rules and notification are read harmoniously, it would lead to anomalies if the amount charged, the same in every case. In the present case there was no discrimination between the operators of transport motor vehicles used roads had been pointed by section 9 and the Notification merely laid down the minimum rate and the maximum Rs. 100/ for those who wish to avail of them. The payments which were prescribed were not "may accept." There was no differentiation between operators in public motor vehicle using road has been made, and all operators were equally affected by the Act. (c) Rule 8 and 8 A and the notifications only lay down what the amount of the lumpsum paid must be, if lump sum pay is being paid. The stipulation to this effect was that the amount payable under section 6 shall be in respect of each passenger, but no tax on fares and freights was leviable unless it was. shown that the payment was an adopting one method of payment or the other.

% The appellant a private limited company, having set up an industrial unit in engineering industry, served notice of retrenchment on 56 workmen alleging non availability or raw material to utilise the full installed capacity power shedding limiting the working of the Unit to 5 days a week, and the mounting loss. Subsequently negotiations took place between the union and the appellant leading to an agreement dated 1st April 1974 whereunder the workmen who were sought to be retrenched were taken back in service with continuity of service by the appellant and the workmen on their part agreed to co operate with the management in implementing certain economy measures and in increasing the productivity so as to make the undertaking economically viable. Simultaneously, the workmen demanded a revision of the wage scales and the Appellant pleaded its inability in view of the mount ing losses. Some negotiations took ensued between the Union and the Company leading to agreement dated Ist April 1974 whereby the workmen were sought back in services with continuity Of service by by the workmen and the workers on their own part agreed that the workmen shall be reinstated in service from 1st August 1974 with full back wages, permitting the appellant to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The Labour Court also awarded full back Wages to the said workmen on its finding that the retrenchment was not bona fide and that the non availability of the raw material or recurrent power shedgeding and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance felt by the management consequent upon refusal of the workmen to agree to the terms of settlement contained in the draft dated 5th April 1974 and therefore the retrenchment is illegal.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 I.P.C. for committing the murder of his wife Churl (26). On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant contended that the confession exhibit PH was not admissible in evidence as it was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It was further submitted that the High court erred in confirming the conviction on the confession made by the accused to him as well upon the other circumstances of the case. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The appellant had gone to the film show at Kotkhai and was not present at his house on the day of occurrence. He did not deny that he was with the deceased at his place on the date of occurrence, but stated that he had seen the accused and the deceased together at their house on a particular day and has told him that he saw the accused while they went to the house of the accused 's father. The conduct of the appellant in neither raising hue and cry nor going to the police even though his wife was murdered in his house is hardly consistent with his innocence. [445 G] Nazir Ahmed vs State of Delhi ; , followed. In the absence of any cogent explanation by him, point to his guilt. The evidence of Girju PW 1 shows that the accused had been illtreating Churi deceased and believed that Joginder had been born to her as a result of adulterous conduct.

The respondent sued the appellant for payment of a sum of Rs. 89,485 12 plus costs. The mortgage was exe cuted on the 13th June, 1936. The appellant filed a suit against his brothers and mother for an amount of Rs., 80,000. The said suit having been dismissed he applied to the High Court under section 115 C. P.C. for setting aside the order granting full ad valorem cost. The High Court held that it was not necessary in any detail as they were given in full in the two judgments of the High Courts. Held further (per Bhagwati, Bose and MUKHERJEA JJ.) : (i) When parties enter into a mortgage they know, or must be taken to know, that the law of mortgage provides for this very question of contribution. It confers rights on the mortgagor who redeems and directs that in the absence of a contract to the contrary, he shall be liable to contribute rateably to the debt secured by the mortgage. The parties are at liberty to vary these rights and liabilities by special contract to avoid different conditions, but if they do not do so, 1 can see no reason why these provisions should be abrogated in favour of a section in the Contract Act which does not deal with mortgages. Mohammad Sher Khan vs Seth Swami Dayal, (1922) 49 I.A. 192, relied on. (ii)Section 82 must exclude section 43 because when there is a general law and a special law dealing with a particular matter, the special excludes the general. In the instant case, apart from the mortgage the obligations arising out of a transaction of mort gage are now statutory and embodied in the Transfer of Property Act read with the Civil Procedure Code as also the rules framed thereunder, and not only giving an overall picture. The object being to avoid multiplicity of disputes between parties on the one side and the promisee on the other, it is open to the court to give a plaintiff such general or other relief as it deems just to the same extent as if it had been asked for, provided that occasions no prejudice to the other side beyond what can be compensated for in costs. Taibai vs Wasudeorao, A.I.R. , approved.

% The Karnataka Univer sity, by Notification dated 4th April, 1985 invited applications for recruitment of Asstt. Engineers (Civil) and (Mech.) for Public Works Department. The selections were to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and marks secured in the interview. Thus the marks allotted for inter view amounted to 33.3% of the total marks. The selection of the appellants was challenged by the respondent State which dismissed their petitions. The High Court dismissed them. Hence this appeal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Unless the marks for interview were kept even at 15% of that total marks and merit list is prepared according ly then both the appellants were bound to be selected and a large number of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appel lant. [422H] Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. S.C.R., 657; Mohinder Sain Garg vs State Of Punjab and Ors., J.T. 3, referred to. In view of the fact that the result of the impugned selections was declared in 1987 and the selected candidates have already joined the posts, the Court does not consider it just and proper to quash the selection on the above ground. [416G H; 417A] Ashok kumar Yadav & Ant. vs ly Haryana & ors., ; , followed. 2. The Government has already framed new rules, and as such, there is no allegation of any mala fides in the matter of the said selections. However, the Rules are clearly in violation of the dictum laid down by this Court in Ashok Kumar yan Yadav & Anr.

The appellants were put on trial along with the appel lants. The prosecution alleged that they had been duped and tricked and started to withdraw from them. The Commissioner dismissed the appeal filed by Sadanand Tripathi, which was rejected by the High Court in death reference 3 of 1984. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The confessions of a co accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the Court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence. [428B] 1.2 In cases involving the killing of District Magistrate in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken keen care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the right time in ac cordance with law. It is unfortunate that lapses have occur ed. P.W. 10 stated: " The people who caught of him started to assault him and began to ask him why has he killed the Collector. On being asked, he replied that he had hit the Collector by bomb at the orders of Guru Sant Gyaneshwar and one bomb has been left in the Jhola". P.Ws. 5, 12, 15, 40 and 57. In his own statement recorded under section 164 of the Code before a Magistrate, being Exhibit 44 and the other is extra judi cial confession. dealing with an offence against a person, the court cannot start with the con fession of a sub accused person, it must begin with other evidence adduced by the prosecution and after it has formed its opinion with regard to the quality and effect of the said evi dence, then it is permissible to turn to the confession in order to receive assurance to the conclusion of guilt which the judicial mind is about to reach on the said other evidence. It would thus be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [414C E] Kashmira Singh vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; at p. 414; Hari Charan Kurmi & Anr. vs State o f Bihar, ; , followed. Kashmira singh & Anr., vs State Of Madhya Pradesh; , referred to. In such a situation the judicial confession has to be kept out of considerations. There is evidence that Yadav was beaten up badly after being apprehended by the mob soon after the bombuh ary, and many prosecution witnesses have spoken about Yadav having been injured by the terror soon before the bombs. All that he said which can be used against Sadanand is the next aspect for consid eration. Obviously, when Yadav was picked up, he must have been anxious to ensure their release from jail custody. His plea in such a situa tion would neither be voluntary nor natural. It will not be proper to rely upon the same for any purpose. The appellants, who are the respondents in C.A. No. 272 of 1962 and the first respondent company, was the first Company and its main activity was to invest money in manufacturing concerns and sickness products with the textile industry. The last two companies were controlled by the first company namely Greaves Cotton and Crompton Parkinson Private Limited and its subsidiary business was distribution of the products amongst the four companies. The third company is Ruston and Hornsby (India) Private Ltd., and a service repair concern known as Cromapton Parkin Parkinsonson, incorporated in one way or the other and that is how the main dispute relating to wages and dearness allowance was dealt with together by the Tribunal. There were two references each with respect to the first three companies and the three references with respect mainly related to the second company. The fourth company was Konyon Greaves Private Ltd. In both the appeals, there was quite a difference between them, and that in view of certain circumstances, namely, that Greaves cotton Cotton and Co., is the controlling Company of the other three companies, which is in the main concern, it would be proper to put greater emphasis on the industry part of the formula if there were large number of industrial concerns in the same region carrying on the same industry; in such a case, in order that production cost may not be unequal and there may be equal competition, wages should generally be fixed on the basis of comparable industries, namely: (i) industries of the same kind ' while others similarly situated, as compared to other comparable concerns; (ii) industries which are engaged in different lines of business for the work of clerical and subordinate staff is more or less the same in all kinds of concerns; and (iii) industry cum region formula assumes greater importance particularly with reference to clerical and subordi nate staff. The Tribunal after a comparison of wages and the dearness allowance prevalent in the four factories, with wages and 7 1/2 times the maximum, awarded by it as well as by the dearness allowances prevalent in comparable concerns revised them. The main attack on behalf of the appellants was that in making such adjustments, the Tribunal completely overlooked the wages prevalent for these categories in concerns which it had considered comparable. It was, further urged that there was no justification to interfere with the order fixing the wage structure including basic wages and other dearness allowance as it should have done after taking into account factors germane to the fixation of wages by the tribunal, which had arbitrarily fixed the same rates of dearness allowance for subordinate staff and factory workmen as in the case of clerical staff.

The plaintiffs respondents executed a usufructuary mortgage (Ex. D 51) in favour of one N. The decree provided that the mortgagees would bear the expenses of the Nand Deep and debit the same to the mortgagors in the mortgage account. On March 10, 1900, the mortgagees by a Kabuliyat applied to the Mamlatdar alleging that the mortgaged property was Devasthan Inam and prayed for the cancellation of the transfer in favour which they claimed to be the legal representative of both the brothers and N. After considering all the pleas raised before him, the Mamlatdar held that the Rajinama executed by his brother conveyed only his interest and nothing more. The mortgagees appealed to the District Court against this order. In second appeal the High Court dismissed both the appeals on March 15, 1909, but that appeal was dismissed in February, 1892. On November 1, 1937, the defendants respondents applied to and obtained from the High court a special leave under Art 136 of the Constitution for the same reliefs. The respondents contended that the judgment of the Division Bench had become final so far as he was concerned. Held, that the decision of the High Courts in Letters Patent Appeal was correct on a correct interpretation of section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Act and the principal contention urged before us must be rejected. Section 74 does not confer any right or imposes certain obligations on the registered occupant as laid down in the Code but it does not mean that the other persons in whose favour the occupancy is relinquished cease to have any right. That their right as occupants remains is clearly recognised by the opening paragraph of section which gives an occupant a right to relinquish his occupancy either absolutely or in favour or of a specified person. The right given to all occupants, if there are more than one for the singular include the plural. It is true that no specific reference was made in the judgment to section 74, but the actual decision in that case, quite clearly indicates the court 's understanding of the law applicable to those facts and that law was nothing but the provisions of section 73 of the Code.

The respondents 1 to 4 were employed by the appellant Mills at various places in the State of U.P. and They closed their mill at Bulandshahr in or about 1955. The General Manager, E.W.1, in his evidence stated that the interim bonus of the said factory as ordered by the Government was Rs. 1,000 while for Amroha it: was nearly 1 1/2 lacs; that the bonus for last year at 1948 would be probably equal to 11 months ' wages and at Bulandshahr equal to about 4 or 5 days ' wages. The respondents were employed as seasonal masons in the year 1946 and 1955 respectively but they closed the mill at their request. On January 19, 1955, the General Manager served a notice on the respondents stating that they had disobeyed his orders and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. L(a). They were asked to submit their explanation as to why action should not be taken against them under the Standing Order. The Labour Union, by its order dated February 6, 1956, held that the management was within its rights and that as the respondents 1, to 4 had disobey ed the order of the management they were properly dismissed by the management. But the workmen raised an industrial dispute which was referred for decision to the State Industrial Tribunal. The Government by its notification dated November 7, 1955 exempted all the references made under the standing orders No. II and IV of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950 from the application of the mind of the workman to the termination of service and also to the award of damages in respect of each of the employees who had been employed in a business or a concern and the question whether an employer has the inherent right to transfer his employee from one concern to another of his in the circumstances of this case was not valid or amounted to victimization. The workmen raised a industrial dispute, which was held to be within its jurisdiction as the employers had disobeying the orders of the Management under Standing Orders No. l(a) which required that action should be taken under theStanding Orders. Held also that in all the said decisions the workers had been paid at once and if so, could it be said that such a term was implied between the parties ? The question whether the employer has inherent right of transfer to his employees from one business to another by reason of his refusal to obey the orders or not did not arise. If so, can it be contended that such an term had to be necessarily implied between any of the contracting parties when the idea of starting new factories at different places was not in contemplation. Mary (Anamalai Plantation ' Workers ' Union vs Seliparai Estate, ; and United Provinces Bank Ltd. vs Ali Hasan, [1956] 1 L.L.J. 344, referred to.

The appellant is engaged in the production and maintenance of hospitals, dispensaries and other institutions. Chapter V A was inserted by section 20 of the , with effect from July l, 1973. The provisions of the Chapter were deemed to have effect on and from July 1, 1973, but that exemption was withdrawn with effect form May 31, 1969 by a notification dated June 30, 1969 issued under section 73 I0 of the Act. The appellant company challenged the vires of Chapter VA by filing a writ petition. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the contribution payable under Chapter V were a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate rendering any service or conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment, and that sections 28 and 24 clearly showed that the scheme could not be implemented straight away circu nated. The writ appeal with special leave against the decision of the learned Single judge was dismissed by a Division Bench on September 7, 1971. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. When extending the Act to different establishments, the relevant (1) ; ; 6 SCR I 1092 Government is given the power to constitute a Corpora tion for the administration of the scheme of Employees ' State Insurance. The course adopted by modern legislatures in dealing with welfare scheme has uniformly conformed to the same pattern. The legislature evolves a scheme of socioeconomic welfare, makes elaborate provisions in respect of it and leaves it to the Government concerned to decide when, how and in what manner the scheme should be introduced. [1092C E] 2. When giving the Act is brought into force in the whole of India, it would not be necessary to retain this Chapter. Then all contributions will be made under Chapter IV. It may be noted that Chapter VA was inserted, as pointed out above, by an amending Act only in 1951. The object of the amendment was to make an equitable distribution of contribution by all employers. [ 1091C] 3. In view of the change in the nature of things it would have been impossible for the legislature to decide in what areas and in respect thereof the benefit provisions were extended should alone make contributions and thereby help to set up a Corporation. Therefore, the amendment provides that employers of regions to which the benefit clauses are not extended must also make their contribution though at a lesser rate. [1000E G] 4. If the charge was to be levied as a fee, it appears to us be justifiable on that basis too. It is not disputed and indeed it is difficult to say that such payment, contribution or whatever name is given to it should be so pigeon hold and fitted in stems from a misunderstanding of the Scheme of our Constitution in regard to social welfare legislation. [1001C] 5.

The petitioners demanded regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of a Diamond Mining Project, Panna. The management denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that they have been continued on rolls for several years even though there was no work for them. In fact, the petitioners were being paid their daily wages in spite of their being no work available for them, and as such, there is no question of regularising the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a short time. The writ petition was filed by the respondents contending that there was a scheme whereby industrialisation offering considerable amount to the workers towards their daily rated workers has been framed, which is Annexure R V to the counter affidavit. Dismissing the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: (1) It has also been stated in support of their contention that a voluntary Retirement Scheme offered considerable amount of retrenchment compensation and the ex gratia payment offered to the 63 daily rated employees under this scheme. The 54 petitioners are included therein. It was at the hearing, that 9 out of these 63 daily newspaper rated workers mentioned in Annexure RV have accepted this Scheme of Voluntary Retire ment and respondent No. 2 is prepared to give benefit of the same even to those who may not have agitated their claim. [638E F] (2) The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment 'to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same Work is taken from him. [625B] (3) The doctrine of regularisation is not the position. This principle has been reiterated at the heating before this Court in Subsequi nnment Petition dismissed.

The appellant was tried along with the other accused persons under section 302 read with sections 34 and 109 of the Indian Penal Code for the murder of his brother Baga Rao, and sentenced to death. His appeal to the High Court failed, as a result of which he appealed in further appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the non compliance with the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A (3) had caused prejudice to the accused. Held, that even though the crucial provisions of section 173(2) were not complied with for failure on the part of the police officers concerned to supply the necessary copies, the omission complained of in the instant case should not have a more farreaching effect than the omission to carry out the provisions Of section 162 or section 360. Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor (A.I.R. referred to. Held further, that non compliance contravenes section 537 of the Code. Abdul Kin vs The Emperor ([1947] I.L.R,. Pandu Venkataswami Iyer vs The State of Madras ([1953] S.C.R., 558), followed. In the instant ease, the failure of justice within a few hours after the occurrence was not fatal to the prosecution case inasmuch as the irregularity involved by the non appearance of the accused persons at the earliest opportunity in the first information report which was lodged without any avoidable delay within a period of two days after the murder. Abdul Muddha vs The Queen ([1952] L.R . 74 I.A. 27) referred to and distinguished.

The appellant was the owner of a chemical works discharged effluent in very large quantities with calcium, sodium and other chromates through Katcha Channels thereby corrupting potable water of the wells in the surrounding area so as to render it unfit for any use by the public or is prejudicially affecting the fertility of the soil in the nearby area. The Municipality issued a notice under section 153A(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901, giving him a reasonable opportunity of being heard. In response to the said notice the appellant replied that since the water of some of the villagers in the areas known as Harijanvas and Kolivas close to the vicinity of the channel might be affected another channel was constructed for discharging the effluent which was at a considerable distance away from Kolivas and Harijanvas, still further away. The Special Officer decided issues Nos. 2 and 3 that the appellant should arrange the discharge of the effluent through a covered pucca drain for pumping it over a distance of about 8 miles as shown in the plan annexed to the notice. He also appointed a special officer under the provisions of section 153 A(3) of Act to hold an enquiry into the matter and to complete it within three months from the date of the notification. The appellant replied to this notice by a letter dated the 10th July, 1956, pointing out that until 1943 through a Katcha channel running parallel to the railway line in the direction of Halvad, all the papers and reports relating to the tests carried out periodically by the appellant were available for inspection by the respondent Municipality and that they could be inspected by appointment. The State Government also issued another notice under sub section (3) to the effect that the discharge should be of the effluents through a bound pucca drain and for pumping water over a passage of about eight miles by a drain through a Abdul Khazat but it was stated in its notice dated July 14, 1956 that "the question whether the discharge Of the effluent from the factory of the respondent company is polluting water and adversely affects the fertiletility of soil in surrounding area by percolation. ". The Special officer also held that the question whether a nuisance existed his order must be set aside. Thereafter on August 18, 1956 the Municipality served a notice dated June 21, 1956 to the appellant under section 188 of the Act requiring him to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge in accordance with the requisition. On September 24, 1956 another advocate was appointed as a Special Officer to hold a enquiry into this matter and report from the Officer. The Committee recommended that the amount of Rs. 50 lakhs which the Municipality proposed to be paid to the Municipality should not exceed Rs. 5 lakhs within six months i.e. upto June 30, 1959, would be payable by the Municipality. On October 9, 1956 on behalf of the appellant it was contended: (i) The provisions of sections 153A and 153B of the Maharashtra District Municipal Corporation Act, 1904 were infringed in as much as they infringed articles 14 and 31 of the Constitution; (ii) The scheme of section 155A of the was to permit the Municipality, if it is satisfied that a nuisance exists as well as on finding that it does exist to proceed further and to do something more then the fact in question is not collateral but a part of the very issue which the municipality has to enquire into; and (iii) The Special Judge had no power under section 154(3), to direct the Municipality if it was satisfied that he should arrange for certain maintenance work. The Municipal Board, by its order dated September 24. 1956, fixed a date for hearing after giving a notice to the parties of the proceeding as well including the appellant as the respondent No. 1. On the same day, the Court dismissed the appeal against which also failed.

The appellant was found in possession of railway stores and kept in 11 bags, and made a report to the effect that they were all railway stores being parts of a railway engine. His conviction under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955, was maintained by the Sessions Judge and the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conviction was without any evidence because no such finding had been given in his testimony before the court nor that he had produced him for cross examination. HELD: (i) Since the prosecution is not called upon to prove that the goods belong to any particular railway administration it has to establish that the articles were the property of a Railway Administration. Evidence to the extent that the said goods conformed to the Railway Standards it held that they belonged to any such Railway Administration and as such the question of punishment under section 1 '3 did not arise. [19A] (ii) One Jaswant Singh described as an expert of railway machinery parts and Foreman and Chief Inspector of N.E. Kotwali Chowk, Lucknow, examined the goods said to be railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act. The evidence in this case did not establish that goods were Railway stores within Indian meaning of s 2(b). [19B] In the present case there was no evidence before the courts to prove the articles seized were railway stores. Evidence had to be led to the conclusion that they had been manufactured for such a long time, that the appellants did not offer any satisfactory explanation of his possession of the goods.

The appellants had leased out the demised premises to the respondent landlord on payment of monthly rent of Rs. 18 which expired on March 31, 1965. The respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under Section 106 of Transfer of Property Act but she remained in possession and enjoyment of the shop carrying on small kirana business. She died in September 1966. The said premises were governed by the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 for short the 'Act '. Section 13(1)(a), thus postulates that "notwithstanding anything contained in any law or contract, no court shall pass any decree or make any order in favour of the landlord, whether in execution of a decree or otherwise evicting the tenant so long as he is ready and willing to pay rent thereof to the full extent allowable by the Act" unless the landlord proves to the satisfaction of the Court any one of the grounds enumerated in Clauses 'a ' to 'k ' thereof. The action for ejectment was initiated by the respondent on the premise that on the death of the tenant, the appellants have no right to continue in occupation of the demised shop. The Trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that Smt. Anandi paid and the respondent accepted the rent after determination of the lease. So she was a tenant holding over. During the pendency of the appeal, the Act was amended by Act 14 of 1976. In the meantime, the Rent Control Act was replaced by the West Bengal Amendment Act. This amendment was replaced in the Rajasthan Premes (Control) Act of 1975 which was replaced with effect from April 1, 1979 introducing to Section 3 clause (vii), thus: "Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in any laws or contract no Court shall pass an decree or making any order In favour of landlord whether in terms of a sentence or otherwise evict the tenant on the termination of a contractual tenancy or until an eviction order is passed against him, continues on the same terms and conditions as before and he cannot be evicted unless a ground is made out for his eviction according to the State Rent Act. " The appellants paid and accepted the rental after determination by the lease but she was not allowed to carry on business with her till date of her death. The eviction petition was dismissed by the Trial Court. In Second Appeal, the High Court held that as the appellants had not carried on the business with the tenant during her life time as family business they were not entitled to the benefit of the amended definition of the 'tenant ' in Section 3(vii)(a) of the Act, she was entitled to ing the continuance of the tenancy. The appel lants contended that the lease hold right is an heritable estate and on death of a tenant in September, 1966, the tenancy rights held by Smt. A. Anand i.e., on payment Of monthly rent December 18, 1969 was opened and the appellants being Class I heirs under the inherited by intestate succession the lease holding estate in the tenancy right held by her deceased husband. According to them preceding the Amendment Act the commercial or business tenancy was not heritable as held in J.C. The finding recorded by all the courts is that Smt Anandi was the tenant. The appellants have been paying and the re spondent accepted rent after deter mining of the contractual tenancy, and they were entitled to enjoy the protection of the said Act. On a reference made at the instance of the appellant it was held that the respond ent landlord after termination of the contract, received the rent from her and thereby she became tenant holding full till date by virtue of intestate succession. The legal representatives of the deceased tenant, did not acquire heritable interest in the commercial tenancy under that Act.

The appellant Board 's claim to the pension fund for its employees who were on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies, was rejected by the Government of Bihar. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there should be a contributory provident fund scheme on the basis of basic wages or total wages; and that there could be no distinction between the Board ' Contributory Provident Fund Scheme and the scheme under the Employees ' Provident Fund and Gratuity Fund Act. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: The Board 'was running at a loss. [44G] Gramophone Co. vs Its Workmen, [1964] II L.L.J 131, and Gramophinone Co., vs its Workmen, ; , referred to. Gramophnone Co operative. vs its Workers and Employees ' Employees Fund Act does not apply. The Board maintains a Contributory Provident fund where the contribution is on the principles of statutory obligations and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciation reserve. These and other matters cannot be properly decided in the absence of a detailed examination of the finances of the Board. [45A B] Gram phone Co, vs its workmen, ; and Gramanthophone Cooperative vs Its Workers and Workmen. , distinguished. The contribution to the gratuity reserve is a statutory obligation and is an definite proportion while it is subject lo a reasonable restriction like any other expense including wages and if the financial position shows that the burden of payment of provident fund and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer that burden will have to be borne by the employer like the burden, of wage structure in the interest of social justice. [46C] Gramphone Co Co. V Its Workmen; ; , applied.

The respondent, who was the wife of the appellant filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 for grant of maintenance to her on the ground that her husband had been guilty of wilful neglect and was unable to fulfil his primary responsibility of discharging his marital obligations. The Magistrate rejected the application on the view that the denial of maintenance by the wife was not just a just cause for refusing to live with the husband, and accordingly refused maintenance to the respondent. Thereafter, the matter was taken up in revision before the High Court which differed from the view taken by the Magistrate and held that the husband having been found to be impotent, this should he a just ground for the wife to refuse to live alongwith her husband on the grounds: (1) that her father being impotently and unable to discharge his marital obligation, he could not persuade herself to live so with him; (2) that as he was impotable and unable at all to perform his marital liabilities. The appellant further held that it was now well settled by decisions of the Bombay High Court in Munnalal Anandayammal vs Smt. Mahrul Nisa, ; and Vizhinama vs Suresh Chandra Misra, ; that a wife is not an active participant in the sexual life and therefore, the sexual pleasure to the wife is of no consequence and therefore cannot amount to cruelty; (3) that it would not be a just reason for the husband to refuse live with her husband when it appeared to the Court that there are "just grounds" passing such an order. This finding was challenged before this Court by Special Leave on behalf of the respondent, and it was contended that it is now wellsettled by a long course of decisions of various High Courts that impotency jurisdiction is no good ground or reason for refusing maintenance to livewith her husband; (4) that in cases under the Hindu law, there is no valid ground for grantof maintenance to: the wife. It is true that Bakshi J., in that case seems to have been influenced more by the concept of neglect rather than by the reasonableness of the ground on which the refusal of the wife could based but this would certainly be a 'relief ' and even if the husband refused to cohabit, that would not render the amendment redundant; (5) that the court must look at the entire evidence and decide whether the allegations made are such in any way inconsistent with the normal ideas of the status and emancipation of women, in which women were subjected to a mental cruelty of living with a husband, who had taken a second wife or a mistress on the pain of being deprived of any maintenance if they chose to live separately from such a husband; and (6) that on the facts found there was "just ground", passed an order granting maintenance against the appellant. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. If the husband was impecotent and unable, to discharge the marital obligations, how could he fulfil the main object of marriage, more particularly under the Mahomedan law, where marriage is a sacrosanct contract and not a purely religious ceremony as in the case of Hindu Law. This would certainly amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a valid ground within the meaning of the second proviso so as to make the refusal, of the husband 's refusal to live With her husband fully justified and entitled to maintenance. [707E F] 2.1 The provisions of section 488 of the Criminal Procedure 1898 are liable to be construed strictly. As per section 125, Cr. P.C., this provision has been incorporated as Explanation to the second sub section (3).

The appellant was a class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer and he was charged under section 161 Indian Penal Code for having induced the said Nanak Singh to deliver currency notes of the value of Rs. 150 by dishonest representation that be could secure a job for one Kallu, that be would secure a jobs for the said Kallu and he could secure an job for the that purpose, it was held that no case under section 420 I.P.C. was made out but he was acquitted of that charge. The appellant contended that the word 'officer ' meant some person employed to exercise in some way and in certain circumstances a delegated function would be "immediately auxiliary to those of the Government". Held, that a public servant was an officer within the meaning of section 21(9) and therefore a public Servant within the operation of section 2 Of the Prevention of Corruption Act II of 1947. Ram Krishan vs Delhi State ([1952] S.C R. 589), distinguished. In order to determine whether a person is an officer of the government, the nature of his duties was not stated, because this objection was not taken at the trial. But merely on a narrow interpretation of the dicta of West J in 12 Bombay High Court Reports 1, an officer in the service or pay of the Govern ment performing as such a public duty entrusted to him by the Government and was therefore an officer "acting" within the terms of section21(9), Indian Penal code. Ram Krishna vs DelhiState ([1952) S. C. R. 930), referred to.

The respondent along with another person applied to the Excise and Taxation Department (Excise and Taxation) for a permanent injunction restraining the State and the Collector cum Deputy Excise and appel lant from auctioning his said half share. The auction in respect of this share was notified for June 14,1977. Just a day prior to the holding of the said auction sale the respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala for a di recting the transfer or creation of a charge by the Respondent of his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 511. Khasra No. 39710 19 situate in village Ghagga with a building constructed thereon. The respondent filed 847 suit against the State of Punjab and the Excise Department for a perpetual injunction restraining that State and Collector from auction ing his half portion share. Thereafter, recovery proceedings were started by the department and the collector. Excise andTaxation Department, Patiala issued a proclamation prohibiting the transfer of or creation or creation any charge by him of his part ty in an immoveable property consisting olve plot of Land bearing K Khatauni No.374, Khatoni NO. 512. Khasra Nos. 397 1019 situated in village saddhwith a building erected thereon. When recovery proceedings under the said Act were started, the department issued a notice prohibiting the re spondent from auction taking his half per share and that the auction in question was notified by the Excise & Taxation Department of the State Government. The Collector cum District Judge dismissed it with costs. The Respondent then filed an appeal to the District Judge, Patiala being Civil Appeal No. 554 of 5 979.9.79 before the Additional District Judge Patiala who dismissed it as well as the first appellate court. The High Court allowed the second appeal holding that the portion of the building used for residence was exempt from attachment and sale under clause (ccc) of the proviso to section 60, while that portion in which the liquor shop was situated was liable to be attached, and accordingly issued a permanent injti cation with regard to the portion in question which the respondent was residing. Against this judgment and decree of the High Court the appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply to an attachment and re sale under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said section is concerned it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue due to the State therefore it contains complete code provides for the mode and machineryfor recovery of outstanding dues. The attachment in a question was levied under the provisions of the Act and the sale which was notified was also under the provi sions of the Central Act. [848F; 849D] 2.1 In the instant case, it contains (a) a complete Code providing for modes and manner for recovery o/s dues of revenue.[849B C] 2(a) Section 60 has no application to an attached attachment and sales under any Of her statute making expressly applicable thereof. So long as the Act contains a specific code providing that, section has no applic ly to attachment and .sale, in execution of a decree there is no provision in the said provi dent corresponding to cl.

The lands in question were acquired under the Land Acquisition Act by two separate awards of the Special Deputy Collector on January 31, 1963 and March 19, 1965 respectively. On March 19 4, 1965 the special Deputy Collector awarded a total compensation of Rs. 20,000 for these lands which was received in April 945 by the heirs of Rashid, namely, his widow Mrs. Freny Chenai and son Shapoor Rashid Chenai on whom the estate of Rashid devolved in equal shares. On the death of Rashid on November 4, 1963, Mrs. Ereny chenai became the appellant in C.A No. 996/66. The Estate Duty assessment was made at Rs. 26,550. This compensation was received by Rashid himself during his lifetime. Later two more parcels of agricultural land (admeasuring 22 Acres 24 Guntas and 8 Acres 23 Guntas) situated at Moosapet village belonging to Shri Rashid Shapil Chenai were acquired for the Synthetic Drugs Project Factory of the Indian Drugs and Pharmaceutical Ltd. by the Andhra Pradesh Government Notification dated June 19, 1961 under the the Land Acquisi tion Act. The Special Deputy Collec tor of Land Acquisition awarded a compensation of RS. 20 lakhs on two grounds: (a) that after compensation had been awarded by the Special Dy.
