Collector under section 11 of the Land Act the heirs Of the deceased had merely exercised a right to sue for further compensation which was merely a hope or an chance that the compensation might be enhanced, that such expector opportunity could not be elevated to the status of an asset or property and as such not asset chargeable to estate duty had escaped assessment and (b) that even assuming that any asset or asset chargeable lo estate duty bad escaped assessment, the notice was illegal and without jurisdiction because such escapement was not due to any omission or failure on the part of the accountable person to disclose fully and truly material facts necessary for making the assessment. 20 On the second aspect the High Court held that having regard to the enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the lands such property (meaning lands) had been undervalued in the original assessment and as Such it had escapedassessment to duty. The respondent as well as the High court proceeded on the wrong assumption that the acquired lands formed part of tho estate of the deceased and passed on his death, for this reason that the lands might no longer formed part thereof and, therefore, it was merely the right to receive compensation which could not form part of assessment record and he so called mistake apparent from the record. The High Court accordingly quashed the order of rectification. Allowing the appeals by certificate, the Court HELD: 1.1 The very issue issuance of the notice under section 59(a) which was done on a basis clearly unsustainable in law is liable to be quashed on this ground. [320E] 1.2 In the instant case, the ward made by the special Dy. Controller of Estate Duty, Bangalore had issued a notice purporting to act under section 61(a), and therefore the same was liable to he quashed on that ground. Thus, since in the instant cases the wards made by Mr. Rashid Shaptoor the Special Collector were not accepted or are accepted under protest and the claimant seeks land references in C Courts, the right of compensation must be regarded as having survived or kept alive by the claimants and it is that property (right to compensation) which will have to be evaluated by the assessing authority as; on the date of the death.

% The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986 and he was elected on 18.8.1986 as one of the Directors of the Bank from the Breeperpuri Ag ­ Agricultral Sales and Purchase Society, Maharashtra State Cooperative Land Development Bank and the election was not called in question according to the procedure prescribed by the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act 1960. On 8.1.1987, the District Deputy Registrar of the Cooperative Societies by his order dated 7.12.1987 removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors of a bank holding that he was defaulter under Section 73FF(1) of the Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act, 1960 and rejected the appellant 's contention that Section 73 FF came into force on 12.5.1986. The appellant challenged before the Divisional Joint Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Nagpur by means of a Writ Petition in the High Court praying for quashing the said order as well as for setting aside the election of the appellant as also for restoring him from the Board of Directors. The Writ Petition was dismissed by the High court holding that Section 75 FF vested no right on the appellant to continue as Director or executive member for a period exceeding six months in view of the provisions contained in section 73FFF(1)(b) as the appellant had not paid all the debts on 21.10.86 and he had committed defaults after the coming into force of the Act. The High Court held that since it was a default, the appellant became defaulter under section 73 FFF(I) of Maharashtra State co operative Societies Rules 1960. Allowing the appeal by Special Leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The disqualification as defaulter continued after the election and since the appellant gave all the creditors on 21 10.86 yet he could not be "absolved of the disqualification on the date he contested the election". [679A] 1.2 There was no room for holding that the appellant was in arrear in respect of instalments on the dates of his election and till 21.4.1986 i.e. both prior and posterior to his election on 18 8.86 i. e. both previous and subsequent to his elections on 18th August, 1986. [679B] 1:3 The question of generalibus specialia derogant special things take from general or generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, therefore, does not arise. What was stated in para 36 of the report in Hundraj Kanayalal Sajnani vs Union of India, ; at 1121 will not be relevant. [680E] 1 :4 In Maharashtra State Board of Education vs Paritosh Sheth, ; followed. The provisions relating to election have to be interpreted harmoniously with other provisions of the Electricity Act such as in section 78(1). Under sub section (1) thereof a person shall be disqualified for being elected as and for being a member, of the committee of any specified society, if he is so disqualified by or under any other provision of this Act. Section 144T deals with powers of removal of committees or members thereof provides as follows: "82(1): If in the opinion of the Registrar, the committee or any member of such committee makes default or is negligent in the performance of the duties imposed on it or him by this Act or the rules or the bye laws, or commits any act which is prejudicial to the interest of the society or its members, or wilfully disobeys directions issued by the State Government or is otherwise not discharging its functions properly and diligently and the business of the Society has or is likely to come to a standstill, or where any member who fails the payment of any instalment of the loan granted to him; xxx xxx xxx" Sub section (2) of Section 73F says that a member who has incurred any disqualification under sub section(1), shall cease to be a member of the Committee and his seat shall thereupon be deemed to be vacant".

Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules empowers Government to reduce or withdraw a pension. Rule 189 contemplates withholding or withdrawing of a pension or any part of it if the pensioner be convicted of grave misconduct while he was in service and after completion of his service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a government servant depend upon the good conduct of the Government servant. Rendering satisfactory service maintaining good conduct is a necessary condition for the grant and continuation of pension. Rules 189 and 189 relevant for our purpose are as under: "188. Government may withhold or withdraw any part thereof if the pensioners be convicted without him: Provided that before any order reducing or withdrawing any part, of the pension is made by the competent authority the pensioner must be given opportunity of defence in accordance to the procedure specified in Note I to Rule 33 of the Rules. Under Note 1 to Rule 35 of the said Rules, Government may withholding or withdrawal of a part of the Pension payable to a Government servant for misconduct which he may have committed while in service. The respondent challenged the validity of the order by means of writ petition before the High Court on various grounds such as (1) that the State Government had no authority to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from service, (2) that there was no relevant rule restricting the exercise of power of reduction of pension; and (3) that even though a Government Servant retired from Service on attaining the age of superannuation he could not escape the liability for misconduct and negligence or financial irregularities committed by him during the period of his retirement. Allowing the appeal partly, this Court, HELD: The High Court committed serious error in holding that the respondent 's action was helpful to Shri Khatavane to sell sugar in the black market, and it amounted to a serious default on his part as a Government employee. [189 G H] B.J. Shelet vs State of Gujarat & Ors., [87] 2 SCC 179; The reduction of 50 per cent was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the Respondent. In this view, the reduction by 50 per 100 per cent in respect of his pension was too severe harsh and pursuitsment to the respondent.

The appellants who were the tenants of a shop in the suit premises, applied for permission to sue the respondents under section 3 (1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 on the ground that the said permission had been refused by him; whereupon they moved the Commissioner in his revisions jurisdiction under section 5(3) of 'the Act. The Commissioner dismissed their revision petitions. Thereafter the respondents applied to the Commissioner, who ordered the reversal of the decree passed by them. The appellants then moved the High Court for a certificate granted by the High court which was rejected. In appeal before this Court it was contended that section 3 of the Act provides a self contained code for the grant of permission and all questions in relation to the grant or refusal of such permission have to be decided by the appropriate authorities constituted under the Act, as the words "the State Government may call for the record of any case granting or refusing to grant permission" indicate that intention. was to confer wide jurisdiction on the Commissioner; and that the words used in sections 188 and 191 of the Sea Customs Act (1878) were clear and unambiguous and the only question which could be raised before a civil court in relation lo orders passed under the relevant provisions of the Acts, could be the applicability of section 3(4) and section 16. HELD : The appeal must be allowed. It was well settled that a party can move the Commissioner under section3(3), in cases where the District Magistrate just refuse to make an order on the application made by the landlord for permission brought a suit against the tenant. If the District Court refuses to grant, and the Commissioner thinks that in doing so, he has committed an error, that would be a case where the Regional Magistrate had wrongly refused to act, and that would give the Commissioner jurisdiction to exercise his revisional power. [558 F G] In order to appreciate the validity of this argument it would be necessary to consider the scheme of the relevant provision of the , relating to the granting of permission to the landlord to sue his tenant in ejectment. It is not easy to conceive of a limitation as to jurisdiction being relevant in section 3, because the said provision deals withorders passed by District Magistrates and the District Magistrates normally would have jurisdiction to deal with applications made by landlords. [559 F G; 559 B] The scheme of section 2 is that if a landlord wants to bring a suit to eject his tenant, he must apply to the District magistrate for permission from the Commissioner within 30 days.

The first reference of the kind made by the President of India to this Court under Article 317(1) of the Constitution was in respect of conviction against the Members of the Punjab Public Service Commission. The question for consideration before the Supreme Court was whether the power of the President to make a reference to this court under Article317 (1) is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. This Court cannot, through the medium of a Reference, be called upon to discharge functions which ordinarily fall within the jurisdiction of a trial court civil or criminal [646C] 2.1 The power of this President to issue a reference under Article 316(1), is notsubject to the conditions precedent that it must first has the facts examine by some body or Authority. That Article provides that the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Com mission can only be removed from his office only by the order of the president on the ground of misbehaviour and (ii) the order removing can be passed after the Supreme court has on inquiry reported to the President that the chairman or such other person ought to be removed on any such ground. [647C] 4. There was a sharp difference between the rival views submitted before this Court as to the nature and scope of the evidence which we should allow the parties to lead. The attention is not always easy of Court to appreciate and interpret the pleadings in this matter. [ 648B C] 5. If an examination and assessment of facts is made by this Court instead of being made by a Magistrate or a Munsif, if a full opportunity is given to the parties concerned to prove and rebut the facts in issue as in a regular trial, it is an idle complaint that the evidence has been examined and found upon by the Supreme and not by a court of first instance.

% The respondents, who were the appellants and the respondent, filed a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 ( 'the Act '). The Subordinate Judge decreed the appellant plaintiffs suit holding that the deity installed in the temple was a family deity and the endowment being of a private nature, the Act had no application and the order passed by the respondent regarding the management was set aside. The respondents preferred an appeal before the Sub Divisional Judge which was heard by the Division Bench which held that the temple and the deity install therein being a public endowment fell within the four corners of section 2(f) read with section 2 (5) of Act 4 of 1939 Act, consequently, it was to be governed by the Act. The High Court reversed the decision of the Subordinate Judge and held that in order to effectuate the spiritual benefit to the family of the founders and its descendants and to perpetuate the memory of the founder, they were fully entitled to pass orders for its management. Hence this appeal by certificate. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 In a public trust, where all trusts are public trusts of a purely charitable nature, there is no document or revenue entry to prove its origin, the task of the court becomes difficult and it has to rely merely on circumstantial evidence regarding the nature of user of the temple. It is well settled that under the Hindu law, however, it is not only permissible but also very common to have private endowments which though are meant for charitable purposes yet the dominant intention of the propotye and their descendants and To perpetuate the confidence of the settlor. [830E G] 1.2 In addition to the unimpeachable documentary evidence discussed above, even the oral evidence to prove that the endowment was of a public nature, is clear and has not been rebutted by the defence. [822F] 2.1 The onus of proving this chain lies heavily on the appellants in view of the provisions contained in section 2 of Act 1 of 1939. [824G H] 3.2 To get home the findings of fact arrived at by the High Court, the burden is shifted on the respondents to prove their existence. [823H] 4. The civil court cannot take care of the documents produced and the evidence collected in the case, which would go against the appellants. [825A] 5. There was no mention in any of the letters to show that there was any such stipulation for taking offerings from the members of the public. The mere fact that the members were not allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that the member of the community had a right to worship in the Temple. [828E F] 6. All other necessary expenses of the Jatra (festivals) repairing of the Temple, utensils and the ornaments of the deity, etc. will be done according to the income.

The appellant Bank entered into certain contracts and undertook to finance the contracts. The appellant was also authorised to sue for, recover and receive moneys due in connection with the contract with the approval of MaLhotra, to conduct and defend proceedings in consultation with him and to take steps in his name and on his behalf. Malhotra agreed that the company would pay out of its assets in their hands the costs of this appeal as also the interest thereon. The agreement recited that "we are working as contractors to the Government in its various departments and have entered into various contracts to finance contracts and to advance us sums of money against supply bills for payments to be received by us under the contracts directly in their own name or in our names in payment of such bills or other amounts and to cash and to receive the amount thereof and appropriate such receipts towards repayment of the advances made or to be made hereafter and all other monies due from us to the attorneys in any account what soever". The appellant bank entered into an agreement with the appellant against his bills for supplies under the contract. For the purpose of carrying out this arrangement, Malhotra executed an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appeLlant on July 13, 1946. The Power of attorney recited: "Whereas we are working for as contractors for the Government and other authorities." On a proper construction of the document it was necessary to bear in mind that the relationship of the two parties, Bhushan Chetty and the Bank was that of borrower and lender and that the document was brought into existence in connection therewith with a proposed transaction of financing of Malhotra 's contracts.

The appellant was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd. The said Company had a Provident Fund Scheme for its employees. But that provident fund was not recognised by the Income tax Officer. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order but on further appeal to the Tribunal, the tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ', the same was his salary as defined in section 17 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (to be hereinafter referred to as the Act); the same having not been assessed as his salary the assessment order relating to that item of receipt was not legal. At the instance of the Commissioner, the Tribunal referred the question to the High Court for its opinion: "Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case and having regard to the provisions of section 17 (3) (ii) of the Act, the amount Rs. 27,948/ representing the interest on the amount of the assessee 's own contributions to an unrecognised provident fund is assessable under the residuary section 56 of the said Act ? " The High Court answered that question in the negative and against the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, HELD: The receipt of Rs. 28,948 by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary though undoubtedly that is an income. What is meant by "profits in lieu of salaries", does not include from the scope of that expression any payments received by the assesses from a Provident fund his own contributions tO to the fund or any interest on such contribution. From that it follows that the receipts of Rs 27,949/ by the appellant in the concerned accounting year could not be considered ' as salary although undoubtedly that was an income and that it cannot be said to be either interest on securities; income from house pro perty; profits and gains of business or profession or capital gains. It has to be considered that as "income from other sources" and brought to tax under section 56.

Section 1(3) of the Bihar Act defines " cow" as including a female calf of a cow, bull bullock or heifer and a new schedule specifying only (1) cows, (2) male and male buffaloes and (3) buffalo and (4) goat and sheep. The petitioners who were dealers in cattle and cattle challenged the constitutional validity of these Acts on the grounds inter alia that they infringed their fundamental rights under article 19(1)(g); that the impugned Acts, if enforced, would compel them at once to close down their business and will, in effect, amount to a complete denial of their right to carry oil their occupation, trade or business in spite of the mandatory provisions of article 19 (1), (g) and that the Act is not ultra vires. Held, further that the Bihar Preven tion Act which restricts the slaughter of buffaloes of all ages and calves of cows and calve of buffaloes was constitutionally valid and there could be no question of any contravention or contravention of any provision of the law relating to slaughtering of her buffaloes, breeding bulls and working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) which were useful as milch or breeding or draught animals. The Bihar Act also did not place a total ban on the slaughter Of buffaloes of every description in the last part of article 48. The two Acts, however, provided for the protection and improvement of stock and that its real object was not to take away or abridge the rights guaranteed by article 19; and that, as regards the Madhya Pradesh Act which restricted the slaughter from cattle of all age and cales of cows it was open to the State Legislature to enact a law relating inter alia to prohibiting the slaughter in respect of such cattle. The provisions of sections 3, 4, 6 and 7 of the Act were valid as they purported to completely prohibit the slaughter.

The respondent, a public limited company having its registered office at Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh, its Manager and Assistant Manager, was charged with misconduct under Standing Orders 16(1) (b), (c), (d) of the Bombay Electricity Supply Act, 1946. The Company submitted his explanation on December 3, 1955, marked a copy thereof to one of its directors of the company. On December 2, 1955 an order of suspension was made against the respondent which stated that his services would stand terminated as from January 31, 1956 and that the said order was illegal and ultra vires and a prayer for certain other reliefs. The Labour Commissioner dismissed the application but granted leave to appeal to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution filed by the company by special leave. Held: (i) Under the provisions of the Central Provinces and Berar Industrial Disputes Settlement Act, 1947, the expression ' Standing Orders ' means rules relating to matters set out in the Schedule, and section 3 requires that within six months from the date on which the central Act becomes applicable to an industrial establishment the employer shall submit to the certifying officer five copies of the draft proposed Standing Orders proposed by him for adoption in his industrial establishment; and where model Standing Orders have been prescribed, the draft shall so far as practicable be in conformity with such model. The words ' whose names and ticket numbers are included in the departmental musterers will not exclude employees who do not possess tickets or to whom tickets have not been issued and consequently whose names only are so entered. Therefore, the respondent was an employee within the meaning of the Standing Orders and, therefore, his service has been terminated in accordance with Standing Order No. 16. (ii) Under section 30 of the local Act no workman shall be dismissed from service unless he was specifically informed that he would take legal action against the proposed action.

The appellant company was an undertaking owned, controlled and managed by a Government Company. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act for the year 1965 631 1966 on the plea that this Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until either this Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this Project went into production. The tribunal found that alloy Steel Projects were divided into two classes and their meaning had been defined. In appeal to this Court it was contended (i) that the word establishment ' has been used in section 2 sub section (15) of the Act to indicate a "Company" as called in common parlance; (ii) that an establishment is owned, managed controlled or managed by or under a corporation; (iii) that if an establishment consists of separate departments, undertakings or branches which are owned, supervised and managedby a person or body other than a Government company or a corpora tion of the nature described in that clause, there will be no deduction @ 8.5 per cent of the paid up equity share capital as envisaged by section 6(d) and the Third Schedule of the ,; and (iv) that even if alloy steel Project is treated as a separate concern, or is to be treated as part of the main establishment owned by the company, it will not be covered by the definition in cl. (16). HELD: The Tribunal was wrong in ignoring the fact that separate balance sheet and profit & loss accounts are maintained for each separate unit and the consolidated accounts are prepared only for the purpose of complying with the requirements of the companies Act. [631B C] Section , 3 cannot be resorted to at all when the Act itself is inapplicable in view of the provision contained in section 1, sub section. It was so held by this Court in section R. T. Kapur and others vs The Textile Labour Association, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 435 that even though there is no evidence at all that in any year, after Alloy steel project was set up bonus was paid to the employees of all the units on the basis of consolidated profits of all such units. In the present case there is very clear evidence that although the Company, Hindustan Steel Ltd., has a number of undertakings, 635 Separate accounts are kept for each unit and separate profit and Loss account for each Unit for purposes of the Companies Act. Therefore from this, even if Alloy Engineering Project or other units of the Company are treated as separate establishments and available surplus is calculated separately for each units, there would be no deducted @ 8 5 per centof the paidup equity share Capital as envisaged in section 6 (d), and the third Schedule of .

The appellants were the sugar mill and later was adjo nised by a Notification issued under section 3 of the Prevention and Control of Pollution Act, 1974. The Act provides for the constitution of joint boards which include the details of which need not detain us. The Cess Act is intended to ensure that the domestic and industrial affluence are not allowed to be discharged into water coars without adequate treatment. This Act is now in force in almost all states. The Central Government and State Boards constituted for the prevention and control of Water pollution, and section 3 provides for levy of cess on water consumed by persons carrying on certain industries which have assumed considerable importance and urgency in recent years as a result of increasing industrialisation and urbanation. Section 3 of Cess Act provides that there shall be levied and collected a cess for the purposes of and utilisation thereunder. The cess is payable by every person who carries on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed. Section 4 provides for imposition of cess in respect of water taken by persons bringing on certain undertakings specified in the Schedule, at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in Sch. I. The appellants challenged the constitutional validity of the Act on the ground that it falls within entry 15 of Schedule I to the empowers the Central Government & State Boards to levy and collect the cess provided under the Cess Act. This was dismissed by this Court. However, on the other hand the Andhra Pradesh High Court allowed the appeal of the sugar mills in part and also took the view that sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products". On the other band it was held that sugar con tinence would come under Entry 15 which is "process ing of animal or vege table products industry" and therefore, falls within Entry 8 of Schedule 1. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power to levy cess is on water taken away from a person carrying on the industries specified in entry 15. But in the context in which the word "vegetable" is used in Entry 15. [528C] 2.1 The Act must be strictly construed in order to find out whether a liability is fas tened on a particular industry. The subject is not to be taxed without clear words for that purpose, and also that every Act of Parliament must be read according to its natural construction of words. Otherwise, it would not be possible to conclude sugar cane as vegetable. [525D E] 2(a) Public purpose will be served if the cess is levied on a person who has carried on any inter alia specified industry. [500E G] 3.2 The word "pro cess" cannot be said to refer to edible plants or parts of edible plants. The expression "who processes any goods" in the Karnataka Sales Tax was held to refer only to edible products, but not to any particular kind of plant life or plant product. On the contrary, it is a transformation of an article which is commercially different from the one which is converted. [600E F] 2.(b) In order to bring an industry within any of the entires in Schedule I it has to be seen what is the end product produced by that industry. Sugar cane is not a vegetable though it may be an agricultural product. If the botanic meaning of vegetable as referring to any and every kind of equipment plant life is to be given then some of the indus tries listed in Schedule 1 like paper industry and Textile Industry and even chemical industry which are covered by other entries could also be brought within Entry No. 15. The word vegetable in the instant case does not attract the botsic meaning.

The respondent, an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant, his tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who was carrying on the business of manufacturing art jewellery in the premises. The trial Court passed an order of eviction against the appellant. Before the High Court it was contended by the Appellant that there was a clear distinction between 'business ' and 'profession ', and that the practice of a liberal profession like that of an Advocate or Doctor which had nothing commercial about it was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3)(a) (iii). Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression 'business" occurring in section 10( 3)(a)(iii) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice as of the legal profession. The word must be interpreted in the context of the statute in which it occurs and not in the background of other statutes or in a manner alien to the context in which the term has been understood in the several statutes do not necessarily throw any light on the manner in which tho term should be understood generally. [14C E] 1.2 The expression business ' is given a narrow meaning so as not to include any profession. There is no reason why a landlord who is a member of the cooperative or medical professions and who requires the premises to carry on the practice for his profession should be wholly debarred from obtaining possession of the premises.[15D E] In the instant case, the Court was clearly wrong in holding that the use of the expression 'trade ' in section 1(3) (a)(ii) is not restricted to any classes of landlords. The question in that case was about the right to compensation for goodwill attached to the premises where the business" or "profession" was being carried on. [16D E; F] M.P. Sethurama Menon vs Thaiparambath Kunhukutty Amma, A.I.R. 1967 Kerala 88 and Stuchbery & Ors. vs General Accident Fire and Life Assurance Corporation Ltd., ; , referred to.

The respondent deposited a sum of Rs. 4,00,000 in the appellant 's account under an agreement and that it was payable on demand. The respondent filed the suit for recovery of certain amount with interest and costs. The suit was dismissed as time barred by limitation and the High Court allowed the appeal holding, (1) article 60 of the Indian Limitation Act 1908 was the relevant Article; if is a case of money deposited under an agreements that it would be paid on demand and therefore the limitation would commence from the date of demand and (2) Article 60 would not come into play during the year 1942. Dismissing the appeal for special leave, HELD : (1)(a) The appellant 'sets including Lakshmi Rattan Cotton Mills were running accounts. It would be more consistent to hold that by allowing India Supplies a deposit of Rs 4 lakhs would be relieved of the situation of repaying the money immediately. [577 E F] (b) The transaction was between the parties, and the respondent. The claim for money could not have proceeded from that date. The appellant had acted as bankers. The money in specie was not a case where money is deposited under any agreement that the same would be made on demand or whether it was a case for an ordinary loan of Rs to 4 lacs. [578 G H] (2)(a). A demand in the year 1943 for a part of the amount would not be effective because there were common partners in the firms of the respondent and the appellant. [576 C] (c) The statement of account was not produced. Therefore, the High 'Court was correct in decreeing the suit. [580 D E] (d)There was merely an endorsement that the money had been deposited with the respondent under an arrangement. In the year 1941 there was a dispute between the appellant and Lakshmi Rattan cotton Mills on the one hand and Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills and it would, therefore, have evidentiary value to show as to how the parties treated and understood their financial dealings. [574 D G] (3)There were disputes between the partners of the various businesses in which the Singhania and Gupta groups were interested. These disputes were before the arbitrators. One of the terms in the award was that the award in respect of Lakshmi Rattan Mill and India Supplies "do not cover the advances which either party or their separate firms may have made to all or any of them or their moneys which may be in deposit with them and they shall be payable and paid in their usual course". If, therefore. the respondent acted as banker bankers. [575 B] (4)There is a presumption that the appellant had accepted the money before it was credited in order to avoid unnecessary harassment to him of being made in order that the amount should not be adjusted against the loan advanced by him.] (5)The loss of money would arise only when there were mutual dealings between two groups. [583 F G] 3(a) There is a difference between the words " deposits karaya" appearing without any doubt to have been written at the same time as the rest of the writing. It will depend on the facts of each case whether the transaction was clothed with the character of a deposit or loan and it will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each ease, whether the transactions are clothed with character of deposits of money. The surrounding circumstances at the time when the respondent demanded the money by a letter dated 27 4 the appellant in their reply dated 5/6 May 1953 (exhibit 7) totally denied the claim. [557 G H, 576 A] V. E. Annamalai Chettiar & Anr. vs sectionV. Veerappa Chettiar, ; , followed.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance on February 28, 1986, made in exercise of powers vested under section 3(1) of the , which provided that "Every summons issued by a Court under this Code shall be in writing in the case, signed by the presiding officer of such court or by such other officer as the High Court may, from time to time, by rule direct and shall bear the seal of the Court. The petitioner was directed to surrender to Jail at any time he lied. He was arrested for a period of one year on March 27, 1987. On February 28 the orders of detention came to be made, the detenu was remanded to the judicial custody on 27th February, 1986 and was again taken into custody and produced before the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate who ramand ed him to custody on March 28,1986. Since the detenu had already surrendered in respect of the criminal charge against him he filed a writ petition in this Court. Allowing the Writ Petition the High court had directed that if any misconduct or any other activity comes to their notice which required the revocation of the parole, the petitioner shall surrender to custody to undergo remaining period of detention. In view of these facts, the order of detention was set aside, and it was held: [849C D] 480 The fact remains that only one contention had been raised. There is absolutely no basis for the alle gation in paragraph 2 of the writ petition that if the Court had indicated to Mr. Jethmalani in course of arguments that the submission on this limited point did not find favour with the Court he would have proceeded to argue the other points. [844G] Kantilal Ishwarlal Shah vs State of Maharashtra, ; and Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Burdwan & Ramesh Yadav vs District Magis trate, Etah; , followed.

The petitioners were working as Casual Labour under the Posts and Telegraphs Department. They had produced a order of the Director General, Posts and telegraphs department bearing No. 28 II/77 SR/STN dated 15 5 1980 which prescribes the rate or rates of wages payable to casual labour in the Telecommunication Wing of the Department. The said order was followed by another order bearing No 10 4/83 R dated 26 7 1984 which prescribed the rate of daily wages for the semi skilled/skilled/s unskilled labour who has not completed 720 days of service over a period of three years at the rate, of 240 days per annum with the Department as on 1.4.80. The petitioners were not satisfied with the above reply received by them. They filed a statement of demands through Secretary General, BPTEF, New Delhi, of which they were members, claiming regularisation of casual labourers, payment of interim relief, payment for overtime relief, supply of dresses, leave and medical facilities etc. They received a reply from the Department on January 10, 1986 which read as under: "Sub Demands of casual labour daily rated workers. Ref: Your letter No. PF/Casual Labour/86 dated 13 12 1985. Please refer to your above cited letter. The position regarding the various demands in their said cited letter is as below: (i) Regularisation of Casual Labour. This is being done as per existing instructions of Department of Personnel & Training as against the vacancies as and when they arise. (ii) Payment of interim Relief. Revision of wages is done once in a year for casual labourers of category 1 (those who have not completed 7 days of Service) over aperiod of 5 years or more. ^ HELD: The benefit of increased rates of daily wage will not be admissible to the casual semi skilled /skilled labour in whose case the continuous spells of duty are intervened by a period more than six months. [609G] 519 In the instant case, since the petitioners belong to the category of casual Labour and are not being regularly employed, they are not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees are enjoying. It cannot be so because there is so much of development to be carried out in the communications department that you need more workers. [ 608A B] (i)(a) The petitioners have not been regularly recruited but many of them have been engaged as casual labourers for nearly ten years. They are rendering the same kind of service which is being rendered by the regular employee doing the same type of work. Clause (2) of Article 38 of the Constitution provides that "the State shall, in particular, strive to minimise the inequalities in income, and endeavour to eliminate inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities, not only amongst individuals but also amongst groups of people residing in different areas or engaged in different vacations". Even though the above Directive Principle may not be enforced as such by virtue of Article 37 of the constitution of India, it may be relied upon by the petitioners to show that in the instant ease they have been subjected to hostile discrimination. [06B C] (b) The fact that non regularisation of temporary employees or casual labour for a long period is not a wise policy.

The Income tax Officer found that in the account year corresponding to the assessment year 1945 46 there were six cash credits aggregating to Rs. 59,026 in the name of the assessee and that he was also assessed on it for the assessment years 1945 46 and 1945 46. The Income tax officer included the sum of Rs.59,027 6 as income from that account. Before the Income tax 's assessment Officer he did not act on this return but on February 27, 1950 issued a notice purporting to be under section 34 of the Indian Income tax Act calling upon the assessee to submit his return. The assessee submitted a " voluntary " return on January 5, 1950 showing a total net income of Rs, 1,935. He added a foot note to the return to the following effect: " My wife has sold her old ornaments and deposited the sum Of Rs. 50 in the firm of Assar Syndicate in which I am a partner". The Income Tax Officer included this amount in the total income of the asses see. Before however, the Income 'tax Officer included the amount in his total income the assessee but assessed him on it as such for the purpose of section 22(1) of the Act to the High Court of Bombay, which took the view that there was no scope for the issuance of a notice under section 24(2) within the assessmentyear or a notice thereunder and that the reassessment completed on February 26, 1951 was invalid. The Tribunal however dismissed his contentions but the Tribunal in appeal by special leave applied the words "allowed" occurring in section 22 (1), and held that the notice issued under section 14(3) was valid in law. On appeal to this Court it was contended: (i) The assessment proceedings commence with the issue of a public notice, and that section 34 does not apply where in answer to the public notice a return is made whether of taxable income or not. The words "admitted" in section 2(a) of Act indicate that there must be an assessment order for each assessment year and it cannot be said that there has been no omission or failure as mentioned in cls. (a) or (b). Nor does the Income Tax officer act on that return to be a 'voluntary ' return ' when it is filed, disclose an income which was below the taxable limit, so as to bring the matter within section 34(1)(a), of the Income_ tax Act. (ii) The words ' Aiyar" in the Section are wide enough to include all kinds of information relating to each assessment years. The word "assessment order" in cl. (c) also includes proceedings for making a return which shows no assessable income, but such as are required by cls. 4 and 6 of section 28. HELD: The notice under s 34 is only necessary if at the end of the assessment Year no return has been made by the assessee. [121 C] The words in cl.(c) may now be quoted. But it can not be said to have meant that the return was to be treated as a return filed under section 22, and therefore, the return in the case must be treated in answer on the safe side. [122 H; 123 A B]. (iii) The notice issued by the Income 8 tax Officer on March 3, 1950, which was not complied with in section 24, is not invalid because it was filed beyond time under section 25. There was no justification for it to hold that the amount noted in the footnote was really the assessee 's income and in which case an assessable income would have been found and the tax could be charged thereon.

% The petitioners are the principal office bearers of a nationalised bank. They are aggrieved by circular dated 23,8.1982 (Annexure A) issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, (Banking Division), New Delhi and claimed that the circular is contrary to the mandate of the Banking Companies (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 and the Natio nalised Banks (Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Scheme 1980. They further contend ed that Clause 3 of the Nationalised Banks ( Management and Miscellaneous provisions) Scheme ' provides for the constitution of the Board of Directors so as to include representatives of the employees and other speci fied categories. The petitioners contend ed, inter alia, that there is no justification whatsoever to issue any such circular for the very object of the Act is to encourage democratic selec tion of the Directors who will truly represent the interests of the various categories of persons mentioned in the Act. Allowing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The object of Section 9 of the , insofar as it is material, is to empower the Central Government to make a scheme for the consul tation of the Boards of Directors, so as, to include representative of the ap peals of the concerned employees and others as a highly sensitive commercial enterprise. Neither the election nor the nomination should be conducted in a manner unmindful of the distinctiveness of the banking industry.

The respondent who was an assessee having been imposed penalties under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961 for concealment of particular income and furnishing inaccurate particulars filed returns before the Income Tax Officer. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal declined to stay the proceedings as also the collection of penalty pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. The High Court held in a reference under section 256 that the power to stay was incidental to and implicit in the appellate jurisdiction created by s,64. It was further directed to dispose of the stay application in accordance with law without granting any stay. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Appellate Tribunal had no power to grant such a prayer as it thought fit after giving full hearing to both the parties to the appeal; and that the High Court was not right in issuing a writ. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The power conferred by section 254 upon the Appellate tribunal with widest possible amplitude must carry with them by necessary implication all powers and duties incidental and necessary to make the exercise of those powers fully effective. [69E] The power to pass such orders as it thinks fit after granting full hearing is an incidental or ancillary to an appellate jurisdiction vested in the court under section 254(1) which is confined only to the stage of pendency in an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The power of stay by the Tribunal is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter of course in view of special nature of taxation and revenue. [70B; 71D] D. Polini vs Grey, [1962] 1 S.C.R. 799, followed. Section 258(5) does empower the AppellateTribunal to regulate its own procedure but it is very doubtful if the power of staying can be spelt out from that provision. When section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction, it impliedly grants the powerof doing all such acts, or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. A certain apprehension may legitimately arise in the minds of the authorities administering the Act that if the Appellate Tribunals proceed to stay recovery of taxes or penalties payable by or imposed on them as a matters of course the revenue will be put to great loss because of the inordinate delay in the disposal of appeals by the Appellate tribunals. It is needless to point out that the powers which have been conferred by s.254 on the Appellate Tribu nal with widest practicable amplitude must therefore carry with it by necessary implications all powers incidental and duty and incidental to make these exercise of such powers fully operative. In substance, from a provision in section 222(6) of Income tax Reve nue Act this power is not intended to be restricted as by their express con tained therein.

The respondent was appointed a constable in the U. P. Police Force. On December 1, 1945, he was promoted to the rank of head constable and in May 1952 he was posted as officer incharge of police station, Intiathok, District Gonda. complaints were received by the Sub Divisional Magistrate who directed the sub Divisional Magistrate to make an enquiry in respect of the said complaints. The respondent submitted his explanation on November 29, 1952, but on December 17, 1952 he dismissed from service with effect from the said date as mentioned therein. Before the expiry of his leave he was reverted to his substantive post of head Constable and transferred to Sitapur. On February 17, 1953, he filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the order of dismissal on various grounds : (1) that the Governor exercised his pleasure through the Superintendent of Police, and as the police Regulations were only administrative directions, the non compliance therewith would not affect the validity of the order dismissing; (2) that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries do not affect his question; and (3) that there was no magisterial inquiry in respect thereof. Held : (i) On the facts of this case it cannot be said that a magisterial enquiry is held in regard to practically all the charges, the subject matter of the departmental trial, the case is not covered by the provisions of para 486 of the Police Regulations. In the circumstances it would be hypertechnical to hold that there is no magical inquiry in the matter which was the subject of the trial, and therefore it falls within the express terms of para 489(2). The fact that in a interregnum the Police received further complaint or that he made further inquiries do not effect affect the question, if substantially the subject matters of the magisterial Inquiry and the departmental enquiry is the same.

The Central Health Service Rules 1963 were amended by the Central Health Services (Amendment) Rules 1966. Under this scheme all 29 posts in supertime grade I and super time grade II were absorbed either in Joint Director 's or in General Duty Officers, Grade I or Specialists ' Grade ' with a view to constituting the Service. Rule 7A(1) and 7A provided for absorbing departmental candidates holding post in categories 'A ' and B ' under 1963 Rules in posts in Supertime grade 1. The Rules envisaged categorisation of personnel manning the Service into five different categories, namely, category I comprising super time scale Rs. 1600 2000, category II consists of Specialists ` grade Rs. 1800 2250; Category II consists Of Specialists Grade I Rs. 1250, category III includes General Duty officers ' grade II Rs. 450 1200 and category IV comprises General Duty Officer Rs. 350 900. On account of various imponderables the Service could not be constituted and 1963 Rules were amended in 1966. Rules 6 to 24 provided for absorption departmental candidates in posts of Supertime Grade I and its super time pay scale. The rules envisaged categorisation 'of personnel manned the Service as into five categories, to wit, category 'A" supertime scale Rs 1600, category `B ' supertime Scale Rs. 1300, category 11 includes General duty Officers grade 1 Rs.450, and category III include General Duty officer Rs.260 900. It was provided that there would be a pool of 19 unspecified Specialists " posts in the super time grades II and 9 unspecified posts also in super time Grade II. The appellant 's promotion to supertime Grade II on February 8, 1971 was challenged by the appellant on diverse grounds but the principal contention is that their promotions were in contravention of rule 8 of 1966 Rules inasmuch as they were in violation of Rule 8 of 1969 Rules. The main grievance is that although the posts were in Specialists grade I, ipso facto they could only be filled in by promotion and not in any other manner and particularly not by transfer. Dismissing the appeal ^ HELD: 1. When a post from amongst unspecified specialists ' posts is converted to a specified post which means specified in the speciality in which a need has been felt from among those in the specialists, " grade I or general duty officers" grade II is converted and made a specifiedpost in a speciality it is an addition to the strength of that speciality and the post can be filled filled in either by promotion or by direct recruitment as the situation warrants according to the rule and as determined by the quota rule. But it was very strenuously contended that when a post is created in a certain grade, category or cadre cannot be transferred to that post and the posts so vacated by him can be filling in, the manner prescribed.

The Preamble to the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 states that 'small land owner ' has in the State held no more than the permissible area and that land acquired by an heir by inheritance is saved from utilisation by the State. In view of the fact that the lands were taken over for settling tenants and others, the petitioner executed a gift of 182 bighas land to his son, which was accepted by the Collector in favour of the petitioner 's sons whereby he sought to stow away some of his lands, shed some of the excess lands and look slim on as a small holder before the law Language permiting, the Court as interpretedor must fulfil not frustrate the legislative mission. 123 The Collector took into consideration the fact of the larger land owners to defeat the land reform law included securing simulactral decrees from civil courts against themselves in favour by their close relations, thus using the judicial process to have. their excess lands secreted in the names of their dear and near near. This invited legislative attention and an amendment of the Act was made viz., section 10A whereby decrees and orders of courts were to be ignored in dealing with surplus lands. Section 19B does not affect the petitioner who has purchased the land beyond the permissible limit, but is given the option to choose there best area he desires to keep, called 'reserved area ' for re settlement of ejected tenants ejected or to be ejected under cl. (i) of sub section (1) or section 9. This creation of a surplus pool or reservoir is vital to the success of the statutory project since, by distribution of such lands, rehabilitation of ejected tenant and landless persons is to be "accomplished". Even if a person is a smallholder it is quite on the cards that, by inheritance or other operation of law, or by voluntary transfer he may acquire lands in excess of the permissible limits. The section does not say that even if the source of the surplus area is inheritance, bequest of gift, the capacity to own is conditioned by the permissible restriction but such a provision must fulfil, not frustrate it, defeat the legislative intent and renders it ineffective. [628G H; 629A B] Amar Singh vs State of Haryana ; , followed. The scheme of the Punjab Act is not a radical agrarian measure which has provided for ignoring decrees diminishing surplus lands and has otherwise prevented the escape of excess area by voluntary transfers, cannot conceivably be intended to permit inherited excesses. [643D & E] Amar Sinahit vs State Of Rajasthan & ors., ; , referred to.

The suit property in dispute was originally owned by the appellant and two branches of Sakru and Kajur. The branch of Hiru (who was a member of the family) had five sons: Hiru, Sakru, Kajur and Raju. The branches of Vasu and Kajodai became extinct with the death of Amarshah upon Pratapshah and Zamindari devolved on Ashah. After his death, Amarsaha devised his estate in their favour. In 1951 he assumed management of the estate. He made an application before the Compensation Officer stating that the Zamindari was impartible and that the decision of the Governor was binding upon all the heirs, that as against those two branches all the proprietary rights devolved upon them under a will executed on December 3, 1950, whereby Amarsh devised his Estate in their favo rated favour. He further claimed that the other property including Malguzari lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951 had become impartible, that the suit property formed part of the joint family estate of Amathi barsha and that on the death Of Amarsachar was granted to him as an impartible estate devolving by the rule of primogeniture; that the tenure of the Zamindari depended upon the death, of the holder on the male relative who is the senior most in age, and not on the eldest member in the senior line. The suit was contested by the defendants on the basis that the village which was impar tible was impartable and was governed by the rules of prim Generiture; and that at the time when the Act came into force, it was incumbent upon Amarshi to execute the will set up by the plaintiffs. The trial court held in favour of the defendants. In appeal the High Court, however, set aside the decree passed by the trial court holding that the will dated December 3 1950 set up on by the defend ant was genuine and that as the tenure as recorded in the Wajib ul arz devolved upon the first plaintiff became entitled to the Zamindari, that it had devolved on the first defendant Dayaram as he was found suitable to hold the same. On appeal by special leave: HELD : (1) A suit challenging an order to set aside a decision must be filed within two months from the date of the order. That is also clear from the terms of section 35(7) of Act 1. Therefore, it cannot be said that the High court was in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awardable to the plaintiffs.[330 A C] (2) The judgment of the High 'Court is set aside.

A suit for recovery of possession of a portion of the ground floor on the ground that the appellants were in arrears of rent. The trial court gave a decree, in favour of the respondent for possession of the premises and against which an appeal to the appellate Court was dismissed by the High Court. In a revision application before the Gujarat High Court, it held that the tenant could raise a dispute as to standard rent by raising an issue as to the standard rent in his written statement in answer to the suit and in 630 such a case, the provisions of section 12 (3) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act 1947 would apply. On appeal to this Court, HELD: 1(i) Under section 12 of the Act the landlord shall not be entitled to the recovery of the possession of any premises so long as the tenant pays or tenders in court regularly such rent and permitted increases till the suit is finally decided and also pays costs of the suit as directed by the court. [632 E F] 2(i). The Bombay High Court took the view that the question is one which is in existence at the date of the notice or at any rate before the exiry of one month from the date it of its service and not the one raised subsequently in a written statement with a view to avoiding the operation of section 10(3) of that Act. [533 G] In order to attract the applicability of section.12 (3), it is only when an application disputing rent is made within the time contemplated by sub section (2) of section 11 that the provisions in sub section(3 and 4 of section LlII505051 are attracted. The Bombay view is that disputing within one month of the service of the Notice terminating the tenancy is one mode of raising a dispute and there is another mode of raise the dispute at any stage of the litigation. [650 A C] (ii) Section 12(1 ) of the ' Act deals with orders which may be passed by the Court during the pendency of the application disputing the rent. Provisions in section 11(4) of tho Act deal with Orders which may he passed consequent upon disputes as to rent. It is only where an application denying rent is filed within the period prescribed by Explanation 1 to s 12 of . that the said provisions are attracted, it would be sufficient to oust the operationof section 12(3)(a) and would take the suit out of the provisions. [66 G] 2 (iii).

The respondent company was a company incorporated in what was then British India having a capital of Rs. 3,600 divided into 360,000 shares of Rs 10 each. The Aluminium Ltd., the respondent company held 21 shares in the chargeable accounting periods ending on December 31, 1941 and December 31st, 1940, and December31, 1943, and February 1, 1950, and March 31, 195o, and June 1, 1948, respectively, and September 31, 1943. By a resolution passed by the directors of the respondent Company the Aluminium Ltd appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of respondent company. By article 90 of the articles of association of the company provided: "90. Where a company registered under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act or not is a member of this company, a person duly appointed to represent such company at a meeting of the Company in accordance with the provisions Of section 80 of the I.P.C. shall not be deemed to be a proxy but shall be entitled to vote for such company on a show of hands and to exercise the same power on behalf of the said company which he represents as if he were an individual member of the Companies including the power to appoint a proxy whether special or general, and the production at the meeting of a company of such resolution appointing such representative duly signed by one director of such company and by the secretary (if any) and certified by them or him as being a true copy of the resolution shall on production at be accepted by this company as sufficient evidence of the validity of his appointment." The respondent company contended that it should be regarded as a company the directors who had a controlling interest therein, inasmuch as Mr. L. G. Bash 's appointed three of its permanent directors in terms of section 2 (21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940 read with section 66(1) Of the Indian Income tax Act, had a "a controlling interest" in it as contemplated by section 2(21). Held, that the shares in question which give the controlling interest are neither held by Mr.L. G . Bash but on behalf ' of the Aluminium Company Ltd. and although he may be bound to cast the vote according to the directions of his principals, the Aluminium company and may be answerable to the latter if he acts in breach of their duty, nevertheless as long as their authority is not revoked, as far as the respondent was concerned, the majority of its votes carrying shares are subject directly or indirectly to his will and ordering, therefore, the controlling interests which the holder of the majority share has never passed to the agent.

The respondent in the appeal was serving as Accountant Grade II, in the Electricity Department of the former State of 61 Hydabad. On 1st October 1957, the Mysore State Electricity Board was constituted under the Indian Electricity (Supply.) Act. The recruitment and promotion of employees of the Electricity Board Regulation 1960 were governed by the Indian Contract Labour Engi tions (Supply) Act, 1948. In 1959 on the reorganisation of the States in pursuance of the , the respondent was allotted to the new State of Mysore with effect from November 1, 1956. The post which he held came to be equated with that of I Division Clerk in the former 'State of Mysore. On January 1st Octo ber 1957, he opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effectfrom that date. In 1960, the Electricity Regis terator framed Recruitment and Promo tions Regulations in exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Act. As a result of the amendment of the Rules by the Electricity (Suppl.) Board of Directors ment dated January 21, 1970, some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on the basis of seniority cum merit on their passing Part I and II of the S.A.S. examination while promotion was denied to him as he had not passed the examination. The respondent made several representations one such representation being on 24th December, 1970. On 21st November 1972, the Board framed Recruitment & Promo tion Regulations in the exercise of powers conferred upon it under sections 79(C) and 79(e) of Electricity Act. In May 1973, some person junior to him were promoted as Accounts Superin tendent. On 31st October 1966, some senior to the respond ent were promoted. The resolu tioner 's representations were rejected by the Board. A writ petition filed before the High Court challenging the action of the Board was dismissed. Hence this appeal by the State Electricity board contending that the respondent is exempted from complying with the requirement of passing the examination and therefore, it was no longer open to the Respondent to rely on the Resolution dated 19th May 1969, in view of the later resolution of the Boards on 31st December, 1966.

The petitioner 's son was taken from his home in police custody at about 8 a.m. on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, Jaraikela Police Outpost under Police Station Bisra, Distt. Sundergarh in Orissa. The dead body of her son was found on the railway track near a bridge at some distance from the Jaraiobizepur Railway station. There were multiple injuries on the body of Suman Behera when it was found and obviously his death was unnatural, caused by those injuries. Respondent No. 6, Sar at Barikpur was taken in police detention in connection with the investigation of an offence of theft and detained at the Police Out Post, under Police Chakraborty Station, Distt., Sundergarh. In the mean time the petitioner came to know that the dead body was found near a Bridge crossing some distance away from the plane railway station, and therefore his death is unnatural, causing death. The petitioner claimed compensation for contravention of fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution on the ground that he had managed to escape from police custody. The State contended that the responsibility of respondent No 2 for the safety of Suman beed by him in view of the injuries inflicted to him while he was in police remand, and it was likely that he was run over by a pass train after he had escaped from police officer. Allowing the writ petition and directing for payment of compensation to the petitioner, this Court, HELD: 1. The claim in public law for compensation ' for contravention under Article 32 of the Constitu tion is an acknowledged remedy remedy for enforcement and protection of such rights, and such a claim based on strict liability made by resorting to a constitutional remedy provided for the enforcement of fundamental rights is 'distinct from, and in addition to the remedy in private law for damages for the tort ' resulting from the contravention of the fundamental right. [596D E] 2.

The two prisoners, who were sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of their sentence are reported to have been rejected by the President recently. The petitioners in this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution seek a writ of mandamus or any other appropriate writ or direction directing the respondents particularly the Delhi Administration and Superintendent of Jail, Tihar, to allow her to interview two convicts Billa and Ranga who are under a sentence of death. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The constitutional right to freedom of speech conferred by Article 19(1)(a) of the constitution includes freedom of Press, is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the press to have an unrestricted access to means of information. [1186H; 1187B] 2. [For example, the rule 552A cannot be denied the right of an interview under clause (4) of Rule 549.] There is a provision in the rules that if a person who desires to interview a prisoner is a female she can be searched only by a matron or a female warden. In giving an individual appraising his task he may properly do so, but no such consideration has been pressed upon us and there fore, the Court cannot overlook that rule 552 A also provides that all reasonable indulgence should be allowed to a condemned prisoner in the matter of interviews with relatives, friends, legal advisers and approved religious ministers. Surprisingly, but this does not mean that they can always and without good reasons be denied, the opportunity to interview and therefore, it would have been impossible for us to pass an order directing that the petitioner should be permitted to interview them. [1108C] 3. The Court cannot ignore the constitutional right of interview under cl. (4), because, for example, rule 552B provides for a search of the person who wanted to interview compelled a prisoner. If it is thought necessary that such a search should be taken, a person whose liberty may have to subject himself or herself to the search in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the interviews. There is no reason why the petitioner shall not be allowedto interview the two convicts billa andanga.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden, called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s Das Bank Ltd. on January 19, 1950. The bank applied for appointment of a Receiver. But the court ordered that the Bank should nominate a ' receiver in terms of clause 12 of the mortgage deed, first the Secretary of the Bank and later another employee called Adhir Ranjan Dutta was appointed as the Receiver subject to his furnishing security before the District Judge. On February 26, 1950 the tea garden was damaged by fire which destroyed over 3,000 tea saplings. The respondent moved an application asking for damages from the court of the Subordinate Judge, P.W. on the ground that the fire had occurred due to his negligence in the performance of his duties as a Receiver and indeed parties had made pleas from time to time as to whether the tea plant was managed by the Receiver economically and efficiently. The application was heard along with the mortgage suit. On these objections the Subordinate judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but he allowed the respondent 's cross objections and enhanced the damages to Rs. 4,525. In appeal the appellant contended that the bond was executed both be the Receiver and the appellant in favour of "Sri Ramani Mohan Goswami, the District judge has no power or authority in respect of the tea gardens; and (2) Under the terms of the bond, the appellant is not answerable for the loss caused to the tea plantation by fire. Both these contentions turn on the terms "as aforesaid" which qualify the words "in relation to his duties". The surety bond was a part of the proceedings pending before the Sub Judge and even if the court directed the Receiver to pay the amount within two months, failing which the amount should be recovered from the security of Rs. 50,000. Held: (i) Under section 150 of the C.P.C., save as otherwise provided, where the business of any Court is transferred to any other Court, the transferee court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor Court. The surety ship was a distinct part of proceedings pending against the appellant and as such the order for recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the Receiver could be executed against the appellants to the extent to which it rendered itself liable under the terms Of the bond. There is no substance in the contention either.

Section 3(3) of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 provides that a contract of sale of goods is a contract where the seller agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price paid or promised and a transaction in which an obligation to supply goods is imposed and which does not involve an obligation of entering into a contract cannot be called a "sale" even if the person supplying goods is declared entitled to the value of goods, which is determined and determinable in the manner prescribed. The appellant who was dealers in food grains supplied to Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat in compliance with the provisions of the order of the collector under the U .P. wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959, levied tax on the aggregate price of the wheat, by rejecting the contention that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller. The Assistant Commissioner (Judicial) Sales Tax held that the turnover resulted from supplies of wheat and was not taxable since there was no "sale", within the meaning of the Act. The order was confirmed by the Additional Judge (Revisions) Sales tax. Both the appeals of the State were dismissed by the High Court, following its earlier judgment in Commissioner of Sales Tax vs Sri Vataram Devgonda Sugar Co. Ltd., and M/s. New India Sugar Mills ' case. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the expression "sale of goods" used in section 2(h) of U. P. Sales tax Act, 1947, should be understood in the same sense in which it is (1) (1969) All L.J. 1. Legislature could not legislate for levy of sales tax on a transaction which amounted to sale within the expression 'sale ' under that section and not on any other transaction which was deemed by fiction to be a sale; and (ii) a price in money paid or stipulated, , a transaction cannot be termed as a "Sale" even though the person supplies goods is shown entitled to a value of the goods, for which is deter minable in accordance with the conditions contained or incorporated in the order. HELD : The exemption granted by section 21 of the Uttar Pradesh Sales Tax (Control) Order and the acceptance thereof do not result in a contract Of sale. [673 D E] M/S New India Sugars Ltd. & Anr. vs State of Andhra Pradesh, ; , referred to. Section 7 of the has no application in respect of the place and manner of supply of wheat or payment of controlled price. It contains a bald injunction restraining the appellant from selling the specified percentage of wheat on hand. It does not envisage any consensual arrangement. A sale predicates a contract for sale of Goods between persons competent to contract for a Price paid or agreed; and it does not contemplate any consensual agreement. A sales predicates contracts of sale between persons subject to conditions mentioned in section 3 of the Order, can be regarded as sales.

Under section 10 of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985 a detention order has been made under the Act, the State Government shall within three weeks from the date of detention of a person under the order, place before the Advisory Board the grounds on which the order had been made. The appellant was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was due for release from prison on June 23, 1986. Though acquitted, he was not straightaway released. On August 7, 1986, an order for his detention was passed under the provisions of the Act against him on June 21, 1986 because after the expiry of three months from the detention, he had already retired and a fresh order of detention was made on the same facts on the date. In the meanwhile, the order of deten tion dated June 23. 1986 had been challenged by filing a writ petition in the High Court. Consequent upon the revocation of that order, the appellant was again arrested and deprived of his personal liberty long before the order was revoked and a new fresh order for detention was issued on the basis of the same allegations. In view of the revocation, the writ petition having become infructuous and another writ petitions, out of which the present appeal arises, were questioning the second order of his detention dated August 7 1986. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. An order of detain ment should have been made, knowing full well that there was no Advisory Board in existence to whom a reference could be made under section 11 of the Bombay Prevention of anti Social Activities Ac ture Act 1985 which provides for the making of successive orders of detention so as to bring it in conformity with article 22(4) of the Constitution. If there is to be a collision between article 22 (4), if there is no fresh facts, the maximum period for which a person may be detained shall not extend beyond the expiry Of a period of 3 months from tho date of deten ment under the earlier detention order. [210A C] 2. The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority.

The petitioner is the father of respondent. Both the father and son have been fighting between themselves since more than one decade. The High Court found that the petitioner and the respondent had referred their disputes to one Kantibhai Vaidya, who had intervened between them with the good intention to bring their dispute to an end, and, therefore, they were compelled to rely upon a photo copy of the original award which was produced before it as exhibit 40 and a letter dated 4th September, 1978 addressed to the arbitrator wherein it was stated that both of them had appointed him as an arbitrator to resolve the disputes between them and that he had given an award dated 20th January 1977 in respect of which award there had been continued objections but now they have agreed that both the parties should abide by the award dated 30th January, 1977. On this aspect, it was held that on this aspect the petitioner is not entitled to challenge the award. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the disputes to the arbitration of the named arbitrator and that they made a award, was not set aside under section 30 and (4) that the award was not remitted under section 16(5), and (5) that in this view, there was no such express or implied prohibition nor any inability of the Judge concerned. [ 537D E] A.I.R. 1988 S.C. 205 followed. In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is clear that both parties had re affirmed the acceptance of the award by the arbitrator and, in the light thereof, a copy of its agreement was also produced before the Court as Exhibit 40. It was signed by both the brothers as well as their respective advocates. The letter of 14th August, 1978 was replied in the form of a letter addressed to one of the arbitrators wherein it had been stated that all of them have appointed him and given an Award dated 20 January 1977.

The appellants were the successors in interest of the mortgagors and the respondent had become the ' sharers for 999 years. The lessor granted two mining leases each for nine years one in respect of 5/16 share Of the Malias in Mouza Monohar Bahal and the other in respect on an equitable mortgage for the due repayment of the loan of Rs. 100,000 advanced by that firm.
