On March 31, 1922, the said receiver with the permis sion of the Court which had appointed him as receiver granted two leases each under section 36 of the , both for 99 years one being on deposit of the principal amount and interest in the mortgage taken at a court sale and were purchased by Deva Prasanna Mukerjee for Rs. 59,000. The appellants filed a suit which was decreed ex parte on October 30, 1935, on the ground that it did not find favour with the High Court but in appeal to this Court it was contended inter alia (i) that the respondent as a bona fide assignee of the mortgage debt was protected by sub section (5) Of section 36; (ii) that neither the original nor a certified copy of the order made on that date by the executing court on the application of Deva Prasanta Kumar Roy was forthcoming but the parties had definite agreed that the order was substantially and correctly entered in column 20 of exhibit F which was a certified copies of extract from the Register of applications for executions of decrees relating to execution case No. 118 of 1936, and (iii) that in exercise of the powers the Court could exercise all or any of the power and give relief to the borrowers in terms of the prayers of the plaint. Held, further, that the expression "all the rights of the mortgagee" used by them in the passage quoted above, means the rights which have been conferred on the Court or to be exercised either in any suit to which this Act applies or in any proceedings instituted or filed after the 1st day of January 1939, and includes a proceeding in execution for the recovery of a loan advanced before or after the commencement of this Act. The said attachment was clearly intended to provide a remedy for the grievance or inconvenience which is apt to arise where, after an attachment in execution has already been entered, the question arose whether the effect of an order "striking off" was that the attachment made upon application for execution was itself struck off or whether it remained notwithstanding such an order. It was a practice not justified by the Code and in cases where attachments are in execution had already been entering, the questions arose whether : whether the promotion of the respondent 's decree to exemption under proviso (ii), to sub section(1) of section 36 must fail. Ram Kumar De vs Abhoya Pada Bhattacharjee, A.I.R. 1937 Cal. 17, referred to.

Certain questions were raised before the High Court in a petition under article 227 of the Constitution and they were referred to a Full Bench. While dismissing the petition, the Full Bench had held that the appeal presented to them by the respondent was within time if computed after making deductions permitted by section 12 Of the Limitation Act. The matter being contested by two dismissing petitions under article 226 and 227 of tho Constitution, the High COurt held (1) that section 29(2) would not apply to an application for special leave to appeal under sub section (3) of section 417 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that therefore the provisions of section 12 of the Limitation , could be invoked. On appeal by special leave: Held: The words "appeal" in cl. (a) of Art 156(2), show that it is an appeal governed by a special or local law. If any special or other local law prescribes for an appeal, no period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor in the First Schedule, and article 151 referred to in article 156, viz., that apart from those prescribed for appeals and of applications filed beyond time, the provisions Of section 12(2). would be attracted by reason of the provision of cl. 2 of article 156 and it was governed by section 29 (2) of the said Act. In order to do so, it is necessary to specify a period of Limitation to an appeal and, in order to deal with the second ground given by the High court, it must be shown that the special law prescribes a period different from that prescribed therefor by the First schedule.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura challenged the validity of the Order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magis trate, declaring plot Nos. 701 and 703 in the Town Area, Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stand/halting place of Baldev and wherein the stage carriages were directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get into and to get down from the stage carriage carriages in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986 filed before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. That petition was dis missed by the High court on September 8, 1986. The Appellant filed an appeal against the aforesaid order dated August 22, 1985 passed by tho District Magistrate, Mathura to direct the Town limits Committee from collecting the fees payable by the bus operators for making use of the area in question which was within its jurisdiction for stopping their buses in accord ance with the order passed by that District Magmit trate. Relying on the decision in T.P. Ibrahim vs Regional Transport Authority, Tanjore, ; this Court took the view that the fixing and alteration of bus stands was not a purpose for eign to the 'control of transport vehicles ' which was gov erned by Chapter IV of the Act and, therefore, rules could be framed by the State Government regarding the said subject under section 68(2)(r) of the . Allowing the Appeal of the appellant, this Court, HELD: That the District Magistrate fixed the area as a Bus stand. Regarding the authority which had the power to notify an area as bus stand and the Dis trict Magistrate cannot be equated with the Regional Transport Officer constituted under the Act. The High Court was, therefore in error in upholding the impugned order passed on August 22 1985 by the Town Planning Committee. [717C] T.B. Ibrahim 's case (supra). This court took the cis tence that section 76 of the Motor Vehicles Rules, 1940 had nothing to do with the fixation or alteration of a bus Stand and the power of issuing a notification fixing a bus stands implied in section 68 (2)(d) of U.P., Motor Vehicles Act. It only authorises the District magistrate to exercise the powers under section 76, of the said Act which is confined to tho question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the Regional Road Transport Author ity as held by this Court in T .P. Singh vs Regional Road Trans port Authority,Tanjore. [ 718C D] T., Ibrahim vs District Magi trate & Anr., ; , followed.

Under the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order 1959, a truck carrying 75 bags of paddy could be used for transporting paddy to Delhi. The consignee of the paddy was Messrs Devi Dayal Brij Lal, Delhi. It was alleged that Qimat Rai also gave a letter, exhibit P 3 addressed to the consignee Sawan Ram and Chiranji Lal were partners of Messrs Sawan accused and they were also prosecuted. The trial court convicted all of them but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction and sentence of T for the offence of export. On revision, the High Court dismissed the revision petition and acquitted the appellants. Held, that upon the facts found by the lower courts no offence had been committed by the appellants and as a matter of law a preparation for committing an offence is different from attempt to commit it. The preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offence. On the other hand, an attempt to committed the offence is a direct movement towards the commission after preparations are made. In order that a person may be convicted of an attemptto commit 'a crime, he must be shown first to have had an intention to commit the offence and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt. The sufficiency of the actum rea is a question of law which has led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commissionof a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt 'to commit it In order, that a man may be convict of an attempts to commit 'A crime, if he approaches the stack with the matches in his pocket but, if bends down near the stank and lights a match which he extinguishes on perceiving that he is being watched, he may be guilty of an offence of attempt to burn it. In the present case there was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit offence of exporting paddy, Delhi 'and so there was an attempt on them to commit export paddy ' from Delhi and so there Was no attempt to committing the offence for export.

The Sassoons executed in favour of the Sassoon and Company, Singapore by two separate deeds dated the 24th February, 1920 and the 2nd October, 1934, the 3rd September, 1943, and the 27th April, 1943. The Sassoors were assessed to income tax on the basis that they had earned their income by rendering services as Managing Agents for the respective periods that they continued to be the Managing Agent and the transferees had rendered the services for the balance of the periods completing the full year of accounting and had earned the proportionate commission and therefore the amount of commission which the latter actually received included the Sas Soons ' share of the joint income, by virtue of the assignment in their favour was in a position to collect. income, it was contended that the Sassoon and Company Ltd., having been assigned the managing Agency commission for the calendar year 1943 they had merely earned the commission or remuneration for the period of actual services rendered by them to the company and the portions of the Managing Agency commission proportionate to the services actually rendered by the Sasbeons to the companies had accrued to them in the chargeable accounting period though it was ascertained and paid to the transferees in 1944, had not been shown as having earned any part of the consideration as required by section 26(2) of the Indian Income tax Act. Held, that the provisions of sections 26(1) and 26(3) of tho Indian Income Tax Act do not help the transferees because it is only when the person succeeded has acquired an actual share of income profits or gains of the previous year that he is liable to tax in respect thereof and as set out herein above no part of such commission actually accrued to or became a debt due by the company to the Sashions on the dates of the respective transfers of the managing Agencies to the transferee. In fact, for computing the taxable income of the assignee, it may be mentioned that in the normal run of events the contract for remuneration under the Managing Agents Agreement was an indivisible contract for a whole year 's remuneration and not for a portion thereof and therefore no commission became due to the shares, because the mere ownership of the agency could not as a matter of law be treated as the source of income. Lakshminarayan Ram Gopal and Son, Ltd., vs The Government of Hyderabad, , followed. Chetty vs K. Gounden, [1947] A.C. 415; British Columbia Electric Lights Limited vs Cavas, ; and South Wales Electric Supply Co. Ltd., (1924) L.R. 60 I.A. 357, applied.

The appellant was a resident of the Dehradun house in the District of Gonda. He submitted his first application before the Sessions Judge for withdrawing and for withdrawing his second application as he was not in the house. The Sessions judge on appeal found that the extra judicial confession was admissible against him but convicted the accused under section 302 I.P.C. On a consideration of the entire evidence came to the conclusion that Sahoo murdered Sunderpatti. In that view, he sentenced the accused to death. On appeal by special leave it was contended that the soliloquy of the accused admitting his guilt was not an extra judicial confessional confession as the Courts below found it to be. Dismissing the appeal. HELD: 1. The fact that the appellant 's second application before him in respect of his first appli cation also got dismissed by the Sessions judge does not depend upon its communication to another, though just like any other piece of evidence, it can be admitted in evidence only on proof. [89C D] 2. A confessional solil purporting to have been made by a witness within the meaning of section 157 meant only "something that is stated" and the element of communication was not necessary before "s something that is mentioned". The test laid down by this Court in Bhogilal Chunilal Pandya vs State of Bombay, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C R. 310 is applicable to the case. [91B C] 3. Section 157 of the Evidence Act places them in the category of relevant evidence, presumably on the ground that, as they are declarations against the interest of the person making them, they are probably true. The probative value of an admission or a confession does not depends upon its Communication to another though just because no other piece Of evidence, It may be an expression of conflict of emotion; a conscious effort to stifle the pricked conscience; an argument to find excuse or justification for his act; or a penitent or remorseful act of exaggeration of his part in the crime. The tone may be soft and low; the words may be confused; they may be capable of conflicting interpretations depending on witnesses, whether they are biased or honest, intelligent or ignorant, imaginative or prosaic, as the case may be. Generally they are mutterings of a confused mind. [90E F] 4. A confession is a direct piece of incriminating evidence and it may be neither an expression Of conflict of falsehood; a reasoned effort to scuttle the concept; an attack on voluntary surrender. What does the expression "statement" mean? The dictionary meaning of the word "statement ' is not a species and confession is the sub species. [92B C]. 5. In the instant case, however, since the appellant has made no attempt to urge that his second applica tion was withdrawn by the prosecution he cannot be convicted under section 3 or 4 of the Penal Code. The circumstances found by the High Court which it have stated earlier lead to the only conclusion that the accused must have committed the murder. No other reasonable hypothesis was or could be suggested. [93C] 6. A statement whether communicated or not, admitting guilt is a confession of guilt. But there is a clear distinction between the admissibility of an evidence and the weight to be attached to it. Under section 157 the Evidence Amendment Act the Magistrate may place them in a category of application of statements, both oral and written statements. [94F] 7. A retracted solil Navigation is a well known circumstance and cannot be made the sole ground of conviction. The answers given by the accused persons in criminal cases. But the expression 'confession ' is defined not defined. A perusal of the provisions of sections 17 to 30 of the Indian Evidence Act discloses that as one learned author put it, that statement was a genus. admission is the species and statement made by an accused admitting its guilt.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi, the general insurance business was nationalised and its management was taken over by the Central Government under General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance 1971 replaced by Act 57 of 1972. Section 7 of the Act provides that every whole time officer or other employee of an existing insurer employed in connection with his General Insurance business immediately before the appointed day, shall become an officer/employee of the Indian Insurance Co. in which the undertaking of the insurer to which the service of the officer relates has vested and would hold his office on the same terms and conditions as would have been admissible to him if there had been no such vesting, and shall continue to do so unless and until his appointment is terminated. The appellant was kept under suspension pending investigation into embezzlement, Explanation was called for on October 16, 1973 in response thereto, the appellant submitted his reply on August 7, 1974. While dropping the proceeding, the management was served with termination order dated April 17, 1975 issued by the respondent which came into force on May 1, 1976, and after dropping the proceedings, the services of the appellant and others stood transferred and vested with the custodian. Under the Act, the employees were transferred and vest with the Custodian under Section 16 of the under the Act and the Rules. By Notification dated April 29, 1976 the Central Govt. also framed the scheme called the General Insurance(Rationalisation of pay scales and other conditions of service of officers and other employees wherever necessary. Pursuant thereto, by Rule 3, the undertaking was transferred to the respondent; under Rule 5, the existing whole time officers etc. became the officer of the transferee company (New Indian Assurance Co. Ltd) and could hold his Office on the said terms and condition as would had been admissible under him if it had been No such transfer, as referred to in paragraph 3. After dropping the matter the appellant was served alongwith termination order issued by respondent. The question before the Court was whether the view of the Board of Directors that there was no need for the services to continue the employee 's service operated subsists which would be based on the relevant material. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 5 does not become arbitrary. unreasonable or void offending Article 14. In D.T.C. vs D. T.C., Mazdoor Congress & Ors., 225 Judgment today, today is correct. But from the facts, it is clear that the Board worked out a decision, whether the need to continue his employee 'S service subsist which would he based on relevant material; consequently, there was a presumption in favour of constitutionality of a legislation or statutory Rule unless ex facie it violates the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution. If the provisions of law or the rule are construed in such a manner as would make it consistent with the constitution and another interpretation would render the provision or the Rule unconstitutional, the court would lean in favour to the former construction. [224A B] D.S.R.C vs DT. C Mazdoor Congress and Ors., 228 225 Judgment recently passed in the case of D.J. Transport Corporation Service Regulation, 1974, at page 225, applied. D.P.M. & Anr. V.D. T.,C. Mazdoor Congress Pvt. Ltd & Ors. , 225 Judgment Today has no application.

The tenders were accepted and the successful bidder was permitted to enter into the prescribed register. The successful bidder deposited Rs. 329/ by way of deposit in the High Court with the allega tion that he had been found not acting according to law as the State Government had issued instructions to him not to issue the licenses, and that it was a tax which was not contemplated by section 38 of the Act, and was in excess of the rule making power of the Board. The High Court, on appeal, quashed the aforesaid direction for re auctioning the license and declared that Rule 103 (1) of the Rules was ultra vires the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (i) the State had no authority to direct withhold and reauc tioning of the licenses and (ii) the order of the State Govt. dated August 19, 1970 was valid because it purported to stock in black money with the stipulation that the auction price for a license was not excise duty within the meaning of Entry 51 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and it was not open to the Collector to follow the process of auctioning for deter mining the licence fee. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1)(a) The power under section 29(2) (a) to grant the exclusive privilege within any specified area, sub section (2) provides that no grantee shall exercise it "unless or until he has received a license in that behalf from the Collector or Excise Commissioner.

The prosecution case was that accused No. 2 and 3 were charged with having entered into crimi nal conspiracy with approver Dinkar Sakharam between 19 December, 1967 and 4 January 1968 at Deolali Camp in bungalow No. 17 for the purpose of committing the murder of Narendra Kumar and com mitted house breaking and thefts in the house of his grand father Dr Nanavati and to murder his grandson Narendra. The trial court acquitted the accused and also convicted accused No . 3 under section 302 read with section 120B, I.P.C. against him. On appeal by the State the High Court reduced the punishment of accused No 1 to rigorous imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was corroboration of the evidence which connected accused No 2 and therefore no corroboration could be given in regard to accused No3; that there had been corroboration of their actual participation in the crime and that the creditor 's story about the conspiracy was not corroborated. HELD: (i) In view of the fact that there were civil and criminal proceedings between him and Dr. Nanavati, the circumstantial evidence was only of creating a common intention with accused No., 2, that an accomplice is competent to depose but as a rule of caution it will be unsafe to convict upon his testimony alone. [621 E] (ii) The law with regard to appreciation of approver 's evidence is based on the effect of sections 133 and 114 illustration(b). [628 B] (iii) It is clear that when the circumstantial circumstances are true, the court has to be satisfied that there is nothing inherently impossible in evidence. The rule as to corroboration is based upon the reasoning that there must be corroborative evidence in material particulars to connect the accused with the crime. In the present case the prosecution story was that the murder and the theft formed the same transaction and were committed by the same persons. [625 C F] (iv) The High Court also rightly came to the conclusion that there 'also was corroboration in material iden tice in regard lo the accused No, 2. [650 G] (v) It was not necessary for the prosecution to find out whether there was evidence to connect accused Nos. 3 and 4 with murder. If a witness says that the accused & he stole the sheep and he put the skins in a certain place, the discovery of the skins into that place would not corroborate the evidence of the witness as against the accused. But if the skins were found in the accused 's house, this would corroborerate because it could tend to confirm the statement that the 2 accused had some hand in the theft.

On July 4, 1967 a draft scheme was published which included among other lands an area admeasuring 1,37,961 sq. meters of which appellant as Karta of a Hindu undivided family was the lessee. On May 10, 1968 Government granted sanction to the draft scheme. By order made on November 4, 1971 the town planning officer awarded compensation at the rate of Rs. 2.40 p. per sq. On June 26, 1965 the Town Planning Officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rates of Rs2.40p. per / . Not satisfied with the decision of the Town planning Officer the appellant preferred an appeal before the Board of Appeal which reduced his claim to Rs. 9.50 p. from Rs. 50 p.m. by a letter dated November 4 1971. By its order dated November 3, 1971 respondent No. 2 determined the compensation payable to the lessee at the aforesaid rate on account of cost of construction and maintenance of roads etc. The appellant challenged the order of the Board in a writ petition in which certain provisions of the Bombay Town Planning Act were also challenged as unconstitutional and it was claimed that the town Planning Scheme was invalid. The respondent No 2 contended that the Town Plan was therefore invalid as the Act did not provide an appeal from a decision of Town Planning officer on matters dealt with by him in his order dated ' November 4 , 1971. The Gujarat High Court dismissed the writ petition agreeing with the Board 's view that the appeal was incompetent and dismissed the petition as incompetent, holding that the Appeal was not maintainable. It held that the appeals were not maintainable against the order rejecting the appellant 's claim. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The appeal must be dismissed. [92B] 2.1 In computing the difference between the total of values of the original plots and the total value of the plots included in the final scheme, the Town Development Officer under section 32 (1) (iii) has to find out the market value of each of the erstwhile plots at the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme. The property or right which is injuriously affected by the making of a town planning scheme is a property or ' right other than that acquired for the purposes of the scheme. When under the Act a plot of land is taken for the purpose of a Town Planning Scheme, it cannot be suggested that land itself is injuded; such a view is unsupportable both as a matter of language and having regard to the scheme of the Act.

One Viswanatha Iyer died in 1934 leaving two daughters surviving him who were minors at the time of his death. He had a brother Seetharama Iyer (Hindu) who was the third son of the testator bequeathed certain lands to them out of the income of the properties in May 1942. In 1949, he appointed his brother, with the aid of a will by which he created the trust in favour of the daughters and provided that as soon as his minor daughters attained majority they should give to them per head One veli nanja land and one veli of punja land in vattam No. 149 in village Nagampadi 976. In 1950, the two daughters claimed possession of their lands on the ground that they were entitled in law having regard to the provisions of the will to select their respective one vela from out of them out Of the income from the properties devised to them after the death of the legatees. The appellant resisted the suit inter alia by his brother V and contended, (i) that the testator had expressly indicated that the selection was made by the legatee not for the daughter to make the selection but was only for 4 months; (ii) that it was not necessary to import the artificial rule of construction evolved in England to avoid uncertainty, and making the subject of gift reducible to certainty. Held:(i) The testator 's intention was clearly to select the house himself to be given to each son and therefore there could be no question of the dispositions making the selection in the order in which they were named in the will; (iii) the legatee intended that each daughter would select the land devised out of vattom and that, therefore, there was no necessity to make it certain; (iv) there was nothing in the words from which it could be inferred that the deceased testator intended that the daughters should get the area of land devised to their daughters taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. Knapton vs Hindle, Cal. 981, referred to.

The appellant 's brother who had inherited certain land from his brother 's widow, situated far away from the place where the widow was living, took undue advantage of the confi dence reposed in them by their widowed sister in law and having painted a rosy picture of honestly managing the property. The plaintiff and defendants were in joint possession of plots in dispute being co bhumidars, because after the abolition of Zamindari by the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the appellant became Bhumidars of the plots in question, being co Giridars, as after the abolished of Zamindari. The allegation of the plaintiff that the defendants had committed fraud was stoutly denied, and the District Judge decreed the suit for joint possession in respect of Chakbandi plot No. 201 and 274 only. As regards plot Nos. 93, 94 and 106, the dismissal of the appellant ' s suit by the trial Court was upheld. In second appeal filed by the plaintiff against the decree of the Trial Court, the High Court allowed the second appeal holding that there was nothing to show that any fraud was practised upon the consolidation authorities so as to make the order a nullity; and held that the plaintiff should be deemed to have been ousted from possession on the ground of constructive trustees 's notice under Section 9 of the Act. The High Court also took into consideration the fact that a clear fraud was committed during the consolidation operation, either by the defendants or by somebody else as a result of which the rights of the appel lant were sought to be extinguished. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the defendant respondents: (1) admittedly the possession of the defendants apart from being in the nature of constructive trustee would be in law the possession and possession of 'the plaintiff 's predecessor in title should he deemed to be protected by the trustees. (2) The respondents had practised a fraud on her by giving her an assurance that her share would be properly looked after by them and on this distinct understanding she had left the entire management of the properties to the defendants who also used to manage them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) If 1 was a co sharer with the plaintiff in the khewat and had also sirdari tenants under them, how could the sirdarri tenants occupy the land of anyone of the co sharers leaving the defendants alone so that the plots were re allotted to them. [867A] (ii) The possession of defendants apart was being in possession of constructive trust trustees would be In law the actual possession of a person interested or having acquired any rights of a Sirdar under the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Rules, 1950 and he would become constructive trustee on behalf thereof and the right of the Respondent would be deemed protected by him.

One V belonging to the Union Government took the oath as the other ministers were required to take. In view of the fact that the Constitution describing him as the Prime Minister while being sworn into office, he describes himself as the Chief Minister and this practice is in vogue eversince 1950. The oath register was by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other Ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing the respondent as his Deputy Prime Minister was descriptive only and for all purposes he is a Minister and there was no 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Minis ter as such. Relying on a bench decision of this Court in the case of Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., , it was contended that the prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. Dismissing the petition for the reasons indicated above, this Court, HELD: 1. The essential requirement of Article 173 read with Form VII A was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. [3 H] 2. There is no force in the contention that Respondent No. 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Prime Ministers but the description of it as Deputy Chief Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Ministers along with his other submis sions, would he the first contention raised by the petition er. [4 F G] 3. It is true that the oath register register is by the chief incumbent signed by a Prime Minister, and all the other minister sign as ministers are required to act as Ministers in vogue on evers explain able days of their nomination as a candidate. The words which precede this portion are merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as as a candidates. [5 G] 4. In the instant case, the oath roll register is signed by the Chief Secretary signed as Chief Minister, having been described by the respondent himself as Deputy Government Chief Minister but the nature of it contains an sub starntial part is descriptive only, for all purpose he is the Minister and thereafter his nomination is to be divided in two parts. [6 G] 5. It must be maintained that yet in view of his categorical statement made in the affidavit of Respondent No 1 that he is just than a Ministers like other member of the councils though he had been described the respondent he describes him as "his Prime Minister", while being being sworn on office, and that practice is being in vogue. The evidence does not support this plea.

On November 1, 1948, the management of the appellant firm stopped work on the night of the 1st November. The strike ended completely. By 10 p.m., it ended completely and the apparent cause for strike was that the management had expressed its inability to comply with the request of the workers to declare, to forenoon of the Ist November 1948 as a holiday for solar eclipse. On the 3rd November, the strike ended totally. The apparent cause, for the strike was: (1) that the Management of the Mills had expressed their inability to do so; and (2) that by a notification dated March 23, 1946, the workers who participated in such strike were not entitled to holidays with pay under sec. 49 B(1). Held, that non permitted absence from work even for half an hour or less in the course of a working day amounted to a strike. The action was clearly one which was concerted action on the part of the management and fell within the definition of the expression "strike" as given in section 2(q) of the and it was not necessary that the workmen were acting in concert. Held, further that the action of the 859 workers on the day of the first November clearly fell within its definition of 'strike ' in section 1(q)(1) of . The decision of the Industrial Appellate Tribunal on this point is set aside. In view of the facts and circumstances detailed in the adjudicator 's award, this contention cannot be seriously considered.

P. C. notwithstanding. The prosecution alleged that the fascinating title was misleadingly foul and beguiled the guileless into degeneracy. It did not enter appearance as a result of any defect in the film being duly certified by the Central Board of Film Censorors, in view of their bona fide belief that the certificate of the Central Government was "A" certificate by the Ministry of FilmCensors and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious nor any material to quash the proceedings. The Analyst after examining some witnesses took cognizance of the offence and issued notice to the accused. Thereafter, the producer filed a petition before the High Court under section 482 Cr. P C. seeking quashing the criminal proceeding as being abuse of the judicial process and engineered by ulterior considerations and that no complaint could be taken cognisance of in the facts and circumstances of this case. The High Court dismissed the petition. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: (1) Misconduct is an offence, definitionally speaking but; a forbidden act may not spell inevitable guilt if the law itself declares that in certain special circumstances it is not to be regarded as an offence. The chapter on General Exceptions operates in this province.[516C D] (2) Section 79 makes an offence a non offence. When ? Only when the offending act is actually justified by law or is bona fide believed by mistake of fact to be so justified, and if, as here, the Board has liled from the court that one had sufficient reason for doing that which i.e. is called to answer; the ground for such a plea. [516E] (3) The resolution of the problem raised in this case thus becomes simplified. Such an act can be stultified by a simple prosecution of a shower of prosecutions for an offenceunder section 292 l.P .C., driving the producer to satisfy a 'lay ' magistrate that the Certifi cate issued under it by expert authority cannot be prematurely invied by a mere prosecution of shower or in good faith believed that he was justified by Law in committing the act, then, the weapon of section 79 demolishes the prosecution.

The petitioner, a lawyer and the Advocate General of Bihar, invited applications for the grant or renewal of his licence as part of professional estate. The petitioner challenged the power of Government like any other litigant to appoint, any other lawyer except under him and never by excluding him. It was contended on behalf of the State that (1) the official income expected from this heavy harvest of cases, of Rs. In support of this alleged injustice the petitioner had pressed into service section 2(7), Civil Procedure Code which runs thus: "2.(7). 'Government Pleader includes any officer appointed by the State Government to perform all or any of the functions expressly imposed by this Code on the Government Pleader and also any pleader acting under the directions of the Government Advocate; (8) It is not the case that in future he would not be given such cases. (60) The fact that Government Pleader of the Patna High Court was employed by the P.S.D. and not by the petitioner does not take into account all the aspects of the matter. (769 G H; 771 G) The scheme and standards laid down in the Bihar Government Rules for fees of Government Pleaders in subordinate courts, is quasi judicial. There are thus conflicting provisions with the heading "order 27 Rule 5B" which empowers the State to adjourn the proceedings. [766 D E] (2) If a Government pleader employs his Advocate in court or exercises control over such surrogates, he must be held to be a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. He holds a public Office and the function must depend on its capacity and responsibility. [769 A] (3) The State is expected to fight and win its cases and sheer patronage is misuse of power. One effective method is of achieving this object is to act on the advice of the District Judge regarding the choice of Government pleaders. When there were several thousand cases in the Patna Courts and hundreds of cases before a plurality of tribunals it was but right that Government did not sacrifice the speedy conduct of cases by not appointing a number of pleaders on its behalf, for the sake of the lucrative practice of a single Government Pleader. It is inconceivable how he would have discharged his duties to the Court and to his client if this crowd of land acquisition cases were posted in several courts more or less at the same time. Scheduled Castes and Assistant should not pamper and thereby inflate the system of costs.

The appellants held out of a total issue as well as other shareholders of the Mills, who had purchased 5,000 shares in the company. The shares were allotted at a premium of Rs. 50 but the shares were issued at a certain premium of RS. 50 and the shares being issued at premium of R. 51. The shareholders had to pay Rs. 100 for each new share. The Mills as the holder of 5,00 shares became entitled to receive 1,66,62 shares of the Bank of India at the rate of Rs 100 per share. From a resolution passed by the Mills in truth transferring a right of the value of Rs 200 for each share held by it in favour of the appellants, the Mills gave effect to the terms of the deed and in the absence of such resolution, the mills was entitled to exercise the rights to take over only 66 shares out of the shares offered and resolved that the right to the remaining 1,600 shares be distributed amongst its shareholders. The High Court held that the distribution amounted to a distribution of "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the sale of the rights amounted to distribution of dividend within the ambit of section 25(1)(a) of that Act and was taxable as income in the hands of the appellant. The concept of "scheduled" is a progressive distributive share of the profits or income of a company given to its shareholders, though taxable under section 12 of the Act, which had a monetary value. But by the form of the resolution sanctioning the distribution, the true character of the Resolution could not be altered. The Tribunal had referred the question whether the receipts by the appellants amounted to dividend only within the extended definition of that expression in section 2 (6A). The appeal was rightly disposed of.

On May 3, 1983 the appellant filed an application for permission to produce and examine witnesses whose names were set out in the appropriate paragraphs of the election petition. The Court after hearing the parties passed an order upholding the objection raised by the returned candidate that the purpose for which the witnesses were offered is not mentioned in the list and therefore the election petitioner could not be permitted to examine more witnesses whose name had not been mentioned in that list. Aggrieved by this order the appellant appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub rule (1) of Rule 1 of Order XVI is in respect of witnesses to procure whose attendance the party needs the assistance of the court. When a summons is issued by the Court for procuring the presence of a witness, it has certain consequences in law. If the summons is served and the person served fails to comply with the same, certain consequences would ensue as provided in Rule 10 of Order XVII. [532C E] 1.2 In exercise of the powers conferred by clauses 27 and 35 of the Letters Patent and Section 129 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 the High Court of Punjab framed Rules styled as 'Rules of Procedure and Guidance in the matter of trial of Election Petitions under Part VI of the '1951 Act ' lays down the procedure for trial of election petitions. Rule 22 of the said rules is relevant. It reads as under: "21(1) A party desirous of obtaining any summons for the attendance of any person shall file in Court an application stating therein the purpose which the witness is proposed to be summoned. (3) The court may, for reasons to be recorded, permit a party to call, whether by summoning through court or otherwise any witness, any witness other than those whose names appear in the List referred to in sub rule(1), if such party shows sufficient cause for the omission to mention the name of such witness in the said list. (4) The provisions of the (1 of 1872), shall, subject to the provisions of this Act be deemed to apply in all respects to the trial of any election petition." [533C] 2.1 Rule 1A is in the nature of a proviso and does not attract its operation as it prohibits the court from dealing with witnesses to secure their attendance on the date fixed for recording his evidence, or if it is satisfied that the party has sufficient cause. The object of this sub rule is to protect the interest of the general public by punishing improper means for unduly protect a witness whose presence will be procured with the assistance by the process of the Supreme Court. It provides for satisfactory procedure in dealing with serious allegations affecting the fairness and fair trial of an election petition to prevent illegal omission or improper conduct of a party that such corrupt practice is likely to take place during the hearing of the case. [540H; 541A] 2:2 The object and purpose underlying sub rule 1A, 1 and Rule 1 A are to protect individual voters. The scheme is that after the Court framed issues which give notice to the parties what facts they have to prove for succeeding in the matters which notice would enable the parties to determine what evidence oral and documentary it would like to lead, the party should file a list of witness with the gist of evidence of each witness in a Court within the period prescribed by sub rule.(1). This advance filing of list is necessary because summoning the witnesses by the court is a time consuming process and to avoid avoidable delay an obligation is cast on the party to file a List of witnesses whose presence the party desires to procure with the aid of the Court.

% The appellant a double M.A. and holding a Doctorate applied in response to an advertisement that appeared in Hindi Daily Bhirgu A Chetna and Dainik Jagran on May 18, 1980 for the post of principal of Shrinath Intermediate College. The Selection Committee constituted by section 16F of the Intermediate Education Act, 1921 held the interview on April 12, 1981. On receipt of this letter, the Manager of the Institution issued an appointment order dated April 27,1981 to the appellant informing him that as permitted by him he has assumed charge of the post, and he has convened an urgent meeting of the staff to be held on the same day after college hours in the teachers room. The appellant submitted a statement before the Manager contending that as desired by him his letter was addressed to the Chairman of the College on May 1, 1981 addressed by the District Inspector of Schools, Ballia to the manager of Shrineshwar Intermediate College which he had given intimation to him that the Committee of Management of the college vide its Resolution No. 3 dated April 19, 1981 had appointed the appellant as Principal on one year probation in the scale of 550 1200 at initial pay alongwith DA admissible under the rules. The respondent submitted an affidavit stating that as permitting by him for taking charge was not by means of communication made to the District Superintendent of Schools. On July 1, 1982, he published a notice inviting tenders for the posts held on April 3, 1981 and invited all fresh selections and appointments of Principals. It was stated that this offer was accepted. The letter also referred to the communication addressed by his letter dated May 1;1981 to both the teachers of the institution to the Principal, wherein it was stated: " As soon as G.O. No. 1701/l5 7 FI1(27)/81 dated 7.4.1981 in regard to the prohibition on appointments is received in this office, it has been sent by letter No. 60/81 82 dated 8.4." The appellant however filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the appellant on the ground that he had no power to make the selection on April 27 1981 and therefore the appointment was not valid. It also contended that assuming such a power to issue radiogram was available to the State Government, if the appointment is made without the knowledge of the order contained in the radiograms, the appointment would be invalid. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. However, it held that the radiugram dated April 7, 1981 contained an order of the State Govern ment in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing power of appointment of Principal and teachers, including Principal and therefore, the Committee had no jurisdiction to set up a selection committee nor the selection committee had any power to appoint. 973 Dismissing the appeals of the Appellant, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment was otherwise valid though ineffective and if appellant under the orders of the High court functioned as Principal, discharged his duties and was paid, no question of recovery of amount paid to him could arise and neither the Government nor the Committee, of Management or the Institution would be entitled to recover any salary paid to the appel lant. [975 G] 2. The power of appointments including the appointment to a head of an institution and sub section (2) of section 9 which has been extracted hereinbefore confers power on the State Govt without making any reference to the Board to make, modify or rescind any regulation as also make such other order consistent with the provisions of the Act as it deems necessary and in particular. may by such order modify or make any regulation in respect of any matter. [978 B C] 3.

The respondents were manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric is supplied "impregnate the fabric with rubber and, on being asked for the reason why this particular type of goods of the petitioners were exempted from sales tax. The Income Tax Officer assessed these goods to sales tax but later dropped due to some preliminary objections. Fresh notices were issued on them to the respondents proposing to reopen the assessments on the ground that the sales of these goods had wrongly escaped assessment and accepted the case of the respondents that they were exempt from taxation. The petitioners contended that what was brought into the "end product" for the mills which manufacture cloth, but it was the raw material for tailors and for those who make ready made clothes to sell them. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. A textile fabric does not cover everything which could be made into a fabric. It is true that the term fabric has a wide meaning. Its first meaning given in the Oxford English Dictionary is "A product of skilled workmanship". The first example of such a product is: "an edifice, a building." The fourth example of the first meaning is: 'a manufactured material; now only a y Textiles fabrics". It must acquire a body and a texture. Presumably it is not just the skeleton of a textile. Apparently, it is more than that. But, against pushing this point of view too far it may be urged that in the technical and commercial parlance the taxing authorities should be left to determine whether the "tyre cord fabric" is more correctly capable of being described as a fabric or as merely cordending to pass off as ar textile fabric This is really a technical question. [502C D] 2. There is no absence of jurisdiction of the taxing Authorities who had the power to decide the question either rightly or wrongly. In any case, its view is that on what appeared to the High Court to be a question of fact, it should not decide whether the product under consideration constitutes a fabric entitled to exemption.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal on contract basis, in different collieries and also doing allied work. Shivaji Prasad Sinha respondent No. 4 was a Senior Supervisor in the Company 's establishment at Dhanbad. It is said that he was caught red handed when carrying 55 pieces of electromagnetic clutch plates kept concealed in the tool box of his scooter, and was dismissed from service. The dispute arising therefrom was referred under section 10(1)(c) of the Act to Labour Court Dhanbad for adjudication. The Labour Court registered the case as refer ence case No.4 of 1988 and issued notice to the parties. The parties entered appearance and filed their respective pleadings. When the matter is thus pending consideration the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating therein that it would be difficult for him to attend the labour court since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would he convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour court, Patna. That application was made without intimation to the management. The Government acceded to the request of the respondent and without opportu nity to the Management transferred the case to Labour Cola nation, Patna and transfer the said proceeding from the Labour Court, Patna for speedy disposal from the stage at which the case was transferred. Respondent No. 2 thereupon moved the High Court by way of writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution to have the Notification quashed. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition with an observation: "Since no prejudice is being caused to the petitioner and no allegation of mala fide has been made against the presiding officer, Patna, we are not inclined to interfere with the order under challenge. This application is dismissed." Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The requirement about the statement of reasons to be recorded must be complied with both in substance and in letter. To say that it is expedient to withdraw a case from one tribu nal and transfer it to another does not amount to giving any reasons as required by the section. [297B C] 2. It was essential for the Government to record reasons in support of its decision. Reasons would be life of the decision. Failure to give reasons or giving reasons not germane would be fatal to the decision.[295E G] 4. The necessary safeguards which are implicit by the duty to act fairly has been explained by Lord Pearson in Pioneer Ltd. vs Labour Court Gorakhpur, [1983] III LLJ 2 18 has also expressed similar views. After the leading English case of Ridge vs Baldwin, I Crl. No. 295/83 dt.

The respondent was the manager of the hotel. A dispute arose between the management and its workmen in October 1955. The present reference was made to a Tribunal under section 12 (4) of the , and a decision was taken by the tribunal on February 27, 1956. It pointed out that the company which was the management of the Hotel and its employees, which were mentioned as its workmen, were not involved in the dispute. Held, that though more than three years have passed since the reference was referred for adjudication it is unnecessary for the purposes of section 10 where the dispute is of a general nature relating to the terms of employment or conditions of labour of a body of workmen, to mention the names of such workmen who might have been responsible for the dispute; and in this case, the dispute was also about workmen to whom notice of dismissal had been given and in that connection no obligation can be held to lie on the Government to ascertain particulars of the disputes before making a reference under section 10(1) or to specify them therein in the order. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy ; , followed.

% The appellant imported certain goods manufactured by the importer. In respect of some of these items, it claimed to be component parts of the engine as also the parts of internal combustion piston engines. The Assistant Collector and the Collec tor of Customs (Judicial) overruled the contention of the appellant that 'the impugned goods were part of a motor vehicle which was imported by the appellant, therefore, they were not entitled to the benefit of exemption under the aforesaid Notification. The Custom Authorities held that the bushings and bearings were the same as those of the bearings come under Heading No. 84.63 and not under Heading 84.06. They took the view that the goods imported by them were component parts 'of the engine or engines in question and was therefore, part of the engines referred to in Heading No 84.6 which did not refer to 'parts ' of such engines. It also rejected the contention that Heading No .84.06 should be read as "parts" and not as "sub heading No. 805". The Customs authorities then applied Rule 9 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 (for short, mentioned 'the Rules), which was followed by the Appellate Tribunal. The appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal. On a reference under section 130E of the , it was held that Heading 8406 did not contain or refer to the parts parts of external combustion pists Dharmendra engine engines, but also to "part and parts thereof" because these words were not mentioned under Heading Law Nos. 21 and 22. The appellant contended before this Court that as Heading 84 had not mention 'the parts ', the Notification was inapplicable to the part parts, which fell under heading No 84, and that the question of any exemption under notification did not arise. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: The Notification exempts also parts of an engine, but it does not say "partes thereof". In the absence of any clear and unambiguous provision that exemption will be granted in respect of parts of engines, which must be all the parts constituting the engineor or engines, it is clear that the Notification has not only intended to grant exemption to internal combustion Piston engine engines but also specifically mentioned the "part 's thereof.

The 1st respondent, a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway, was allotted house rent allowance to him from the 19th August 1948 after he had been offered by the Government quarters suitable to his post but refused to occupy the same. On the question whether House Rent Allowance claimed by the 1st Respondent came within the purview of the definition of "wages" contained in the Act, HELD : The rules which must be included in the terms of the contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one 173 1352 of the specified places would be entitled to house rent allowances; but that as soon as he is offered Government quarters for his accommodation, he ceases to be so entitled. [1348 B] The fixation of house rent rooms does not create any indefeasible right in the employee at all places wherever he may be posted and in all circumstances irrespective of whether or not he has been offered Government quarter. But the statutory rules framed by the Railway governing the grant of house Rent Allowance do not make it unconditional and absolute in terms. [1448 D] The position in law is that there is no absolute right in an employee at any place where he may cease to be entitled, whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarters offered to him. Therefore the grant must be in such absolute terms. What was required was that house rent Allowance which might in certain circumstances as aforesaid be included therein in "wages ' is not the same thing as the value of any house accommodation referred to in the section and that therefore the grant can not create an indefeasible right on the employee into the house rent claim allowance. [1548 E F G] Section 23 of the Act prohibits an employee from relinquishing such a right as is the subject matter of rule 3(i) of the Rules framed by Government governing the granting of house accommodation Rent Allowance without anything more, in other words, if the house Rent allowed had been granted without any conditions or with conditions, if any, which were unenforceable in law.

Dismissing the writ petition, and directing release of his detention to be set aside. ^ HELD: The failure and the belated supply of the writ of habeas corpus have vitiated the detention. [351 F] Khudiram Das vs The State of West Bengal & Ors., , ; Khudi Ram Das vs Union of India, ; and Khudi Ran Das vs State of W.P. No. 435/80, decided on April 23, 1980, referred to. 'The constitutional imperatives enacted in Article 22(5) are two fold: (i) the detaining authority must, as soon as may be, that is, as immediately as practicable after the detention communicate to the detenu the grounds on which the order has been made; and (ii) the detained authority must afford the detenu an earliest opportunity of making a representation against the detention order. In the context 'grounds ' does not merely mean a recital or reproduction of a ground of satisfaction of the authority in the language of section 3; nor is its connotation restricted to a bare statement of conclusion of fact. 'Nothing less than all the basic facts and materials which influenced the detaining Authority in making the order of detention must be communicated to the detenue. This is the ratio of the decision in Khudi Gulab Das vs the State ofWest Bengal & ors., to which one of us (Sarkaria J.) was a party. [352 A B] In the instant case, the grounds contain only the substance of the statements while the detenu had asked for copies of the full text of those statements; and the full texts of those statement. It is not possible to say that the disclosure of the entire texts of their statements would endanger their safety or harm public interest. In these circumstances, furnishing of copies of statements and documents relied upon in the grounds for detaining the detenu at this stage, would not be in public interest and there was an infraction of the constitutional imperative because it relied on presumption under Section 123 of the Customs Act, 1962. [353 B] Khududiram Dass vs The Union of ' India,[1980] I SCR 996; Khudi ram Das vs Commissioner of Income Tax, West Bengal and Ors., to Which one of the us (Hind) was a Party. This principle has been enunciated after an exhaustive survey of the authorities by Bhagwati, J. who delivered the opinion of the Court.

Section 419 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides, inter alia, that every appeal shall be made in the form of a petition in writing presented by the appellant (1) A.I.R. 1960 S.C. 449 and (2) A L.R., 1961 Guj. 877. 1278 as required by section 419(2)(c). The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 419 and sentenced to various terms of imprisonment. After a protracted trial the High Court came to the conclusion that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Cr. P.C., as disclosed by these sections, and particularly by section 418 is against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against an order acquitting several accused persons tried jointly. On reference under section 258 of the Criminal Proce dure Code and came to its con tended conclusion that r. 6 in Chapter XXVI of the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, 1960, is invalid. The Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court, however, recorded a very lengthily order though the reasoning in support of the non maintainability of the joint appeal is confined to a couple of pages only and dismissed the appeals without going into the merits. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the State that r 6 in chapter XXVI of Bombay High court Appellate Side Rule (which are applicable to the proceedings in Gujarat High court) was inconsistent with Chapter XXXI, which provides for an appeal in a case of acquittal by the state against a common order acquitting any accused person tried jointly and convicted is competent. HELD : 1. The findings of the High Courts on the construction of sections and the other provisions of the code also do not militate against the jurisdic tion of the Full Bench on the basis of which it mainly proceeds merely to lay down the correct rule of law, then there cannot be much difficult in upholding the maintainability or of a Joint appeal by State against more than one accused persons. [879 H] 2.

The appellant, an assessee, was a firm registered under section 26 of the Income tax Act, 1922. Prior to its constitution as the firm the partners were members of a Hindu undivided family and it was assessed under the Indian Income tax Acts 1918. There was a disruption of the joint family status on June 2, 1938, and thereafter the members of the family continued the business as partners. The family which consisted of Meyyappa Chettiar had earlier claimed that having regard to the severance of joint family character, the income from the partnership business in India could not be treated under section 3 of the 1918 Act but only receipts of the income in British India were assessed to income tax twice; it was claimed by the respondent assessee in respect of business carried on outside India. The Income Tax Officer accepted the fact of partition amongst the members and rejected the contention that the family was not liable to pay tax on the profits for the said period. The Appellate Tribunal 's view was, however, reversed by the High Court which held that there was no discontinuance of the business within the meaning of section 25(3) and accordingly answered both the questions in favour of the Department. In appeal to this Court, HELD: Under section 3 the charge was made on the receipt of income in India and as the income received by the assessee was derived from the foreign business and was in relation to the foreign tax business, it must be taken that there had been an assessment to tax on income of the previous year. [ 907 A B] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs section V.R.M Palaniappa Chettiar ; , followed.

The respondent entered into a contract with Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department. The assessee made an application under Section 52 of the Bombay Sales lax Act, 1959 on November 19, 1967 to the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax, to determine the question whether the said supplies of bricks by the assessee to the Public Works De partment were sales or works contract. The Deputy Commissioner held that the supply of bricks was sales. At the instance of the assesee, the Tribunal referred the following question of law to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the Public works Department of Government (1) 14 S.T.C. 766; 119641 2 S.C R. 879, 2197 2 S C.R. 878, and (2) whether on the materials placed in the instant case it was a works contract." The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee holding that the transaction was a work contract. However, the High 'Court held that as per the ratio laid down by this Court in Chandra Bhan Gosain vs The State of Gujarat & Ors., ; , the contracts in dispute were for sale of bricks and were therefore permissive clauses and were substantially the same. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In Chandra Bhan Sone Gosain 's case, the contract in this case was a contract of sale and not a works contractor. The contracts in that case are a contract for work and labour is often a fine one. A contract of Sale is said to say, the contractor is bound to complete the work and or to supply materials at the rates mentioned in the contract. [162 G] 1.2 There is no standard formula by which one can distinguish a contract from contract for sale. [163 C] Chandra Bhanos Gosain`s case (supra) discussed. Chandra Bhan Referring; in Chandra Kumar Nayak 's Case, ,.
