The validity of the two Proclamations of Emergency issued on 3.8.75, as required by cl. (2) of Article 352 of the Constitution (as it stood at the relevant time read as follows: "352(1) If the President is satisfied that a grave emergency exists whereby the security of India or of any part of the territory thereof is threatened whether by war or internal disturbance he may, by Proclamation, make a declaration to that effect. . (c) shall cease to operate at the expiration of two months unless before the expiration 7th day of that period it has been approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament: Provided that if any such Proclamation is issued at a time when the House of People has been dissolved or the dissolution of the House" of the People takes place during the period of two yea, referred to in sub clause (c), and if a resolution approving the Proclimations has been passed by the Council of States, but no resolution with respect to such Proclamation has been issued by that House of the people. On 12.3.75 when India was attacked by Pakistan on May 27, 1975 under the Enemy Act the President issued a proclamation stating that he had formed a state of emergency existed between His Majesty and Germany which were published in the Gazette on June 21, 1975. In exercise of powers conferred by sub cl. 2 of article 352 of ' the Constitution, Parliament passed an ordinance declaring that a serious emergency exists within whereby the Security of India is threatened, inter alia, by internal disturbance. The aforesaid Proclamation was put up before both Houses by Parliament and eventually a resolution was passed by two Houses of parliament approving the said Proclams of Emergency as required under cl.2) for further information:NMENT OF EMERGENCY In exercise Of the powers conferred under sub clause(b) of cls. (1) and (4), Parliament enacted the , namely, the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly (Extension of duration) Act 1976 (Act 30 of 1976). The said ordinance was subsequently replaced by an order dated September 3, 1975 by which the period was extended for a period of one year. In August 1975 when India came into force, the President promulgated the Constitution of India. Clause (1)(a) of clause (2), however, provided that if both or either of the said two Procer tions cease to function before the expiry of two years the Proclamation shall cease operates at the expiry Of a period: Provided further that the said period may, while a proclamation is in operation, be extended by Parliament by law for a further period not exceeding one year at atime and not extending in any case beyond a period Of six months after the proclamation has ceased to operate. The petitioner filed writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of this Ordinance and the constitutional validity of these two resolutions. It was contended that (1 ) there was no evidence to show that the Proctor had ever issued the two Proclamation of Emergency dated 3rd December 1971 as required in cl.4(2) which recognised the Pro visions of Emergency under clause (3); (2)(a), and (b) no resolution approving a Proclay was passed, and therefore the proclamation of emergency was liable to be quashed. It were further contended that even though it was not expressly provided that the resolutions passed by both Houses should be published in 'the official Gazette, they could have been published for the very same reason which compelled the Government to publish the Provelations in the official gazette. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the decision of the said authorities. The District Judge, Madurai decreed the suit in favour of the appellant holding that the aforesaid premises did not constitute a temple within the meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951. In appeal, the High Court reversed those finding and decree. On further appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The High Court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that the property was the private property of the family capable of alienation. The subject matter of the dispute has to be ascertained with reference to the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the respondents the property is the private properties of the Hindu Family capable of trans pecting property, the suit was not capable of valuation. [157 D F] (2) Both parties have agreed on the question whether the property in dispute is a private or a public temple as held by the High ' Court. The question therefore to be determined with reference would to the answer to this question and the appellant will pay to him the costs of this appeal. [158 E, G] (3) The Division Bench was wrong, in proceeding thereon on the aforesaid assumption. [155 A C] (4) The direction given by the Single Judge for deciding the application for leave in accordance with the observations made in this Court judgment.

The respondents ' Union claimed that the appellant should be given cash allowance in lieu of tiffin arrangements at present made by the appellant. The respondent pleaded that the practice started by the appel lant was not based solely on humanitarian grounds and therefore, the appellant could not be blamed on that account; but the Tribunal held that under the relevant provisions of the Factories Act a canteen had been started by it, but set aside the award on the ground that the Industrial Tribunal had overlooked the fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted in the appellant 's concern and that the Tribunal was justified in law in making an award in respect of the cash allowance for tiffins. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the limited direction issued by an award was either improper or unjustified and therefore in view of r. 571(a) of the Bengal Chamber of Commerce Formula, no relief could be granted in regard to the cash allowances. HELD: The fact that a re employed person has made an admission supporting the said practice cannot have any material bearing on dealing with the point; nor can he be blamed for that reason. [ 571 D] It is not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the tiff in its employees. A Cabinet decision which was taken by the State Government could have no material bearing in dealing with this point. The history of the relations between the parties coupled with the prevailing practice in comparable concerns shows that the respondents felt that the policy adopted by the company in re employing the retired personnel was not supported solely on sympathetic grounds.

The Government of India created a Provident Fund Account in sterling in the United Kingdom. The sum of money remained under the control of the Railway Administration until the money was converted into sterling and transmitted by the Reserve Bank to Browne, the money remained at the disposal of the railway administration. The Union of India then invited applications for removal of attachment on the ground that the money represented provident fund money which by section 3 of the , was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was void ab initio. The respondent claimed immunity from attachment of the cheques on the grounds that they represented Provident Fund money which had by section3 of the . Held, that section 50 of the Indian Contract Act is applicable to a case where a creditor has directed the debtor to send him the amount owed by him to the creditor in a certain manner. In the instant case the order of attachment was contrary to the terms of section 3 9 of the Act and was therefore void ab so long as it was found that the property in the hands of the Reserve bank had ceased to be provident fund moneys and was liable to be attached. The High Court was right in holding that the amount was in the hand of the Government and did not fall within the provisions of section 50, Indian Contract act, and was not immune from being attached as claimed by the objector The Union Government of Delhi vs P. L. [1960] 1 S.C.R. 461, applied. Corto. M.M. Cotton Spinning & Weaving Co. Ltd. vs The State of Bombay, [1962] Supp. 2 S. C. R. 231, distinguished.

The appellant, a permanent employee of the respondent company, was dismissed for misconduct by the management on the ground that he had lost confidence in the employee. The management raised an industrial dispute and the dispute was referred by the Labour Court to the labour court for adjudication. The reference ran thus "Whether the termination of services of Shri L L Michael is illegal and/or unjustified and if so, to what reliefs are necessary in this respect ?" Both sides stated their cases in their pleadings that the employer had lost his confidence in him, though he did vaguely refer to the termination order of service as wrongful and malafide. The Labour Court held: (1) that the action being a simple termination without a sting process and consequence of a disciplinary action was not attracted, and (2) that even in a case like the present the requirement of bona fides was essential and if the termination was a colourable exercise of the power or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice the industrial tribunal would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. In appeal by special leave: HELD : (1 ) The appellant 's denial of leaking out office secrets was an after thought pleaded only in the rejoinder and therefore liable to be discredited. [419E] (2)(a) The impugned action is not bona fide. Besides, since there is no speck of record or any hint of written material in support of the story that the management had credible information of the appellant betraying sensitive secrets of business. [490C D] (b) If the reasons including termination were victimisation, unfair labour practices or misconduct, it was foul play to avoid a fair enquiry and fall back upon the power to terminate simpliciter there is bad faith in discharge simpliciter. [493D] (c) The management 's motive behind the recording of evidence and that the motive for the first time before the Labour court, the workman in his statement did not even file a counter affidavit and the Counsel for the Union and the workman agreed that the order of termination was not a disguise or cloak for dismissing the employee and hence liable tobe set aside. [492)(d) The industrial tribunal has misled itself on the law land. [52E] In view of what we have indicated, it is clear that loss of confidence is often a subjective feeling or individual reaction to an objective set facts and motivations. The Court is concerned with the latter and not with the former though circumstances may exist which justify a genuine exercise of a power of simple termination. [53B C] (3) In the light of what have been stated, it has been clear that losses of confidence are often a irrelevant consideration for the management; otherwise security of tenure, ensured by the new industrial Jurisprudence and authenticated by a catena of cases of this Court can be subverted by this neo formula. [482E] Sections 2(a) and 2(g).

By the Government of Uttar Pradesh, the 'Eye Camp ' intended to extend facilities of expert Ophthal mic surgical services to the residents of the town. A dispute arose regarding the supply of microbi ture from a certain M/s Mehtaad Company, Jaipur under Invoice No. 1533. Originally, the four respondents were the State of U.P., Dr. R.M. Sahay of the Sahay Hospital, Jaipur and his team of doctors and para medical staff arrived in Khurja on 21st April, 1986 examined about 122 patients. One hundred and eight patients were operated upon, 88 of them for Cataract which with modern advances in Ophricular Cavities of the operated eyes. Dr. Arif was also operated upon but on lesser scale affecting some patients, repeated itself at Moradabad. Some of the victims were later sent to and treated at Dr. Sahay 's Hospital at Jaipur. But their condition did not improve. It is now undisputed that this terrible medical mishap was due to common contaminating source. The suggestion in the Report of the 245 enquiries that ensued is that, in all probability, the source of the infection, referred to as E coli malignure of such a scale possible and evolve proper guide lines which will prevent recurrence of such tragedies; and that Government do conduct a thorough investigation as to the conditions which rendered a medical misadventure ofsuch a scale reasonably likely and evolve detailed guidelines for the conduct of eye camp work without ensuring a strict compliance with the conditions prescribed in the guidelines issued by the Central Government was submitted before this Court. The Indian Medical Council after its impleadment in these proceedings also constituted a sub committee with Dr. A.M., the Committee deliberated on the issue and its recommendations in regard to the norms for the conducting and management of eye camps have been filed before this court. In order to suggest that some points made in the report and Recommendation of the expert subcommittee of the Indian Medical council may be considered by the Union Government for incorporation in their Revised Guidelines dated 9.2.1988 arrived at after a careful study of all aspects of the problem are quite comprehensive. However, the Court instead of deciding the matter by directing the State to initiate appropriate action against those responsible for the tragedy is concerned, has suggested that some point made in this Report and Recommendations of the Expert sub committee of theIndian Medical Council may be consid ered by the said sub Committee of the Society. It cannot be said that the guidelines prescribing norms and conditions for the Conduct of 'eye camps ' are sufficiently comprehensive to ensure the protection of the patients who are generally drawn from the poorer and less affluent sec tion of society or whether any further guide lines would require to be evolved? At this stage, it was also submitted by Dr. Ghosh that the victims who constitute the 'ey eti nied camp ' were acting pursuant to and under the authority of Government and that on the doctrine of State action the activity must be reckoned as that of the State itself which must, accordingly, be held vicariously liable. Dismissing these petitions, this Court HELD: (1) The medical advice given by the expert committee is prima facie valid. [253E] (2) The guidelines issued to the Union Govern ment on 9.3.1988 clearly indicate that a Committee under the Chairmanship of the Union Health Minister with six State Health Ministers and four experts as members to re examine and update the existing guidelines or evolve fresh ones.

In a suit for declaration that a deed of gift was void and inoperative beyond the lifetime of Sumitra Devi and was not binding on her reversion, as she had only a life interest in the corpus of the property and there was no justifying legal necessity for the alienation made by her. Held (per section K. Das jj.), that having regard to the terms of the contract between the parties, it could not be said that the gift was made at the time of the marriage. It was open to a Hindu widow to make an effective gift in favour of her daughter subsequent to the marriage, if the conditions laid down were fulfilled. There is no consideration nor any discussion of the texts bearing on the question whether a particular gift is reasonable or not will have to be judged according to the state of the family at the date of the gift. Churaman Sahu vs Go pi Sahu, (1933) L.R. 59 I.A. 104, relied on. Per section K J. Section 123 does not deal with nor did it affect the power of a Hindu wife to make a gift in respect of a reasonable portion of her husband 's estate in favour. A gift made long after the marriage may be supported upon the ground that the gifts when made fulfil that moral or religious obligation. Per Subba Rao J. In order to decide whether a valid gift is unreasonable, it must be proved (1) that the donor intended thereby had been induced to make such a gift; (2) that on the facts of this case it could be said in law that the donee who had made the gift had made a voluntary gift of the four houses. The expression "whether acquired before or after the commencement of the Act" was not retrospective in effect. The Explanation further postulates that by reason of the use of the expression " whether acquired before, or after her marriage " the section was retrospective in operation. Held further (per Das J., dissenting) that a gift made earlier prior to the execution of a deed could be valid only if it fulfilled the moral obligation flowing from the ante nuptial agreement; and that it did not affect the powers of a ' Hindu widow under section 123(1). Gurumo Ram vsgo Devi, (I.L.R] , distinguished. Held also, further, that a conveyance made long before the marriage might be supported on proof of such a condition as being necessary for making an gift at the later stage of the agreement. The intention of the Legislature was not to make any distinction between "other than the donor and his wife in favour but to make it impossible to affect them. Sheo Ram vs Banarsi Das, (1935) L L. R. 59 1.A I. 104 and Churabman Sahu 's case, , relied on by the Full Bench of the High Court. Chimuraman Rampur Sahu vs G Fixeda Collieries Ltd., [1863] 3 N. D. 309, relied upon. Held, further that the essential or obligatory acts could not make a valid gifts unless it was proved that there was antenuptial arrangement by Sumitra Devi that she would give four houses at Asansol. Per Sarkar J. (dissenting) 1. Section P. Maintenance of Internal Security Act, 1950 did not deal merely with nor does it affect its power of the parent to make or execute a deed. It had no application to the present case because there was none such stipulation in section 123 that it was made prior to or after its amendment by Act VI of 1937. The conditions laid under section P. maintenance Act were "a condition precedent for making gifts" and "that there was, therefore, no scope for doubt than the Explanation to section 123.

The appellant, a rival candidate under the Punjab and Haryana High Court (Tej. Singh) filed an election petition for challenging the election of the 7th respondent on the ground that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices and detailed in the petition an(l in the statement of facts. The petition was contested by both the parties. The evidence led by the parties showed that the allegations of corrupt practices indulged in by Tej Singh were clearly proved. In these circumstances it is imperative to defeat the dictatorial Congress in those elections. Civil Appeal No. 420/79, filed by one of the candidates against Tej Singh, and Avtar Singh challenging the validity of the election on the grounds (1) that he had got circulated pamphlets and posters among the voters of the constituency wherein he had mentioned that Ruplal had withdrawn his candidature and any vote given to him was deemed to be a vote for Ruplod; and (2) that in view of the very narrow margin of votes (123), the election would have fallen to the appellant. On behalf of the appellant it was contended: (1 ) that the evidence showed that Tej Singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the posters; (2 ) that he made payments for the entire posters which was printed at the instance of Tej Singh on a perusal of the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by the respondents, in view the very wide margin of difference between the votes secured by Tej. Singh and Avtar singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of his candidate would have gone to the appellants (Airlines Singh) and therefore, the result of the Election would have been materially altered; and consequently the appellant had incurred serious losses and prejudice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Pratap Singh had indulged in corrupt practice particularly when the printing was clearly admitted by him as indicated above. [419D E] 2. In view of section 123(2) of the Act having been adopted by the first respondent as his separate petition challenging the appellant 's election, the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tejwant Singh had admittedly paid for posters which they were printed. [420A B] 3. The result is that the appeal is allowed, the judgment of the High Court is quashed and the election is set aside.

The appellant, a Forest Minister of the State in Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal was personally keen on giving him an office of profit. The Ordinance inter alia provided that the constitution of a Forest Development Board would be constituted with a view to appointing the said Devinder Sharma as its Chairman. On 15.3.1983, the Secretary, Government of the Government of Punjab issued a rule nisi which stated that a decision on the question whether a particular Devinder ' was a forest Minister in the Council of the Ministers headed with Shri Bhajanlal. The aforesaid Ordinance inter fered that the said Marinder Sharma was constituted with the view to appoint the said Saminder Sharma, as its chairman. It was also alleged by the appellant that after having failed to threaten and demoralise the appellant through indirect means the respondent, the respondent called him to his official residence on July 26, 1983 through the Acting Chief Conservator of Forests and criminally intimidated him to withdraw the writ petition and pursuant to that, eleven officers withdrew from the petition. Later, the appellant filed an application for contempt against the respondent in the High Court complaining of interference by the Respondent with the due course of judicial proceedings. The application was admitted and a rule was issued upon the Respondent. The respondent appeared in the rule and opposed the same by filing an affidavit denying all the allegations made against him by the appel lant. The learned Single Judge of the High COurt, after considering the application, affidavits and the submissions made on behalf of the parties took the view that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the Court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In that view of the matter, the learned Judge dismissed the application and discharged the Rule nisi. It is apparent from the facts stated above that the allegations ' made by the Appellant, if proved would consitute a criminal contempt. The appeal filed against this order has been incompetent and is, accordingly, dismissed. Allowing the appeal in part, 892 HELD: 1.1. An appeal will lie under section 19(I) of the Act only when the High court makes an order or decision in exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt. It does not, however, mean that when theHigh Court erroneously acquits a contemnor after hearing the parties and after considering them the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Courts cannot be said to be exercising its jurisdiction or power to punishfor contempt under article 215 of the Constitution. [894C D] 1.2.

The respondents were the daughter and grand sons of one Vinayakbhat. The lessee paid a premium of Rs. 999 for the lease, and also agreed to pay a yearly rent of Rs 80 to chos during her lifetime. After his death a yearly sum equal to the assessment of the two lands to the heirs of VENKATARAMA was payable by them. The appellant instituted a suit against eleven persons, alleging that he had committed default in payment of rent, that he sent a notice on 21st January, 1941, terminating the lease and asked for immediate action to be taken for recovery of arrears of rent from him. The trial court dismissed the suit. It was contended by the respondents that there was no forfeiture because no rent was fixed in respect of the suit property and also because it was for the plaintiff to approach the defendants and not for the defendants to go to the plaintiff and pay it, therefore, he should have sent a communication according to law if he wanted to enforce the right of forfeiture and had not done so. There was no waiver or breach by the appellant which could legally be inferred from sub section (g) of section 111(g), as amended in 1929, that the court ordinarily would grant relief against forfeiture for non payment of arrears rent under section 114 of the and that if at the time relief is asked for the position has been altered so that no injustice will be done there is no real discretion and the court should make the order and give the relief. Held: A landlord can never take advantage of the proviso for re entry in order to avoid a lease which, by the terms of it, is to be void on the non performance of covenants, it seems clear that to put an end to this licence, the grantor should have given notice of his intention so to do, and though section 114 has no application, equity and good conscience and according to it the institution of a suit for ejectment would be sufficient indication on the part of the landlord for determination of the lease. The courts below erred in coming to such conclusion. It has to be seen that when the Act is so express to provide a wide discretion , meaning no doubt, to prevent one man from forfeiting what in fair dealing belongs to some one else, by taking advantage of a breach from which he is not conversant and irreparably damaged, it is not advisable to lay down any rigid rules for guiding that discretion. In the present case as the Act provides that if during the period the relief is called for the purpose of giving notice before a right of re entry accrues to the landlord, section 114(g) falls. The restrictions on the exercise of the discretion in cases where statutory provisions were made to the contrary, were imposed from time to time, and after 1st April, 1930, the principle of equity applicable is the one contained in sub section 2 of section III and that no notice as required by section 111 (g), was necessary. The law in India and England on this subject is not the same and it cannot be said that this sub section enacts or enunciates any general principle of justice; equity and justice, therefore applies to leases executed prior to 1929 or even prior to the coming into force of the , or to leases made after 1th April, ,885. The rights and obligations under those leases have to be determined according to the rules of law prevailing at the date and only rule applicable seems to be that a tenant cannot by his unilateral act and by his own wrong determine the lease unless the lessor gives an indication by some unequivocal expression of intention on his part of taking advantage by the breach. On no principle of Equity, equity or good conscience can be invoked in the case of a tenant of this description.

Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 provides that certain persons occupying land for not less than ten years to be deemed tenants notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in section 52 or any other provision of the , or any law, custom or usage, shall be deemed to be a tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was in occupation of such land on the 11th day of April, 1957, on the basis of that deed, notwithstanding the fact that the lease was granted by a person who had no right over the land or who was not competent to lease the land. The appellant, who was a tenant in respect of the lands, surrendered lease hold rights but continued in possession to be so deemed tenants despite the terms fixed under the agreement. The High Court held that the benefit of section would apply only to persons whose occupa tion had a lawful origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believe to be competent to grant such leases or had come into posses sion with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the exclu sive basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the expression "in occupation" occurring in section 7D must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation". On the other hand, it was not within the contemplation of the legisla ture to confer the benefit on persons who had wilfully trespassed upon lands belonging to others and whose occupation was unlawful in its origin; (2) the finding of fact entered by the High Court is that the appel lant had come with possession of the land by trespass, and his plea before the Courts below was that he was himself the owner of the area having acquired title to it by adverse posses tion. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The intention of the legislature in enacting section 7E must be interpreted as meaning 'in lawful occupa ties". [114F G] 2. In the instant case, the finding that the appellant had come to possession of lands by trespass was entered by him with his plea, before the courts below as well as by the Receiver, and a further amount of Rs.50,000 should be deposited by the respondents in the trial court within a period of three months from today, whereupon the appellant will be at liberty to withdraw the said amount from Court without furnishing any security.

The appellant, a manufacturer of gold and diamonds, was found in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967. He had produced before the customs officers a challan under section 110 of the . The value of 7200 cigarette lighters was stated as Rs. 14400/ and of 250 tins of flints as Rs 15,000/ on which customs duty of Rs. 15,840/ and Rs. 10,500/ respectively was alleged to be payable. In the complaint filed on 30 October 1968, by the Assistant Collector of Central Excise, Marine and Prevention Division, Bombay it is alleged that the cigarette vendor members and others were in possession with all that was contained in it. It was also alleged that he had not given any evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. In reply, he asserted that he was not only in possession but knew something about the incriminating nature of their contents. The trial Court confirmed the conviction. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant had failed to prove his contention and consequently convicted him under section 135(1)(ii) of the for which he was acquitted. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 123 of the Art provides a procedural rule. They could be applied when the case came up for trial before the Presidency Magistrate who actually decided it on 15 7 1969. Further, the complaint itself was filed on 5 1968. It is immaterial that the prosecution was found to have been in possession on 21st April 1967. There is further another objection to the applicability of section 123(1) of Act. The appellant had not produced evidence to prove that the goods were legally brought into India. [541 B C] 3. What Section 123, read with section 114, was sufficient to enable the prosecution to ask the Court to presume that the appellants knew that the Customs must have been smuggled or imported in contravention of the law. [542 A C] 4. The onus of proving innocent possession of these goods upon the appellant is on the person from whose possession the goods are seized.

The question which arose for consideration in the appeal was whether the provisions of section 4 Of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935, were applicable to a case on the basis of the provision in section 4(2) of the Rewa state Companies Act. Held: (i) The suit before the District Court was not one for accounts of a dissolved firm but for accounts and accounts of an illegal association which was in existence at the relevant period for which accounts were asked, the only course for the courts to pursue is to say that he is not entitled to any relief on the allegations made as the courts cannot adjudicate in respect of contracts which the law declares to be illegal (Senaji Kapurchand vs Pannaji Devichand ([1867] L.R. 52 I.A. 126), 128, 129, 130 131 132 132 133 135 134 135 and 132 135 138 and 136) because under the , an unregistered firm is not illegal; there was no direct compulsion in any partnership firm to be registered though the disabilities consequent on non registration may be extremely inconvenient. (ii) The analogy does not really apply. For the reasons given above, this Court directed that the parties must bear their own costs of the hearing in this Court and the High Court, for adjudicating the preliminary objection raised by the appellants. [773 A B] Surajmull Nargoremull vs Triton Insurance Company Ltd., (1948) L. R. 52 1.A I. A. 129, distinguished. (iii) Since the suits were not one of accounts of dissolved firm and but for account of an alleged illegal association against another member on the footing that the said association should be treated as legal in order to give rise to a liability to render accounts in respect Of the transac tions of the association, the suit must fail.

The Superintendent, District Jail, Amritsar, in exercise of powers under section 482 Cr. P.C., issued a charge sheet against the three respondents on three charges: (a) that on 8.6.1986 at 2 P.M., they along with two others named in the complaint, shot and killed an elephant in compartment No. 13 of Kundurugutu Range Forest and removed the ivory tusks of the elephant; (b) that the elephants were removed for being carried out by the person who was the driver, as they then were along with another driver, and that a case had been registered under sections 447, 429 and 379 IPC read with section 54 and 39 of the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972; and (c) that he alongwith two others, named in th complaint, fired shots and killed one elephant. The learned Magistrate took cognisance of this offence and ordered issue of process to the accused. It would appear that at the Police Station Souna, a case was registered under section 447,44 and 379 I.P.C. read with Section 54 and 40 of the Northern India Forests Act, 1934. The respondents moved the High Court under section 483 Cr. Procedure or quashing the order of the Magistrate taking cognizance. The High Court quashed the proceedings against the accused as it was violative of the provisions of sections 100(1), 101(2) and 149 I. P .C. 1973 on the ground (a). that an investigation by the Police was in progress in relation to the same offence, the learned Magistrate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaint and call for a report in the matter from the police; and that the learned trial Magistrate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of the offence and ordering issue of summons. The State filed Special Leave Petitions before this Court contending: (i) that section 210(1) Cr.P, 1973 was attracted and that as an investigation was in pending relation to a same offence the learned Magis trate would be obliged to stay proceedings on that complaint and calling for a final report in respect of it from the Police; and, (ii) that tuskks and had been seized by the police. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1(a) The expression "any act or omission which constitutes any offence under this Act" in section 56 of the has not done much to lessen the difficulty in applying the tests to identifying the legal common denomnators of "same offence". [463C] (b). There is no reason why such a construction should be avoided. The wide language used by the legislature would convey that what would constitute the offences under two different laws i.e., they should be identical. if, however, the two offences are distinct then notwithstanding that the allegations of facts in the two complaints might be substantially similar, the benefit of the ban cannot be invoked. [463E G] (c). An act or an omission can amount to and constitute an offence under the IPC and at the same time constitute an. offence under any other law. The person doing it is not obligatory for him to bring his case before the court, but has to do so before he comes in to Court. [453G H] PG NO 483 2(a). It is also not permissible that the section may be attracted even where a Magistrate takes cognisance when another offence is alleged under two or more enactments, then the offender shall be liable to be prosecuted and punished under either or any of those enactments, but shall not be liable for being punished twice for the same offences. [452C E] (d). The prohibition in section 8(1)(a) of the is attracted the same act must constitute an " offence" under more than one Act. If there two distinct and separate offences with different ingredients under two enactments, a double punishment is not barred. [459D G] 2(b).

The petitioner, who had been suretyship abroad for a non bailable offence either as undertrial or as convict who has appealed or sought special leave, challenged the order of the magistrate refusing to accept the suretyship and the court granted bail. In appeal to this Court, it was contended by the defence that bait loosely used, was comprehensive enough to cover release on ones own bond with or without sureties, that there is no definition of bail in the Code and that therefore there are no guidelines which prevailed with the Supreme Court when granting suspension of sentence must, in a broad sense, have relevance to what the Code indicates except where special circumstances call for a different course. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 In order to invoke section 43(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, it is necessary that the magistrate must always bear in mind that monetary bail is not a necessary element of the criminal process and even if risk of monetary loss is a deterrent against fleeing from justice, it will be not the only deterrent and there are other factors which are sufficient deterrents against flight. [430C D] 1:2 The Supreme Court 's power to enlarge a person during the pendency of a Special Leave Petition or of an appeal is very wide; as order 21 Rule 27 of the Supreme court Rules disclose. In that sense, a consideration of the question (1) Report of the Legal Aid Committee appointed by the Govt. Of Gujarat (2) Report dated the Expert Committee on Legal Aid Processual Justice to the People, May 1973. 345 as to whether the High Court or the subordinate courts have powers to enlarge the person on his own bond without sureties may not strictly arise.

The assessee company took loan from the respondent assessee for the purpose of manufacturing 'Eldee '. In 1951 52, the assessee claimed under section 15C of the Income tax Act, 1922 exemption from tax in respect of 6% of its capital employed in 'E '. ' as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of the capital so employed Rs. 3,21,460 advanced to it. The Income tax Officer rejected this claim but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to 'Castle ' in the calculation of the Capital invested for the purposes of 429 section 15 C of the Act. Upon an application under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax , 1922, to the Tribunal to refer a question which was subsequently raised by a Commissioner arose out of the order of the Tribunal was rejected and the petition of the Commissioner under section 11(2) for an order directing the Tribunal not state the case on the ground that no question of law arose out. The High Court declined to require the Tribunal 's finding that the finding of the Appellate Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from the non inclusion by the Income Tax Officer in the assessment in question of income of 'C 'astle and that the factor taken into consideration by the Appellate reached by the Tribunal in coming to its conclusion, it did "was a relevant factor." Held, that the High Court had misdirected itself in law in arriving at its finding. The Tribunal had considered evidence covering all the essential matters before arriving at a conclusion. If the conclusion of the Tribnnn is based upon some evidence ignoring other important matters , it cannot be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. Non inclusion of the income of assessee 'C,astle, being separately assessed at Bombay in the status of a registered firm apparently refer to assessment of that business in subsequent years and not in the year of assessment 1951 52.

The Minister concerned had passed a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The writ petition was then amended and 97 in the amended petition Duggal respondent also challenged the validity of the subsequent order of February 18; and at the resumed hearing of the writ petition the High Court directed that the Minister concerned might give a personal hearing to the parties and thereafter pass the necessary orders in the matter. Aggrieved by this direction, the appellants have come up before this Court for relief by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The direction for impleading the Minister as a party was given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the petition. [971C] In the instant case, the directions for impleading of the Minister and directing that the Chief Minister be impleaded as a respondent were given by this Court with a com plication to apprise it the Minister for the allegation that he had deviated from the normal procedure while passing the order dated February 18. 1975 inasmuch as he had dealt with the matter directly and by passed the Secretary of the Department. The High Court was, therefore in error in directing the Minister to file his affidavit. [962D E] The direction of the High COurt to the impleaded of the Ministers as a parties was given with a clear view to informing the Minister that the Government should file his personal affidavit. It is essentially for the Minister alone concerned to decide in the light of the allegation made in tile petition as to whether he should or should not file an affidavit. The other part of the order whereby the Minister, concerned was directed to file His personal affidavit is set aside.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant under section 259 of the Cantonment Act. In 1938, the appellant filed an application before the magistrate for realisation of arrears of rent on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of rents on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent. The Magistrate held that he had jurisdiction and issued warrants for attachment of movable property of the 'respondent on June 13, 1961. Thereupon the respondent went in revision to the Sessions Judge which allowed the application holding that rent under a lease could not be recovered under section259 of the Act and made a reference to the High Court under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court also held that since it was an application under article 227, section 259 was not applicable to a case where the Magistrate did not take into account the objections of the respondents. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The jurisdiction of the High court in hearing a reference under section 435 of the code is controlled by the words "claimable by a Board" and that it is not any sum that could be described as rent or fee which could be recovered by a Magistrate under the general law of the land. Since section 259 provides for recovery by suit also and as such it wilI not be possible for the Board to recover rent from the tenant, section 257(1) cannot be applied to a simple case of money due to the Board on contract of lease.

The appellant was employed as a Section Salesman for the districts of Bikaner, Ganganagar, Merta and Barmer in Rajasthan with his head quarters at Bikaner. Two other local salesmen and local Trav elling companies were appointed for certain number of districts and in the area of each section salesman a number of local sales men and local travelling salesmen were appointed. The appellant was ap pointed as a section Salesman and his services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. Some correspondence and other evidence produced before the Labour Court showed that the appellant was engaged to do canvassing and 551 induce them to canvass and promote the sales of the company 's product in his area. The Tribunal also found and in fact it had referred to as an admitted case of both the parties that the respondent Company sells its product i.e. cigarettes manu factured by it directly through their wholesalers who in turn sell the product to various dealers appointed by the company in the areas. The section salesmen 'and the local salesman and local trav eling salesmen are employed by the Company in order to canvass, and promote sales of them by the companies. From 475 perusal of the records produced before this Court it is seen that the appel lant is required to send reports about the publicity and advertisement of placing posters, holders, cinema slides etc. These duties do require the imaginative and creative mind which could not be termed as either manual, skilled, unskilled or clerical in nature. The supervising work of other local Salesmen was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the Areas of his operation. Such a person cannot be termed 'workman 'as defined under the Industrial Disputes Act as it stood in the year 1973 when the appellant 's service was terminated, the employee has to be under the employment to do the work of one of the types of work referred to in the section i. e. manual, unskilled and/or clerical nature and that the provisions of the Industrial Dispute Act were not ap plicable and the reference, therefore, was incompetent. It is against this order the appeal has been filed. In order to come within the definition of workman under Section the Industrial Re spondent company as it then stood in 1973 when he appellant ' s service was termin ed, the employ ment was terminated. The petitioner claimed that the termination itself was illegal and should have been treated as not a 'workman" and that therefore the reference was incompetent and it was incompetent for this Court to interfere with the finding on the question whether the appellant is a workman employed for manual,killed, unskilled, or clerical nature. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act (the award was not applicable to him and in view of the fact that a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. [401E G] 2.1 The contention whether the appe lant was a workman is also the ratio of the decision of this Court in Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distribution Company vs Burmah South Management and Staff; ; , D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal & Ors., 1973 F.J. (42) P. 440, J. Dec suppose Distributor vs State 476 Kerala & others, [1974 11 LLJ 926). [402G] 2(a) The word 'sales promotion ' in the Industrial Dis bur tion Act was not used to absolve from the definition that of workman. In the context of the Act and the employees covered by the enactment also go to show that persons employed for sales promotion normally would not come within those categories. Therefore a direction to the management to pay some compensation is necessary to meet the ends of justice.

The appellant Company entered into a contract of lease with M.P. Government for a period of 10 years in Samvat 1999. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years in the Samvat 2000. When proceedings were initiated on 16.7.1952 to eject the company, the Company filed Suit No. 14 of 1960 for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The Trial Court dismissed the suit in terms of Section 182 of the MP Land Revenue Code, 1959. The Company preferred second Appeal No. 1 of 1961 before the Madhya Pradesh High Court which was also dismissed by its judgment dated 30.6.1964 in First Appeal No 1 of 1962. Thereafter the State entered into an agreement with the company to grant a fresh lease for a term of 10 year renewable ten years from 9.2.1971 subject to payment of enhanced rent as agreed upon between the parties. Since the Company failed to pay the agreed rents and thus contravened the conditions of the lease, proceedings were started by the Additional Collector by his Order dated 1.10.1977 for eviction of the Company from the land in question. The High Court held that the Company was not a 'pakka ' tenant ' and did not enjoy the status of a ' Gair Maurusi ' tenant. Hence this appeal by the State. Allowing the Appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. Section 182(2)(i) of the M. P. Land Revenue Act, Samvat 2007 defines 'phakta ' as "a person holding land from the State Government under section 181", Section 181 provides that a Government lessee may be ejected from his land by order of a Revenue Officer on one or more of the following grounds namely: (i) that he has failed to pays the rent for a Period of three months from the date on which it became due; or (ii) that, he has used such land for purpose other than for which it was granted; or that the term of his lease has expired or under the newly stipulated terms of the original lease, the company has been holding the land from, the State Govern ment and it had never been an ordinary term as defined in the M P. Act No. 66 of 1950. [179D E] 2. Section 183 of the Code provides that the Additional Collec tor made his order for eviction where he is satisfied that the tenant has failed and to pay rent for more than three months. The finding of the High Court that large amounts are due and payable by the Company as rent and that the rents have remained unpaid for aperiod far in excess of three month from the dates on which they became due, shows that large amount are due.

By section 1(3) of the principal Act, "the interest of the person to whom the surplus lands relate and of all land holders mediately or immediately under whom the excess lands are being held shall stand extinguished and the said lands shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances. " By a notification dated December 9, 1965 the State Government issued certain provisions of the Principal Act other than those contained in Chs. III and IV of the Orissa Land Reforms (Amendment) Act 15 of 1965 which included sections 40, 41 and 42 in Ch. III (sections 24 to 37 dealing with resumption for personal cultivation of any land held by a tenant and related matters) and also provided for payment of compensation at a rate which was less than the market value of the land falling within the ceiling limit as originally fixed under 1960. The original Chs I and IV were substituted by fresh provisions. By section 37 it was provided that "the remaining provisions of this Chapter shall, A mutatis mutandis apply where lands acquired and held under personal cultivation prior to the commencement of this Act by any person through inheritance, request, gift, family settlement, purchase or otherwise together with the lands 'in his personalcultivation at the time of such acquisition exceeds his ceiling limit. By a Notification issued on September 25, 1968 certain provisions were brought into force in respect of "seiling area" and the consequences of failure to submit the return. " Section 43 provided for revision of compensation. It was provided by section 37 that "where any law made by the State of any estate or of any rights therein or the extinguishment or modification of any such rights, or (b) (c) (d) shall be deemed to be void on the ground that it is tent with, or takes away or abridges any of the ferred by Article 14, article 19 or article 31 598. The Act was amended on October 17, 1960 and the amending Act 13 of 1965 were both Acts enacted for ensuring agrarian reform, and the lands held by the petitioners were "estates" within the meaning of article 31 A.

A deed of surrender has been executed by a Hindu widow and it is not the intention of the widow to retain her property but for the surrender made by the widow, and the mere execution of a surrender in favour of the latter does not affect her right. The fact that a surrender may and in the majority of cases does take the form of transfer, e.g., when the widow conveys the entire estate of her husband without consideration and not as a mere device to share the estate with the reversioner, in favour Of the latter, does not invalidate a surrender as having been held by this Privy Council in Sreeramulu vs Kristamma, I.L.R. 1 All. 511. In deciding this case the High Court took the view that there was no reason why it should be necessary that the estate must remain with the widow before she could exercise her power of surrender and the widow could sue for possession at once by 34 5 evicting the defendants and were not bound to wait till the widow actually died. Held, further, that in case of alienation by a second wife of her deceased husband 's property without any justification or in the case of a stranger acquiring title by adverse Possession against her the interest created is to be deemed to be severed from the inheritance and if a surrender is made subsequently by the widows the surrenders must take it subject to such prior interest. Sreersamulu v Kumaraswami Sastri, I .L. R. , approved. Held further, also, that where there is no necessity for alienation, the interests which she herself holds and which she can convey to others is not an indefeasible life estate but an estate liable to be defeated on the happening of certain events which in Hindu law cause extinction of the widows 's estate, and if the title of such person has been completed already, it could not be defeated by a surrender made again by the proposer. The effect of a surrendered by a co widow is not to spilt up the husband ' 's Estate into two parts or to give to the alienee an interest necessarily co extensive with her lifetime. When once shells her husband ' estate in her favour, she does so on the direction of the court. In any event, it cannot be said that she has gifted neither lost her title nor vested her title in her by adverse possession, there is, no principle of law under which the acts of the reversioners could bind him.

In October, 1977, an extraordinary general meeting of the Swadeshi Polytex Ltd. was held which it had been informed by a telegram that the appointment of Shri Sitaram Jaipuria as Managing Director of the Cotton Mills Company be and is hereby terminated subject to certain conditions: (i) For the year 1976, the Gold Mill Company had acquired 10 lakhs shares of Rs. 10 each from Brooke Bond and other industrial units belonging to the Cotton Mill Company; (ii) On receipt of a notice dated February 11, 1984 under section 169 of the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958, (as amended in 1976), Shri Sitaram went into voluntary liquidation with effect from March 3, 1979. The requisitionists sent a requisition to the Polytex Company on 15th February, 1984 for sanction of its extraordinary general meetings of the company and for appointment of Sitaram Jaupuria as a Director. Subsequently, the requisitionists under section 173(2) and (5) read with section 190 of the Companies Act were appointed by two of them to consider the said notice. The meeting also referred to the resolution passed by the Board of Directors on March 14, 1984 in respect of the shares in question and ordered that a meeting be held in accordance with the order of the High Court notwithstanding any order of injunction etc. issued by any other court or authority. In the year, 1976, Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Ltd., filed a petition under sections 397 and 398 against the Polycell Company alleging oppression and mismanagement of the Poly Schtex Company, impleading Shri Sitaram Kaipuria and other directors of the Jute Mill Company as parties, contending that in view of the impending general meeting held with effect on June 30, 1981, the acquisition of 13 lakhs shares out of the said 10 lakhs share, by its entire company 's creditors would not be sufficient to issue the said requisition notice. It was contended that since a Receiver had been appointed by the Collector in respect thereof the attachment of the 9 lakhs shares and also the pledge of 3,50,000 shares out was invalid as there was no other legal or equitable right which would prevail over it, the impugned order of acquisition was bad. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that since the Receiver had already been appointed on March 12, 1979 his right to exercise its voting rights in respect o the said shares continued to have vested with the Cotton mills Company and could not claim any right whatsoever or interest therein. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that (i). the Board and the Directors of a company had no power to take over the management of the affairs of the Mill Company in respect whereof the said company had acquired the shares of the Mills Company; and (ii). the requisition under section 17(1) (a) of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act 1951 was a piece of colourable legislation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, ^ HELD: There is no provision in the Code for charging orders, but on the Original Side of the high Courts which has inherited the older jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery, it is the practice in cases where it is considered undesirable to grant immediate execution to make a charging order in the form made in the case of Kewny vs Attril, [1967] 2 S.C.R. 889, 891 (as a result of which the winding up petition has been filed, that it would not have the effect of depriving the holder of the share of his title to the shares.

The petitioners were plaintiffs. They instituted a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure for a declaration that they were the owners in possession of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala, District Sangrur in the State of Punjab (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act) had no sort of right in the suit lands and that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. The trial court framed an issue relating to its jurisdiction and tried it as a preliminary issue. It held that since the question involved in the case was simply one of title to the suit property and it was not necessary for the Civil Court to decide whether the suit Land was shamlat deh or not, and that even if the land had validly vested in the Panchayat or not being shamlat mallat deh, it had jurisdiction to try the suit. Aggrieved by the said finding, the Panchayat filed a revision petition before the High Court which came to be dismissed with leave to prefer an appeal against the decision of the High court. Allowing the Special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: The view taken by the High Courts is clearly distinguishable from the facts in this case since in this matter the Panchayat which had been impleaded as defendant has raised the plea that the land was a part of shamlat and that they had no right or title in it. This question has to be decided by the Collector only under section 11 of the Act, and not by the Civil court. [835G H] The above decision is clearly inapplicable from the present case since it is the Panchayat who had been impleading as a defendant had raised the pleas that the plaintiff land was shamil deh. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil Court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was sham Tel deh or was not and whether it belonged to the Panchayat concerned or not. Reliance was also placed by the counsel for the petitioners on a decision of this Court in Bhagu & Ors., vs Ram Sarup and Ors., [1985] Punjab Law Journal Page 366 in which the suit had been held to be maintainable in a civil court even though the defendant had contended that the said land was not shamlat Dev deh.

Section 59 of the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board General Conditions of Supply Act, 1981 empowers the Board to notify the terms and conditions upon which it will supply electricity to a person. Clause (6) further provides that in the event of a consumer failing to pay to the Board any sum which may become due for payment to the Controller on the dates fixed for payment thereof, the Board may, in addition to and without prejudice to the other rights of the Board, appropriate a part or whole of such deposit towards the sum due from the consumer. The clause stipulated that if there be any delay in payment, the consumer shall pay surcharge thereon equal to 1% per month or such other percentage to be fixed by the Board from time to time, of the demanded amount for each month of delay or part thereof. The deposited was liable to be reviewed by the Electricity Board fromtime to time and having regard to the factors mentioned in clause (ii) of the General Conditions and conditions of supply it observed that no interest would be payable on security deposit since it had direct hearing to the level of supply in consumption of electricity. On the question whether the law could be held to be violative of the freedom guaranteed by Article 19(1)(f) & (g) as imposing an unreasonable restraint in the interests of the consumers, this Court, HELD: 1. The essential condition of supply requiring a consumption security deposit has a direct bearing on the operations of the plant with the meters and such other methods adopted by the consumers. [259 B] 2. There is nothing to indicate under the scheme of the Act or Schedule VI of the Supply Act that interest must be paid on the security deposit. The regulation prescribed for payment of interest at certain rate, in the case of a Rajasthan and Orissa the Board have clearly stipulated that no Interest would be liable on security deposits. Section 4(2)(g) of The Electricity (Supply) Act provides that the requisition for supply of energy by the company is to be made under proviso (a) after a written contract is duly executed with sufficient security. The payment is in terms of the agreement between the Board and the consumer, interpreting the conditions of the supply, HELD : There is no legal obligation to pay interest on a deposit made by the consumer with the Board in terms thereof. [260 D F] 3. The true nature of the transaction, in these cases is one of advance payment of charges for consumption of Electricity estimated for a period of nearly 3 months.

The petitioners, an officer of the Telecommunication Research Centre, were recruited in four batches in 1965 and 1971. The Class I posts in the Tele patiec tion Research Centre consisted of the following posts: 1. Director (Senior Inspec tive Grade Level I) 2. Additional Director (Junior Administrative Grade Level II) 3. Deputy Directors (Senior Selection Grade I). The Posts of the Deputy Directors, Assistant Directors and S.T.Os Grade I are filled by the following methods: 1010 (a) by direct recruitment through the Union Public Service Commission; (I) by transfer of Group A Field Officers recruited through the P&T Board of the Ministry. (II) by Transfer of Group B Field Officers who are Posts and Telegraphs departmental promotees belonging to the Indian Telecommunications Service Group A and Group B. For the first time the UnionPublic Service Commission advertised for the recruitment of 10 Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I in the Telegraph Research Centre under the Recruitment Rules. These were General Central Service Class I post and they continue to be so till today. In response to the said advertisement petitioners 2,3 and 4 applied for recruitment and they were selected for appointment to the posts of Assistant Directors or Deputy Directors since 1975. The direct recruits to which category the petitioners belong and the transferred Field Officers Group A working in the P & T Board of Director (Telecommunications) were recruited at the entry level of Junior Class I Officers of S & T.Os, Grade I and they continued to be en ged so till now. In view of the fact that the offi cers who are likely to be affected by the decision are not impleaded as parties by name to these petitions, this Court, HELD: 1:1 The direct recruit tions to which categories the petitioners belonged belongs are not given any Special Pay in those grades and they are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It is not deputation allowance. It was paid for the arduous and special nature of the functions to be discharged in the Telephone Training Centre. [1010C E] 1:2 The two categories of persons who are similarly getting Special Pay are of the order of 275 while only about 25 officers who are direct recruits working in P &T Board Control Centre are not give ing any special Pay in these grades and that they are giving only the benefit at the same rates to the transferred officers working in that centre with effect from the date which the transferred officer have been drawing the Special Pay.

The appellant, an employee of an industry governed by the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, framed a charge sheet against him in respect of certain acts of misconduct, gross negligence of duty insubordination etc. on May 13, 1965. An enquiry held on May 15, after receipt of written statement from Nathu, holding that the charges were proved, the employer dismissed the third respondent with effect from August 1, 1965 on the ground that the charge sheet was not proper. That order was confirmed by the Labour Court in appeal and revision filed before the State Industrial Tribunal contending inter alia that the finding was based only on his statement and in particular his cross examination. The High Court allowed the 'appeal of the appellant holding that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42(4) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour court under section 7 8 (1)D). Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (i) The scheme of Chapter VIII seems to be that in regard to any "change" in an industrial matter there must be compliance with the provisions of that Chapter. [737 A] (ii) The object of which was to make numerous changes in the Act shows in its Statement of Objects and Reasons that clause 31 of the Bill was meant to 'enlarge the powers of the Labour Courts under section 78(1) D.P.C., it is not necessary to take note of other Chapters excepting section 123 in Chapter VIII headed "changes". The scheme underlying the Act is that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the Industrial Court. [ 739 D, H] (iii) Sub section (5) of section 78 which provides for award of compensation against an offence is provided for, determines the compensation and order it, payment; C require any employer to (a) withdraw any change which is held by it to be illegal or withdraw temporarily any change the legality of which is a matter of issue in any proceeding pending final decision, or (b) carry out any change provided such change is a matters in issue in the proceedings before it.

The contesting respondents have been occupying the property under a registered lease for a period of 20 years which expired on 31.7.1971. They served a notice on the appel lants claiming the right to contin ue in possession after 31.07.1971 as tenants from month to month. The appellants did not accept the claim and filed before Munsif, Ranchi a case purporting to be an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent & Evic tion) Control Act, 1947 before the Munsif was not maintain able. The respondents filed a regular appeal from the decision before the District Judge, Ranchi designated as Judicial Commissioner, and he also went into the entire controversy thoroughly. The parties led full evidence both oral and documentary. On an elaborate trial the learned Tribu nal accepted the appellants ' case that they were the successors in interest of the lessor company, and the legal representatives of late S.N. Ganguli had formed a partnership as a result of which a new month to months tenancy was created, and that the respondents, therefore, were not liable to eviction. The trial court accordingly directed the respond ents to vacate the premises. On appeal by the respondents the learned Judicial Commis sioner agreed with the findings of the Trial Court on merits and concluded in paragraph 48 of thejudg ment thus: "In view of the findings on the disputed issues of fact between the parties, they are not necessary to be detailed". The parties lead full evidence, both oral & documentary. on the admitted issues and after an elaborate adduce ence the learned Munsif accepted the appell lants ' case; that he is the successors of late M/s. Ganapathi Properties (Pvt) Ltd. Limited, the predecessor in title of the appellants. The company has granted the lease in favour of one S.M. Ganguli who on his death was succeeded by his legal representatives. There was due attornment of the tenancy and lessees were liable to vacate t he premises on 31st July, 1971, but did not receive any orders from the landlords and their heirs. No month to year tenan cy had been created; and that they have formed a fresh partnership in September 1977 and approached the High Court by way of second appeal, presum ably because the Judicial Commit tment after deciding the disputed issue in favour o f the present appellants instead of confirming the decree of 977 the Munsif directed them to file a fresh application under sec. 12(3) of the Act for evicting the responds if they did not vacate within the time allowed by court, and accordingly modified the decision of the trial Court in so far as the learned Munsiff had directed that his order would be executed and the respondents would be evicted from the premises on their failure to vacate within time. The respondent 's revision application preferred before the Patna High Court was dis missed. The learned Judicial Commissioner who heard the case held that in absence of a month 's notice under section 10(1) from the tenant, the application of the appe lants was not maintainable before the Munsiff and the entire proceeding was mis conceived, and directed the respondents to vacate. On further appeal by thorities, the Judicial Commissioner agreed with t he findings of fact that the appellants are the successorsin interest of late Mrs. S. N. Ganguli, Advocate, appearing for them before him, designated as judicial Com missioner, and also went up to decide the issues between the par ties and granting one month 'fine time to the respondents (appellants before him) for vacating the premises and further held that the appeLants would have to make an application u/s 12(2) of and thus the appellants would have made another applica tion under section 13(3). The learned judicial Commissioner confined his decision to deciding the issues.

The appellant a registered Society filed the suit against one Hari Narain Swami through his Secretary who was numbered as Suit No. 11 of 1973, in respect of an immovable property through its then Secretary which was numbered at serial No. 116/ 1974. After the institution of the suit, an election of the office bearers of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as the Secretary. On 4.9.74 a prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by Hari Narain Vidhya through another lawyer claiming to have been elected as its Secretary on 4.8.1974, and according t he appellant ' s case one Shri Laxman Das Mahant Swami was also elected as Secretary. The trial court after holding that the appellant had 's application filed under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable proceeded further to consider the question as to who was the duly elected Secretary of the appellant Society, entitled to prosecute or withdraw the suit and accepted the case of Hari Narain Pandit. Being aggrieved by the order withdrawal of the Suit, Hari Narain S/o Shri Laxman S/O Shri Badri Narain Swami filed a civil miscellaneous application before the High Court praying for recalling the order of withdrawal and restoring the suit to its file. The prayer was contested and the trial court rejected the application. The High Court agreed with the trial Court that the application under section15 1 of CPC was not entertainable. While agreeing with the argument of the appel lant that the Trial Court has jurisdiction to cancel the order permitting the withdrawal of suit under its inherent power, if it is ultimately satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree on a fraudulent repre sentation made to it that the party had actually consented to it. However, since no notice was given of his applica tion for withdrawal of t he suit either to the then Secretary Laxman Das Shree or to the learned advocates Sri Satya Narain Sharma or Sri Shyam Bihari Agarwal, through whom the suit had been instituted, none of them had any knowledge of the order passed by the Court. Later, in the next election another Secretary named Jeeva Nand Swami was chosen, and when he learnt about the fate of the complaint, an application was filed for recalling of the said order and restoring that suit to his file. Aggrieved by the aforesaid order, Hari Narayan Swami filed an appeal before the Division Bench, which was also dismissed by the impugned judgment. It is contended on behalf of the respond ent 's that the trial chal lenged the order allowing withdrawal of its suit under inherent power and the High Courts have rightly held that the only remedy of the the appellant is to file a fresh suit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The case has to go back to the trial courts for reconsideration of the evidence on merits. [237D E] 2.1 A dispute relating to election of its Secretary had arisen between the parties which ultimately went before the Registrar o f the Cooperative Societies who decided the matter in 237 favour of Laxman Dasr Swami and against Hari Narain super president. A writ petition filed thereafter by Hari Narayan S/0 Shri Badri Narayan S Kulkarni, was dismissed.

The appellant who was the accused No. 1 before the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate 's Court, Bombay was charged along with others for having transferred by sale of High Denomination Bank Notes of Denomination of Rs. 1000 each to one Velji Lakhamshi Joshi for Rs. 1000 at the rate of Rs 180 per note and thereby contravening the provisions of section 4 of the Ordinance read with section 109 Of the Indian Penal Code. The trial ended in his conviction and sentence against him along with the co accused of the offence with which they had been charged. He was sentenced to pay a fine of Rs . 8,000 and in default suffer six months ' rigorous imprisonment and the co Accused of the appellant were awarded varying sentences of fine with which however the appellant was not concerned. The High Court agreed with the trial court that Ordinance I of 1946 promulgated by the Governor General on January 12, 1946, was in operation on July 11, 1953 when the offence under section 7 read with s. 4 thereof was committed by the appellant and the appellant 's conviction for offences punishable under sections 7 & 8 were confirmed by the High Court. It was contended that the Ordinance did not cease to be in operation under the date when the Act was promulgated and that therefore the prosecution was not maintainable. Held, that the imposition of punishment by imprisonment under section 3 Of the Ordinance, would be without any limitation. The ordinance having been promulgated during the period between June 27, 1940 and April 1, 1946 was perpetual in duration and continued in force until it was repealed. It is not necessary to refer to the other Ordinances appearing in this compilation but suffice it to say that in respect of all the Ordinances which were thus promulgated by him, the continuance thereof even after April 1 was predicated and the adaptations prescribed in the Adaptation of Laws Order, 1950 issued under the Constitution of India were made applicable thereto.

Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) A decision on a question of sentence depending upon the facts and circumstances of a particular case can never be regarded as a binding precedent much less 'law declared ' within the meaning of Article 141 of the Constitution so as to bind all Courts in the country. [1073 C D] Rajendra Prasad vs State of Maharashtra ; , followed. (2) In order to discard it is to disobey the Constitution and such subversiveness of the rule of law, in a crucial area of life and death, will spell judicial disorder. To day, the law is what Rajendra Prasad has for his own advocate the death penalty for certain classes of offenders, (I) Sentencing and Probation National College of the State Judiciary, Reno, Neveda p.68. [ 1074 A] (3) The process at the sentencing stage is a functional failure because of the casual way the punishment factors are dealt with as if the nature of the crime was the sole determinant of the punishment; and (4) the judicial discretion vested in the Court regarding its imposition on an accused are constitutionally valid. That decision, it may incidentally be pointed out has adverted to the "well settled principles" which have all these years governed the exercise of proper judicial discretion. [1007 E] (4). It is not within the province of the court while dealing with an appeal confined to sentence under Article 136, to curtail the scope of death sentence under section 302 I.P.C., 1860, nor is it constitutionally or legally permissible for this Court while hearing such an appeal to lay down that on grounds of compassion and humanism the sentence of death on a conviction for murder under section 304/109, as a rule of universal application, be substituted by a sentence of imprisonment for life, irrespective of the gravity of the clime as the surrounding circumstances is not for the Parliament to decide. [1000 B] (5) If the general observations on sentencing jurisprudence made in Rajendra Prasad 's case are to be regarded 'law so declared by this Court within the expression "special reasons" necessary for imposing death penalty must relate, not to the crime as such but to the criminal". The question of abolition of capital punishment is a difficult and controversial subject, long and hotly debated. It has evoked during the past two decades strong conflicting views, as was pointed out by me in Rajendra P. Sharma vs Shri S.I.T. . ; applied. (6) Section 302 I I. P.C. confers upon the Court a discretion in the matter of the sentence to be imposed for an offence of murder and the court has to choose between a sentence one of death and a sentence Of imprisonment for Life; while under section 354(3) Cr.P., 1973, the Court is enjoined with a duty to record "special reason ' in case the extreme penalty is awarded.
