But the question whether the death sentence should be awarded or not must, in my view, be left to the discretion of the Judge trying the accused and the question of awarding sentence must depend upon the fact and circumstances obtaining in such cases. [1018 E G] (7) Expert opinion based on the combined effect of (i) and (ii) above (iii) is the material element in the decision for it determines 1074 finally their rights and liabilities in relation to the subject matter of action. The court has, therefore, power to choose either between a Judge of law and a ' sentence of life imprisonment.

The appellant was in service upto 30th April 1958 when he was prematurely retired. One of the defences urged before the authorities related to confused nature of charges characterised by him as "vague, overlapping", intermingled" and wrongly joined together. He also pleaded that there had been an enquiry in 1949 by Shri A. K. Bose, Deputy Director Investigation or against whom charges were framed on 30th December, 1953, and about others in 1952 by Shri R. N. Srivastava, another Inspecting Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax, Meerut, which was conducted by Shri G. section Srivastava, Inspecting Assistant Commissioners (Income tax). The second charge given particulars of thirteen assessment cases in which the appellant was alleged to have been either "grossly negligent or careless, inefficient and/or corrupt in the performance of his duties as Income tax Officer". The appellant 's defence was that he had made various investments in the name of various members of his family far in excess of and disproportionate to the known sources of his income. He further contended that there bad been an inquiry by Shri P. R. Gupta, Inspecting Assist ant Commissioner regarding some of the matters mentioned in the charges. He pleaded complaints that a fresh enquiry into the same charges was not permissible under the Departmental rules and was also barred by rules of natural justice. The trial court upheld these pleas and granted certificate to appeal to this Court on the ground that some material facts were suppressed or misrepresented for this purpose. 501 Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The plea raised by the appellant that there has been an ' enquiry in 1948 by Shri S. Srivastava and Shri R.[583 C] If an inquiry is held at a particular stage possibly to determine whether regular proceedings should be drawn up or started, it does not debar a departmental trial. That was the nature of the previous enquiries. It would depend upon the circumstances of each case. This confidence tends to be shaken if there is excessive delay between hearing of arguments and delivery of judgments. Justice, as we have often observed must not only be done but must manifestly appear to be done. On 4th March, 1971, however, the High Court refusing the certificate of fitness of the case for appeal to the Supreme Court observed that questions had been attempted to be raised before it in asking for certification which had not been argued at the time when the first appeal was heard by the High court.

The appellants, who were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh, were assessed to sales tax under section 3(a) of the . The High Court came to the conclusion that the contracts between the appel lants and M M.M.T.C. were interlinked with the contract entered into by M.S.C., the first respondent and M.A. who was the exporter and shipper of the goods, holding that these contracts were distinct and independent con tract of sale entered into in the course of export. The High COurt took the view that the appellants were the first purchasers within the state and therefore they were liable to pay the tax. The Court also held that the contract between the appellant and M/M.Stictico nary did not render these contracts F.O.B. contracts with the M.E.C and that the actual exportation of the materials. The Union of India appealed, by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1. There was no privity of contract between M/s.ticoan nary purchasers and the foreign buyers from the S.T .C. on board the ship. [444A C] 2. unless there is a single sale which itself causes the export or is in progress or process of export, there cannot be two last purchasers in the sale of same goods within the same State. Similarly, there could not be two contracts either inte grated or the contract to between the merchant and the S .T.E., an F. O.B., a contract with a foreign buyer. This Court in Serajuddin 's case referred to. In the instant case, it was said that the agreement between the M/Sticohanan nanded on board ship were in the way of exportation pursuant to the export sale (See Serajiduddin ' 's Case). [444E] 3. In view of the fact that the first appellant and the third appel tants entered into direct contract with their foreign buyers on F.0.B, the contracts were different. Since they are two separate and independent contracts of sale there cannot have been two or more sales in the cueeenment of export of goods within it. [548D] 4. It is not because of any peculiarity of F.o.B contracts but because in this type of contract the seller 's duty is to deliver the goods F.Os.B Thus, even if they are different contracts, as they are in the present case, the last purchaser within the Government is the M .M.F.C.[444C] 5. The first appellant was the importers and shippers of the, goods. In Serajuluddin ' s case (supra) this Court relied on FO.A., the decision in National Tractors Hubli vs Commissioner of Commercial Taxes Bangalore ; , followed.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974 with effect from 19st October,1974 on the grounds inter alia that he was not found suitable for the Post to which he was appointed. The Labour Court held that the termination was neither illegal nor improper but unjustified and consequently it held that his termination would not constitute retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) read with section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. With this award the appellant filed an appeal before the Labour Court, Delhi. During the pendency of the appeal, the respondent again moved for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate in the proceedings which motion was granted. The respondent contended that he had been a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of this extended period of probation his services were terminated by letters dated 12.10.1974, 24th April 1976 and 13.1079 whereby he informed the appellant that his service should have been terminated on the expiration of initial period of extension, namely, June 8, 1974. The labour Court found in favour of the respondent and it was held that there was nothing in the two aforementioned decisions which is inconsistent with each other and taking note of the decision in Delhi Cloth & General Mills Ltd. vs Shambu Nath Mukerjee; , , setting aside ex parte orders as well as for granting permission to appear in the proceeding. The appellant contended (1) that the Labour court on evaluation of evidence both oral and documentary, held that termination was not illegal nor unjustified and therefore the claim of the appellant was negatived; and (2) that even assuming that this note incorporates all the necessary rules and regulations in the contract of employment, it was incumbent upon the respondent to show that even when appointment is not shown to be on probation in the order of appointment, in view of the rules governing the contract for employment. it would nonetheless be a retrenchment within section 2 (oo) and in the absence of strict compliance with the requirements of section 25 F, termination was held invalid. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 In the present case, the appellant is employed and was on duty from December 8, 1973 to October 19, 1974 when his service was terminated. 1096 (2)(a) and he must be deemed to be in continuous service for a period of one year for the purpose of Chapter VA. It is not necessary for the purposes of sub section (2), to determine first the relevant date, i.e., the date of termination of services which is complained of as retrenchment. After that date was ascertained, move backward to a period 1 of 12 months just preceding the dateof retrenchment and then ascertain whether within the period of 12 calendar months, the workman has rendered service for 240 days.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. He was served with a charge sheet on February 22, 1955 and after making his explanation to the charge sheet he was called upon to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against him. He submitted his explanation before the Settlement Officer and the Deputy Commissioner by order of March 17, 1955 ordered that the services of Madan Gopal Inspector be terminated forthwith and that in lieu of notice he would get one month 's pay as required by the rules and that he will get one months 's salary as required under the Punjab Holdings (Disciplinary &Dismissi tion) Rules. The appellant was served a charge sheeted on February 23, 1955 which was followed by an order dated March 17th, 1955. He challenged the authority of the Settlement officer to hold the enquiry and submit a memorial to the Minister for Revenue affairs. After considering his explanation the Deputy Commis sioner passed an order dismissing him from service. The High Court held that the appellant was not dismissed or removed from service but his employment was terminated by the impugned order, and that the order of dismissal from service was in contravention of article 311 (2) of the Constitution as no reasonable opportunity to showcause against the order had been given. Held, further, that in view of the settlement Officer with which view the Deputy Commissioners agreed the misdemeanor was proved, the appellant could not be dismissed or removing from service until he had been communicated, such an enquiry and order consequent upon the report made in the enquiry will not fall within the principle of Ram Narayan Das 's case (1). Held further that the fact of the holding of the an enquiry is not decisive of the question. What is decisive is whether the order is by way of punishment ,in the light of the tests laid down in Parshotam Lal Dhingra case and State of Orissa vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, [1958) S.C.R.828, relied on.

The respondent, a Professor of a College affiliated to the University of Jammu and Kashmir, claimed that he should be promoted as Professor in accordance with the law. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government 's order on its merits. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD : 1. The question whether the requirement for consulting the Commission is mandatory or not does not arise in this case because it is not disputed that and was in fact the case of the appellant State that the Commission was consulted. [872H; 873A] 2. On the facts brought on the record, that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. The State Government had stated in its reply to the writ peti tion that for every post of Professor, names of four Lecturers strictly in order of seniority were sent to the Commission "at its direction" and they were interviewed by the Selection Committee which was "formed" by the Commission and a member of the Commission, was appointed its Chairman. The Commission set out the reasons for its decision, and finally made its recommendation on merits. [888B] 3. It is not provided in section 133 that all the members of the commission should have interviewed all or any of the candidates, or that it was not permissible for the Commission to entrust the selection to a Committee consisting of only one of its members, so long as the Commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility.

The petitioner filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of the House of Commons and a writ of mandamus to restrain the Committee from publishing the proceedings of the Assembly. The controversy in this case was as regards privilege based on the fundamental right guaranteed by article 19(1) (a) of the constitution. It was contended, inter alia: that the privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the freedom conferred on a citizen under article 19 (1) of that Constitution and the Act does not fall within the purview of the article; the privileges and immunities enjoyed by the House or Houses are subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by articles 19(2), 19. (3) that the powers, privileges and immunity of the State of Bihar conferred on Parliament were not excluded in article 19, because the provisions of article 194(3) were confined only to matters specified in cls. (1), (2) and (4) respectively of Article 194 which provided for restrictions made under cl. (5) of article 84, which dealt with the power, privileges, immunities and immunities of the Houses of Parliament and of its members and committees thereof. It is also contended that on the facts of the case, there was no violation of the provisions contained in article 194; (ii) that even if section 194(2) were to be read as a whole, it must be held that the legislature of a "State" had the privilege to prevent any citizen from publishing or publish anything relating to the proceedings, and not to a case of privilege having been made by the Legislature for over a century; (iii) The fundamental right under article19(1)(a), inasmuch as the petitioner was given freedom to speech and expression which includes freedom of propagation of ideas and their publication, it did not necessarily mean that it is not so subject, and that the several clauses of articles 194 or article 105 should be taken as subject to this provisions of the Act which gives freedom of speech and option. Held, also, that article 194 of the Indian Constitution does not in express terms make that clause subject to article 19 must be deemed to have been made subject to any provisions of law made by Parliament or declared a particular law to be in force unless modified by Parliament; (iv)that even if article 194 was to operate as an exemption from such operation, it would still be void under article 13(2); and (v) that though the privilege was not expressly made subject, the restrictions imposed were within the ambit of article 19. State of Madras vs Gannon Dunkerley & Co., ; , followed.

A private college was taken over by the Government in pursuance of the unanimous resolution of the managing committee of February 18, 1970 and later transferred to the Government. The Government took over the management of the College on and from March 9, 1971. This was done as a going educational concern and it went without saying that it must be administered on sound lines having regard to the quality, efficiency and progress in all respects. It was also decided that the services of those not found suitable by the P.S.C. will also be terminated by giving one month 's notice in each case. The Respondents filed a writ petition before this Court against the validity of the circular on the ground that they were drawing as Reader salary less than Rs.600/ and that since under the terms of the take over, they were drawn monthly salary less Rs.640/ on the date of taking over. their names were not referred to the Public Service Commission for consid eration of their suitability for appointment as Readers in the Government College. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the Respondents were entitled to consideration by the Public Services Commission for appointment to posts as Readers ' and hence they had no rela tence, whatsoever. In appeal it was contended on behalf of the Respondents that since the P .S.S., Class II (Lecturer 's grade) in Government service, they are not enti tled to be considered by the Govern ment for appointment since Government may not undertake to take over all the employees by maintaining the billabong of a status quo ante. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The requirement of 8 years of teaching experience is clearly violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. When a fairly well recognised institution, as in this case run for more than a century, is completely taken over, by the Gov ernment for management, it is not merely taking over the land and buildings, tables andduces Accountants but also improvements. It has to tackle, at the same time, a human problem, that is to say, the fate of the teachers and the staff serving that institu tion.

The appellants made applications for temporary permits to ply their vehicles on the route. The U.P. State Road Transport Corporation (Corporation for short) also made an application for grant of three temporary permits for the same purpose and the application was rejected on the ground that once a scheme has been published in view of the provision contained in section 68 F(1 A), the Corporation alone to the exclusion of others, is entitled to apply for temporary permit and if such application is made by the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled, to obtain a temporary permit. The appellants moved the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and writ petition to the High Court did not meet with success. It was common ground that in respect of the route a scheme had been prepared and published under section 68 C of Chapter IV A of the . The route in question was an inter regional route and therefore an application made for temporary Permit for the period intervening between the date of publication of the scheme and the date on publication of approved or modified scheme has to be made to the State transport Authority under sec. 68(1) C. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: There are 7 vacancies for which 4 temporary permits could be issued by the State ' Transport Corporation on this inter regional highway route. Therefore, therefore, there were 6 vacancies for temporary temporary permits and the Corporation was able to provide only one vehicle and there is felt need for providing transport service on the routes in question.

The appellant was the son of 'L ' and, in virtue of a registered mortgage deed executed by him under which his father inherited certain properties from his maternal grandfather, the ancestor of respondents I to 9 for Rs. 5,000. In suit No. 145 of 1946 filed by the appel lant the appellant claimed a declaration that the two transactions of mortgage and sale in question did not bind his own reversionary rights, because the impugned alienation were without consideration and were not supported by any legal necessity. The trial judge held that the property in dispute was ancestral qua the appellant 1101 and that the impugned alienations were not effected for consideration or for legal necessity and dismissed the suit. In appeal to the District Court, it was contended on behalf of the appeli lant: (i) that the suit had abated in the trial court as a result of the death of one of the defendants pending the decision of the trial judge; and (ii) that by virtue of Hindu Law the properties inherited by the respondent were not ancestral property because the said transactions were without considera tion. Held, that on the terms of a proper mortgage deed, which was found to be performed in good faith, it could be safely presumed that it was executed for legal purposes. The doctrine of stare decisis is not so imperative or inflexible as to preclude a departure therefrom in any case. Even if an earlier decision had been reversed by the subsequent Full Bench in 1950, the said decision must be taken to have been overruled. Once this Court decided on the question whether the property inherited from his paternal grandfather was ancestral property or not, it would be difficult to say that the doctrine of pronounce stare decisis applied because the previous decision in the case of N. K. Ponnuswami vs Veerarathnam Mudaliar (1908) L. R. 45 I.A. 203, referred to.

The appellants were tried and convicted under section 449 and section 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The Sessions Judge accepted that verdict and convicted them all under sections 449 and 307 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for four years under section 448. He also sentenced them under section 324/34 'of the Indian penal Code and to two years under s. 450 of the I.P.C., and one year under section 458, I. P.C. The other three appellants appealed to the High Court which dismissed their appeal. A Bench of the High court gave the appellant a certificate that this was a fit case for appeal to this Court. Held, (i) that there is no substance in either of these contentions. Section 449 prescribes the punishment for house trespass if it is done "in order to" the committing of any offence punishable with imprisonment. The words "inorder to" have been used by the legislature not only in section 449 I.C but in the two succeeding sections 450, 451 and 457. The act did not result in death of one of the other persons to kill Ebrar Ali with the dagger on the neck as if the act had been done by himself alone. (ii) Section 449 I .P. C. prescribes the punishments for house imprisonment trespass if they are committed "in" order to 'the committing of theft. There could be no doubt that the words " in order to have been use by the Legislature not onlyin section cattle but also in section 457, I0I49 and 457, and more so sections 451, 454 and 457 will apply it the house trespass or lurking house trespass, or lharking house breaking by night or house breaking of night. But once it is decided that the act is so done by a number of persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, the legal position that results is that each person shall be held to have committed the entire criminal act. (iii) Section 459 I.A. has no application as it overlooks the legal fiction that the acts committed by a particular number of people shall in the circumstances mentioned in section 34 I0o49 I45 and not in section 454 and section 457 should apply it in the present case.

In the partition of India a portion of the land in village Bhadroya was acquired for the Kangra Valley Railway and a sum of Rs. 1,539 7 0 was awarded to Musammat Melo. On an objection by the appellant that the properties in suit being in possession of tenants the suit was not maintainable in view of the provisions of the Indian Succession Act relating to succession certificates the Sub Judge held (i) that the lands in suit were non ancestral and (ii) that in view, in view Of section 23 of the Hindu Succession Act, it was necessary for him to produce a Riwaj i am which is a reliable and trustworthy document. On appeal by the respondent the High Court held that though the appellant 's father had not filed any nomination paper before the Sub judge as required by section 2(i)(b) of the , he had failed to discharge the burden that was initially on him by producing in evidence showing the custom in Rattigan 's Digest. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (i ) that in any case there was no custom whereunder the collaterals of the father who was the last male holder excluded the daughter from succession to the self acquired property of her father and had, therefore, failed to discharged his onus by producing documentary evidence showing that the collateral 's of one Harnam Singh who was also a Sarswat Brahmin of the Gurdaspur district were reliable and unimpeachable documents. (2) that even if the presumption as to the correctness of the Riwazi am be weak, the respondent had not cited a single instance of a daughter having excluded the collateral in succession to self acquired properties of her deceased father; (3) that if on production by the appel lant of the Qaw i am of the jawaj i m of the Kpali district prepared by Mr. Kennaway himself in 1913 and (4) a Rwaj i Am of 1913 showing that defendant ever excluded the executant from succession, his father would lead to a result favourable to the collateralS; and (5) the appellant must succeed. Held: (1) that on production of Riwraj i am a reliable document, has been carefully prepared and does not contain within its four corners contradictory statements of custom and in the opinion of the Settlement Officer is not a record of the wishes of the persons appearing before him as to what the custom should be, it would be a presumptive piece of evidence in proof of the special custom set up.

The respondent, at the material time the Managing Director of Messrs Bird and Co., Ltd. was acting as a sole trustee of certain companies registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. He was also a director of a number of Companies, registered under Indian Companies Acts, 1913, as being acting as an executor or administrator of estates of deceased persons and as trustees of various estates. The Collector referred the matter to the High Court under section 57(2) of the Indian Stamp Act which stated his own opinion that the stamp duty was payable on the power for as many respective capacities as the principal executes the power. The reference, was heard by a Bench consisting of the Chief Justice Das, Das, J., and section R. Das Gupta, J. who differed in their opinion. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word "matters" in section 5 is synonymous with the word 'description ' occurring in section 6. Held, further (per curiam), that it would fall under article 48(a) in whatever capacity it was executed, and that when two persons join in executing a power of attorney in respect of all matters in which he could act, it should be held to comprise distinct matters, and as the instrument in question did not contain separate words, section 5 would apply even when the instrument consisted matters of the same description. The transaction is a single transaction whereby the donor constitutes the donees jointly and severally his attorneys for him and in his name and on his behalf to act for him in his individual capacity and also in his capacity as managing director, director, managing agent etc., dealing with various affairs with which he was concerned. Held further, that though enjoying different capacities, he is the same individual who functions though he in different capacities and conducts his affairs in the various capacities which he enjoys but as a single individual. The fact that the donor of the power of Attorney executes it in different capacity is not sufficient to constitute the instrument one comprising distinct matters and thus requiring to be stamped with the aggregate amount of the duties with which separate instruments each comprising or relating to one of such matters would be chargeable under the Act, within the meaning of section 5. The. transaction is one whereby the donee constitutes the doinges jointly with the donor in favour of the doneves constituting the donee his attorney to act on behalf for him, and in its instance he held that if that was the position, it was but logical that whatever acts the donor was capable of performing whether in his personal capacity or in his representative capacity as trustee or as executor or Administrator were also comprised within the instrument and were not distinct matters to be dealt with as such so as to attract the operation of section S.5.

The assessee company was the assessee in each of these appeals which were filed before the High Court under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The said appeal was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner which held that the expression "or which would have been allowed to him if the Indian income tax Act 1922 had actually been in force in Saurashtra in the past" did not permit the Income tax Officer to make any deduction under this head. In second appeals the High court held that since the assessee assessee was carrying on business in Bhavnagar which was formerly an Indian State and in 1948 he could not be said to have made a claim for the depreciation allowance and so no depreciation allowance would then be allowed to the assessee if the Bombay Income tax Ordinance, 1949, had been in operation by the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) amendment of 1950 was not retrospective; (ii) the words "if a claim had been made" in para 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order were vague and indefinite because, at the relevant time there was no dispute about the depreciation allowed under the Saurashtra Income tax ordinance and therefore no depreciation could be allowed in computing the written down value. HELD: The provisions of this paragraph applied to these two cases of assessment for 1951 52 and under them the depreciation already availed of by the assessees under the Bhavnagar War Profits Act had to be deducted in ascertaining the written up value, but the deletion of this part was not by way of profit making allowance; (iii) that the words actually used were not sufficient to express and give effect to this intention. [225 E G] Although section 10(5)(b) of a Part B State Act which provides that certain difficulties had arisen in giving effect to the provisions of any of the Acts, rules or orders extended by section 3 or section II to any State or merged territory, the order was made by the Central Government on December 2, 1950, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 12 of the Finance Act, 1950. That provision ran thus: " All depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a part B State relating to income tax and super tax or any law relating to tax on profits of business shall be taken into account in computing its written down values under section 10 (5) (b) Of the Indian Incometax Act, [225 G] (iv) The words "actually allowed" in section 13(5) are not "depreciation allowed" but "deatuity applicable" is a law relating of income tax which was law of a.

One of the conditions for submission of tender forms namely: (a) Audited Balance Sheet/certificate from Chartered Ac countant for preceding three years; (b) Contest income tax clearance Certificate; The issue of blank tender books was to be between 23rd January to 27th January 1989 and the completed tender books had to be submitted by 3.00 p.m. on 6.2.89. These were scrutinised with reference to the prequal qualifying requirements and data on experience, work done etc. as furnished by each of the applicants. The Tender Authority submitted its recom ments for grant of contract forms for the construction work of a plant at an estimated cost of about Rs. 1.8 crores. In view of the fact that M.C.,C. did not comply with the pre scribed condition, it rejected the petitioner 's tender. On appeal, the Karnataka Power Corpora tion Ltd. (K.P.C.), an instrumentality of the State of Karnataka in favour of the Mysore Construction Co., (M .C. C.) filed a writ petition and a further Writ Appeal in the Karnataka High Court having been unsuccessful, he has preferred this Special Leave Petition from the judgment of the High Court in the writ appeal. The facts necessary for the disposal of the appeal are: (i) There was nothing unfair or arbitrary about the award of the contract tO the M. C.C.; and (ii) The High Court did not express any opinion as to the nature of the requirements set out in Para V but was satisfied on an overall view that there was nothing unreasonable or arbitraryality about the awarding of the Contract. Allowing the Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1. It is well settled that while exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution, it is not for this Court to reap praise the facts on merits and come to one conclusion or other with regard to these aspects of the matter. [234B] 1.2 The second consequence, indicated by this Court in Ramana 's case (supra) will be readily applied by Courts to a case where a person complains that a departure from the qualifi cations has kept him out of the race injustice is less apparent where the attempt of the applicant before court is only to gain immunity from competition. [237G] 1:3. Even if para V cannot but be read with para I and that the supply of some of the documents referred to in para V is indispensable to assess whether the applicant fulfills the pre qualification, it has not deprived the appellant of its right to be considered for the contract; on the other hand, its tender has received due and full consideration. If, save for the delay in filing one of the relevant docu ments, M.D.C.(C.I.), it is open to the K.P.,C., to decline relief. [236E F] 1 :4. The action of the first respondent in accepting the tender of 4th respondents even though they did not satisfy the pre qualifica tion stipulated under the pre em plation, was clearly discriminatory. Since this Court had already directed in Ramna 's Case (supra), that only a person running a regis tered.
