Held:(i) The contention that the revisional power could not be exercised when there was an appeal provided but no appeal is filed after notice was a general and open remand where all questions on the merits are to be reconsidered or was only a limited remand and if so what the limitations are.

The appellant Union made a claim for bonus for the relevant four years prior to 1965, when trouble began. The dispute was founded on tradition or custom or condition of service and in that light the references to the Industrial Tribunal relating to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 were not such as a matter which had to be adjudicated, and it also did not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act. However, in his view, the Bonus Act was a complete code, and no species of bonus could survive outside the contours of that statute. The Tribunal found, although the demand for bonus was barred by res judicata, the industrial dispute referred by the State Government to the Tribunal was a matter relating to a totally different type of bonus, namely, customary bonus or one which was a term of the employment itself and that as such fell squarely within the Bonus act. On an application made before it by the appellant Union for relief under article 226, it was dismissed in limine on the ground that the demand was barred either by resjudicata; the arbitration tribunal did not enter the merits of the claim but dismissed it in limine. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the respondent, it had been urged that articles 14, 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution were unnecessary for the respondents to substantiate the plea that the claim put forward by the workers was not based on profits or the financial results of the employers but was based on custom. HELD: (Per Gajendragadkar, J.) The award of the Industrial tribunal relating to both the claims must fail. [610 E] (1) In the instant case, the Tribunal failed to enter the merit of the claims; and it could not therefore be annihilated by implication, other distinct and different categories of bonus such as the one oriented on custom, and service condition not one based on profit. [600 F G] (2) The main question about the policy of the Parliament that was agitated in that case turned on the availability of the as an independent method of claiming profit bonus de hors the Bonus Acts and that it would be subversive of the scheme of the Act to allow an invasion from the flank in that manner. [599 C] (3)(a) The reasons for considering this question were: (1 ) Where a plurality of unions pollute workers ' unity and create situations calling for investigation into the representativeacy of the party appearing before it or court, (2 ) whether the bonus Act provides for an award to persons employed in certain establishments not in all establishments; (3) whether such a demand can be legitimately made by the workmen ' were set out in that decision. [501 D E] In the present case, therefore the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to try the dispute referred to it and no question of customary or contract bonus was urged for the year 1965 1965 and so, the mere fact that the reference was based only on a claim of profit did not detract from the claim of customary bonus. [ 604 C D] (b) The Industrial Tribunal rightly rejected this contention on the grounds of res judicata. Since the bonus has not been related by reference to any festival by the respondents in their pleadings, the scope and reasons of the BonusAAct is different. [106 A B] (4)(a). A perusal of the Statement of the case shows that it relates to a case of profit bonus urged under the two sets of workmen, engaged by establishments which are either excluded or exempted from the Bonus Scheme. The main grievance raised in this appeal was not merely a claim based on an implied agreement but also for a consequential point covered by the reference. [ 610 A B]. (5)(a); and (b).

The writ petitioners in the two Writ Petitions are promotees and those who were promoted to the Higher Judicial Service from the Haryana Superior Judicial Service. Some of the members of the judicial service of the State as Additional District & Sessions Judges for two or three years prior to the appointment of Respondent 3 directly to that Service lost their seniority over him by being allotted a date of confirmation which was one day later than the date on which he completed his probationary period. These rules were previously framed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court, in exercise of the powers conferred under Article 309 of the Constitution. Rule 12 as it originally stood originally was revived with effect from April 1, 1970 with retrospective effect from March 9, 1976 with retrospective operation from April 9,1976 and July 2, 1977 with retrospective from April 3, 1977. It is alleged that the seniority of the promotees and direct recruits was wrongly determined by the length of continuous officiation in a post in the Superior Judicial Services. The petitioners in writ petitions Nos. 4228 to 4230 of 1978 assailed the validity of the rules on the ground that their seniority qua direct recruits is wrongly made, unjustly made to depend upon the fortuitous circumstance of the date of their confirmation in the Higher judicial Service; that even if a substantive vacancy is available, the confirmation of a promotee in that vacancy is postponed arbitrarily and indefinitely, that promotees are treated with an unequal hand qua direct recruit for example, a promotee despite his satisfactory performance and availability of a substantive vacancies in which he can be confirmed, is continued in an officiating capacity until after a direct recruit completes his probation and is due for confirmation, and that the High Courts applied the principle of rotation as between promotees and promotees at the time of their regularisation when on December 31, 1976, the Governor had amended the rules in 1972 with retrospective effective effect from January 9, 1970. The High Court rejected the writ petitions against which W.P. 266/79 filed in this court by twenty two promotees a petition under Article 32 of the constitution was also dismissed on December 13, 1977 as time barred, and hence this appeal. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. A combined reading of Articles 235 and 309 would yield the result that though the control over Subordinate Courts is vested in the High court, the appropriate legislature and until that legislature acts, the President of the High COurt has the power to make rules regulating the recruitment and conditions of service of judicial officers of the state. The power to legislate on seniority being subject to all other provisions of the Supreme Court cannot be exercised in a manner which will affect or be detrimental to the control vested in an High Court by Article 235. [1057G H, 1058A] 2. Though the legislature or the Governor has the right to regulate seniority of judicial officer by laying down rules of general application, that power cannot be invoked in a way which will defeat or be prejudicial to the administration vested in it by law.

% The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, B. Kumara Swamy and G. Amarender, filed a writ petition before the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal contending for promotion from Senior Assistant to Assistant Commercial Taxes Officer, Zonal Seniority of Warangal local area comprising of War downangal, Khammam, Karimnagar and Adila bad is the criteria. The Adilabad division consisting of Adilabad and Karimnagar Districts of the Commercial Taxes Division cannot be treated to be a zone and the divisional seniority prepared by the department is bad in law. It was held that in the im pugned order that G.O.Ms. No. 1648 was issued under Para 5(2)(c) of the Andhra pra Pra desh Public Employment (Organisa tion of Local Cadres and Regulation of Direct Recruitment) Order 1975 for that "the order" no allotment of cadre in terms of para 4 of the order was issued. The G. O.Ms, No. 1658 dated November 20, 1982 was quashed by this Court in R.P. No . 1615/ 1984, which was dismissed on December 7, 1987. Hence these appeals after obtaining special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Clause 3(7) of Andhra Pradesh Public Employment)(Organu tion of local Cadres is violative of Articles 14 and 21 & 21 and also because it is only relatable to the power given by the Presi dent to the State Government to organise local cadres within a zone for the Commercial Tax Department. [568C] 1.2 In exercise of the power under proviso to paragraph 3(1) the President has issued the order organising the local cadres and zone V consists of Revenue Districts, namely, Adilabad, Karim nagar, Warangal and Waran gal was declared as local area for local cadres of the Department. In exercise o t a power under Proviso to paragraph 2(i)(j) the State Govern ment shall within a period of twelve months from the date of commencement of the Order organise class or classes of posts in the civil services of and class or Class or classes thereof, under the State into different local cadres for different parts of the State to the extent, and in the manner therein provided. No doubt in common particu larity, the word 'otherwise ' is of 'wide ' amplitude. Therefore, the phrase 'constituted otherwise ' is to be understood in that context and purpose which Article 371 D and the Presidential Order seek to achieve. Consequently, the State Go vernment have no inherent power in creating a zone or organising local cadre within the zones except in accordance with the provisions made in the Andhra Pra dita Public Employment(Organia tion of Sal traction of Local Cadre and Regulation for Direct Recruitment).

The appellant was the manager and Karta of a joint Hindu family. During the pendency of these proceedings, it appears that the 5th November, 1925, Wazir Narain Singh granted a permanent lease of four villages Nawadih, Koldih and Chihutia by a registered patta to one Hiraman Ram who was the Manager and karta of his Joint Hindu Family. The Permanent lease was taken by him in his own name and in the name of his son Chohan Ram. An agreement was subsequently arrived at between the Bank and Wazir Narain singh that if Wazir Narain, Singh paid to the Bank or before 16th August, 1926, the sum of Rs. 1,10,631 4 0 the sale would be set aside. The plaintiff 's father Dilo Ram died after the mortgage decree but Hiraman, his son Koldh, continued in actual possession of the disputed villages and the plaintiff therefore filed the 16th November 1939, the suit out of which this appeal arises. In the Court of the Additional Subordinate Judge, the High Court held that the appellant was subrogated to the position of the Bank. It further held that since the mortgagor had in good faith granted the lease for a limited term a fair and reasonable rent, the mortgagee or the purchaser in execution of his decree could not repudiate it, specially as the mortgage deed did not prohibit the grant of temporary leases to middlemen or cultivators; appeal, the District Judge affirmed this view and declined to accept the broad contention that leases of all description granted by a mortgagor were void against the mortgagee. Held: (i) The appellant was entitled to khas possession of four particular villages of which the defendants were in wrongful possession, and the appellant had ample opportunity to redeem the mortgage if they so desired but did not choose to exercise their right of redemption; even though the lease was good as between himself and the mortgagor who granted it, the paramount title of the mortgagee may be asserted against both of them. The question whether the mortgagor in possession has power to lease the mortgaged property has got to be determined with reference to the authority of the mortgagor as the bailiff or agent for the mortgagee to deal with the property in the usual course of management. Held also that the High Courts were right in holding that the sale was valid and operative against the plaintiff, since no allegation was made by the defendants that the grant was a dealing with the mortgaged properties in the ordinary course of administration, it could not have been validly pleaded or proved.

The petitioner sent bills on July 12, 1979 but payment was not made. The respondent filed an arbitration suits in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5, 12 and 33 of the for short the Act. The Single Judge held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation. In appeal. the Division Bench held that since the claim had been made long after 10 years the arbitration cannot be proceeded with. Hence these special leave petitions. 2. On behalf of the respondent it was contended that clause 68 of the contract provided for appointment of an arbitrator and when the petitioner has legally invoked clause 68 and issued notice to the Respondent, the notice under section 5 of the Act must have been given. It was further submitted that clause 70 was also within the purview of Section 37 of the as the arbitration agreement subsisted. The High Court misconceived this procedure in exercising its discretion under section 6 of the Limitation Act which is illegal and ultra vires. It would be relevant to refer to a few paragraphs of the Agreement which deal with the interpretation on clauses 68, 69 and 95. Clause 68 provides that when any disputes or differences has arisen, they should approach the Engineer in the first instance seeking reference of it to an arbitration. It empowers either party to issue notice calling upon the Engineer to refer the dispute or difference for arbitration. The jurisdiction vested by the Court under section 51 of the , is illegal. Section 37 stipulates that there must be an order of appointment of arbitrator and thereafter the same cannot be revoked except with the leave of the Court, unless a contrary intention is expressed in the agreement. That sub section postulates that there should in the second instance be an Order appointing an arbitrator or umpire and thereafter it cannot be revoke except with leave of this Court, without a contrary intent is expressed In the instant case, the arbitration clause will cease to have effect with respect to the difference or dispute referred in the notice of the petitioner.

A decree holder, who had obtained a preliminary decree on June 26, 1947 on the basis of a mortgage, filed a petition before the executing court for passing a final decree and also to execute the mortgage decree against the mortgaged property. The execution court dismissed the suit on October 1, 1956. Thereafter, the mortgagees applied under section 14 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 and got determined the compensation to which they were entitled under the Act. The objection raised by the judgment debtors was overruled by the executing Court but reversed in second appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of dismissal and execution application was barred under section 4(d) of the Act as there was no necessity for the legislature to enact rule 9 Order 9, Civil Procedure Code which in specific term say that where a suit is wholly or partly dismissed under rule 8, the plaintiff shall be precluded from bringing a fresh suit in respect of the same cause of action. HELD : Though at one stage, learned Counsel for the appellants decree holders attempted to bring the case within Explanation 5, section 11, C.P.C., he did not pursue that line of argument but tried to support his contention on the broader principles of res judicata. [914 D E] Although under act vesting of the Estates and the deemed settlement of raiyats rights in respect thereof, a part of the mortgaged estate vested in the State absolutely free from all encumbrances. Under the circumstances of this case it is not open to the appellants to proceed with the execution. Their only remedy open to them was that provided in Chap. IV of the . [915 E F] (ii) The principle of resjudicata which has been held applicable in the earlier decision of this Court in Sidheshwar Prasad Singh vs Ram Saroop Singh, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 564 is not correct. [963 B C].

% The first proviso to Rule 4 of the Civil Services Examination Rules (C.S.E. Rules) introduced by Notification No. 13016/4/86 AIS(1) dated 13.12.1986 provided that a candidate who has already been allocated to the I.P.S., or to a Central Services Group 'A ' and who has been permitted to abstain from the probationary training in order to appear at the next Civil Services examination, shall not be eligible to appear again in the Civil Service Examination unless he has first resigned from the service. The proviso further provided that the candidate should have expressed his intention to appear in the next C.S./C.B. and must have expressed its intention to stay the operation of the order. In O.A.No. 206/89 on which date the Tribunal rendered its main judgment in O.As. No. 206 of 1989, and the connected batch of Civil Appeals. In both these cases, the Tribunal held that the approval of the Commission for admission to the competitive examination was necessary as the candidate who had been allocated were not within the permissible age limit under the Rules, whether it could be said that the reasons given by the Government to justify the introduction of the proviso could have any rational nexus to the object of the scheme of recruitment to the All India Services or/and whether such reasons were arbitrary, unfair and unjust. In the appeals preferred before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) it did not examine the merits of the case as no opportunity had been afforded to the re spondents of being heard; (ii) the State Government should have granted relaxation in the matter of deciding whether the applications were at all entertained. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The second proviso to rule 4 of C.SC.S Rules does not travel beyond the intent of the main Rule putting any unjustifiable embargo and that the proviso is not ultra vires regulation 4 (iii) a) of Regulation 4 of Regulations 1955 on the ground it makes the candidates ineligible who are otherwise eligible in terms of clauses (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) or (v). 2.1 There are 46 Group 'C ' serv ice listed in the C.C. Examination to which only for 16 Group 'B ' services, recruitment is made through the Civil serv ices conducted by UPSC annually and it is only in respect of such candidates that the impugned proviso imposes an onerous restriction that they should first resign in order of to appear before the next civil service examination failing which their allocation to the Service based on one or both the examinations as the case may be, will stand cancelled. [97A D] 2.2 In all, there are 46 Groups 'C Service listed in tile C.T.

The appellant challenged his order of detention under Section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short). The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal before this Court, it was contended that if the detaining authority had been assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise, he should have been allowed the assistance of a 'friend '. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The refusal by the Advisory Board to permit the appellant to be assisted by Sundararajan as a friend was bad and continued detention of the appellant became vitiated. [792E] 2. The High Courts were right in holding that the refusal by detaining the Advisory board to permit him to be aided by the detenu was not justified. [789D] 3. If the detaining Authority or the Government takes the aid of a legal practitioner or a legal adviser before the Advisory Boards, the detenu must be allowed the facility of appearing before the Board through a legal witness. [788C] 4. The detaining authority or the government to appear before the detaining Board with the aid and with a view to justifying the detention orders. If that be so, it would be difficult to say that the detaining authorities or the Govern ment should have the facility. [ 789B] 5. It is not for this Court to examine and assess what prejudice has been caused to the appellant on account of such denial. This Court has reiterated the position that matters relating to preventive detention are strict proceedings and warrant full compliance with the requirements of law. [ 788E G] 6. As has been indicated by this court, what cannot be permitted directly should not be allowed to be done in an indirect way.

In 1946 there was food shortage in the country, that is, September 30, 1946, and the Government issued a notice under sub r. (2) of r. 75 A(2) for acquiring the requisitioned goods i.e., the said goods on September 30. The appellants contended inter alia that they were entitled to have their requisition confirmed by the Ministry of Defence as required by r. 74 A (2), and there was no service of the orders in this case, and relied on a decision of the High Court in K. N. Banerjee vs Union Of India, [1954] S.C.R. 829, holding that. it was not necessary to serve them with notice under r, 75 A (1) C.P.C., and the High court also held that the action of requisition and notices of acquisition were valid and binding on them. Held, that it was incumbent for the Government to have served the said orders by issuing proper notices to the appellants after they had notice of the acquisition. In the present case there was a specific provision for service of summons under r. 77 A(1) of the Defence of India Rules which laid down that where a notice of acquisition has been served on the owner, then at the beginning of the day on which the notice is so served, the property shall vest in Government free from any mortgage, pledge, lien or other similar encumbrance and the period of the requisition thereof shall end. The service of notices of the Acquisition Officer was effective by service on the appellants as owners for the purpose of rs 75 A, C. P.C.; 834 (2). Since it was only in the case of orders of requisition made by the Government, prohibiting the corporation from acquiring the acquired goods and taking delivery of the goods an order of requisition was made under r . 75 A of the Rules. Held also that service of notice of Acquisition Officer in this Case on the managing agents of the mills was effective service on them as owners taking part with their respective activities, though for the purposes of r, 25 A(3) read with 0. XX r. 2 (a), C.p.C.) and the impugned order of requisitioning were valid. It was not correct to say that under R. 75A(2), the service of such an order was necessary on the person who can place the goods in question at the disposal of the requisitioning authority and until that is done there cannot be any valid and effective requisition. Held further, that when r. 76 A ( 2) expressly provided for publication with notice, making it clear that the provisions of rr. 74(a) did not speak of an order in writing as was the case not in r.75 issued to the Government. The effect of being that certain notices were served on a company or a corporation. The fact that they had been served with the notices of acquisi tion under R, 45 A C.

The assessee is a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. Sometime in 1955 56, the a notice was issued to the assessee under section 23A of the Income Tax Act 1922, and for the assessment year 1963 64, on the ground that it may become liable to pay additional tax under the said provision. The assessee submitted that the said sum was a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal. By the date this appeal was taken up for hearing, another appeal preferred by the assessee relating to the assessment years 1964 65 was also before the Tribunal. The said appeal arose under the provisions of the Companies Surtax Profits Act, 1964 which replaced the . The appeal relating to assessment year 1964 65 related to the re spondents. On an application made by it in the High Court, the correctness of that view is questioned. It held that no action can be taken against the assessee. On behalf of the Revenue it was contended in this appeal that inasmuch as no order levying additional tax had been made on or before the date relevant to the assess ment year 1963 65, the said amount cannot be treated as a provision. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding it to be a provision and not a reserve. [111C] 2. In Metal Box Company of India Ltd. vs Their Workmen, [1969] 3 S.T.R. 891, the distinction between a provision of and reserve is stated in the following words: "The difference between a pro duction and a reserve is in commercial accountancy fairly well known". Provisions made against anticipated losses and contingencies are charges against profits and therefore to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L accounts and the balance sheet. On the other hand reserves are appropriations of profits, the assets by which they are rep resented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. [113E G] 3. While approving the said statement it was stated in Vazir Sultan: "In other words the broad distinction between the two is that whereas a provision is a charge against the profits to be takes into account, against gross receipt in the p.& L. accounts, a reserve was in appropriation of profits and the asset or assets by that it is represented being retained lo form part thereof. [114F] 4. While approved the said statements it was mentioned in V strict Sultan 's: "in other words, the broad difference between the present class is that while a provision was a charge sheeted against the profit to be took into account as against gross dis receipts in view of which they were made whereas general reserves and reserve funds are shown as part of .the proprietor 's interest". [114A B] 5.

% The petitioners were appointed to temporary posts on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority was reckoned on the basis of the written examinations. The respondents, who were holding the posts of Civil Engineers (Class 1) and (Officers ' at places), contended that some Officers were recruited in Class I service and supported their claim on diverse grounds but they produced two different sets of books which contained an integrated scheme for the recruitment of personnel into those that were recruited by selection. The petitioners, who claimed to be members of a Federation of Temporary Officers Association (Indian Railways) joined with them, their President, Vice President and Secretary of the aforesaid Federation as writ petitioners. The Railway Board decided in favour of the employees holding that the officers so absorbed were appointed validly appointed from the date of their absorption into the Indian Railway Service of Engineers. The Union Public Service Commission by order dated September 17, 1965 took a decision to the effect that the Officers so absorbed into the 'Indian Railway Service would be given weightage in seniority "on the basis for half the total years of continuous service in working posts in Railways prior to their permanent absorption into Class. 1. The Assistant Engineers challenged the said order before the High Court by filing writ petitions and claimed that officers were appointed on temporary posts in the cadre they were recruited on the prior to the permanent absorption in Class. The High Court allowed the writ petitions, quashed the classification of temporary Assistant Officers and that the seniority had to be reckoned on basis of their length of continuous serv ice, though they conceded that in any given year, the candidates appointed as Engineers on the ground that they were appointed as Engineering Officers on the same basis of selection by the Union Public Services Commission. Hence these appeals by special leave against the decision of this Court in Katyani Dayal 's case. Allowing the appeals and dismissing writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution it was, HELD: 1.1 To find fault with it, at this juncture again on the touch stone of equality dimension would be to unsettle a settled position. That venture is neither in the interest of justice nor in the Interest of service. When there has been complete absorption of personnel of one service into the other, and the seniority of the absorbers is to be counted from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of half the length of service subject to a maximum of five years, it would otherwise be imprudent now at this point of time to dig up old issues. [1023C E] 1.2 In Katyoni Dayal ' 's Case (supra) this court was concerned primarily on the question of seniority between the officers in a representative capacity and Engineers not so represented in Katnayani Dayal case (supra). This Court in Chal984 Lal Gupta vs Secretary, Home (Police), Department, Government of Bihar & Ors., [1988] Supp. SCC 519 and Direct Recruit Class II Engineering of officers Association vs State of Maharashtra & Ors, ; held that the principle of constructive res judicata would bar the re agitation of the issues decided in Katakyani Lal 's cases if not the strict principles of res judicata. [1324C D] 1:3 The distinction between,, the two services was well marked in Katmayani Dayal vs Secretary Home (police), Department Government of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. ; and Direct Publicruit Class Il Engineering of Officers Association v State of Maharash tra & Ors ; , followed.

Section 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance, 1949, authorised the State Government to constitute Special Courts for such areas as may be specified in the notification and section 10 provided that the period of limitation for appeal to the High Court was curtailed. Under section 11, the State Govern ment is expected to select only such offences or classes of offences or class of cases for being tried by the Special Court under the former Act but this part authorises the State Govt. to direct any case to be tried by a special court constituted under the latter Act. The appellant contended that sections 69 and 118 Of the Bombay Ordinance were discriminatory in that they offended article 14 Of the Constitution as much as section 11 authorised the Government to appoint a Special judge, to preside over a Special Court constituted under section 9 for such area as might be specified therein in the Notification; and (4) that section 11 was violative of article 14 of the Constitu tion. Held, (per curiam): The State Legislature has left it to the State Legislature to classify offences or categories of offences for the purpose of the Ordinance for the State Governments is in a better position to judge the needs and exigencies of the State and the Court will not lightly interfere with the decision of the Government. Benoarilal 's case, , M/s. Benooarilal vs The State of Saurashtra, ; , referred to. King Emperor vs Sibnath Banerjee, L. R. 45 I.A. 256; applied. It is well settled that article 14 must be read as a whole and "the State Legislature cannot enact an Act which is in any way restricted by article 14 or section 10. The use of the said clause implies that classification made by the State legislature should be based on some intelligible differentia distinguishing the offences grouped together from others, such differentia must have a reasonable relation to the object of the Act as recited in the preamble; and it is not intended as a mode of legislation, nor would any question arise as to its constitutionality. The power conferred under section 11(1) of the Bombay Act of 1946,, which purports to amend section 5 (1), does not offend against the equal protection clause of the Constitution; it merely refers to the need to provide for public safety, maintenance of public order and tranquility in the State of Orissa, that is to say a classification which must fulfil both conditions, namely, that it must be based upon some intelligible distinguishing differentia distinguishing them from other offences and that differentia must has a reasonable nexus to the objects of the statute as recited therein. It may well be regarded as an instance of conditional legislation and where it is found that the offence is committed fully in all respects it can be said that there must have been an intelligible differentia which distinguishes the offences left out of other offences, and in each case it was permissible to take the view that on a rational basis the classification made would be an unreasonable and arbitrary one. It will be for the Court to consider the nature of the offence committed by the accused persons constituting the offence under section 7(1)(a) and the circumstances in which the offence was committed, that those offences must have reasonable relation with the object which would be served if it were possible to take that a different view could be taken. It was not necessary for the purposes of the particular legislation as recited by its preamble. The Legislature has right to classify persons who are involved on the basis that it can classify offences and classes of crimes or categories for the pur pose of the ordinance, under which the Special judge directed them to forward their cases before the Special Judge constituted under that Act, and the State is in the better position than to judge its needs and necessities of the state.

The prosecution alleged that on the day of occurrence, one Mauji Lal had reported by his father that some of the accused persons were playing in a tin shed situate north of his house and he was cleaning the door of the western kotha. On hearing some commotion when the occupants entered the northern kothakha of the house they suddenly jumped into their courtyard and pause towards a tree and started beating the deceased and P.W.2 who were sleeping in the tin shed, as a result whereof his brother and several other persons went to the house of Mauji Lai Lal, Pradhan, and others attacked him with lathis, spears and lathis. P.Ws. 2 and 8 were injured. The trial court acquitted all of them on the ground that they had witnessed the occurrence, in fact the appellants armed with various weapons could not have been present there in the vicinity of the scene of occurrence and that they would have implicated the accused for the occurrence in this case and have succeeded in getting up that lacuna which was not suggested by the prosecution. The High Court dismissed the appeals filed by nine accused persons on the basis of the evidence of P. Ws. 1, 7 and 8 and the High Court confirmed the conviction as against them. In appeal to this Court it was contended: (1) There was no reason whatsoever for rejecting the evidence; (2) It is a well known rule that in all cases of circumstantial evidence conviction can be based on the testimony of an eye witness only if there are circumstances and the chain of proof is complete so far as no reasonable explanation can be laid down. (3) The principle of law applicable to criminal trials has not been followed consistently with the principles of law enunciated by this Court in Bhajan Singh vs State of Punjab, [1985] Supp. SCR p. 384; (4) A conviction can also be based upon circumstantial evidence and unless there are compelling reasons to do so, the court should lean against them ; (5) Where, however, it is found that the eye witness has given a correct account of his injury, it cannot be said that he has been present at the time of occurrence or see what was reasonable. In other words, there must be some strong reason for accepting the evidence and giving any explanation about the injuries caused to the accused, and unless these circumstances are satisfactorily established the court will be justified in interfering with such a conviction. (6) Where there is no doubt about the participation by all the eyewitnesses that the culprits were moving in and out of the deceased, the fact that they received the injuries at the hands of the assailants immediately after the incident would not be possible to reject the evidence as of P 's eye witness altogether. The learned Judges of the High court have observed that it is not probable that these appellants had been seen by them with their arms such as guns, pistols, axe and lathis could have been in the kotkha together at the same time at the instance of the prosecution witnesses.

The respondent being a temporary employee of the appellant Corporation was dismissed from service on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity to cross examine the witnesses. The order of discharge having been grounded upon unsatisfactory service during the period of probation, it has been urged by counsel for the appellant, that the workmen were probationers and the orders of termination had also been bad for non compliance with section 25F of the Act inasmuch as the services had been terminated on the grounds of unsuitability. The respondent, however, relied on the decision in Management of M/s. Shiba Prasad Jaiswal & Ors., ; and that the three Judge Bench decision of this Court in Sundara Money 's case was not at all inconsistent with what has been held in State Bank of India vs N. Sundara money, Hindustan Steel Ltd. vs The Presiding Officer Labour Court, Orissa & Ors, [1970] 1 SCR 586, that even though the termination of service was not due to discharge of surplus labour force and, therefore, did not amount to retrenchment. Allowing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: The three Judge decisions in Sundari Money ' 's Case have been correctly considered by this Court and must be treated per. [790G] I. In the instant case the requirement of section 25 F had not complied with in these cases. It was not necessary to dilate on the point nor to refer to the earlier decisions of this court to both of which one of us was a party. [789H; 788A B] The idea is to protect the weak against the strong and strong policy of comprehensive definition has been effectuated. Termination embraces not merely the act of termination by the employer but the fact of termination howsoever produced. Then came the decision when the view expressed in Bank of U.P. vs Nousan, ; and L.J. Godse vs Management of Bamoudagea & Anr., [1970)1 SCR 597, applied. The three Judges decision in Ranade Chemical Works Ltd. (supra) has been given to its own facts. The view indicated therein had rightly been reiterated by this court in the earlier two decisions of This Court in L. J. God fruitful vs State Bank Of Patiala, ; , and Bharat Cloth & General Mills Ltd. V. Workmen, [1971] 1 S.C.R. 590, referred to.

The assessee South Eastern Railway disposed of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. On 1 April, 1952 the assessee applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of the registration of the assessee as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act in respect of unconnected or unclaimed goods. The Commercial Tax officer held that the sale effected by the assessee was sales under the provisions of Section 56 of the Indian Railways Act, 1940 and therefore he could be treated as a 'dealer ' under the Act. On 6 June, 1959 the assessee made an order rejecting the application on the basis that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the asses see 's activities and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act, and that the assessee did fell within tile scope of section 2(c) of the Bengal Amendment Act. The revision petition filed by the Revenue was dismissed by the Additional Commissioner of Commercial Taxes who dealt with the case, by order dated 17 June, 1960. In these appeals the question is whether the assessee Railway in each case is a " dealer" for the purpose of as sessment under theBengal Finance ( Sales Tax) act, 1941 and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. Allowing Civil Appeal No. 1069 of 1975, this Court, HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of Goods by the Railway. It seems to South Eastern Railways was a "business" for purposes of the said Bengal Finance Act 1941. [781F] 2. In the case of the appellant South Eastern railway, what were sold were unclaimed goods but the Railway was a carrier of the goods and if at the stage of delivery goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway Was entitled to dispose them of. There can be no doubt that the activity of such so disposing was adj tractive to its principal activity as carrier of goods by the railway. It, therefore, seems to the South Eastern Rail Railway was engaged in selling scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. In other cases the assessee Eastern Railway, what are sold were loose goods.

These three appeals arose out of a case which was referred to the Supreme Court by R. P. Gurha, the Director of the appellant company, under section 120 read with section 409 I.P.C., and all of them except Vishnu Prasad were also convicted of certain offences arising out of the overt acts committed by them. sessions judge of the High Court found that Dalmia had the necessary criminal intent as what Chokhani did was known to him and was under his instructions, was that of Raghunath Rai, Secretary cum Account of the Bharat Insurance Company. Held, that, R. J., acting power of attorney on behalf of Dalmia and Bharat Union Agencies, told the brokers at the time he gave business of Bharat Union agencies to them that it was the business of Dalmia that of Dalmia. If Dalmia 's statement about Mittal 's communication to him be correct, it would appear that when the Bombay Office of the Union Agencies was not in a position to meet the losses, Dalmia would not be of arranging, on his own funds to meet these losses and would then be responsible for the mis doing of that way. Held further, that R. K., acting under authority of the company itself, did not acquire any such powers as he had no power under section 411 J, and section 409 C. The contract directed delivery of the securities at Delhi was a mere ruse to show to him that it had suffered losses as a result of sharespeculation business in 1954 55 and therefore Dalmia was liable for prosecution.

The Inspector of the Secretariat Service of the State moved a petition in the High Court for an order directing the State Government to treat its order dated August 19, 1966 as "illegal, void and of no effect" and to forbear from enforcing its order treating the persons whose names were specified in the annexure to the order as servants of the "Secretariat Cadre". The Government which was the authority made under article 309 of the Constitution directed that the officers mentioned therein "should be treated to have been regularly appointed in the posts shown against their names in column 4 of the statement with effect from the date shown in column 5 in the Departments mentioned in column 6. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants : (1) that the order violated r. 138 of the Recruitment Rules in that it altered the conditions of service of the applicants; and (2) that therefore it violated r . 138 by fixing a uniform method for recruitment to the ministerial service, that rule made under Article 309 of 1061 did not contravene article 311 of the Constitu tion inasmuch as the order purported to amalgamate the former Saurashtra and Kutch States and was contrary to the terms of r. 141 of the Rules. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The view that recruitment to ministerial staff in the Secretariat could only be by nomination or by promotion from among members of the Lower Division of nomination being on the result of a competitive examination held by the Public Service Commission and promotion being from the subordinate staff. [519 G] N. Raghavendra Rao vs Deputy Commissioner, South Kanara, Mangalore; , followed. (1)(a) By virtue of section 8 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 the new State of Bombay which included the territories of the Union Territories of Saurashtra and Region which were formed. under section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act 37 of 1956 the newly constituted State of Gujarat came into existence. Under section 81(c) of the Government of India Act, 1935 a guarantee was given to every allotted public servant that his conditions of services shall not be changed except with the prior approval of the Central Government and at the time of preparation of a provisional gradation list, six were specified therein. The condition of service applicable immediately before the appointed day in the case of any person who is allotted to another State cannot be varied to his disadvantage except with previous approval of Central Government. [525 C] (b) Rule 138 only dealt with the existing servants and did not prevent any additional members from being amalgamated in the ministerial establishment of the Gujarat State Secretariat. The appointments did not amount to absorption in equivalent posts. This construction was quite clearly contrary to r. 13 of the recruitment rules, and could not be allowed to be removed by the rules made by the State subsequent to November 1, 1956 unless the previous approval was obtained thereto. [500 G H] (c) By the proviso to sub section(7) section 115 a guarantee that the conditions Of service applicable Immediately before the appointment day in tho case of a person who was allotted to other State cannot he varied to their disadvantage except without the previous permission of the authority of the former then Saurashtra and detaining states personnel in the subordinate offices. [436 A] N .

Section 5 of the Central Sales tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 provides that in respect of declared goods the tax (sales or purchase) shall not exceed the prescribed limit and shall not be levied on the purchase or sale of such goods at more than one stage. A single Judge of the High Court quashed the Punjab Amendment on the view taken by the Full Bench of that Court in the case of Madras State, when there was a discrimination between the imported goods and local goods. Accordingly, a writ petition was filed in this court challenging the constitutional validity of the Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment & Validation) Ordinance 1967 as again amended by Punjab Legislature and the Punjab Sales Tax Act. The contention of the State that section 2(ff) of the Act which guarantees the levy of tax on declared goods within a State is unconstitutional being rejected by this Court, HELD : Rule 3 of the Haryana General Sales tax Rules, 1957 for taxing purchases of cotton was issued in a rect to meet the inconvenience and hardship caused to dealers in the matter of taxation. The policy underlying section 5(2)(a) of that Act is that the tax can be collected only at one stage, in appeal or review as provided by the Punjab GeneriI Sales Tax Amendment and Validation Act. It has been amended in relation to the area of that State and it was inconceivable that this could not be within the competence of the Legislature.

The appellants filed a suit for enforcement of a mortgage against the present respondent, who was defendant No. 1 in the suit and six other persons alleging that he too was an agriculturist and therefore entitled to the benefits of the Act. During the pendency of these appeals a final decree was passed by which a sum of Rs. 49,255 with interest thereon at 6% per annum from 1st October 1937 was directed to be paid by defendant No 1 in default of which the plaintiffs were declared entitled to apply for a final deci sion for sale of the mortgaged properties and the suit was dismissed against respondent No. 2. On appeal, both parties agreed to receive Rs. 24,000 only towards part satisfaction of the decree. The Court found that the amount due by the appellant under the decree was to be settled at Rs. 37,500 with interest thereupon at 6 % per annum on payment of which 10 % per cent per annum was passed as against the original respondent. On this finding, the appeals were set down for final hearing and by their judgment dated March 23, 1942, the learned Judges of the High Court accepted these findings of the trial judge but held that the appellant 's claim to any relief under the Agriculturists ' Relief Act was not entertainable by the lower court and that accordingly dismissed the appeal. On certificate, the appellants were contended that before the execution proceedings for execution of the final decree the High court had no jurisdiction to condone the default made in making payment of the amount as the Court had no power to extend the period or extend it beyond the time given by the section. Held: The High Court was right in holding that by virtue of the provisions of the Agriculturists Relief Act, a non agriculturist could indirectly get relief which he cannot directly get. It is not lawful for a party claiming any benefit in viola tion of this clause to raise a ground of equity. The general law undoubtedly is that a mortgage decree is one and indivisible and exception to this rule are admitted in special circumstances where the integrity of the mortgage has been disrupted at the instance of the mortgagee himself; e,g., when there is severance of the interest of the mort gagor with the consent of the mortgagor or a portion of the equity of redemption is vested in the latter. It was not necessary for purposes of this case to express any opinion as to the correctness or otherwise of these deci vations. The ratio decidendi in all these cases is not applicable to the case before us.

The respondents were sub tenants of a premises in the City Civil Court which was situate at the time of their letting out their premises to the appellants. The first respondent filed a suit against it, inter alia, for eviction of the first respondent on the ground that he had since the coming into operation of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, sublet the premises or assigned or transferred in any other manner his interest therein. The City Civil Judge held that the first appellant having not lawfully sublet the same to them as sub tenants the provisions of section 10 of the Act were violative of the right of the respondents and consequently dismissed the suit on the grounds inter alia that there had been a lawful subletting by the first plaintiff of the premises to them. He accordingly passed a decree for eviction against all the appellants, who were the appellants in this Court. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the City civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit, because (i) there had failed to comply with section 10 Of the Act as the first and second respondent had not lawfully let the premises; and (ii) the dispute between the parties in the First Civil Court was one which arose out of the provisions Of section 28 of the said Act. Held: (i)(a) The contention that the suit in the city civil court was not one between a landlord and a tenant cannot be accepted. [437 G] (b)In a suit under section 28, a question of title to premises which does not arise out of tho Act or any of its provisions may be determined incidentally. Any party aggrieved by such determination would be free to sue in a competent court to establish his title to such premises by virtue of the provision of section 29A.

The appellant, a private company, was incorporated under the name and style of Oriental Metal Pressing Works. On May 26, 1955, the respondent transferred his business to the appellant Govind and had started to take over the aforesaid business. The appellant claimed that he became a director on account of his failure to attend the directors ' meetings. The respondent contended (1) that he was not an employee as defined by section 312 or his services were terminated in contravention of section 312; (2) that the appointment of the appellant was void and inoperative, (3) that section 312 did not prevent him from appointing his successor, he having been lawfully appointed, the managing director ceased to be a director. Held, that the power to appoint an alternate directors by the articles was not given by the old Act but had been given by articles, such an appointment would be void under section 312 and the appellant could not be held to have been duly appointed at all. The word "assignment" in the section included "appointment". The proviso to section 86B did not apply where a managing director has been appointed otherwise than by the company in a general meeting and, on a true construction of the sections, it was clear that in certain circumstances an appointment by a directors in his place might be deemed to be an assignment and would not therefore be rendered void by the section. In order, however, that a managing Director may exercise this power of appointment he had no power under the articles to appoint another person as an alternate director to act for him during an absence of not less than three months from the district in which meetings of directors were ordinarily held if done with the approval of the board of directors.

The respondent filed an eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm, carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart, on the ground that the appellant had unlawfully sub let the shop to M/S. Adi iron Mart, without joining any of the partners of the said firms as respondents or serving them as partners and hence, the eviction petition was not maintainable at all. The Trial Court held that the 1940 Act was not applicable to the proceedings under the Rent Act either and hence the ratio laid down in Chhotelal Pyarelal, the partnership firm and others vs Shikharchand, In that case an eviction suit was filed by the respondent landlord against the appellant a partnership firm under Section 13(3)(iv) and (vii) of the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949. The Appellate Authority dismissed the said appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appellants. In this appeal by Special Leave, it was urged for the appellant that in the instant case there was no evidence to show that M/M. Adaseshwar Glass1991 was carrying on the business at the said premises and that firm was carried on business as in the premises even for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the opera ties there. Moreover, though a notice was given by the respond ent to the appel lants and M/D. Adarsadeshwar Glass plantation Mart to produce their income tax returns, assessment orders as well as account books ledgers for the relevant period, these were not produced. It was urged that there was evidence to indicate that M was carrying out business at a premises even without joining the partners as respondents. The respondent contended that both the partners, who had sublet the said shop to the appellants, were also joined by them as respec tive partners of M firms. Adeswar Glass Mart and that on the date when the suit was instituted against the appell lants, there was a dispute between the parties. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the order passed by the Appellate Authority, this Court HELD: 1. The finding of subletting must be negatived as it is open to the appellant to amend the eviction application and join the partners in their place. [420E] In the instant ease, no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Civil Leave and it is certainly not open for the appellants to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years. This contention must be rejected. [ 420C] 2. Since there was nothing on record to show as to who M was in possession of the premises or that he had sublet it out to M; the finding recorded by the Appel lant Authority that M had sub let it out was not open to him to raise this objection at such a late stage. [421E] Halsbury 's Laws of England (Vol. 37) pp. 161 & 162; relied on. In Chhotelalsal Pyare Lal vs Prem Chand, A.I.R. 1987 S.C. 156, followed.

% The Andhra Pradesh Ceiling on urban agglomeration Act, 1976 was passed in pursuance of the provisions of Article 254(1) and by clause (1) of article 252, the Central Act imposed a ceiling on holding of land in urban agglomerations other than land which is mainly used for the purpose of agriculture. The proviso thereto stated that if the extent of the holding of a person is in excess of the ceiling area, the person shall be liable to surrender the land held in excess. In 1957, the Andhra Pradesh Act was enacted mainly to provide for the imposition of a ceiling of 10% on urban immovable property and for matters connected therewith, with an object to preventing the concentration of urban land in the hands of a few persons by speculation and profiteering therein and with a view to bringing about a equitable distribution of land In urban agglCeiling and Regulation) Bill 1976 in Parliament. The Andhra Act imposed the ceiling on vacant lands which were mainly used either for the purposes of agriculture or for purposes ancillary thereto and with an aim to preventing concentration of such urban land into the hands off the tenants from being deprived of their wealth by the landlords. The question was whether on a proper construction of the relevant provisions of the Andhra Act, a divided minor son was not liable to be included in "family unit" as defined in section 2(f) of the Central.Act and its definition was materially in the same terms as the definition of "family units." The High Court held that the Andhra Acts violated Articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution and directed the State Legislature to reconsider the question after taking into consideration the representations made by its members and on a reference made by it to the President of India. On behalf of the landholders it was contended that merely because an area may possibly in the future be notified as an urban agglalities under section 2 (n) (A)(ii) of tho Central Act, the State legislature would cease to have competence to legislate with respect to ceiling on land situate within these urban aggl Electoral Area and even if it is so notified it would not be an urbanically agglomeration and the Andhra Legislature would have legislative competence to provide that imposition of ceiling on urban immoveable property in excess Of the ceiling limit was based on a violation of Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of Constitution. It was further urged that since the provisions Of the Andhra P. Act were repugnant to the provisions contained in the Central Acts, so far as the rural agglomeration are concerned it was not within the legislative competence of the State Government to provide the imposition by the impugned Act which authorised the imposition thereof on vacant land situate in those urban agglonments and since then the AndhraP Act was ultra vires and void as being outside the legislative competency of the Parliament. It also urged that merely by a division of one member amongst two or more members would not result in deprivation of the right to hold property. Allowing the Appeals, this Court, HELD: 1(i) The Andhra Poshioneder 's declaration under section 9 of the Act is in the latter terms as it stands and the expression "vacant land" which must be construed ejusdem generis with that of a minor son would clearly be included. (ii) The ceiling area in the case of a family unit consisting of father, mother and three minor sons or daughters, the lands held by all these persons would have to be clubbed together and then the ceiling areas applied to the aggregate holding.

The workmen of the appellant company were employed on various dates between July 5, 1953 and August 18,1953. The notice stated inter alia that in consequence of the illegal strikes which took place on several previous dates, the management had no option but to declare a lock out of the entire Works except for some special shifts, really terminated the services of the workmen, and on September 23, 1953, another notice was issued by the company lifting the lock out with effect from August 24, 1953. In November, 1953 the Union made an application before the Industrial Tribunal under section 33 of the , praying that the services should be taken back as of right without any condition; but this was refused. Against the refusal to give permission, both the workmen and the Union appealed to the Labour Appellate Tribunal, Calcutta, which dismissed the applications on merits. In appeal by special leave, HELD : The two Tribunals below have misdirect ed themselves as to the true scope and effect of the Standing Orders in question and their decision with regard to the seven workmen mentioned above cannot be supported. On merits the case against Samar Sen was that as a result of a regular and proper enquiry, he was found guilty of unauthorised absence and insubordination, etc., and therefore, the Company dismissed him. [688 A B] The two Tribunal 's findings with regard regards the seven employees mentioned above could not be supported, because, on the contrary, the workmen were given continuity of service for the entire period of their absence. It has been somewhat faintly suggested that if an Order was given to discharge by a particular mode then there was no consideration for the condition imposed and the Company could change its mind and ignore the condition. As to Civil Appeal 45, on behalf of the workman in which the prayer is for payment of full compensation, it was sufficient to state that no question of principle is involved. [687 B] In view of the conflicting evidence on the point it would not be possible to proceed on the footing that the workmen themselves understood the notice dated August 23, and they were also found guilty.

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in Department of Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under Section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for Appointment) Act, 1974 held interviews on 20th June, 1989 and selected Dr. Nathawat for the said post. Dr. Smt. Uma Kant neither filed a writ petition in the High Court initially challeng ing the appointment of Dr.Nathawat on the ground that the Selection Committee was not constituted in accordance with law, and objection was also raised that once a selected person joins the post, the reserve list exhausted itself. Dr, Shri Urea Kant as well as the University have come in appeal by grant of special leave. In order to appreciate the controversy it would be apposite to refer to certain provisions of the Act of 1974. The University of Rajasthan is the highest executive body in the university and has also approved the name of Dr Shyam Sundarwat, who was the highest Execu tor in the University for 6 months and that subse quently extended to one year by a resolution passed in its meeting dated 3.12.1983. In the present case Dr. Umakant was selected on 20.6.1989 and was going to retire on 30th September, 1989. The Syndicate by its resolution decided that the reserve List recommended by the Selection Commit tee shall be valid upto 6 months from the date of approval of the Syndicate which was subsequently extended to another year by resolution dated 3 12 1983. In these circumstances it is perfectly valid to select one more person and to keep him in the reserve for being appointed on the regular vacancy which was shortly anticipated on account of retirement of Dr, Mrs. Uma Devi Kant as also the University having come in appeals by grant. of special Leave it is contended for the appellants that a regular vacancy of Professor having arisen on the retirement of Sri Shri Natha Raj as Professor from the reserve lists it was held that once the person selected by the Syndicate has joined that post then selection made by the Committee is exhausted and the reserve so extended to a one year instead of 6 months in a resolution dated 2.12 1983, it was perfectly valid upto six months, that a fresh Selection Committee should have been constituted and no appointment on such post could have been made from the reserved list prepared by the duly constituted Selection Committee on 20rd June,1989 as against Dr. Mrs. Shobha Kant Sharma, that the selection committee was properly constituted. A bare reading of Section 5 with section 6(4) makes it quite clear that the determination of a Selection Committee is necessary for the meeting of a selection committee and sub section (4) of section 6 clearly provides that the selec tion Committee shall prepare a list of candidates selected by it in order of merit and shall further prepare a reserve list in the same order and to the extent of 50% of the vacancies and persons kept in the reserved List would be considered as having been selected for the concerned post and shall be entitled for appointment if any vacancy is caused during the validity period of the reserve provi sions. The respondents, who had filed the writ petition, have submitted that the ap pointment committee was duly constituted; that mere filing of a Writ Petition in the Allahabad High Court would not affect the power to appoint Dr.Usi Kant as valid on the post they were appointed long after the promotion of Dr and Mrs. Asha Kant and others subsequently impleaded Dr. P. Khanna both as one of the respondents in the writ peti tion. The facts are that University of ly has taken a categorical stand that since 1978 not only in the Univer sity of Rajasthan but all other universities in the State of Rajasthan reserve lists were prepared and appointments were being made from reserved List the said list stood exhausted and that once selected person join the post then, selection madeby the Selection com pany Committee is exhaust ing and the Reserve List is of no avail and becomes extinct.

The petitioners were owners of plots of land in areas round about Bombay. They had all similar but separate grievance with respect to the development plan prepared and published under the Act. It was alleged that the list of sites reserved for public purposes was for the first time submitted by the second respondent to the Development Committee on February 8, 1964 showing for the second time that a major portion of the petitioners ' lands were earmarked for a recreation centre. The petitioners contended that they had applied through their architect on January 2, 1962 for permission to change the existing user of their land by putting them to industrial use and had written a letter to the Municipal Commissioner of Bombay for that purpose. the first respondent after considering the proposals made in the tentative development plan and the reports of the Development Plan Committee prepared a development plan: and published it by means of advertisements in approved newspapers and in the Official Gazette and a perusal thereof clearly showed that detailed provisions have been made for giving as wide a publicity as possible, at all stages to the public, and to owners. , The petitioners further alleged that they were bona fide purchasers of plots ' allotted for recreation centres and green belt by the first, second and third respondents in the Development plan finally adopted was in contravention of section 9 of the Act, and prayed that no action should be taken against them for the acquisition of any land designated for public purpose under section 7 of the Gujarat Town Planning Act, 1954. Held, (per Sarkar, jj.), that the objection raised as to the invalidity of sections 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 of the Bombay Town Planning (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1947 which was attacked in these cases was rejected by this Court; (if there were no principles in the Act itself to guide the competent authority in the exercise of his will and pleasure to refuse permission to execute a decree for eviction violated the right to hold property under article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.

The petitioners are five writ petitions under article 32 of the Constitution and three appeals against the decisions of the High Courts were filed in this Court. Firstly, there is no territorial dispute as there was a well established boundary running between India and Pakistan regarding which there were disputes and much friction, and by the award no cession of Indian territory was contemplated. Secondly, apart from the claim to exercise rights to move freely throughout the territory of India under article 19(1)(d), any other right or of any individual citizen was likely to be infringed by the implementation of the award. Thirdly, there was no evidence that it is part of the Great Rann of Kutch as shown in the pre partition maps which needs to be demarcated on the ground. The agreement between the two States was reached purely as an executive act and no legislative sanction was obtained by the Government of the Union of India to its implementation. The contention that the enhancement of the territorial area under the award is admissible only to reports relating to British India, does not support the claim. Thirdly and lastly, even granting that the evidence about the exercise of sovereign authority by the British authorities governing Sind since 1843 over the Rann was inconclusive, the claim by Indian citizens to exercise fundamental rights in respect of the territory in that Sector may be entertained only if it be established that the territory is found to be originally governed by the Maharao of Kutch. Held, that there was not a mere agreement between two States which was reached at purely as arbi trary and effective and is unacceptable. In view of the above fact that the area described in which authority, in this instance exclusively for the protection of activities of private individuals, individuals, is shown to have been displayed by Sind authorities in a manner which is not sporadic but consistent and effective, is Dhara Banni and Chhad Bet. The boundary between the States was indefinite and by virtue of the awards of the Tribunal the true boundary of India and the Pakistan is determined: the award does not purport to, nor did it operate as giving rise to, an obligation to cede Indian territory. Damodar Gordhan vs Deoran Kanji ([1880] 3 C. R. 302), followed.

By virtue of the mortgages the due dates mentioned in Sch. (kha) shall always be treated as mortgaged and security for realising the interest and principal due to the mortgagor according to the terms of the contracts. The trial Judge rejected the defence raised by the contesting defendants and held that as the plaintiff had in her plaint not relied upon dispossession as a ground for extension of the period of limitation, that claim should not have been permitted to be made out by the trial Court. The appellants employed as many as 7.000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to their employees to come to the factories from their respective villages, the appellants provided transport which would pick up passengers from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or Alandi or places enroute to TELCO Factory at Pimpri or Chinchvad and back. The appellants further averred that these amounts were realised by the appellants only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in the supervisory grades. In the course of arguments, it was pointed out that when the company was prepared to grant free transport facilities, it had not levied any charge at all for the transport facilities granted to the employees; they would be provided free transport as in the case of supervisory staff. It was further contended that even if a nominal charge was realised from the employees that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger, so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act. In view of what we have already said, it is not necessary for this Court to go into such meticulous details because the legal position appears to be clear enough. As counsel for the appellants has already undertaken not to charge any amount from the Employees for providing transport facilities and the point had now become more or less academic.

The appellants were the residents of a locality. The cinema house, in which the respondents are the residents, had been running in the locality and hence, a renewal of the licence for a temporary cinema in the same locality would not be proper. Respondent 3 carried out a printing press at various places including the place where the proposed cinema house was to be constructed but, it was interrupted by an extraneous consideration and that a course which was going on, had also been functioning in the premises in question and therefore, a fresh renewal of its licence for the same premises would not he proper. The District Magistrate granted an ex parte temporary licence under the M.P. Cinemas Regulation Rules to the third respondent who was the owner of a hotel building along with a permanent cinema licence for four months. This order was upheld by the State Government on 26th December 1977. A writ petition filed in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order was dismissed. The appellants then moved this Court for relief by special leave. HELD: 1. After considering the objections, if no objection certificate was granted, there ends the matter subject, of course, to any properly constituted legal proceedings, conceivably a writ petition under Article 226. But sub section (3) of section 5 of the Act is unambiguous when it provides for an appeal only at the instance of a person aggrieved by the decision of the licensing authority refusing licence. A fortiori every objector to renewal is not entitled to file an appeal if licence is granted rejecting his objections.

A contract dated August 3, 1957 was entered into between the parties on September 2, 1957. The defendant wrote a letter to the plaintiffs that the subject matter of the contract had been settled on September 1,1957 and that the plaintiff 's offer was unconditional acceptance but on November 6,1957 the plaintiffs did not accept the offer either orally or by any communication sent to the defendant. On November 1, 1957 the plaintiffs filed suit (O.S. No. 46) for specific performance of the contracts. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the plaint in O.S., No. 47 of 1957 was not an acceptance of the offer, not was it intended to be an acceptance. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The plaintiffs had failed to establish the new case. [585 A] There was no concluded contract and the appeal must fail on this ground. [58 E] In re: Pellatt 's Case, ; , relied on. Consequently, if a plaintiff in a suit for specific perform of the conditions mentioned in O .S. 47 could rely upon the oral application for shares he had withdrawn the offer from the defendant at any subsequent date by his letter dated September 2 and there was no completed contract. The court cannot add to an acceptance in view Of its conclusion. [55 E] The fact that the parties were bound to conform to the terms of the letter of September 2 did not mean that there was a concluded contract. In the peculiar facts of Bloxam 's case, a contract to take shares was concluded by an oral application.

The appellants are office bearers of M/s. S.K. G Sugar Ltd., Ltd. within the meaning of section 3(1) of the , as also the, office bearers. The complaint filed in the High Court was investigated. Ch Tika Ram Ramji & ors. vs the State of Bihar, [1962], Supp. 2 S C.R. 435 and M/S. K.G. Sugar Ltd. vs 8 7 Of . HELD : It is idle to contend that a complaint made before the police does not disclose a cognizable cognizable offence and as such the Police could not have taken up investigation of the said complaint.

Under an order dated 12th January, 1977 the procedure was prescribed for obtaining concessions given under the orders referred to earlier. On 12th of January,77 the Government of Karnataka issued another order which recited that the Government, namely, the Government Of Karnataka was committed to a policy of rapid industrialisation and that in pursuance thereof, the Govern ment had on 30th November 1966 issued directions indicating the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries in the Mysore State. The said order dated December 12, 1977 inter alia provided as under: "Consequently, the Governor of Mysore is pleased to sanction the following incentives and concessions to the entrepreneurs for starting new industry in the Bangalore State: (1) Sales Tax A cash refund will be allowed on all sales tax paid by a new industry on raw materials purchased by it for the first five years from the date the industry goes into production, eligibility to the concession being determined on the basis of a certificate to be issued by Department of Industries and Commerce . " By an order made on November 11th August 1975 the procedure prescribed for obtained the concessions given thereunder under the order dated 30th June, 1969 was prescribed. On December 12th, 1977, the State Government issued another Order which stated that the concession of refund of sales tax on raw material purchased by the new enterprises should be limited to 10 per cent of the cost of fixed assets per year, thus not exceeding the total of 50 per cent over a period of five years for which the concession is available.

The Trial Court acquitted A 7 of all the charges except A 1 to A6. The conviction and sentence of A 4 to A 6 was set aside by the High Court, and they were acquit ted on the following reasoning: . . It would be safe to accept the evidence of PW1 and 2 to the extent it is corroborated by the evidence 6 of P.W.3 in so far as the presence and partic ipation of the accused in the attack on the deceased is concerned, that the eye witnesses to the occurrence have been corroborated by them in so insofar as t he participation and parag ing with some unidentified persons. The non applicability of Section i49 I.P.C. is, therefore, no bar in convicting the appellants under 7 section 302 read with Section 34 I. P.C., if the evidence discloses commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intention of the parties all. All of them tried for offences under sections 147, 148, 323, 379 and 302 read ted with 149 I.p.C.; they caused the death of the sen ers with their respective weapons. When the deceased fell down, PW 1 and PW 3 were also armed with sticks. Seven of those weapons were deep penetrating wounds and remaining were abrasions. The injuries caused fracture on the right perietal bone result ing in the opening of the skull. The fourth rib was broken and there were an injury to the lung. There was an injury on the chest, therefore was broken, and there sen ting of the left hand of the PW 1 with the knife. A 2 further gave blows to the deceased on his head, and the deceased died instantaneously on the spot. Thereafter at the asking of A I, A A 2 and A3 dragged the dead body from the field while placed the same on the road.
