The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam, which he had purchased for the price of Rs. 16,500 to his daughter in law and five of his children. The assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 for which the relevant accounting year was the calendar year 1965 was thereafter completed on the normal course and in this assessment no amount was included by way of capital gains in respect of the transfer of the house since the house was sold at the same price at which it purchased and no capital gains accrued or arose to him as a result of the Transfer. On 4th April 1968, however the Income Tax Officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Income tax Act seeking to reopen the assessment of assessee for that year and requiring him to submit a return of income within 30 days of the service of the notice. 48,500 was to be considered as the full value of the consideration declared by the assessee in respect thereof. The assessee submitted a return showing Rs.16,500 shown to be the consideration for the transfer which had accrued or arisen to him. The Income Tax officer issued a show cause notice proposing to reopen assessment and requiring the assessee to submit an explanation within 30(thirty days from the date of service of this notice. By his order dated 4th March 1968 the IncomeTax Officer included Rs. 15,500 as capital gains on that basis. The charges for the year 1966 69 were dropped. The assessing authority accepted the explanation and assessed the amount in respect to the assessment. He also imposed an penalty under section 271(2) of the Act, 1961 for importing capital gains from taxation. The order was confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. Before this court the assessee contended that it was not necessary to state any general pattern of practice governing transfer of property and further that there should be under statement of consideration in respect 'the transfer ' on the date when the transfer took place. HELD: (1) The taxable income for the purpose of bringing a case within sub section (2) is, therefore, liable to tax under the Gift Tax Act, 1958, but it cannot be said that the transaction was effected with the object of avoidance or reduction of his liability under section 45. [653E] (a) There must be cases where the consideration received by the assesee in respect Of the transfer has been understated or even, if the condition of 15% difference between the fair market value of capital asset as on the the dateof transfer and the consideration declaring in respect respect of transfer is not truly declared or disclosed by him, but which were not covered by sub section(1) because the transferee was not directly or indirectly connected with the assessee or the object Or under statement , of the mind is unconnected with tax on capital gains.

The appellant, a businessman, was charged in the Court of Presidency Magistrate as follows: That you on 3 12 1968 at 8.m. in contravention of provisions of Section 2(1)(f) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, sold 450 grams of Til seeds to the Food Inspector and that the Til seeds were unfit for human consumption, and thereby committed an offence under section 16(1) (a)(1) of that Act and within my cognizance". The two witnesses produced to support this charge were D. P Tambe and section P. Gaydhani. They did not even remember who made the cash memo and whether anyone signed it in his presence. He also said he only thinks that he signed it, but on being asked for some Til seeds the accused told him that they were not meant for human use and thus committed an offense under section 6(1). The trial court convicted and sentenced the appellant to imprisonment for 6 months under section 5 of the Act. The High Court (on appeal) maintained the conviction and sentence. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was such vagueness and apparent contradiction in the pictures conveyed by the Food Inspectors and the Food Inspec tive that D. should have so stated; and on not the packets, though they had deposed in his examination in chief that Tambe 's testimony tends to demolish more than to corroborate the version of the Food inspector, he should have known that the appellant had only black Tils used for Pooja. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. Section 10(7) of tho Prevention of food Adulteration Act lays down that "food" means any article used as food or drink for human hire other than drugs and water and includes (a) any article which ordinarily enters into,or is used in the composition of preparation of human food. [316 E] 2. If the appellant was correct to say, they would have been kept for the purpose of being sold only as a substance used for pooja and not as human food and that it could not therefore be said that this case had been repelled by the mere statement of the food Inspector that they can be used as a food also. [341 C] 3. When the case of the appel lant supported by his cash memo, was that the particular black 'Til seeds where meant to be sold only for poojas for pojniment was put into a separate plastic bag and then sealed and labelled by him. He said that he himself divided this quantity into 3 parts each of which was put in a separate type plastic bag, and then labelled by them. The accused was therefore entitled to the benefit of that doubt [353 G] 4. Section 7 prohibits manufacture, sale or storage or distribution of certain types of food`. It is true that some articles such as milk or bread, or butter, or foodgrains are meant for ' human consumption within the meaning of section 7 of the hereinafter referred to as 'the Act '. In order to judge whether the Food En ter Inspector 's version or the accused 's explanation was more credible the prosecution has to prove beyond reasonable doubt that what Was stored or sold was `food '. [353 B] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , distinguished. In view of the fact that the signatures of an Inspector were absent on all those documents on which they would appear have been present if section 10(1), could not be implicitly relied upon in this case. The appellant must get the benefit Of that doubt.

The plaintiff in a civil suit was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13.1.1966, whereupon he preferred an appeal to Divisional Commis sion and that appeal was dismissed on 31.8.1966. The order of dismissal was communicated to the plaintiff on 19.9.1960 asking for a declaration that the order of dismissa tion was inoperative and he continued to be in service. On that day, i.e., on 13th January, 1966, a notice under section 80 Code of Civil Procedure was served on him asking for copies of documents. There were three suits pending in the courts below which were dismissed by the Trial Court in terms of orders dated 18.6.1969 and 22nd April 1950 respectively. The plaintiff filed an appeal before the Divisional Com missioner and that Appeal was dismissed. On 31st August 1966, he gave notice under Section 80 Code C.P.C., on 17th June, 1969 asking for filing of his suit on 30th September, 1969, asking for declaration that his order was inoperative. He filed a fresh suit on 29th September 1969, praying for a declara tion that the said order of termination was inoperative, and he should continue to be service. The Trial Court dismissed the suit in view of the dismissal of the appeal alleging that it had not been filed within three years from the date when cause of action first arose, as required under Article 58, as the period of limitation for pro per sonment was available to the defendant in addition to the period prescribed by section 326. The suit was accordingly dismissed on 28th January 1966. On 30th November 1968, the Divisional Commissioner communicated the order to the appel lant on 19th September 1960. The appellant flied a suit on 6th December 1969 asking that an appeal be heard and then the said notice had been served on the defendant on 7th February, 1971, terminating his earlier stand. He further contended that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court dismissed the suits, decreed the plaintiff 's suit, but the First Appellate Court in second appeal confirmed it in second appeals. The High Court held that on 1st March 1966 when the order was made by the Collec tor, the right to sue first accrued and since the suit filed was within time, the suit would be within time. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 Article 113 of the Act of 1963 corresponding to Article 120 of the old Act is a general one and would apply to suits which no other Article in the schedule applies. These suits outside the purview of the shall continue to gov erned by Article 58. It is proper that the position in such cases should be uniform. However, in every such case only when the appeal or representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of actions shall first accrue and where such order is not made, on the expiry of six months from thedate of preferring of the appeals or making the representation shall be taken to have first arisen. [54E F] 1.2 Article 113 says that "notwithstanding anything contained in this Chapter" any proceedings which are pending before the Court shall continue on the date of accrual of the cause of ' action, there is no get ing behind these words in spite of the apparent inequity of applying the same". [55D E] 1:3 There is nothing in the Indian Law to warrant the suggestion that the decree or order of the Court or tribunal of the first instance be comes final only on the termination of all proceed ings by way of appeal or revision.

The appellant filed a suit for his half share in the properties which originally belonged to the joint family consisting of himself and his father and to this suit he impleaded his father, several alienees from him. His case was that the alienations effected by his father as well as sales held in execution proceedings against his father were not binding on him and so his share in them was not affected by them. Held, that the word "decision" in article 133(1) must be read on the basis that every decree passed in a suit should be held to be a " composite decree made up of several decrees in respect of several claims or reliefs and that the decree appealed from is only that particular decree which is proposed to be brought in appeal to this Court. Where there was a variation in regard to the order as to costs such a variation is not an integral part of the decision or the grounds given for it but the decision of the suit as a whole, even though in form there might be one paper on which one decree is drawn, there could be no doubt that this decision clearly recognises that if the decision were wholly confirmed an intending applicant would not be entitled to come to this court as a matter of right unless there was compliance with a substantial question of law. The test of the value of the subject matter can be taken into consideration by reference to the subject matters which are actually proposed to he brought to this in appeal, and it is well settled that in construing the clause the Court would carefully bear in mind the views expressed by the majority of this Court, but as there was nothing to do with the decision as to the character of the appellate decree, it was not a case of affirmance. The principle underlying an appeal has to be ascertained on a consideration of the whole, and then whether the appellate court altered the order of the trial court so as to interfere with that order. The correct test is whether the variation as to cost is made in favour of one party or the other. If there was such a difference, then such variation would not confer a right of appeal as regards matters unconnected with the matter in respect thereof, and if it was felt necessary to take the decree as a part of it, then, such variation could not affect the character or validity of the original order.

Section 3, Code Of Civil Proce dure empowered the High Courts jurisdiction over specified cases and power was also conferred by section 115 to the District Judges. Under section 115 C. P.C., the revisional powers were separately mentioned. Section 115 provided that notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, any amendment made or provision inserted in the Code of civil Procedure by a State Legislature before the 1st February, 1978 would stand repealed except insofar as such amendment or provision was consistent with the Code as amended by the said Amendment Act. The proviso prescribed revisional jurisdiction in the High court alone and an additional remedy in respect thereof was provided for. Section 6, U.P., Civil Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976 provided that section 115 as now amended by section 2, U P. Civil Laws Amendment Act, 1973 would not apply to nor affect any proceeding for revision which had been admitted after the preliminary hearing, before 1st Febru ary, 1977 and every such proceeding for Revision would be disposed of as if section 43 had not come into force. The High Court in the writ petitions under section 11, UP., was directed to dispose of the application expeditiously within a specified time, failing which the District judge would deli cute an unnecessary exercise in accordance with law. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that the revisional power vested by section 151 C.l.C was plenary and not judicial; while applying the principle contained in Har Parasad Singh and others vs Ram Swarup and others and the main question raised before this Court, the High 'Court had jurisdiction under section 3 of the Code to hear such revision petition at a later date. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The legislative intention behind the amendment was to relieve the High If a revision application is permitted to the high Court against the revisional order of District Judge arising out of a suit of a value less than Rs.

The respondent owned Khasra No. 383 area 14 bighas 16 biswas situate in village Madrampura on the outskirts of Jaipur City. On June 25, 1975, the Special Officer issued a notice under section 52 (2) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 read with Rule 10 of Rules 10 and 18 of Rules 37 and 38 and 39 of the Rules framed thereunder requiring the reasons as to why a writ in the nature of mandamus should not be issued directing the appellants herein, the State Government by a letter dated April 4 , 1977 informed the respondents that there was no possibility of an exemption being granted under section 20 of the Act in their favour allowing them to retain vacant land in excess of 6,000 square yards for the construction of a three Three Star Hotel. The State Government in its special leave petition have explained that the notification under section52 (1) was issued on June 25 , 1975 and the necessary procedure as laid down in sub section (3) thereof followed. As a result of this , the State Govern ment issued the impugned notification dated February 8, 1984 under section 53(1) Or the Act and the notified land vested in the State government free from all encumbrances. The respondent filed an application to the State Govt . seeking exemption of the notified lands under section 50 (a)(e)(e) (f) (1 1 ) for the grant of an appropriate writ , direction or order under Article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that they needed the said land to start new business in the state, and for this purpose to utilize the notified Land for establishment of a branch office and for construction of residential houses for their Director and other Senior Executives. The application was not contested. The High Court dismissed the application. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that the petition filed by the respondent purporting to be under article 226 , is undoubtedly maintainable as there is no violation of Article 14 of the constitution or to make the declaration prayed for by the State which is not an integral part of the cause of action within the meaning of article 226(2) . Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The service of notice under sub section 2 of section 52 of the , on the respondents at their registered office at 18 B , Brabourne Road , Calcutta i.e., within the territorial limits of the State of West Bengal could not give rise to a cause of actions within that territory unless the service of such notice was an integral component part of ' cause of ' action. [605F G] 2. The notification dated Feb 8,1984 issued by the Government under section 51(1 ) Or the . Act became effective the moment it was published in the official gazette as thereupon the notified ' land became vested in State Government free from All encumbrances.

The appellant company entered into three several contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and other works at Ranchi. After the work was completed, disputes arose between the parties over the bills and eventually by an agreement dated February 6, 1948 they were referred to arbitration of one Col. A. W. section Smith. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948, and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The respondents thereupon filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award which was dismissed by the Subordinate Judge but granted a certificate under articles 132 and 133(1) of the Constitution. Held (per C., J., Kapur and Venkatarama Aiyar, jj.), that as the copy of the Award was sent to the Government would appear to have been insufficiently stamped it could not be validated merely because in the original the document which was unstamped or was insufficiently Stamp. But the language used must be interpreted literally and if a document purporting to have scribed a particular mode in which authority must be conferred is sufficient compliance with the Act. If that was so, it would not make any difference of opinion between the arbitrator and the Government. In the present case the title suit had been transferred by a party thereto and the same having been accepted, the document was new and fresh Construction of the original contract was effected in its place in the present form. 936 But the copy was sent as was sent again to the State Government would have considerable importance for the purpose of being defeated if it had been produced but then the Government failed to produce the same. The Government has failed to discharge the statutory obligations under section 35 of the Stamp Act and a valid reference could not validate the award only on an unstretly stamped or insufficiently stamp paper actually produced in court not and that the order was also one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of bills.

The respondent company was managed by a firm which after the death of 12 Nageswara Rao Panthulu, the widow of Nageswara rajuna Rao. The company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913 to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". In September 1936 it was managed for Rs. 5,50,0001 paid in the form of 2,500 ordinary and 3,000 preference shares of Rs. 100/each and the issued and paid up capital was 2,5500 ordinary, and 3200 ordinary and three,000 ordinary preference shares. The respondent company took over the business conducted by Nageswara Ramayamma for Rs 5,00,01 paid as in the forms of 2 and 500 ordinary preference fully paid up shares. This company was run by a Company which after its death was managed and managed by another firm which on August 12, 1955, issued and pay up capital of 2 500 ordinary and 61 per cent on the ordinary shares which was considerably less than sixty per cent of the amount available for distribution as computed under section 23 A of the Income tax Act. As it stood at the material time, no order could be passed in respect of any company in which the public were substantially interested and to a subsidiary company of such a Company if the whole of the share capital of such subsidiary company was held by the shareholders including Ramayma, widow of N. K. section 23A of the Act provided for total dividend of Rs 38,750/ . The proviso to section 23B of the Indian Income tax Officer served a notice after obtaining the approval of the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax and re quired the respondent company to show cause why an order under section23 A should not be passed against the company. After considering the objections raised by the assessee company ordered on March 31, 1953 that undistributed portion of the assessable income of the company as computed for income tax purposes and reduced by the amount of income tax and super tax payable by the company in respect thereof, shall be deemed to have been distributed as dividend amongst the shareholders as at the date of the respective general meetings. The order was confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Com missioner and the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) The Explanation to sub section (1), of section 23E of the , by which the provisions of section 24A were correctly applied for the three relevant years, did not define the expression "company in which and the explanation should be construed; (2) the explanation was against the Act as it stood in 1955 under which the Public were substantially con tended, and (3) the Explanation to that sub section was inapplicable as there existed no controlling interest in a group of persons. so as to bring the case within the third proviso. Held: The Explanation did not purport to define a company in Which the public are substantially interested, but only limited its limits were enjoyed by the controlling group.

The first appellant is the General Manager of a mill and he was sentenced to two months rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2,00,000 on each count. The second appellant is one of the Directors of the Mills. He was sentenced for two months ' rigorous imprisonment under section 7 and 9 of the Essential Supplies Act (No. XXIV of 1946) on two counts : (i) as shown above, the property in the goods had passed and so the first appellant no longer had title to them; (ii) Dwarkadas Khetan & Company were the sole selling agents of the mills. He is given a receipt for the money paid: At the same time Dwarkad as Khetan and Company sent the first appel lant an " advice slip" telling it that the money has been received, and asking it to prepare a delivery order. The appellants who are the Directors or their agent do not submit true and accurate information relating to his undertakings "to the Textile Commissioner C.S.T. Section at Bombay contended that even if there was physical delivery to Dwarkadash Resolution Dwarkadasa it would be wrong to say that there had been anything beyond a technical and unintentional breach of the law. Held, that the charge on the second count relating to the 6 bales was a similar one and the facts follow the same pattern. Those facts were truly and accurately given according to the popular and natural meaning of the words used; nothing was hidden ; it would not be correct to say, that there has been anything more beyond a jurisdictional technical and purpotic breach of law The fact that the goods did reach the683 market would not make any difference since the goods were actually delivered. Dwarkadhatas Khetan vs Bhagwan Narain, [1953] S.C.R. 763, considered.

The respondent was a Senior Lecturer with the University of Ahmedabad. In April 1964, the Physics practical examination for the first year B.Sc. had been to be held by the Gujarat University. One of the centres was Surendranagar and the other centres were Surendhanagar. Dwivedi had been appointed as an Examiner for Physics. He was alleged to have accepted gratification of Rs. 500/ other than legal remuneration for showing favour to a candidate Jayendra Jayantilal Shah by giving him more marks than he deserved in the Physicsology. It is also alleged that in April 1964 the Physics economic examination for first year M.Sc., was to be conducted by the Rajasthan University. A question arose whether an Examiner of the University as such can be regarded as a public servant within the meaning of the Ninth clause of section 21, Indian Penal Code. HELD : The use of corrupt or illegal means is essential before the amendment made in 1964 under the twelfth clause. But it is not necessary that the public servant while misconducting himself should have done so in the discharge of his official duty. [317H; 318A] In the instant case, the High Court had, on the evidence produced, come to the conclusion that Saxena taking advantage of his own position as an employee in the Chief Commissioner 's Office and Ram Narain 's ignorance and anxiety to get the license, had induced him to part with the money on ( 1 ) ; [317B C] Dhaneshwar Narain Saxena vs Delhi Administration, ; , distinguished.

% The petitioners filed a Writ Petition under Article 32 of the Constitution contending that notwithstanding the fact that each of them had put in continuous service for quite a long period, the Railway Administration, respondent herein, had not treated them as temporary servants and had applied discriminatory rates of wages. They also asked for reinstatement in the regular cadre on completion of 120 days of service as against 180 days which was the previous requirement. The Senior Signal & Telecom Engineer (Power Signalling) has filed a counter affidavit. At the hearing of the applications, counsel for the petitioners as also the respondents contended that the Respondent Railways had not treat them as permanent servants and as such they were entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in the Regular cadre in the permanent category as per Railway circulars issued by the Respondents. On behalf of the Administration it was contended that out of forty four petitioners who had put less than 360 days of continuous service, they had been empanelled and of them five have been given temporary appointments; eleven are said to have refused to join and seventeen are still continuing with temporary status. Allowing the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The Railway Establishment Manual has made provisions for their protection but implementation is not P effective. Several instructions issued by Railway Board and the Northern Railway Headquarters were placed before us to show that the Administration is anxious to take appropriate steps to remove them difficulties faced by the casual labour but there is perhaps slackness in enforcing them. It would have taken away inequality which is main grievance of the petitioners. The respondents shall have a direction to consider the claims of each of the Petitioners promptly and make appropriate orders for their regularisation. For over ten years, litigations of this type have been coming to the Court. About three years back, this court directed a scheme for absorption in Yadav 's case which has been framed and is operative. Casual labour seems to be the requirement of the Railway administration and cannot be avoided. The writ petitions are disposed of with the directions indicated above without any order for costs.

By a notification issued under section 12 of the Forward Markets Act, 1952, r. 52A(1) was made by the Central Government in exercise of power conferred on it by one of its provisions. The appellants who were members of a Association entered into contracts with other persons for settlements in February 1956 and May 1956. There was no dispute that these contracts were in accordance with the bye laws of the Association as they stood at the date when the contracts went into, on which the bye law came into force, and that the provisions of cl. (f) of section 4 were not in either case Subordinate legislation under section 11 or 12 as the case may be, of the Act and they would therefore be squarely fall within the words 'under the Act '. Held:(i) The appellants had entered into a contract for Settlement in February, 1956, whereby the Forward market Commission was to follow certain bye laws framed by it. On January 21, 1956 the Central Govern ment notified a new bye law 52AA which came into operation on January 21. Under cl. 2 of that bye law also all hedge contracts in so far as cotton is uncalled thereunder and relating to the delivery or deliveries notified under cl. 3(1), entered into between members and a member and a non member then outstanding shall be deemed closed out at such rates as shall be fixed by the Forward Market Commission and the provisions Of el. 11 of el. 2 in so insofar as they apply to hedge and on call contracts shallapply as if the formed part of this bye law. The words 'except under cl.(b) of the section show that the power was conferred in the interests of India, held to be a power which could be assigned to it by or under the Act. (ii) The notification dated January 24, 1956 by the Board was illegal and the appellants would be entitled to issue of a writ of mandamus unless retrospective operation was given to the provisions by el. 1(f), indicated that the Commission can perform its functions assigned to them by or tinder the Act, or as may be prescribed by the rules made under the Indian , for if the said phrase takes in a rule, the word 'prescribed ' becomes redundant; (iii) tile notification was illegal because the Central Govt., had no power to make a bye law under section 13 of the Indian .

The assessee company, a shareholder of a company called the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd., had received dividend from the Company and became its member. On November 7, 1948, the Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the company for the grant of long term mining lease was not taxable as dividend but as income of the assessee from "other sources" and taxed it under section 12. On second appeal, Tribunal held that the entire sum for each year was income in the hands of the asses see, but only a part of it being dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of Act, was liable to be grosed up. The High Court also observed that it had no recorded final answers on all the questions in the negative and held that it was agreed between the parties that the answers in the affirmative on all questions were subject to the final decision in appeals filed against the orders made in Income tax References Nos. 131 of 1961 and 3 of 1964. In the appeal to this Court, HELD : The order passed by the High Court is set aside and the case remanded to the High court for disposal according to law. [35B] The appeal is remitted to the Tribunal for disposal in accordance with law.

The State, Kerala Forest Act, 1961 aims to prevent depleting forests, conservation thereof and protection of wild life in the country to maintain ecological balance. The Karnataka Forest Act prescribes procedure for preservation of forest and regulates possession of the forest produce, failing of trees in the forest area and removal from the forest or reserved forest area by transit permits etc. When Sandalwood Oil either was found in transit or in possession of manufacturers it was seized in the respective cases and laid the complaints under section 5 1(1) (or contravened thereof. The jurisdictional question before the High Court was whether "sandlewood oil" is forest produce within the meaning of section 2(f)(i) of the Act. While accepting the contention of the State, the High court quashed the complaint holding that Sandal Wood Oil is a wood oil and not wood oil as defined under section 2 (f) (1) of Kerala Forest dcture Oil. Dismissing the appeals by Special Leave the Court, HELD: 1. The view taken by the High Courts appears to be correct. It can, however, be said that the Union of India had no authority in the matter. [505E] 2. The expression "wood oil", as defined in section 2 of the Kerala Forest Produce Act, is an inclusive definition and it cannot be restricted in a narrow circumference as was done by the learned Single Judge. so as to defeat the object and purpose of the act.[505B C] 3. The primary purpose of interpreting word " wood" in section2(f) is to conserve forest wealth which is very dear for preservation to maintain ecology. Forest produce defined under s 2 (o) is an exhaustive definition. It is settled law that the word 'include" is generally used as a word of extension. When used in an interpretation clause, it seeks to enlarge the meaning Of the words or pharases occuring in the body of the statute. The prosecution alleged that there was no evidence against the appellants sufficient to warrant a conviction and (2) there were no compelling reasons for reversal of the judgment of acquittal. Held, that the High Court should not set aside an order of conviction unless there are " substantial and compelling ' reasons for doing so. The conclusions of the High court had been taken into consideration by the Sessions Judge who treated the dying declarations as a reliable one and which were accepted by him though they were rejected by the trial judge. It was, therefore, that not proper to contradict the statement of a man who was present at the spot by using the statement to make a dying declaration, improbable. The learned judges of the Madras High Court had proceeded on a consideration of the testimony of one eye witness Hazari and Bega, and not being satisfied with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon. Where the evidence was such that no Tribunal could legitimately infer from it that the accused is guilty of this court would set aside the conviction. [859 A C] Case law considered. Emperor vs The King ; , Emperor vs Ganappa, (1933) L.R. 73 I.A. 33 and Queen Empress vs The State of Madhya Pradesh, Aher Raja Khima vs The Sate oforageastra, ; disapproved. Stephen Seneviratne v The King, (1883) 9 L.W. 1, followed. Further, the infirmities which the testimony were put to him by the prosecution in support of the correctness of the two dying declarations or could the statement be relied upon as sufficient to support the conviction of the accused.

Section 10(2) of the , provides that without prejudice to the generality of the power in sub section (1), such regulations may provide inter alia for the manner in which trade unions and their rules shall be registered. In pursuance of the powers conferred by sub sec.(2) Of Sec. 10, the Registrar of Trade Unions issued a letter dated January 21, 1963 by which the Secretary of the said union informed the District Manager that the disputes referred to above were " those set out in the agreement and state 554 and were between the management of the appellant company 's factory at Jamshedpur and their workmen represented by the Indoxco Labour Union." The appellant company, from time to time claimed bonus for overtime work but did not pay any overtime rates. But, it claimed that the dispute raised by the union was in respect of employees of the Company wherever they may be stationed. The Tribunal held that the constitution of the .said ' Indox co Labour Union came into force with effect from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the company and the workmen of all the establishments of the appellants" in Bihar eligible for its membership, there was no difference that the name of IndoxCo Labour Union as representing the workmen concerned was mentioned in the said agreement and the said statement and the statement of the parties were wrong. Accordingly, the Tribunal awarded a special leave to attend the law courts for matters connected with the workers and the management to attend to annual conventions of their federation, to attend on the general festival of their association. The appellant contended that (i) under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act it could be made liable to pay overtime work at the rate provided in that Act; (ii) even assuming that the Indrasan Labour Union validly amended its constitution so as to extend its membership to the Company 's other workmen in its other establishments, inasmuch as the disputes refer ed to the Tribunal were only those set forth in the agreements and the statements and no other dispu sions of the Indian Oxygen Workers ' Union were allowed to attend with the firm 's meetings without loss of pay; this was not sufficient for the employer to .be entitled to claim parity between the workmen working at Jamshedpur, because if facilities were given to the workmen to conduct the administration of the union themselves, there would be less possibility of outside elements establishing their hold on the union. HELD: The Tribunal 's award is operative in respect to the labourers of the company wherever they might be stationed and thus the appellant Company was justified in obliging the appellant to grant special leave demanded by the Union. [550 B] (i). In considering such a demand, the first question which strikes one is as to why the meetings of the executive committee of the Union cannot be held outside the hours of work. But emergencies are not of regular occurrence and if there be one, the representatives can certainly sacrifice one of their earned leave. [551 E] (ii). The workmen getting various types of paid leave. As the figures of such leave are not correctly stated in the award, it is impossible to say that the Tribunal erred in doing so or act unjustly. [553 G] (iii) In conceding the demand of the Unions the Tribunal does not appear to have considered the adverse effect on the company ' production if further absent absenteeism were to be allowed especially when the crying need of the country s economy is more and more production and employers are exhorted to streamline their management to achieve this objective and to bring down their cost in line with international cost.

The assessee was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918 in respect of income from business inter alia in timber at Abdullapur. In 1948 there was a partition of a Hindu undivided family and five members of that family entered into a partnership to carry on business in timber which was carried on by the undivided family. Accounts of this firm were settled till March 31, 1939, and the firm was dissolved. The timber business of the assessee firm was taken over by two partners of the firm Gajjan Mal and Jodha Mal, who entered into an agreement of partnership to carrying on the business in the name of R. B. Jodhar Mal Kuthiala son of Lala Khem Chand Sahib Sud of the other part residents of Haroli, District Hoshiarpur ( Simla), and all the partners had become separate from April 1, 1939. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm M/s Hakam Mal Tani Mal was dissolved on March 31,. 1939 before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 Of 1939, which came into force and that it succeeded to the business after April 1. 1939, after Act 7 of 1939 was brought into force relief under section 25(4) was not admissible. The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub sections (3) or (4) of section 25 of the Indian Incometax Act 1922, and thus assessed the assessee under section25(4). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order holding that succession to the family firm was having taken place on April 1., 1939, when the firm had come into force. ^ Held: (1) The provisions of section 66(2) were applicable where a deed recites that a transaction is effective from a particular date it has to be determined in the context in which that expression occurs, whether the date mentioned has to been excluded or to be included. Once an agreement was arrived at between the partners on April. 1, 1938, and upto March 31 1939, the business of M firm started till the midnight of March 31 and immediately thereafter the business came into being at the precise point of time when the Indian income tax ( Amendment) Act 6 of 1939 came into operation and it could not be said that the assessee was not carrying on business at the commencement of the Income Tax (Amendment). (2) A deed recites in the agreement that a certain transaction is voluntary from a specified date, it has further to be deter mined in the light in which the expression occurs ' whether the day mentioned has been excluded. (3A B) (4B) and the words "or" occurring in section 25 were not intended to give any meaning to the term "in coming within the meaning of that word.

The appellant was granted stage carriage permit under section 48 of the (briefly the Act) for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by its order dated May 3, 1963. Some of them preferred appeals against the said order to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and obtained stay of the order on the ground that the Secretary to the Regional Transport Authority had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 after a lapse of such a long time from the date of the grant of the permit. The appeal filed by the appellant to the Revenue Appellate Tribunal against the order of the State Road Transport Appellate tribunal was dismissed on September 27, 1963 and the impugned orders were challenged in this Court. HELD : An appeal lay under section 64 against an order issuing a permit in pursuance of the earlier resolution of the Regional Authority granting the permit: Issuance of the certificate is only a ministerial act necessarily following the grant granting of the permits. The appeals before the State RTA were, therefore, not competent under section 58(1) of the Act to entertain the appeals and to interfere with the order granting the permits which had already been affirmed in appeal by the State and further in second appeal by Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunals while affirming that view. [6412H] The High Court was, therefore right in dismissing the writ application of the appellant which ought to have been allowed. Though arguments were addressed by counsel with regard to old rule 151 and r. 119 of Mysore Motor Vehicle Rules,1963, this Court did not think called upon to pronounce upon the legal effect of these rules in this appeal.

The appellant was elected to the Lok Sabha from Hapur Parliamentary Constituency in the year 1967. The election symbol of an Kamil Party which was headed by a Congress party. At that meeting respondent Prakash Vir Shastri secured 1,49,943 votes while the appellant secured 34,274 votes while that the appellant obtained 36,272 votes while his supporters were standing and assaulted the workers of the appellant tore posters, abused the appellant and threatened his workers. In support of these allegations the appellant relied on two oral testimony of PW 11 P.W. 12 P. W. 11, P.Ws. P. 10, P 10,P.W 19, P 15, P 16 and P 17 which confirmed that position. The gist of the case is that at the meeting held the respondent Prakash had spoken at an election meeting at Hapur, but did not mention or refer to any meeting on behalf of respondent Prakash. He was prosecuted under section 123(3A) of the Act in respect of the attack on the office of the Republican Party. The High Court dismissed the Election Petition holding that there was no discussion of the oral evidence of P. Ws. 8 and 2, who were the supporters of the Congress Party, could not be allowed to make that case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf Of the appellant that the statements in Exhibit 22 did not make any reflection on the moral or mental nature of the respondent. The appellant relied mainly on the oral testimony, of PWs. 11 and 12, P 9, P 13, P 14, P 20 and P 26, and that the evidence in support of the contention was only one which was reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospects of the election of the person. HELD: (i) The offending news item in the journal 'Vir Arjun ' Exhibit 22 does not offend the provisions of either sub section(3 A) or sub section (4) of section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. [900 D] (ii) The publication in the newspaper 'Vit Arjun ' was an appeal on behalf by respondent Prakash, since the appellant had participated in the meeting which was held at Hapur in support thereof and his election agent was not made to have the consent of the candidate or his election office agent. It was only after the publication was not tainted by corrupt practice that the respondent could be said to offend the provision relating to corrupt practices as contemplated in the Representation Of the People (XLIII) Act, 1950. [902 E] (iii) The appellant had acted with due care and caution. It would be unfair to hold that it is an offence, if committed, which was not by the workers. There is no violation of any provision contained in sub section 3(A). A candidate may have been convicted under section corrupt section by a competent Court on proof only of the allegation that he made the statement. The expression 'partisan feeling and there is absence of such element. [986 E F] (iv) The objections to his being allowed to be withdrawn or not filed, were also taken to be adjudicated by the Election Tribunal. [987 A B] Badat & Company vs Kultar Singh, ; , followed.

The mortgagee decree holder in execution of the final decree for mortgage himself purchase the disputed property in auction sale held on July 14, 1978 at a sum of Rs.30,000. On September 20, 1978, the judgment debtor Ganpat Singh, since deceased, the predecessor in interest of the appellant filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. Two other petitions of objections were filed by one Chiranji Lal and another judgment debtor Mst. Abhey Kanwar. All these objections including the applica tion of Ganpat Singh under order XXI Rule 95 of the C.P.C., were dismissed for default and, consequently, the sale was con firmed by the District Judge on January 2, 1979. On July 17, 1980, that is more than one year after the sale, was confirmed, the decree holder auction purchaser filed an applica tions under Order 21 Rule 95 CPC for setting it aside the said sale which was opposed by the judgment debtors Ganpat Singh on the ground that as the application was filed more than 30 years after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by limitation under Article 134 of the . 360 It was held by the learned District Judge that in view of the provision of Explanation I1 of section 47 read with Article 136 of the , an application for settingaside the sale may be made within one year from the date on which the decree or order becomes enforceable or where the decree, or any subsequent order directs payment of money or the delivery of any property to be made at a certain date or at recurring periods when default in making such payment or delivery in respect of which execution is sought, takes place. After a decree was out into execution within the period of limitation under article 136, questions relating to execution, discharge or satisfaction of the decree may arise and such question including the question as to the delivery Of posses sion of the property to such purchaser of immovable property would be questions relating thereto to the execution of tho decree and, as such, Arti cle 136 and not Article 134. The certificate dated July 21, 1979 was refused by the executing court on April 26, 197 1. On August 14, 1947, the judg ment debtor Ganpat w/o Sh. Ram Phool Chand for the suit premises were put in auction on July 17; 1980 at a price of Rs '30, 000. On October 7, 1980 the judgment debt holder auction sale purchaser filed a applica tor under Order XXII Rule 90 CPC for bringing aside the Sale. Two more other applications were also filed by another judgment debtors in respect thereof.

In the election to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from Mattancherry Constituency No. 73, appellant was declared elected by a margin of 1873 votes over his nearest rival, the first respondent. The appellant filed an elec tion petition claiming a declaration that he 's election was void on the ground that the appellant had committed two corrupt practices within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Representation of Peoples Act, 1951. In support of the petition, the appellant stated various corrupt practices by including (i) printing and publication on March 22, 1987, a day prior to the election; (ii) printing of a wall poster both maligning the personal character and conduct of the first res pondent; and (iii) publication of a got printed news item in daily "Malayala Manorama" dated May 22, 1983 and (iv) publication by a newspaper circulation paper. Both these witnesses denied those allegations and also denied the allegations of corrupt practice made against them. The High Court rejected all the said corrupt practices except two namely (i). printing and publications on March 23, 1987 a day before prior to March 22. 1987, leading to the filing of the Election Petition but did not record an order as to how it shall create such an impression amongst the electorate, and (ii). the pamphlet containing the reprint of the daily " MalayalaManorama", which was printed at the instance of the appellant and with his consent and connivance as well as of his election agent. Aggrieved by the said decision and order, the election of the appel lant to the State Assembly from the Mattanapalli Constituency was declared void on that ground. The election petition filed on behalf of the returned candidate was dismissed by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 An Election Petition has been riled and it is not necessary to plead in the pleadings that particular acts were alleged to be defamatory in their natural and ordinary meaning and whether the literal or inferential meaning, and those in which the jewellato ry meaning is a secondary meaning derived from extrinsic or special facts or matters, so that a legal or true innuendo must be pleaded. [776C] 1.2 In the instant case since the election petitioner had proved that the theatre belonged to Chowd hary 's sons and that Chowdhary was the Minister in charge of the Rajasthan Canal it should be held that the returned candidates had reasonably calculated the voters or at any rate the voters in and about the locality where the theatre was being put up, had knowledge of the fact that it was being constructed by the Minister or his sons, and that such extrinsics facts could not have been unknown to the voters. It is not a case where the first respond ents are related to the third respondent, who had stated in his petition that the pamphlet was printed and distributed with a view to create false impression among the elector ate that he was a murderer, he has not stated as to why it would create such a impression amongst them. [76H; 77A B] 1:3 In the absence of any allegation by the appellant that it is in the name of the election Committee. The first respondent, even in his complaint had relied on an innuited statement made before him that he had not seen the act of pasting of exhibit P1 and he did not know who pasted exhibit P 1 nor was there anything more to show that the poster was affixed prior to election by the workers of the Appellant with their knowledge and consent.

The respondent No. 5 proposed to construct a five star hotel on a tract of land measuring 44,820.49 square yards at Bandra, Bombay bearing R.S. Nos. 416 (Part) and 417. The land in question had been purchased by the respondent No 5 from its erstwhile owner, Byramji Jeejeebhoy Pvt. Ltd., In the 1966 sanctioned development plan of Greater Bombay, the said land was shown in the residential zone and a contiguous parcel of land was indicated as a green belt. With a view to developing the disputed land, the Respondent No.5 submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of GreaterBombay for the construction of five star hotels. The Commissioner of the Municipal Corpora tion, however, rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said plot under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the respondent no. 5 preferred an appeal before the Government under section 47 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966. The appellants filed a writ petition challenging the legality and validity of the resolution dated 14.3.1974 and also the provisions of sections 46 and 31(6) of the Act. A Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that even the proposed revision could be taken into account as one of the relevant factors, while in granting exemption to the Respondent 5, the authority concerned has violated the relevant guidelines and also provision of section 20 of the Urban Land Ceiling Act. In appeal to this Court, the appellants contended that the Municipal Corpo ration had decided to revise the 1966 Development Plan, but they were entitled to take into consideration other relevant facts including the contemplated revision of plan apart from those mentioned in sections 46, 47 and 31 (6) thereof. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The ground for rejecting the plan submitted by the Respondent no.5 was not tenable, and the appellate authority was justified in allowing the appeal. [922D] 2.1. It is apparent that in granting sanction to the Plan, the Municipal Commissioner had, subsequent to the judgment of theHigh Court, prepared and published on April 30, 1984 a draft revised development plan. The plan of the respondent NO 5 is not inconsistent with the draft revised Development Plan. [936F G] 3.2 In granting sanction of the building, the Corporation has acted in public interest by imposing the conditions mentioned above. There is, in our opinion, some force in the contention made by the appellants against the sanction of this plan. [948B C] Life Insurance Corporation of India and Another vs Municipal Corporation.

A complaint was filed by the employer against one of the appellant companies, and both the applications were dismissed in limine. The Union thereupon filed two special civil applications in Bombay High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution questioning the correctness of the decision of the Industrial Court. Both the applications filed by them were dismissed. Thereafter the management filed two writ petitions before the High Court challenging the correctness or otherwise of the Tribunal 's judgment, and contended that they had closed and irrevocably closed the industrial undertaking; and that there was partial resumption of manufacturing process. The High Court dismissed both the writ petitions in limine, holding that there is a closure of the industrial undertakings and it was not a case of lock out. In appeals to this Court on behalf of the employers, it was contended that the Industrial undertakings had never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that the old workmen were not being re employed. Dismissing the Appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 While examining whether the employer has imposed a lockout or has closed down the industrial activity, it is not necessary to approach the matter from this angle that the closure has to be irrevocable, final and permanent and that lockout is necessarily temporary or for a period. The employer may close down industrial activity bonafide on such eventualities as suffering continuous loss, no possibility of revival of business or inability for various reasons to continue the industrial activities [69H; 70E] 1.2 When it is claimed that the employer had resorted to closure fide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial process he can not do so on the pain that the closing down of the new industrial activity was a consequence of imposing lock out or the owner employer had decided to close down the Industrial activity. [70G] 1:3 The question whether the closure is brought about malafide and whether it could have been avoided are matters irrelevant and what is to be seen is whether in fact and in effect there is any closure or not. [71D E] 2. When it was claimed that it has resorted to a closure bonafide wants to revive, revived and re started the industrial operation he can no do so. On the other hand closure implies closing of the industry as a consequence thereof of which workmen are rendered jobless. The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the employer at the time of closure but is not decisive of the matter. [72E, G] 2:1. It is to he determined with accuracy whether the closing up of the undertaking was a device or pretence to determine whether the industrial establishment was a activities consequence of imposed by imposing lockout out or has closing down the business.

The assessee company acquired shares of the value of Rs. 1,33,930 and during the year ending 30th June, 1940 no purchases were made with the exception of a few shares of Loyal Mills Ltd. taken under which debentures held by the assessee company in the Sassoon Group of Mills were redeemed and the proceeds were to be paid to creditors in payment of the loan granted by them. From the year ended 30th September, 1943, reconstruction scheme of the Appollo Mills Ltd., 48 took place under which debenture held by a registered office of the company were redeemed. The Income tax authorities accepted the plea of the assessee and treated it as a dealer for the assessment years 1940 41 to 1948 49, excepting the year 1947 48. At the instance of the assesee company the issue of shares made by the company in Appollu Mills Ltd 48 took over from the retiring staff. The return filed by the assesment company was accepted only on March 6, 1944 and after the return had been filed for the year 1943 44, the assessee Company withdrew its return and filed a revised return on March 7, 1944 contending that it was not a 49 dealer but merely an investor. On April 8, 1944, the Income tax department issued notice to the asses see company who in turn made a claim every year being treated as a "dealer" in investments and properties but this contention was repelled by the Income Tax Officer and on appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Tribunal held that the assessee was a dealer in shares, securities and immovable property under misapprehension and without appreciation of the correct facts. On reference by the High Court to the High court the question whether the assessee appellant company was a "residing in investments" and properties or whether it was a mere investor will have to be judged on a proper scrutiny of the transactions themselves considered in the light of the circumstances in which the transactions both of purchase and sale had been brought about. Accordingly, the High COurt set aside the order of the Tribunal. The assessee company contended that the real controversy in this case was not reflected in the two questions framed by this Court in its judgment dated May 22, 1957, but it was purely a question of law.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif. He was again promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge, and on June 19, 1950. After a period of 15 days he had been suspended from service. In view of the enquiry pending against him the respondent contended that by reason of the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules 1953 which had been published by the Andhra Government in October 1953, it was only a Tribunal as provided in Rule 4(1)(a). Held: The order passed by the High Court on January 28, 1954 is merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government and such an order is neither one of dismissal nor removal from service within article 311 of the Constitution. It was not correct to say that because under the proviso to Rule 4 of the A Civil Services Rules it was obligatory on the part of the Government to refer the cases of all. Government servants drawing a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above could dismiss or remove him from service, and such order is outside the rule. The order in question falls within this rule and is perfectly intra vires. Held further, that the High court had no authority under the rules to suspend a judicial officer pending final enquiries into grave charges under r. 17(e) if it considered necessary to do so. Sri Krishna Deo vs C. T. & Ors. , held inapplicable. After the service of the respondent was terminated in view of his enquiry, the High: Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with it.

The respondent obtained probate of various shares of a private Limited Company A ' with its registered office in Bombay. The company had issued letters of Administration "durante absentia" to the estate of A ' as his share to tax under section 24A of the Income Tax Act, 1922. Under an order made by the Income tax Officer under section 23A of that Act certain undistributed parts of the assessable income of the Company shall be deemed to have been distributed as dividends amongst the shareholders, and by the express provision contained in the statute the proportionate share of the dividend of each shareholder has to be included in the total income of such shareholder for the purpose of assessing his total income. The respondent claimed that the dividend deemed to be distributed was only an effective device to avoid tax on receipts by legal representative of a deceased person in the years of assessment succeeding the year of account in which such person died and that therefore he should not be taxed as his income in the hands of the legal representatives, since the provisions of section 24B had been given rise to a notional income. Held, that the respondent 's action by way of taxation was valid when it purported to tax all assessable incomes, and income received by a legal representative by virtue of a personal order made under section 22A of Income Tax (Second Amendment) Act 18 of 1933 in respect of calls upon shares whether made during the life time of the holder or after his death in that previous year became assessable to tax in the relevant assessment year but not receipts by the legal representative, who was himself not a member is as valid if he were a member at the time of execution of the transfer. Amarchand Shroffs case, [1953] S.C.R., p. 67, followed. Commissioner of Income tax Bombay City II vs Shakumtala and others, , approved.

The appellant was the Ruler of the State of Baster. After passing the Indian Independence Act, 1947 the appellant executed an Instrument of Accession to the Dominion of India on August 14, 1947, whereby he ceded the State to the Government of India to be integrated with the Central Provinces and Berar (now State of Madhya Pradesh) in such manner as the Government thought fit. The appellant was a Ruler of Baser ' within the meaning of article 366(22) of the Constitution and therefore he could not conceivably be a maufidar. He relied on article 6 of the Instrument of Covenant and it was contended that his rights had been recognized and guaranteed under the agreements entered into by him with the Government Of India which he was entitled to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such villages, that the appellant was not allowed to do so in view of the provisions of article 363(1) of Constitution. Held : Where under any covenant or agreement entered into between the Ruler and of any Indian State before the commencement of the Act, payment of any sums free of tax has been guaranteed or assured by the Government at any time before the Constitution, that would not make him a Ruler for purposes outside the Constitution. The impugned Act did not fall within the category of Estates or Alienated lands but as they did come within the purview of the definition of the word "mahal" contained in the Act. [507 C] The ordinary dictionary meaning of maufi is "Released, exempted, exempt from payment of rent or tax. " In view of section 2(j) of ' the Act the same must be separately assessed to land revenue and as he was also a mahafidar for purposes of the privy purse guaranteed, he was a holder of rent free land, a grantee".

Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The transfer order dated January 29, 1991 in respect of applicant S.L.Abbas was malafide and liable to be quashed. [455D] 2. In the matter of considering transfer of an individual officer, the office Memorandum dated 3.4.1986, educational dislocation of the children and health ground, if all present, deserve special consideration not to pass the order. The said guidelines also do not have statutory force. Who should be transferred where, is a matter for the appropriate authority to decide. Unless the order of transfer is vitiated by malafides or is made in violation of any statutory provisions, the court cannot interfere with it. While ordering the transfer, there is no doubt, the authority must keep in mind the guidelines issued by the Government on the subject. Similarly if a person makes any representation with respect to his transfer, the appropriate Authority must consider the same having regard to the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouses to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees for the other employees. [ 432E] 3. Where a person made any representationwith respect to the transfer of his transfer from any place in India, subordinating the need of the couple living together at another station, he cannot as of right claim to be relieved of the ordinary incidents of all India service and avoid transfer to a different place on the ground that the spouses thereby would be posted at different stations. [ 433E F] 4. The guidelines indicated that as far as possible husband and wife must be posted in one pi" as faras practicable, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as of rights if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. In this case all India Services, the hardship resulting from the two being posted at the same station even if their employers be different. [44C D] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta [1992] 1 S.C.C., 306 referred to. 5. The guideline does not confer upon the Government employee a legally enforceable right. Rules 11 says that as in far as practicable, husband andwife must be posting at thesame place.

The appellants were tried for the murder of one Jawahar. Three charges were framed against them by the Trial Judge and A4, A5 and A6 were al acquitted by the trial Court. On appeal the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A3. It was contended on behalf of the appel lants that the appellants were falsely implicated in the case and that they had no motive for such offence because there was no evidence against them. The trial court while relying upon the evidence convicted both of the accused under section 304 Part I read with Section 34, I.P.C. and sentenced them to undergo Life imprisonment for five years, and this appeal by A1 to A 3 as well as to A2 through a special leave petition was filed against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The intention of the appellants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them came within the parameters of Section 325, I P.C., i.e. section 325 read with 34, IPC, and instead convict them under Section 325 I. P. C.[62E] 2.1. The purpose of setting in view the nature of injuries on the person of the deceased and the facts and circumstances of this case, it is not able to give a finding in favour of the prosecution. Even according to Jawahar 's statement (Exhibit PW 6) all that first accused had remarked was that the attack on him was in retaliation for the injuries Jawahar had caused on the first accused a few weeks earlier. The High Court while setting aside the convic tion of A 4 to A7 but restored the findings in respect.

The respondent firm was nationalised on July 7, 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act V of 1970. The loan amount was admittedly advanced by way of loan by the Bank after its nationalisation. The appellant Bank filed a suit for recovery of the amounts claimed by it on account of the loan together with interest due thereon amounting to Rs.18,14,817.91 being the balance (inclusive of interest) of three principal amounts of Rs.3.00,000 and Rs.80,000 advanced by the bank to the firm under cash credit account on 28 11 1967 3 4 1968 and 17 2 1972 respectively. The said suit was decreed and the Bank preferred an appeal before the High Court which dismissed it. In decreeing the suit, the High court held that no equitable mortgage was created in favour of the Bank and that therefore the Bank was entitled to recover the entire amount without the same being scaled down as provided in section 13 of the Act. Aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the High 'High Court the Bank appealed to this Court by special leave. The questions for determination were: (1) whether the High Courts were justified in decreeing the Bank 's claim only after the scaling down of the debt in accordance with the provisions of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act IV of 1938 which, after the creation of the State of Andhra Pradesh was made applicable to that State as the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Agriculturists Relief Rules, 1937 and the Court therefore had no jurisdiction to decree it; and (2) whether there was any reasonable justification for laying down that the expression `special Indian law ' in section 4(e) of the act means a law enacted by an Act of British Parliament for India. Allowing the appeal in part. HELD: 1. The Banking Companies Act is a special Act enacted by the Federal Parliament. This Court while speaking of any special Indian law, is only speaking of special Indian laws and the provision of section 4 (e) would apply to a corporation which is the creature of a special Indian Law. [970G] 1.2 In view of the definition of `special foreign law ' as made in Krishna Murthy 's case (supra) the expression "special Indian" has a clear and unambiguous meaning and there is no need for its interpretation. There is no reasonable justification to think that the term `special general Indian law" must be an enactment of the British Parliament. If, on the date the Act was passed, there was no Indian Legislature, such an interpretation might be justified, but if there were existence of Indian legislatures including a Legislature at the Centre, it would be quite unreasonable to think 'that `special India law ' must be a law promulgated by the British legislature [970C D] 1.(a) That the said words "in pursuance of" refer to the action taken under the law and not by the law itself in order to come within the purview of section 2(e), would apply.

Section 3 of the , provides for the control of price at which any essential commodity might be bought or sold. Clause (c) of section 3(2) lays down that the Government will take into account in fixing prices and this was done with a view to securing equitable distribution of the commodity to the consumer at a fair price, namely, the consumer. The Central Government by its notification had fixed ex factory prices for all the units of sugar including charges incidental to sale and levy an additional excise duty at the rate of Rs. 17 per maund on any factory failing to deliver its quota of sugar for export. On dispute being raised as to whether the impugned notification was hit by article 19(1)(g) or article 19 (1)(f) of the Constitution, the Government referred two sets of interveners consisting of sugar factories in these areas which did not join the petition. Their case was that the prices fixed were arbitrary and did not take into consideration the cost of production and distribution of sugar, including charges relating to incidental to sales and therefore in any case it was not necessary for them to control the prices elsewhere; nor was there anything in the press note which suggested that the price fixed was just below the cost. Held, (per Hidayatullah, Mudholkar and Shah, JJ.), that section 3 of tho Act is constitutionally valid and must be struck down as unconstitutional on the ground that it does not violate article 14 or article 31 of the constitution and any infringement of the fundamental right under Article 19(6) of India. It was well known that there are three kinds of prices prevalent in the market for a commodity like sugar, namely ex factory price, wholesale price and retail price: The main object of the Act is to maintain the production, supply and distribution thereof trade and commerce therein. Under cl. (c), the prices for the consumer only should be fixed; but this does not mean that the power of the Central Government under section 3 (1) and section 3 are control at a different stages in the interests of general public. It is well known in these circumstances that the wholesale and retail prices depend upon ex factory rates, in the case of a commodity such as sugar, there is no reason why the Government should have fixed wholesale and total wholesale price also. The notification fixing ex factory Price was not bad because it fixes ex factory arbitrarily for the ultimate consumer which must be done under the Act; the impugned notifications did not subserve the purpose of the order and the order appealed to this Court by special leave.

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956 transferred the dispute between the parties to the second industrial Tribunal under section 10 Of the , to that of the Fifth Industrial Tribunal for adjudication of industrial disputes relating to any matter whether specified in the Second Schedule or the Third Schedule. The Fifth Industrial Disputes (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1956 came into force on August 28, 1956, and by virtue of this award, the Tribunal held that there was rise in the cost of living index and that to neutralise the said rise the employees should get an increase of Rs. 7 in dearness allowance on the pay scale up to Rs. 50 and Rs. 5 on the p. pay scale above Rs.50. The company preferred Civil Appeal No. 125 Of 1958 against the award of the Tribunal as modified by the Appellate Tribunal fixed the basic wages and the rate of dearness allowance payable to the employees was worked out, and awarded. On that basis the dearness allowance paid to the workmen was worked over and above that. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the company, inter alia, that though the said principles might be applied at the time of granting special leave once leave, once leave is granted no such restrictions could be imposed or applied at all the time Of granting special Leave; (1) in view of the multiplicity of industries in India and the increase in dearness allowances to which they would have otherwise been entitled on the basis of the rise in cost of live index by dearness allowance could not be permitted, and (2) section 33B inserted in the Act by the Amending Act 18 of 1957 was prospective in operation i.e., it would apply only to proceedings initiated in the tribunal constituted under the Act before the commencement of the Amending Acts came into effect. Held:(1) When a Tribunal has been established before the amendment of 1957, that question arises whether there is substantial change in the working class cost of the living index, in which case the rate will be suitably adjusted. In regard to matters covered by it, the agreement replaced the earlier award and therefore the date of the agreement is the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change. (2)(a) Section 19(6) does not confer a right of appeal to any party from the decision of any tribunal, but it confers a discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal from the order of any Tribunal in the territory of India. Although article 136 is couched in widest terms, it is necessary for this Court to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction only in cases where awards are made in violation of the principles of natural justice, causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raises an important principle of industrial law requiring elucidation, and final decision by this Court or disclosed such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit consideration of this Court. Further the broad test for determination whether there has been substantial change of circumstances which entitled the employees to claim an increase in their dearness allowance was that the Tribunal should have applied all the relevant facts and not merely to individual orders, but also to individual awards so as to effectuate a fair decision by the Supreme court or disclosed and fair decisions by this court or disclose such other special factors which merit the consideration of the Supreme. (3) This Court cannot interfere with the findings of fact given by the Tribunal from different angle must be mentioned; it was not necessary for the Supreme Courts to give any finding on merits of the matter, but only has merely to see whether there had been substantial increase in the price index in the year 1951 or that the principles were applied at a time when the dispute was referred.

The appellant, a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hindus, was taken over by the Board of Hindu Religious Endowments constituted under the Madras Act 11 of 1927. That Act repealed the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act XIX of 1951 by which all schemes settled or modified by a Court of law under the said Act or under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 were deemed to have been settled or dered. It was provided that notwithstanding the repeal of the Madras Acts by virtue of the provisions of the earlier Act, all schemes settle or modified reached by a court of law shall be deemed to be settled or modi cated under the provisions Of section 103(d) and (h). Thereafter the appellant moved the High Court for quashing the notice served on him by the Executive Officer. The said writ petition was allowed. In appeal to this Court it was urged that sections 103(a) and 32 of the Act contravened the fundamental right guaranteed to the appellant under article 19 (1)(f) and; so, it could not be enforced, as it contravened his fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19(1) (f). HELD: The scheme was framed and the Executive Officers were appointed as early as 1939. If the Executive officer was of a particular capacity the authority could not take over the administration of its own body or the properties according to law. In any case, the scheme did not cover the entire property but only covering all those properties held by the appellant. [262 E] R.S. In re : The Telest of Hindu Law , , applied. R. S.A. 259, followed.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools) on the recommendation of the Managing Committee of the school and continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells till May 25, 1986.
