Although the period of summer vacation during all these years was three years, the appellant continued to serving the school from July 12. 1982. However, since he continues to serve till 18.7.1986 he continued until replaced by a candidate from the Select List. He also continued till 18th July 1986 with breaks in between and the petitioner 's appointment was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced after a candidate of one year from the select list. His case, therefore will not come within the preview of the Validation Act and, therefore, the question of issuing any direction to regularise his service in a substantive vacancy because of the validation Act does not arise. [993G H; 994A B] Rattan Lal vs State of Haryana, ; and Rattan Lal v State of Uttar Pradesh ; , referred to. The High Court rightly dismissed the prayer for regularisation and held that the appellant was not entitled to be regularised as Hindi teacher with effect from July, 12,1982. In response to the notice issued in the special Leave Petition, the managing committee through its Secretary cum Head Master stated that the petitioner is still continuing to serve as Hindi clerk in the school under the orders of the managing Committee. The staff of the School who are thus appointed on such ad hoc basis is very large indeed. If the teachers had been appointed regularly, they would have been entitled to the benefits of summer Vacations along with the salary and allowances payable in respect of that period and to all other privileges such as casual leave, medical leave, maternity leave etc. available to all government servants. These benefits are denied to these ad hoc teachers unreasonably on account of this pernicious system of appointment adopted by the state Government. These ad hoc teacher are unnecessarily subjected to an arbitrary `hiring and firing policy. Those teachers who constitute the bulk of the educated unemployed are compelled to accept these jobs on an ad hoc or on after December 31, 1984 and come out with a scheme or any other appropriate measure to regularise their services. [995E F] Rattanlal vs State o Haryana, A.I.R. 1987 S.C.

The respondent, who was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti and the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of a byeC Sabha, challenged the election of the successful candidate in an election petition inter alia on the ground: (1) that he had been disqualified from becoming a member by itself because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time; and (2) that his appointment being an office under the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads Non Ministerial Members ( Payment of Allowances) Rules, 1965 made thereunder, made his office of profits. The trial judge found him guilty and gave his award which was upheld by the High Court in appeal. Dismissing the appeal to this court, HELD: (i) Rule 3 only covers payment to compensate a Chairman for journeys performed by him for his official duties within the district in which the Panchayat is situated, while r. 4 to 7 govern cases where the journey is performed outside the District. Under those earlier Rules of 1961, the Chairman was entitled to draw travelling allowance and daily allowance even when travelling beyond the district. [427 C] (ii) The daily allowance is invariably fixed after estimating what extra expenditure in a day the person concerned would have to incur. A Chairman, it appears, was expected to incur more expenditure per day than a Member, and that seems to be the reason why a higher rate of daily allowance was prescribed for him. [433 H] (iii) The whole purpose of r. 3 is, therefore, basically to ensure that he does not have to spend money out of his own pocket for the purpose of discharging his official work, namely, travelling allowance or daily allowance during tour.

The appellant had a tenancy in the demised shop. The tenanted premises was let out to him for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The respondents purchased the building from the erstwhile owners in 1963, a year later they filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without their consent causing substantial damages to it. The disputed constructed properties include a partition wall in a hail converting the same into two portions and tin sheds shown by letters ABHG and CDGH. The trial court held that the partition wall did not constitute material alteration, its further held that tin shed marked by letters BGHB and C DGH had been constructed by the appellant with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents but the tin shed mark marked with letters CFGH had, been constructed without obtaining the permission of the Cantonment Board. The first appellate court reversed the findings of fact, on which the High Court dismissed the second appeal filed by the tenant and partly affirmed the decree passed by the trial court. On a second appeal by the respondent, a learned Single Judge of the High COurt set aside the order of the first Appellate Court on the finding that no case for eviction had been made out against the appellant in respect of any building under section 14(c) of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act, 1952. On second appeal, a Single Bench of the said High Court set aside both the orders of the First Appellate Court and the Commis sioner 's report and dismissed the respondent 's suit on the findings that none of the construc tions constituted material alteration justifying appellant 's eviction under sec. 14(1)(c). In appeal by special leave it was contended for the tenant that: (i) the mens rea tence which had been done by the respond ents exceeded his jurisdiction and, therefore, he was liable for eviction; (ii) the construction of tin shed could not be held to have materially altered the accommodation; (iii) the constructions were made with out the consent o f the landlord; and (iv) the building contained substantial alterations, as the determination of this question depended on the facts of each ease. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. A permanent construction tends to make changes in the structure of the building without destroying its identity. The word 'materially altered ' means a change in the character, form and the structure o fure without destroying Its identity. In the instant case, the disputed constructions which the appellant has found to be 'material alteration ' consisted of a partition walls of 6 feet height in a hall converting the said two rooms into two rooms and a tin shed yellow storied by letters CDG H on the Eastern side on the open land adjacent to the accommoda tion. [884C D] 2.1 The construction of a tin sheds could not have been held to be materially altered or which was likely to diminish its value substantial ly, but the question whether the constructions materially alteri tions justified the constru cations would be one of fact and law. [876G H] 3.2 In the absence of any legislative defi cition of the aforesaid words it would be useful to refer to the meaning given to these words in dictionaries. Concise Oxford Dictionary defines the word 'alter ' as change in character, position 'Materially ' as an adverbimpor tant essentially concerned with matter not with form. In Words and Phrases (Permanent Edition) one of the meanings of the word "alteration" is 'to make change, to modify, to change, change, a thing from one form and set to another. The expression 'materialally altered ' in t he instant case means 'substantial ' change in in the nature, character, shape and the structures of the build ing without destroying their identity.

The respondent was a resident company in Calcutta. According to the case of the appellant, the appellant Company came to know about the ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent firm. When the respondent was called on 25 3 1975, he filed an application under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. requesting that summons be sent to the registered office of the company and that he be instructed by a registered post. The appellant denied having received the summons. It was alleged that the summons purported to have been served on the respondent on 17 3 1975 and hence the application filed for setting aside the ex exparte decree was not duly served on its company and it came to knowledge about the decree on 29 7 1975. Hence, the respondent filed a suit against the appellant claiming damages to the tune of Rs. 26,000/ on account of the non delivery of certain goods, contending that summons in the suit was sent to registered office at Calcutta and was a good mode of service. The trial Court held that the exparte decree was passed according to law and, therefore, the application of filing was about a week 's time thereafter within time. Accordingly, the suit came to an end on 29th July 1975. On 17 3 1977, the plaintiff filed a revision in the High Court under Section 115 Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court allowed the revision set aside the judgment of the trial Court and upheld the passing of the ex p parte decree. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1. There is only three Rules in it. There are only 3 Rules in its it. Rule 2 is an exhaustive provision providing for all modes of service on the company in the sense as to what is meant by service of summons on the Secretary. 891. In other words, if the serving peon or bailiff is not able to serve the summons on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving officer shall affix a copy of the summons upon the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain, 1032 and shall then return the original to the court from which it was issued, with a report endorsed thereon or annexed thereto stating that he has so affixed the copy, the circumstances under which he did so, and the name and address of the person (if any) by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed. [1032B C; 1033C D] 1.2. The word "Principal Officer" in clause (a) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the Code in Order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summon on natural persons. Sending a summons by post to the Registered office of a company, unless the contrary is shown, will be presumed to be service on that the company itself. But the first part of clause (b) has get to be read in the context of the provision contained in Order5 Rule 17 of the C. P.C., and in other words if the service peon or Bailiff isnot able to served the summons for on the secretary or any Director or any other Principal Officer of the Corporation because either he refuses to sign the summons or is not to be found by the serving person even after due diligence then he can leave the summons at the registered Office of the Company and make a report to that effect. In the instant case, none of the kind was done. [ 1033E F] 1.(a) The judgment and decree passed by the trial court setting aside its decree was correct. There was no error in that judgment much less any error of jurisdiction entitling the High court to interfere with it. [1001H; 1034A] (b).

Under section 145(5) Cr. P.C., the Magistrate, after passing a preliminary order on the 29th July, 1976 (wherein the Magistrate had recorded reasons for his being satisfied that a breach of peace existed and such a finding was implicit in the final order passed by the Magistrate so it was not necessary for the Magistrate to repeat what he had said in the preliminary order also. [95 B] Hari Ram & Ors. vs Banwari Lal & Ors., ; , followed. Hari Ram vs Banwari Lai & Ors, ; , referred to. The High Court was wrong in holding that the final ordered of the Magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of the peace existed at the time when the order was passed and the High Court therefore erred in holding on that ground. [96 B] In the instant case, the Magistrate has observed that there was no clear finding by the magistrate that there is an apprehension of breach of a peace existed even in the said final order. Merely because absence of finding by Magistrate in the earlier final order in the circumstances as mentioned above cannot be said to be such a manifest defect so as to attract the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High court under section 482 Cr. [97 B] R. H. Bhutani vs Banwari lal & Ors; ; , distinguished. Hariram Ram and Ors. v Banwari Lal and Ors., , ; , overruled. Hari Prakash Ram & Others vs Banwarilal Lal & ors. ; , ; applied.

The appellant company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn, and for the purpose of that business it purchases cotton and occasionally sells it. Its profits arose for the most part from the sales of yarn and to some extent from the re sale of cotton. The department did not accept the correctness of the figures as shown in the accounts. It claimed that because of this scheme evolved by the appellant for this purpose it was an integrated scheme for this object, there being nothing unusual in its selling all its yarn to its customers, and that there was nothing unusual or unusual in their selling all their yarn to their customers. Held, (i) that there could be no doubt that the income was assessable under section 66(1). G (ii)that section 42 (3) applied only to non resident persons and not to nonresidents because it was not possible to hold that such persons would have thereby created a liability for payment of income tax on the profits made by them on the sales in question. The Sales Tax Officer had no power to tax such persons as were residents within his powers. It had also been held that under section 42(1) there could not be any right to apply to non residents who had sold their goods manufactured by them and that they did not get a capital from the banks which are controlled by the Government. The mere fact that the profits were disposed of by the assessee 's own constituents would not amount to an accrual of income or of profits under the statute. Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co. (1917) I. T. R. 73, disapproved (iii)that in view of the decision of this Court in Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay City vs Ahmedabhai Umarbhai, it was open to the Tribunal under section 33(1)(c), to refer the question for the decision to the High Court and that it could not therefore merely pass it on for the determination of the court. The facts relating to this matter are that during the periods of assessment with which the appeals were concerned the appellant opened branches in the States of Travancore, Cochin Pudukkottah and Mysore, and sold yarn to them from Pakistan. It was in the course of the business of these merchants and the intermediaries that it was the appellant 's relations and men who had been put up as partners and shareholders of the concerns. The question whether the profits could be taxed only if they were remitted to British India. Held also that section 42 applied only where there was evidence to support it or if it was perverse but that, where there is evidence to consider, which is one of fact and is itself an inference from other facts, it is open to attack on the ground that the basic facts themselves do not constitute evidence in support of the final conclusion a position which does not arise here. The jurisdiction to refer must be exercised judicially and not arbitrarily and should be exercised reasonably and that be done when there is no evidence to prove the case based on such findings. In the present case, the Tribunal had wrongly distinguished the decision in Commissioner, Income tax Bombay City v Ahmedbhai Valabhai Chela, [1964] S.C.R. 140, followed. Commissioner for Income tax vs Ahmed Bahadurbhai Umar Shah and Co., (1966) 66 I.T.R.(P.) 181, discussed (iv)that when a question of law arises out of its order it is not open to review by the court only on the grounds that it is perverse, or if there is an evidence to judge, one way must be rejected.

In terms of the appointment, Shri Vaish got no commission in the first year as the mill suffered a loss. The Income Tax Officer determined a sum of Rs. 5,000 as a reasonable amount payable as commission. Against the disallowance of Rs 70,465 paid as commission to the General Manager, the assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who by his order dated October 31, 1949 found that Rs. 65,430 being not sufficient and it was reasonable to allow the payment of commission at the rate of 121/2 %. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal. In reference under section 66(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 (the question referred for decision to this Court by the assessee was whether in the circumstances of the case, the sum of money paid to Shri Vaish was an amount laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee within the meaning of section 10(2)(xv) of Income Tax. HELD: The fact that the rate for which the machinery was laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for. the purpose for which it was laid up was one of law. [515G] Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. vs C.I.T., U.P. ; Swadeshy Cotton Mills Company, Ltd. V C.l.T,, U. P. ; and Swadeshani Cotton Mills Ltd. v C. I.T. Bombay vs Walchand & Co. Private Ltd., , referred to.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Company, since October 1943. On January 13, 1954, he made an application under section 26(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act praying that he should be excused and his agents should be heard before the disposal of the case. The company resisted this application as being repre sented by its Secretary Fateh Singh. By a notification dated April 29, 1955, the appellant was informed that he had not authorised Fateh Singh to enter into any agreement in his case and praying that the agreement filed in respect of his case should not be accepted. Case law reviewed. On August 28, 1956, the company made an order fixing December 20, 1956 fixing December 1955, "for filing compromise or hearing". On January 31, 1957, a fresh application for time was filed but it was stated that agreement had already been reached on some of the matters and opportunity was asked for to settle the other disputes. The case was adjourned to January 21, 1957 on which date a further petition was again filed for time filed by both the parties stating: (i) that the compromise had already be obtained on some matters and were going to be compromised; (ii) that in spite of everything, the Union did take up this appellant 's case against his dismissal as its own. It was mentioned that the Union had no authority to enter any compromise on behalf of the Union. Held, that the question whether the workman who is a party to a dispute should have a fair hearing must be decided by the Tribunal in that case and not by the High Court, (2)that section 36 of the industrial Disputes Act recognises this position, by providing that the workman, who is one party to the dispute shall be entitled to be represented by an officer of a registered trade union of which he is a member. The scheme of the Act does appear to contemplate that the machinery provided therein should be set in motion to settle only disputes which involve the rights of workmen as a class and that a dispute touching the individual rights of a workman was not intended to be the subject of adjudication under the Act, when the same had not been taken up by the Union or a number of workmen.

The appellants instituted a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against two defendants on the allegation that defendant No. I was the tenant inchief who had sub let the premises to defendant No 2, that the family of the plaintiffs appellants was not a joint Hindu family and that the true facts were that the members were separated, that Lala Ram Chandra Prasad was not karta of the joint Hindu Family, and that he looked after the affairs of the house property; and acted for and on behalf of the family just as other members of the families looked after other affairs including the business belonging to the family. The suit for eviction was decreed against both the defendants and for arrears of rent and arrears against defendant No, 1, and on appeal by defendant No: 2, the District judge set aside the decree for ejectment against Defendant No. 2 with respect to defendant Nos. 1 to 9. On second appeal, the High Court did not decide that question. In appeal to this court it was contended: (1) the deceased appellant and the surviving appellants constituted a joint family and as in the event of the success of the appeal there would be two inconsistent and contradictory decrees; (2) the legal representatives could have instituted the appeal against the entire decree in view of section 1O of the Code, that they were competent to continue the appeal even after the death of the deceased respondents; and (3) the Court could have reversed or varied the whole decree in favour of all the original plaintiffs and granted relief with respect thereto. It was also contended:(1) as the appellants constituted joint Hindu families there was no ground for condoning the delay in filing an affidavit stating that the deceased was a member of the Joint Hindu Family and other relevant facts: (2)(a) the provision of section 4 Of 0. XLI, r. 4 of O.

The appellant tenant of a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent landlord under a letting of May 19, 1954 evidenced by a deed which fixed the term merely as less than a year (a circumstance out of which a minor ripple of legal argument had arisen), and at the time of the lease, the land was first let to him. The landlord filed an eviction petition against the tenant on the ground that no notice to quit had been given nor notice of forfeiture as prescribed by those sections. The Rent Controller dismissed the tenant 's application holding that the vacancy in question had been determined by forfeiture but the High Court allowed the tenant to raise a new plea of statutory tenancy, and held that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111(g) because the TP Act, as amended by the Amending Act of 1929 did not apply proprio vigore. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the lease is one where the time is not limited and therefore section 111 (a) will not apply; (2) since no notice in writing was sent to the tenant of the application for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the grounds that the tenancy stood determined either by efflux of time as provided in section III, since the 07 letting Act did not contain any express statutory provision, the rules of justice, equity and good conscience govern the situation and this element is amply fulfilled by the filing of the eviction petition itself. HELD: (i) The requirement of a written notice in terms of section 111 cannot be said to be based on any general rule of equity. [918C] In the present case, though there was some confusion in this order about the determination of the expression lease being under section III (g) or outside it, the thrust of holding is found in these concluding words: " However, as held by the Supreme Court in Narender Lokmanya Lodhi vs Arvind Bai & Ors. [1974] I SCR 913, it was specifically urged that the tenant remonstrated against this new plea being permitted in appeal but the court construed the statement in the pro forma in column 18 B, that no notices were necessary since the lease was created prior to the extension of the 408 procedural law. The requirement as to written notice provided in the section therefore cannot be held to be a rule of justice. [936E F] (ii) A bare reading of the terms and conditions of the renewal agreement between the parties would make it clear that the intention of the lessor was merely statutory and it cannot trace its origin to any rule of Equity. [949H; 919A B] (iii) The pre amendment provision of section III in 1929 could not be said as having been given to the lessee in the present ease, determination of date of expiry by forfeiture under section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act would not be considered as being consistent with the rules laid down in section 112. [943C E] (iv) Section 111(c) was a procedural law which did not require notice in law for valid determination. [946E F, G] (v) The principle of equity and Good conscience applied proprio scare to transfers. If, therefore, the court is satisfied that the particular principle to which the legislature has now given effect by the amendment to section 111 did in fact represent a principle of justice equity, equity or good conscience, or whether it is merely a procedural and technical rule introduced in the Section by the Legislature and is not based on some general rule or principle of ' Equity.

Section 240(3)(c) of the Government of India Act, 1935 provides that where a person is dismissed or removed from service on the ground of conduct which has led to his conviction on a criminal charge; or (b) where an authority empowered to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank is satisfied that for some reason to be recorded by that authority in writing it was not reasonably practicable to give to that person an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. In exercise of this power the Governor issued orders delegating his powers to the Government on certain dates, namely, May 25, 1969 and December 21, 1969, suspending the right of the President to dismiss a Government servant pending inquiry into disciplinary proceedings but not with an order imposing any penalty on him. The appellant, who was a Superintendent in the State Service as well as in the Indian Army, was dismissed from service by an order made under r. 5(c) on June 7, 1969. Thereafter the Governor made both these orders effective from July 27, 1969 i.e., August 7, 1970 and September 1, 1971, but later on, he continued to be governed by the Government Orders issued in December 1971 onwards. In November 70 a writ petition filed in the High Court challenging the validity of this order was also dismissed by the High court on June 11, 70. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the satisfaction recorded by the Governor under r,. 5(C) is not obligatory since it is not mandatory and (ii) the action in question amounted to an enquiry wherein the Governor is himself the original dismissing authority. HELD: If the satisfaction of the Governor was recorded in the language in which the provision in article 311(2) stood prior to its amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, the fact that the Governor 's attention was not invited to the amended article 311 would not have rendered the order invalid on account of non consultation with the Public Service Commission. [488 E F] Khem Chand vs The Union of India and Others ; , followed. In the first place it is quite obviously necessary that the Government servant should have the opportunity, as soon as he makes a request to show cause against his action proposed or to be proceeded against, explained in the second paragraph. But before an order is passed by the Govern ment under r . 5 (c) must be satisfied that in the interest of the security of the State it was "not expedient" to give the Government ' servant an opportunity or of showing any cause against such action proposed. [489 G H] Khemchand vs The State of U.P., ; , State of UP vs Sanita, A.I.R. 1970 All 114; Hemanta Kumari Chowdhury vs The Chief Secretary in the Department of Personnel & Administrative Reforms, Government of West Bengal and Ors.

The Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi is founded on a religious faith and performance of religious rites and observances. The Shia Community of Mohalla Gaya Nagar (now in the city of Varanasi) was founded on four plots known as Shia Waqf Estate known as Mohammadan Temple situated near Hanuman Mandir near Hanuman Temple, Hill Station, Varanasi in the town of Varanasi, under the U.P. Muslim Waqf Act, 1960, in which certain properties were all situate and structures thereon belonged to the Shia waqf of MohallaDoshipha, Police Station Jaitpura (formerly Adampur) in the City of Varanasi and in particular were sought a declaration that the said plots of land including plot Nos. 245, 246, 247, 248/23/72, 602, 602/1134 and 247/1130 in the said Mohalla and buildings and structures thereof belong to Shia Sunni Waqf of Mohalla from the Shiasdars and that the members of Shia Muslim Community had a right to perform their religious functions and practices on the said properties and structures as also an appropriate writ, direction or order in the nature of mandamus commanding respondents 1 to 4 not to prohibit or restrain from performing their religious function and practices thereon. The petitioners and through them Shia are founded based their customary rights to perform the aforesaid religious rites, practices, observances and functions on several plots and properties situated in the aforesaid Mohalla. The Sunni community of Hotel Line Lal (Gulam Abbas & others) had a common City school School at Doswara whereas the Shiana Central Waqf Board and Sunni Central Wakfs Board constituted under the Act was headed as a Shia Central Waqf board and Sunni central Wakfs Board to which each Central Board had to send its report for the purpose. The provisions of section 5 (1) of the U .P. Muslims Waqf Act 1960 were amended by the Uurt in 1976 whereby it was provided that no suit shall be instituted against the Shiadars or Shias of any religious denomination on the ground that they have a right of worship therein and such right shall be restricted to the period during which the Shiama community is established. The impugned legislation was amended by U. P. Act 62/1133 of 1936 which provided for the prevention of mischief and control culminating in the enactment of section 144 Cr. P.] The petitioners filed a writ petition in the Allahabad High Court challenging the impugned order on the basis that a clear and apparent distinction must be made between title and ownership of the concerned plots of property, title and possession of structures thereon on those plots and structures over the said lands and structures on two sides: (1 ) Decisions of competent civil courts adjudicating these rights in their favour in earlier litigations and (ii) Registration of Shias concerning the plots and structure for performance of these practices and functions under sec. 144 Cr P.C. The High Court found that the order was mis conceived; that the effect of the order had been that no Mohammedan would be allowed to say his prayers in the mosque it was not justified under section 144 and that it would be open to the respondents to agitate question of title either to the plots or to the structures thereon or even the Shina community to perform its religious ceremonies and functions over the plots, and structures thereupon. In appeal by special leave, this Court HELD: The petitioners have established their existing customary rights on the plots as Shias Wakfs under the Notification dated February 26, 1944 issued under section 5(1) read with section 5 of the Act and published in the U Uttar Pradesh Gazette dated 23rd January, 1954 must be held to have become final and conclusive between the members thereof. [1134E G] The contention that the impugned legislation in question belongs to both the sects and no special rights are claimed by the Shiukas over it except those conferred on them under the decree in Suit No.

On a ques tions of the Income tax Officer 's order for the assessment year 1957 58, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the assessee 's claim. The Tribunal, on a reference under section 256(1) of the Incometax Act, 1961, held that there was no genuine loss; it was essentially notional in nature and that the claim for set off to be admissible had been notified by the Income Tax Officer under Section 24(3) of 1922 Act to the assessee by an order in writing. That having not been done, the claim was not admissible. The Revenue went before the High Court and reiterated its claim. Disposing of the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of the provisions of section 74(1)(b) and Section 80 of the latter Act, the High court was Fight in holding that the al low sum amount claimed for the asses see was admissible in law. On a bare reading of these provisions, and without reference to anything more it was not open to the Revenue to contend that the amount claimed was not genuine while dealing with the assessment years 1957 58 and ultimately allowed the asses sees 's appeal. [1166 C] 1.2 When the assessee had made the claim and took note of it, his failure to comply strictly with the requirements of sub section (3) should not be permitted to be taken advantage of by the Revenue, nor should it be used to the prejudice of the assessee. Since set off has been claimed in the assessment yew 1965 66 to which the Act of 1961 applied, it is necessary to turn attention to the relevant provisions thereof and they are in sections 74 and 80.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer in the Defence Science Service. He was posted at the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DTD & P). The recruitment was made from the Defence Department. When recruitment was being made, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service. When the recruit ment was abolished, he became a member of DAQAS. The respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal, who held that respondent K.T. Shastry was entitled to remain in service upto the superannuation age of 60 years and was not liable to be retired at the alleged retirement age of 58 years. The Tribunal also held that the re spondent was not enti tled to the benefit of the power so exercised by it in the facts and circum stances of the case. In an appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of service for members belonging to the different units, and merely because the superannuationage of the members of the DAQS was increased, it could not be held that he belonged to another unit, viz. DAQ, was entitled lo the said benefit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The decision of the Tribunal is both proper and valid. [85C] 2.1 As regards the question whether respondent was also entitled to the bene fit of the said power so mined in the circumstances of the instant case. [86C] 3.2 In spite of the decision of this Court in the case, the denial of the benefit by the enhanced superannuation age to the members is not correct, and there was no substance in the appeal.

The appellant who was a candidate for election from the said ward challenged the election by filing an Election Petition challenging the election of the appellant before the High Court. The first of these was to the effect that the appellant had published all the phmphlets mentioned in the petition and distributed the same amongst the voters and the appellant 's cause of action bad arisen on that date. An application for issuing summons on the two persons was rejected by the Judge as well as by the High court. The High Court dismissed the Petition in limine holding that the order under article 226 was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court, HELD : Under section 21 sub section (1) of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965 which does not contain a similar provision it has been held by this Court that "although. the trial court should be at arms length and the court should not really enter into the dispute as a third party but it is not to be understood that the Court never has the power to summon a witness or to call for a document which would throw light upon the matter, particularly of corrupt practice which is alleged and is being sought to be proved. If the Court was satisfied that a corrupt practice had in fact been perpetrated, may be by one side or the other, it was absolutely necessary to find out who was the author of that corrupt practice. [973 C] The question whether two person were guilty of corrupt practices is of a serious nature and if the appellant was found guilty of the commission thereof, the period of disqualification would certainly not be inappropriate. It is difficult for us to see why two Gazette notifications had become necessary. One seems to be the verbatim reprint of the other. [978 G] There can be no doubt that the Supreme Court has to deal with the provisions of 0. 14 and the quotation from that judgment shows that the powers of the court in this respect are of wide amplitude specially when investigation is being made into allegations about commission of a corrupt practices. It may be that in the instant case, if the two candidates had not been examined, the Judge might well have decided the issue the other way. But, the Act certainly gave him the power of doing so and no exception can be taken to the course adopted by the court although it must be recorded that his earlier order refusing to issue summonses to them in the first instance when asked to do so on the 21st August was hardly justifiable.[974 C] R. Shah vs Labal Singh, [1965] 1 S.C.R. 977; In the instant ease, if this statement was true, naturally any right thinking Muslim would think twice before casting his vote in favour of such a person. There was no error apparent on the face of record before the trial Court and consequently, the jurisdiction under article 227 could not have been exercised on the facts of the case by the issue of a writ of certiorari. Neither could the High.

The Government of Uttar Pradesh imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. On August 1, 1956, the State of Uttar.P. imposed a, taxation of one annas in the rupees on the sales effected between April 1, 1955 and July 31, 1956. The petitioner challenged the validity of this tax by writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution. It was contended that the Validation Act seeks to validate the impugned notification which had been struck down by the High Court as unauthorised and inoperative because it was not in fact validated, and since the Act itself is ultra vires, there is no question of unconstitutionality. Held, that the impugned Validation Act is not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54 in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and the impugned tax is not a sales tax on the occasion of sale, and cannot be imposed with retrospective operation even for a period prior to the constitution. A sale for the purpose of Entry 54 in the State List II in Schedule VII to the Consti tution of India and notification issued under section 3A was intra vires as it was passed before section 3 A was in operation and not thereafter, since the impugned Act is intra vires, the invalidity of the impugned amendment will be no ground for holding that there was, in fact, no imposition of tax. It would be competent for the legislature to enact a law with retrospective effect, which is either prospective or retrospective. The State legislature has derived its authority to enact such a law and it has been held by this Court that a sale for purposes of entry 54 would be ultra vires as the power conferred on Parliament under article 286(2) was plenary and unrestricted subject only to any limitation imposed by the Constitution, but it is not an essential characteristic of a sales Tax. The power of a legislature to legislate with reference to a topic entrusted to it is, as already stated, unqualified subject only, to any limitations imposed by 'the Constitution. In the exercise of such a power, it will be competent to the Legislature to impose a tax (1) [1947] S.C.R. 933 and State of Madras vs Boddu Paidanna & Sons ; , followed.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Court for rape. The sentence of imprisonment was altered to one year R.I. on the ground that he had forgiven the criminal; and that the evidence showed that he has forgiven criminal. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. A non deposit of a condition precedent prejuvenation which is bad enough in a society where women are often socially weak and sexuallymised. [596 G] 2. Judicial notice should be ad dressed to persuade guilt to re fade his sentence of imprison ment. The task of not done by a negative reduction in the prison term would be quite lished by reducing the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for two years. [597 E F, H, 596 A] 3. The special circumstances of this case impell for extenuating a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. It is not done in this Court 's direction because it is not artificatory reduction in prison term. What is more important is a set of positive prescriptions which will ensure his turning a new leaf. One major method in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. Within limits of the Prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or the Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on parole, furlough or orders, the young appellant turns a new tender leaf of normal life. [557 A B] 4. In prison treatment must. therefore be geared to psychic healing, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation apart from training to adapt oneself to the life outside. The functional failure of our pachydermic prison projects, exacerbated by its tension and trauma on the one hand and the reverse ethos inside on the other, deserves judicial cognizance. [593 G H, 597 A] 5. The Court must restore the man. A hyper sexed homo sapiens cannot be stervated via humiliating or harsh treatment, but that is precisely the perversion of unreformed jail Justice which some criminologists have described as the crime of punishment. This Court has held in Sunil Batra 's case and later that constitutionally viewed punitive deprivation, punitive deprivation deprivation of personal freedom must be goal oriented and humanely restorative, apart from being deterrent. [592 C D] 6. Keeping an overall view of the familial and the criminal factors involved the appellant is reduced to rigorous sentence for two year.

The appellant is a limited company dealing in land and maintained its accounts on mercantile system. By an order dated June 21, 1946 under rule 75A(1) of the Defence of India Rules read with section 19 of the the Act certain plots of land measuring about 19.17 acres in village Kankulia in the District of 24 Parganas and belonging to the appellant, were requisitioned by the Government of West Bengal. Subsequently the land was acquired permanently in the State Government under s.5, Requisition of Land (Continuance of Powers) Act 1951 by a notice of acquisition dated December 27, 1952, published in the Gazette dated January 8, 1953. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.2497,249 as compensation payable to the assessee, and the appellant was not satisfied with the amount of compensation, and preferred an appeal before the Arbitrator. 24 Parganas , Calcutta. The Appellate Tribunal accepted the other contention raised by it, but took the view that the amount received related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee and was, therefore, a trading receipt liable to tax. The High Court affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer as well as the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal by certificate granted by the High Court. ^ HELD: 1. A mere claim by the assessee after taking possession of the land, at a particular rate or for a certain sum is not compensation.

The appellants filed a suit against the appellants, landlords. The respondents objected to the execution on the ground that the compromise decree was void and inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961. The executing court accepted the appellant 's objection to the Execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case. The appellants preferred a second miscellaneous appeal before the Madhya P High Court. A learned single Judge following the earlier decision of that Court in Smt. Chandan Bai vs Surja, (1) came to the conclusion that the decree was not a nullity and was executable. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal the Court HELD: 1(i) The provisions of Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot apply to eviction suits governed by the special statutes. [882C] (ii) In order to get a decree or order for eviction against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Act the suitor must make out a case for eviction in accordance with the provisions Of the Act. When the suit is contested the issue goes to trial. The Court passes a decree for eviction only if it is satisfied on evidence that a ground for passing such a decree in accordancewith the requirement of the statute has been established. Even when the trial proceeds ex parte, this is so. [871F] (iii) If, however, parties choose to enter into a compromise due to any reason such as to avoid the risk of protracted litigation expenses, it is open to them to do so. The court can pass a decree on the basis of the compromise.

The assessee company, a limited company doing business as selling agents of a Textile Mill. For the assessment year 1955 56 the assessee was assessed on a total income of Rs. 1,61,089/ and taxes paid were Rs. 69,973/ leaving a distributable surplus of Rs 60,761/ . In this year also the company did not declare any dividend because of the loss referred to earlier. The Income tax Officer in exercise of his powers under section 23A(1) levied additional super tax @ 4/ per rupee on that surplus and in appeal the Asstt. Commissioner took the view that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss and the assessee 's loss was a, capital loss. But all the same as there was no commercial profits in the relevant accounting years it was not reasonable to expect the assessee company to declare any dividends. The Department appealed to the Tribunal which agreed with the conclusions reached by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and held that under the circumstances the Directors were justified in not declaring any dividend in respect of the profits that had accrued in the accounting years. In appeal, this Court HELD : (1) The view is not correct. [858 G] Commissioner of Income tax West Bengal, vs Gangadliar Bannerjee and Co. (Pvt.) Ltd. ; followed. (2) Section 23A.(1) provides for imposition of super tax at 25% in the case of a company whose business consists wholly or mainly in the dealing in or holding Of investments. [864 F G] Union of India vs Amalgamated Coal Concern Limited and Another, , referred to.

The effect of the section is that all taines of the provisions including sections 15, 16 and 30 of the apply to arbitrations in consolidation under section 13(4), shall be determined in accordance with the provisions Of the .
