The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. Since respondent No. 2 was a degree holder, he got the said resolution and was promoted to the said post on that date. The petitioner challenged the said Resolution by way of a Writ Petition in the High Court which dismissed the same. Hence this petition by special leave. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the absence of rule or regulation, the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. The proposition that in the absence absence of rules and regulations, the Authority could act by executive instruction finds direct support in Mysore State Road Transport Corporation vs Gopinath Gundachar char, ; , relied on. 1.2 In the instant case neither the practice followed till 1988 nor the resolution passed by respondent Corporation in 1988 nor any resolution passed in accordance with section 64 of the Act. It is well settled that for the purpose of promotion, a valid classification can made among the members holding the same post on the basis of their qualification. [174E] State of Jummu & Kashmir vs Triloki Nath Khosa and Ors., ; , applied. 1 .3 In the present case, neither the requirement followed till 1987 nor the Resolution passed in compliance with Section 64 of Act. The Court also pointed out that the very Bench which decided Roshan Lal 's case in terms of its own judgment did not hold about a fortnight later in accordance therewith Section 64. [175B C] 2.1 There was no violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. It was a case where no separate quota for promotion to the post was kept for degree holder Junior Engineers and diploma holder Junior engineers. The degree holders Junior Engineer had sought a relief that such a quota be kept. It may be observed that it is not a case of where the classification was already made which was challenged before the Court.

This petition is directed against the judgment of the Bombay High Court and the notifications issued by it in regard to appointments to the Judges in the Supreme Court and various High Courts. The petitioners were practising as Advocates, litigants for several years in the court. They filed applications under Article 32 of the Constitution. These applications are filed in the nature of public interest litigation. The reliefs asked for by the peti tion from this Court is confined to the relief of filling up of vacancies in the Bombay City High Court. Since common kindly were advanced and the relief sought was of similar nature, these applications have been clubbed together and heard by an ad hoc Secretary of the Maharashtra Bar Association; who filed counter affidavit on behalf of the Union of India, the position as on 20th Febru ary 1990 showed that as against the sanctioned strength of 462,368 had been filled up and the vacancies were 94 in all. The Court heard the petitions. The Union of india took the stand through the Attorney General that the petitions are not maintainable, and the filling up the vacancies in superior courts was not a justiciable matter, and it is con tended that this Court has no jurisdiction to entertain these applications. It was further contended on behalf thereof that when there is difference of opinion amongst the constitutional functionaries in regard tO appointment of Judges and the primacy of the position of the institution of Chief Justice of India which would, in our opinion, require re consideration, this Court had no juris diction to interfere with judicial independence; whether at all, and if so under what circumstances, a judge of High Court could be transferred to another High Court without his consent; and as to the crite ria on which an additional Judge was entitled to be made permanent. Disposing of the petition, this court, HELD: 1.1 There are stagnant and com pelling considerations why the views of the Chief Justices of the States and that of the Sura nity of India should be afforded a decisive import unless the executive has some material in its possession which may indicate that the appointment is otherwise undesirable. The view which the four learned Judges shared, in Gup ta 's case, does not recognise the special and pivotal position of tho institution of the chief Justice of Amend ment. [463B] 2.1 It is clear on a plain reading of clause (2) of Article 124 that it is the President, which in effect and substance means the Central Government, which is empowered by the Constitution to appoint Judges of the Supreme Coupa tive High Courts and such other judges of the High Courts as the Central Govern ment may deem it necessary to consult, are merely constitutional functionaries having a consultative role and the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Board. [465C D] 2:2 In view of what has already stated and the assurance held out by the learned Attorney General, it is not possible to contend that the final say is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government.[465E F] 3:3 What has been held out in S.P. Gupta 's Case relating tO the status and importance of functionaries required to be deter mined should be considered by a larger bench. [467G H] 4. The primacy of Chief justice of India in the process of selection would improve the quality of selection. [468C D, E F] 2 :4 The primacy and responsibility of the cabinet which would ensure better efficient functioning of the judicial system in the country require consideration and there is an element of immediacy in the matter. [471D] 5:5 It is not a case for review for appointment of a Judge in a High Court, but is one relating to the status of the Nazial Council.

The Respondent had availed of leave from April 17, 1978 to May 1, 1978 and was allowed an advance of Rs.2,500 on April 19, 1978 under LFC to be adjusted later on his submitting the LFC Bill. He submitted a bill for Rs. 2,800 on May 5, 1978 along with a stamp receipt purporting to have been issued by him in August 1954 but subsequent investigations revealed that the firm of M/s. Shri Manju Travels was a spurious one which indulged in issuing fake travel receipts. Thereupon the respondent was served with a charge sheet dated October 12, 1978 followed by a departmental enquiry. The Enquiry Officer conducted the departmental inquiry against the Respondent and found him guilty and awarded a punishment of discharge on January 14, 1980. The Respondent 's appeal was also dis missed on June 17, 1980 on the ground that "as the original order was without jurisdiction or competence there was nothing for the Appellate Authority to confirm" but the said order had merged in the appellate order, the initial defect, if any, stood removed, was repelled by the learned Judge on the grounds inter alia that: (1) he had been the holder of a de facto facto office and (2) the respondent had not raised any objection to the continuance of the enquiry by the said Shri U.B. Menon at any time during the pendency and till the disposal of the departmental appeal preferred by him. The Division Bench of the High Court, however, allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of punishment and directed that the re spondent be paid all consequential benefits. Hence the appeal. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, the Court, HELD: 1.1. It is for this reason that the de facto doctrine can have no application to the case of a person who is not the holder or of an office but is merely a bank employee, for that matter an ex employee. [200E] 2.1 There can be no doubt that a non official cannot act as a 'dischargee dor or usurper or a total stranger to the office. Obviously the doctrine can be invoked in cases where there is an appointment to office which is defective; but notwithstanding the defect to the title of the office, the decisions made by such a de f facto officer clothed with the powers and functions of the Office would be as efficacious as those made by a de jure officer.[200E G] 2:2.

The respondents were owners and in possession of a building bearing municipal door Nos. 3766 to 3776 situate in the main Chawri Bazar Delhi. They submitted their applications for execution of work consisting of repairs, additions as well alterations to the said building. The Commissioner rejected the said applications on the grounds that the proposal was under acquisition and also effected in the ROW and directed the appellant to accord sanction to the plan for execution. The first respondent thereupon filed a writ petition which accepted the writ petition and issued a mandamus directing the appellant 's to accord the sanction, as asked for by them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant : (1) that the Master Plan prepared by the authority showed that certain areas including gramburini Bazar would be the Central Business District of Delhi and therefore as the proposal regarding the width that a road should have been carved out was not in conformity with the Master plan, section 14 of the Development Act will be violated; and (2) that even if the Masterplan mentioned the width of a proposed road and the width thereof had some construction thereon it could not be stated that when the respondents were attempting to renovate the building they would require more amenities than what was necessary. HELD : (i) The Master Plan contains provisions regarding allotment or reservation of land for roads. Therefore, in order to sustain the validity of the order of rejection passed by the Commissioner, the appellant has to establish that any land or part of a land or a building in a Zone had been dealt with in a particular manner by the Master plans and that it was proposed to be used in a different manner by tho owner Plan and that its area would have to go further to be prepared and has not come into operation for the zone concerned, nevertheless till such a Zonal Development Plan comes into operation. [172 F G] (ii) Even if a Zonal Planning Plan is prepared for the area, before it comes into force in the Zone, the procedure indicated in section 10 will have to be followed and parties will have had to be given an opportunity of putting their objections and suggestions and representations after having all to be duly considered by the Authority concerned. [173 C D] (iii) The appellant is not entitled to any relief because (1 ) under the Master Book, there was no violation of section 14 or of the by the respondents as they have alleged that the permission granted by section 8 is not in contravention of section 25(2) or any other provision of the Corporation Act or of any other Act; and the mere noncompliance with a Master Plan cannot make the order invalid. [ 174 E F] (iv) The High Court was right in holding that the Map plan had been prepared under section 7 by the M issue of the Master Master Plan as required by section 14, which, according to it, will show the approximate location and extents of land uses proposed in a zone for roads; (v) The agreement between the two authorities is not vitiated because there was an obligation on the Authority to prepare the Master Planning Plan simultaneously with the preparation of Master Plan, or as soon as there may be thereafter, no Zonal Development plan has been prepared. That assumes considerable importance in this case because it is the Zonal Development Plans under section 8(2)(a) which will show total location and stipulated number of roads within which the Zonal development plans should have to consist are to mention all buildings operations on either side of the proposed road; (vi) Even assuming that a Master plan had come into existence in accordance with the Calcutta Master Plan there is no violation or any provision of any law.

Held, that a witness against whom an order of acquittal is passed in respect of certain offences under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code with which the accused is charged is entitled to come before an independent and impartial Magistrate who is expected to deal with the case without the Magistrate himself being in any way a partisan or a witness to police activities. Consequently, the trial magistrate could not be said to have committed any error in coming to his aid on the mere ground of misjoinder of the accused in this connection. In cases where the order of conviction is based on no evidence or recorded by him the accused cannot be acquitted unless he has been charged with having committed any wrong or improper motives on the part of the prosecution case or the other facts emanating from his own conduct. If the number of the notes tallied with the numbers of the currency which were handed over to the accused there is no reason why such a large sum should be allowed to be paid for that purpose. Further, in cases where charges have been framed and the accused are charged under section 120 B he cannot be convicted without giving them an opportunity to explain their prejudice. Although charged with the high responsibility and duty of performing a great and essential public service of this State the police cannot afford to run the risk of opprobrium ' even if unfounded they have enlisted the Magistrate in their cause. The power under section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code, when it is alleged by the accused persons or the court who is supposed to deal With the case cannot be too scrutled to allow such recall of witnesses as are not free from doubt in cases governed by this rule and must be exercised with great care. In the present case, however, the statements made by the appellant No. 1 to them were not recorded under section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and it was stated that he had brought these moneys from his home sources into a par with that of the denomination which had been handed over by the police authorities to Nagindas when the raid was organised with the number arrived at by the witnesses on their tallying of the numbers contained in the memo prepared when the trap was organised and which numbers were also specified in the memos prepared at that time was enough to establish the falsity of the allegation made by him. The evidence of these witnesses being thus worthy of credit and the statements, made by them before them were admissible under section 16 Of the Act, Held further, that any alteration or modification of the charge or the conviction must be appealable to the Supreme Court on a consideration of all the circumstances including the fact that the accused had already been charged for the offence committed by him No. 2 and could not therefore be relied upon as inadmissible in evidence.

The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the plaintiff along with the Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the respondent was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. After trial, the Trial Court dismissed the suit. The first appellate court dismissed the appeal of the respondent on the ground of limita tion holding that no law of limitation was applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. The High Court granted a decree of nullity in favour of the re spondent. On the question of jurisdiction, it was contended that Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab police Rules, 1934 mandatorily directs that a police officer judicially sentenced to rigorous imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed; and the direction about the payment of salary and other emoluments was not interfered with by the High Court in the manner it has been done. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The question involved in the suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the Trial court in the way it has already been done [826E F] Sub clause (2)of Section 16.3 requires that a Police officer judicially pun ture to rigorous Tr i469 of Rs. 1050/ more shall be dismissal, and this mandate includes the payment for the period the plaintiff remained out of service because of his being in jail. In the instant case, admittedly, neither of these two questions were pressed by the parties before the trial court and the High court erred in dismissing the second appeal in limine.

The appellant company, a private limited Company in cloth and jute goods purchased pucca delivery orders (in short P.D.Os.) from the Mills. The transactions thus resulted in loss of Rs. 98,534 to the assessee and the assessee claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions were not speculative and the loss could be set off against speculation profits in the future. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on appeal by the assessee held that it was a case where such transactions were of such a nature as to constitute a business, but that the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court, namely D. M. Wadhwana vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh, ; and Commn sation of Income tax vs Romeshway, A.I.R. , referred to. In view of the decision in D.M. Wadhwaniwana 's case, the Tribunal held that sales in question were speculative and consequently the losses suffered by the appellant in these transactions could not be set aside against the profits made by the respondent assessee 's non speculative business High Court on reference following its earlier decisions in D . M. pollwana vs Commissioner of Income Tax, West Bengal, and in the appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the Department took an actual delivery of the goods sold and that therefore there was no completed sale since no property passed, but only an agreement for sale; (2) the sales were not booked by the buyers at all; and (3) the transactions between the assessee to the third parties as agent of the appel lant. HELD: The question referred to the High Court in of Andhra Pra dence applies to this case. [187C] D.

The appellant was a candidate for the reserved seat but his nomination was rejected by the Returning Officer at the scrutiny stage and therefore he was unable to contest the election. On appeals by special leave : HELD: (i) In the absence of attestation in the prescribed manner, attestation of a particular form is required in the case of the candidate himself if there is no signature and no mark the form would have to be rejected and their absence could not be dismissed as technical and unsubs tantial. [485 G] (ii) When the law enjoins the observance of a specified formality it cannot be disregarded and the substance of the thing must be there. The substance of such the matter is the satisfaction of the Returning officer at a particular moment of time about the identity of the person making _a mark in place of writing a signature, but if there was no signature he would have been too late because the attestation and the satisfaction must exist at the presentation stage and a total omission of such an essential feature cannot be subsequently validated any more than the omission of a candidate to sign at all could have been. [490 H] The word "sign" when used in its ordinary sense, includes the making of a mark and as the Act tells us quite clearly how the different types of signature are to be made are indeterminate. [448 A B] (iii) When an act which requires the satisfaction can be dispensed with altogether is not for Courts to decide. What is beyond dispute is that this is regarded as a matter of special moment and that special provision has been made to meet such cases.

The appellants were employees of the Company. During the pendency of the reference No. 336 of 1972 before the Second Labour Court, Bombay for adjudication of a dispute, 344 workmen of the company including the appellants went on an indefinite peaceful strike with effect from August 30, 1972 pursuant to the strike notice given by the Company 's registered union ' in support of its demand for re instatement of three of the Unions who had been dismissed by the company. The Assistant Commissioner thereupon summoned the parties for discussion on July 19, 1973 but his attempts at conciliation did not bear any fruit. Thereafter, the appellants made the aforesaid complaints before the Industrial Tribunal with their result as stated above. On September 7, 1972 the union made a formal demand calling upon the Company to re instle the appellants and others who had were removed from service on the ground that they had abandoned the services of the appellants on the presumption that they were no longer interested to continue in service of the said company and had totally abandoned the company 's service. On October 23, 1972, the union wrote a letter to the Assistant Commissioner stating therein that it did not wish to revise its earlier decision under which their names had been struck off from the rolls of the companies because they had not abandoned their service. The appellants made these complaints before Industrial Tribunal requesting for re dis instatements of its three dismissed leaders and alleging that the said action was by way of victimization for their participation in the strike. In support of the appeal Mr. Ramamurti has contended that the action of the respondent Company in removing the names of the appel lant from its rolls was illegal, arbitrary and that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned the service of their company and did not intend to abandon the services but had also returned the cheques sent by the companies on account of their leave salary gratuity etc. The respondents have contended that there was no abandonment of service on their part in the circumstances. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that (i) what is the true meaning of the expression 'abandonment of service '; and (ii) whether in the circum stances of the case it could be said that the appellant had voluntarily terminated the services by way relaxation of the term of employment unilaterally convert the absence of work into abandonment of employment. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(i) The intention may be inferred from the acts and conduct of the party, and is a question of fact. Temporary absence is not ordinarily sufficient to constitute an abandonment of office. From the connotations reproduced above it clearly follows that to constitute abandonment, there must be total or complete giving up of duties so as to indicate an intention not to resume the same. In Buckingham Co. vs Venkatiah & Ors., it was held by this Court that under common law an inference that an employee has abandoned or relinquished service is not easily drawn unless from the length of absence and from other surrounding circumstances an inference to that effect can be legitimately drawn and it can be assumed that the employee intended to abandon service. Abandonment or relinquishment of service is always a question Of intention, and normally such an intention cannot be attributed to an employee without adequate evizence in that behalf. [616D E] Express Newspapers (P) Ltd. vs Michael Mark & Anr., ; Express Newspaper (P.) Ltd.v Michaenx Mark & Ors. , Express Newspaper, P) Limited v Micha! Mark and Anr. [1976]3 S.C.R. 913, followed. (ii). It may be recalled that the appela lant 's absence from duty was because of their peaceful strike to enforce their demand. It was held that if the employees absent themselves from the work because of strike in enforcement of their demands, there can be no question of abandonment of employ ment by others. [625E F] Express Newspaper Newspaper (p) Limited vs Michashael Marks & Anr. ; Express Newspapers, p.

On a promissory note, the trustees of a public trust mortgaged a house belonging to the Trust. The trustees applied under 0. 21 r. 89 for setting aside the sale and deposited Rs. 250 being 5% of the purchase money for payment to the appellant and Rs. 6 for payment of the mortgage amount. A suit was filed by the trustees against the trustees who had failed to comply with the requirements of section 89. The trial court held that the trustees had no jurisdiction to set aside the auction sale, and directed execution of the decree. On appeal, the District Court reversed the order holding that since the trustees bad failed to complied with the provisions of s. 35 of the Bombay Public Trust Act, they had no power to set it aside. Held: The only non obstante clause in section 36 is intended to confer a right upon the judgment debtor, even after the property was sold, to satisfy the claim of the judgment holder and to compensate the auction purchaser by paying him 5 % of the sale money. The provision imposes a fetter on the power of the trustees: it is not intended thereby to confer upon the Charity Commissioner an overriding authority upon actions of the Civil Court in execution of decrees. The section imposes a restriction upon the powers of the Trustees : it was not intended to defeat the claim for auction purchaser unless the decree is simultaneously satisfied. When the judgment creditor agrees to extend the time for payment, he cannot be deemed to be complied with. It is sufficient to observe that an order setting aside a Court sale in execution can be obtained under 0 . 21 r 89 by merely depositing 5 % amount specified in the proclamation of sale for the recovery of which the sale was ordered. Per Das Gupta, J. (dissenting) The doctrine of mutual consent cannot apply to pending proceedings. It would not include cases where a case affecting a public religious or charitable purpose is involved. Section 37 of the Act does not confer such an absolute right on the judgment debtors and are intended to be made by the trustee for a price; section 36 would only mean transfer of property by the Trustees for a sum equal to 5% and could be enforced only if, Judges do not ignore it. Where a Judge omits to follow that precedent he only regards himself bound by the principle underlying the judgMent and not by the facts of that case. It was therefore held that when a judge or a Division Bench of a Court makes a reference on a question of law arising in a matter before him, on the view that every Judge is entitled to take such view as he chooses of the question of fact arising before him as Venkatarama Aiyar, J., would act contrary to section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act and would also violate the oath of office taken by him when entering upon his duties as a Judge under the Constitution.

Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950, which permits the Central Government to retire a Government serv ant at any time after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service provided that in the public interest to do so. Rule 2 provides no guide line and gives absolute discretion to the Gov ernment. There is no requirement under the rule to act in 'Public Interest '. A person who joins Government Service at the age of 21 years can be retired prematurely under F.R. 56(j) only on the ground that he has attained the age Of 55 years, but cannot be picked up for premature retirement under the Rule. Since no safeguards are provided in the Rule, the discretion is absolute and is capable of being used arbi trarily and with an un even hand. The provisions will have effect from the Ist December, 1962. A bare reading of the memorandum shows that there is an obvious fallacy in the argument of the Union of India. This was issued in anticipation of Fundamental (Sixth Amendment) rule 1965 which inter alia incorporated Rule 56(J) into Fundamental Rules. Even otherwise para 6 of the Memorandum could not and did not add anything to Rule 2 (2) 1/2 of the Pension Rules. Rule 2046 is a statutory rule and is identical to Fundamental Rule 56 (j). In any case, the point before this Court was neither involved nor raised in Narasimhan 's case and as such, Mr. Anil Dev Singh cannot derive any support from the said judgment.

The assessee was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable account ing period was 1 4 1943 to 31st March, 1944. There were two partners of the assessee firm, viz., L. Phoolchand and M/s Biharilal Balkishan each having profits in proportion of 11 annas and 5 annas respectively. The work in connection with the extraction of Katechu was carried on in Nepal by one Phoolchand. The sale of Katocana extracted from 23rd November, 1942 to June 29, 1941 to March 31, 1944, fell in the financial year ending March 31. 1948, sales were effected between 26th July, 1943 to September 29, 1940 and March 31st, 1944 respectively. On April 1, 1941, the business was dis continued. The assessee firm did not maintain any books of account, and the entire record of business transaction was maintained in the books of M/S BiharilalBalkishan in the account styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". The assessee Firm had taken a jungle on lease for this purpose and had extracted Katechhu from October 1940 to September 1941. The sales of kattechu were effected by M/ s Biharilal. Balkrishna were effect ed from 30th May, 1941 in which one of the partners of M.M. were stated to have come to India on 1st April, 1944 for the purpose of the Act and thereafter, each jungle was taken on lease in November 1942 and Katechtu was extracted from December 23, 1942. The Sales Tax Officer valued the stock in trade at cost and held that there could be no profit or loss during the chargeable accounting period.

% The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May, 1978. The qualifications specified for the post were B.Sc. (Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering) of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the Rules of the Tamil Nadu Engineering Subordinate Service (General Branch). It was challenged before the High Court by the petitioners holding Civil Engineering degrees. A common question paper was which contained in category I, questions in civil Engineering and in Category II, questions, in Mechanical Engineering, and both the candidates qualified in Mechanical engineering the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had qualified in Civil Engineering question before a common rank list was prepared by the KPSC as was intened, 8 Writ Petitions were filed in the High Courts holding Civil Engineers degrees. By these writ petitions the preparation of a common gradation list and also the procedure of the examination and a method of selection were challenged. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the applicants who had appeared in the written test conducted by the Kerala Public Services Commission, had to answer the questions indicated in Category 1 on the One hand and Those who had applied for the said post should not rationally be included in a common seniority list after the interview but it was open to him to choose which wing, Civil or Mechanical, suits he most. In that view, the High court allowed the writ petitions and directed the Government of Kerala and the Kerala State Public Service commission to prepare "two lists, namely, one for Civil Bench and the other for the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted". The materials placed before the Court showed that there was a common question pre ferred between the two candidates and those whose applications had already been appointed. On behalf of respondent No. 2 it was contended that he has come high in the Common List prepared by Tamil Nadu Government and that as there was no common list, and since no option was given to the Special Leave Petitioners before this Court for clarity, the said decision should be treated to have been overruled.

The respondent No. 1 filed a suit against the appellant defendant for dissolution of partnership firm and for accounts. The valuation of the suit was put as Rs.150 being the sum of Rs.50 for declaration, Rs. 50 for rendition of account and another sum of profit to the share of the plaintiff arising out of the business. The Court fee payable was accordingly. The appellant defendant No. 2 filed a civil revision application before the Calcutta High Court which was dis missed, on appeal by the Corporation. On the question: whether relief to the tune of lacs of rupees has been claimed by the plaintiff in the suit? Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. It is not uniform. The interpretation put by the learned counsel on the decisions of this Court is not correct and cannot be accepted. None of the two cited judgments relied upon by the appellant helps him. It will be open to the trial court to take into consideration the statement in the plaint that the plaintiff has been ousted from the partnership business. If the Court comes to the conclusion that the tentative valuation of a suit would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction, it shall pass an appropriate order under Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure. [508A C] 2. In A suit for accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose any unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, [1945] ILR XXIV Patna 334 and Shama Pershad Shahi Sinha Shahi vs Sheopershad Singh XLI I.C. 95 (Patna). In Attar Singh Singh vs Manohar Singh, ILR (1947) Nagpur overruled.

The respondent assessees were the assessees in the other five Special Leave Petitions. All these matters raised common issue. The assesses ' claim for exemption from sales tax for certain periods in question was accepted by the High Court in the case of G.S. Dhall & Flour Mills and, following it, in the earlier cases, which had negatived the contention that C.A. 22 1187 should be allowed and that the assesses 's S.L.Ps should be dismissed in limine. On appeal to this Court, on behalf of the State Government, it was contended by counsel for the assessees that (i) the decision in G. S. Dhal & Flour Flour Mills case was itself the subject matter of Special Leave Peti tions in this Court but those petitions (S.LP. Nos. 15688 90/87) were dismissed at the stage of admission on September 9, 1983 with the observations: "It is our opinion that the bar imposed by the Full Bench judgment in G Dhall and Flour Mills cases was not intended to be wider than that of the concurrent Bench decision of this Court in GS.Dhall & Weaving Mills case and (ii) the notification issued under section 12(1)(i) of the Act and a similar scheme should have been quashed by a Single Judge of the High COurt. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The effect of rescinding the exemption granted by the 1981 notification was not to be taken away by certain categories of industries. [617G] 2.1 In view of this interpretation, the 1987 amendment has the effect of deci sions and rescinding it by giving retrospective effect so as to exclude what may be described in brief as `traditional ' industries though, like rule 14 of the defer ment Rules, the exclusion extends even to certain other non traditional units operating in certain situations.

Under Rule 5(2) the inter se seniority of members of Delhi Judicial Service promoted to the Service shall be the same as in the Delhi Higher Judicial Service. The petitioners, who were direct recruits, had made representations to the High Court in 1977 for direc tions that their seniority be determined in accordance with the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional District and Sessions Judges. While so, they filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the validity of Rule 5 on various grounds including that the seniority between promotees and direct recruits must be determined according to the respective date of their actual appointments and since no rule was framed under the proviso to Rule 7 of the Delhi Judicial Rules, 1982, there was no provision for probation for the appointment under Rule 16. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that there was a quota of one third of the substantive posts in the Service, and that the law laid down in Chandramouleshwar Prasad vs Patna High Court & Ors. , that seniority between direct recruits vis a vis promotees shall be determined on accordance with their respective dates on which direct recruits were appointed to their respective vacancies and that direct recruits who are appointed as Additional Sessions Judges after the promotees were so appointed, cannot rank higher in seniority over the promotees. Disposing of the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1. It is necessary to draw attention to Rule 2(d) which provides that a Member of the Service ' means a person appointed in substantive capacity to the service under the provisions of the Rules. [362 C] 1.2. Reading Rule 16 of the rules and 17 of the Schedule to the Delhi High Court Rules, 1981 it is apparent that promotees are appointed to temporary posts in tho Service while under rule 17 they are appointed in a temporary capacity to substantive vacancies in the service. It may bear emphasis that promotees appointed under Rules 16 and 17 have to be on probation for a period of two years.

Section 31 of the Income tax Act, 1922, provided that every assessment made on any partner of a firm or association of persons for a particular year may affect the assessment for the said year on a partner or partners of the firm. The Income tax Officer assessed the assessee under section 33(3)(b) of the Act in respect of the income for the assessment years 1951 52 to 1952 53. In appeal by Debi Parshad, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the said order and directed that the direction for assessing the income in the hands of Debi Parl hut be deleted. The Tribunal referred two questions to the High Court: (1) Whether the Income Tax Officer could give a direction in the case of Ambala Flour Mills to the effect that the income should be assessed in the assessee 's favour after annulling the assessment in the cases of Ambala Sugar Mills ? and (2) whether the order of assessment was not barred by the law of Limitation. The High Court, in appeal, set aside that order and remanded the case to the IncomeTax Officer for making fresh assessment after making such further enquiry as he thinks fit or the Appellate Tribunal may direct. In appeals under this Court, HELD : Under section 31(3) of Income tax an assessee is entitled at the option of himself to such share of the profits that went into the assessment of the year under appeal or revision. Commissioner off Income tax, U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate. and Kailash Nath Singh & Ors., [1966] 2 S.C.R. 840, relied on.

The appellant filed a suit claiming partition of his undivided family properties and other assets. The suit was valued at Rs. 1,000 under section 7(iv)(f) of the Madras Court Fees Act, 1951, and a court fee of Rs. 112 7 0 was paid on the said amount on an ad valorem basis. The appellant contended that he should have deposited court fees under section 6(v) Of the Act in respect of his claim for partition as the appellant 's claim for the value of his relief in substance was a claim for recovery of possession based on title within the meaning of section 7 (iv)(b). Held, that since the suit was triable by a Court which has been given the option to value his claim it was not open to him to value the relief on the memorandum of appeal under section 5 of the Act. Accordingly the presentation of the plaint or the appeal and the defendant or the respondent was generally not interested in such a dispute unless the question of payment of court fees involves also the question whether the suit or memorandum of Appeal should be valued for the purposes of jurisdiction and it is on this valuation alone that the appellant can be legitimately called upon to pay Court fee both on the plaint and on the memo of appeal. It would not be reasonable and proper in such cases to hold the plaintiff bound by the valuation made by him for the purpose of jurisdiction, and to infer that the said valuation should be also taken as the value for the payment of Court fees. That is why, in suits falling under section7 (iv) (b), where the plaintiff seeks to pay the fixed court fee as required by the said article he and his advisers are apt to take the view that it is unnecessary to state the amount for which relief is sought to be claimed for the pur poses of Court fee and the valuation for jurisdiction alone is, therefore, mentioned.

% The New Delhi Municipal Committee (NDMC) sought to impugn the decision of the NDMC dated 18.2.1987 declining sanction to accord sanction to the revised Plans for construction of "Statesman House" a high rise building on plot No 148, Barakhamba Road New Delhi, of which the first respondent was the lessee. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC to convey its formal sanctioning ence of the buildings plans on or before May 4, 1989. In June 1985, however there was it would appear, prohibition on high rise structures. During the course of the order dated 28.4.1989 finally dis posing of the writ peti tion, the High Court after referring to what is considered to be a co operative attitude of the DUAC and other authorities, however, had by its order dated 18th February, 1987 declined to sanction the Revised Plans for the construction of 'Statesman house" a low rise building. The NDMC challenged the decision in this appeal by special leave. Disposing of the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The sanction granted by the NDMC clearly postulated that the local body had itself understood the prescriptions in the bye laws to be flexible and had further limited the extent of the Ref uge Areas to 0.3 sq. metre per person as against 1.0 sq. 270 metres per person set out in bye law 16.4, and 16.2 ' [600D] 1.2 The clearance by the Chief Fire Officer is an indispensable condition for eligibility for sanction, however this clearce, by itself, is not conclusive of the matter nor binding on the NDMC. On the material placed before this Court it is open to the NDMC either examine or decide the question independently of the Chief fire Officer 's clearance? [601F] 1:3 The exemption from the Chief Electrical Fire Offi cer in so far as the Refuge Area is concerned, although such clear ance, had been made, has treated such provisions, it is not unreasonable to presume that the requirements were incorporated in the Bye laws with a similar approach as to their import. [602F] 2.1 No departure from bye laws 16.8.1 provides for refuge areas in the ratio of one sq. metres in height and buildings identified in 6.2.[603A B] 2:2.

The joint family carried on joint business of a grocery shop and liquor shops, a ration shop, a motor bus service and also moneylending under the name of "Sontakke Brothers". He was running a liquor shops in a grocer shop. He was carrying on the business, while defendant No. 4 was running the flour shops. The parties tried to have partition effected between them through their arbitrators but the attempt failed were unsuccessful. On June 29, 1945 all the five brothers filed a suit for partition against the plaintiff of all joint family properties including the accounts of the various businesses. The compromise further declared that the plaintiff was to have one sixth share in the motor garage and that defendants 1 and 2 were to pay the price of one sixth of the income from the said business. The plaintiff contended before the trial court that the compromise was made after due deliberation, that accounts of motor business and grocery shops should actually be taken up to March 31, 1946, that the joint family business would be either altogether stopped after the 31st March, 1946 or would be run by it independently of any of you. None of 'the parties agreed to confine the period of account to March 16, 1946 and that which would have normally extended to the passing of the final decree will appear from the following circumstances: The plaintiff had no real grievance in the matter for although the defendants Nos. 1 and2 who continued to run the motor business, may have made some money with the help of their two old motor buses; but he was anxious to run by him independently of all of them. Held, that a consent decree is as binding on the parties thereto as a decree passed by invitum. The partition having been found not to be vitiated by fraud or misrepresentation, mistake, misrepresentation, misunderstanding or mistake, the decree passed thereon has the binding force of res judicata.

The appellant was the owner of a large open space extending over an area of 400 acres, the works of which were carried on in the premises of the firm. At about a few places pucca platforms exist for fixing the water pump when required to pump water from the sea. When not required, the pump is kept in the office; With the exception of the constructions already mentioned, the entire area of Salt Works was open. On the sea side it has bunds in order to prevent sea water flooding the salt pans. Clause (m) of section 2 of the Act provides that " factory means any premises including the precincts thereof (i) whereon ten or more workers are working, or were working on any day of the preceding 12 months and in any part of which a manufacturing process is being carried on without the aid of power, or is ordinarily so carried on, or (ii) whereon twenty or more persons are working or were employed or working onany day of such preceding twelve months andin any part thereof which a manufacture " is being carry ing on with the aid Of power or is being ordinarily so carry on, but does not include a mine subject to the operation of the , or a railway running shed. The expression " premises " means any Premises including the premises precincts thereof". The word " premises includes precincts and it has been urged that the ,doubtor did not come within the definition of the word " factory" in the Act because, according to the meaning given to the word ' premises " must be restricted to buildings alone. Held, further, that even assuming that the word factory was only put into the condition of a finished article by the processes to which it had been subjected in the hereditament and that no human agency was employed in such conversion, at an earlier stage, in the absence of such words, the use of the expression " manufacturing process " did not amount to manufacture".

The respondent entered the service of the Princely State in 1935 as Instructor in Tailoring and joined duty there on December 1, 1949. One Shri K. Narayanaswamy Chetty who was also an Instructor in tailoring and was also deputed to the occupational Institute at Salem and joined duties there on 12th October, 1949, but he was reverted back to his parent department. Later, the State Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service Commission for examining it and by a communication dated February 2, 1960 made these recommendations in favour of the respondent: "It is stated in the Government letter dated 26 10 1959 that the Director who was the Unit officer for both the departments ordered the transfer of Sri Srinivasa Murthy who was fully qualified as Tailoring Instructor in the Technical Education Department and there was no need to classify the vacancy post to which he was transferred under the then existing rules. Along with him, Sri K. Narayana Chetty, who was junior to him in the parent department and came on deputation to the Polytechnics and joined work there on Decem ber 1, 1964, joined duty on December 13, 1949 and after his reversion as Instructor , in tailalling and he joined duty thereafter from December 1 1949. This appointment was challenged by the respondent in a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution alleging that while his juniors were officiating in the Department of Technical Education with effect from November 28, 1949 to November 21, 1950, they should also be absorbed in the department of Technical education with effect on November 28. 1949 it was contended that this principle of policy was ignored in the case of respondent and that he 's absorption in 1964 was not made in pursuance ' any principle of Policy or statutory rule but was done as a matter of concession. It was further submitted that this condition had been violated by the State Public Service Com mission, and, therefore, the transfer order could not be treated as a break in his service, and that the respondent was entitled to all consequential benefits from such absorption including the benefit of revision of pay scales. Disposing of the appeal, ^ HELD: 1 : There is no principle of law or service rule on the basis of which they can claim such promotions as of right. [259 G H] 1:2 The acceptance of the Respondent 's contentions in the present case cannot lead to any untoward results such as were apprehended in Rajalakshmiah Setty 's cases, and this being the case, the High Court was fully justified in granting the relief, it did, to the respondent. % This writ petition was filed by one Laxmi Kant Pandey, an advocate practising in this Court complaining of malpractices indulged in by social organisations and voluntary agencies engaged in the work of offering Indian children in adoption to foreign parents. The said letter was treated as a writ petition and by an order dated 1st September, 1982 the Court issued notice to Union of India, the Indian Council of Social Welfare and to appear in answer to the writ petition. The respondent Union of india filed its counter affidavit. Stating that the adoption of children by foreign parents need not be stayed since the application for appointment was being made directly without the intervention of a social or child welfare agency in the country of the foreigner, it was prayed that an order appointing the foreign parent as guardian of the child with liberty to him to take the child to his own country with a view to its eventual adoption, and directing the Government to carry out their obligations in the matter of adoption of Indian children byforeign parents. Allowing the writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1. It would be almost impossible for the Court to satisfy itself that the foreigner who wishes to take a child in adoption would be suitable as a parent for the child and whether he would be able to provide a stable and secure family life to the child. [828C D] 2. I This procedure has been observed and followed, whether the foreigner will be a suitable adoptive parent for taking a child out of India and take it to his or her own country for the purpose of adopting it in accordance with the law of that country can be followed. [ 816E F] 3.1 In every foreign country where children from India are taken in adoption, there are social and child welfare agencies licensed or recognised by the Government and it would not therefore cause any difficulty or inconvenience or inconvenience if it is insisted that every application from a foreigner for taking an Indian child in adopt must be sponsored by a social, or child Welfare agency or individual trafficking in children by demanding exorbitant amounts from prospective adoptive parents under the guise of maintenance charges and medical expenses or otherwise, would be virtually eliminated. [ 839A B] 2:1 The recognised social or Child welfare agency sponsoring the application of the foreign parents should also agree to send to the concerned social or Children welfare agency for processing an application of its national for taking into consideration an application by a foreigner as guardian for a child with a particular view to his eventual adoption. [ 837C D, 823A] 3:2 Since an application is made directly with the intervention by a Social or child rehabilitation agency in India, there would hardly be any scope for a social and Child welfare Agency or individual who brings a child from another State for the purposes of being given in adoption by that person of any consent required in connection with the adoption, unless such institution or organisation is licensed as a social welfare institution and under Clause 21 it would be unlawful to make or to give to any person any payment or reward for or in consideration of the grant by that persons of any ternical or childful social agency or Individual trafficking in Children by demanding meagre amounts from prospectively adoptive parents from prospective applicants under the garb of maintenance charge and medical expense or otherwise. [araB] 3 :3 In the instant case, admittedly, it is not necessary that there should be only one social or 'child welfare agency which has a child under its care would have to approach a recognised social/ child welfare Agency if it desires such child to be given in inter country adoption.

The appellant company was a manufacturer of Aluminium Rods, Radio Aerials, Fuse Wires and other products. Its paid up capital is Rs. 2,48,65,450. It employed workmen numbering over 5000. The gross effective salaries and wages of its employees for the relevant accounting year amounts to about Rs. 23,68,785 as available surplus was declared as bonus for the year 1965 66. This amount represented 13 51% of the wage bill. The workmen were dissatisfied with this offer of bonus at 13.51%. In view of the agreement between the parties to refer the claim for additional bonus for adjudication to a Tribunal, the workmen received the bonus at 108 the rate of 13.50% offered by the Company. The Central Government referred for adjudication the dispute "what should be the quantum of bonus payable to the Workmen of the Indian Cable company Limited Calcutta for the accounting year 196566" The Unions contended before the Tribunal that the computa tion of allocable surplus available by the company has not been properly made in accordance with the Act and that several items shown in the profit and loss account as expenditure have to be added back to arrive at its actual gross profits. The Unions further alleged that the Company had spent large amounts for payment of liability for future years with a view to reduce the available surplus and allocable allocable to the available and alloca tionable surplus, which in consequence had resulted in reduction of percentage of bonus. The company on the other hand maintained that it has kept proper accounts which have been audited by a reputed firm of auditors of Messrs Lovelock & Lewes and that the computation of allocables has been properly arrived at having due regard to the provisions of the Act. It also added back the sum of Rs. 21,06,576 being 60% of that available surplus. On this reasoning the Tribunal added back this amount to gross profits as an item of expenditure. The Tribunal took notice of the fact that the Income tax Authorities did not object to deduction of the provision made by the Respondent for payment bonus for accounting year 1964 65 and directed the payment of the balance 6.49% within the period mentioned 109 in the Award. One aspect which has to be acted is that (in calculating the available available surplus, the Tribunal before deducting the amount of Bonus paid for the previous years had to be deducted from the gross profits for calculation of direct tax or alternatively rebate for bonus found payable has to he calculated and 60% Of the rebate has to go through the method of computation regarding bonus which was not adopted by the Tribunal. It held that such a payment was not an item which could be deducted out of the gross profit under the Act as claimed by the management. The appeal to this Court was against the award of the Tribunal and it was contended on behalf of the Unions that (1) the respondent had paid not only bonus due to him but also the extra amount of Rs, 1,05,32,880 as an assessee entitled under section 8 read with sections 10 and 11 of the , and (2) that the payment should be deducted back in computing the gross computed profits. HELD : (i) In view Of the fact, that a ceiling had been fixed under the Companies Act, 1913 to make up for the lesser amount that the employees like Mr. Banerjee will get under the Payment of Bonus Act, this amount of bonus will be Rs. 14,76,706 and not Rs. 20% as awarded by the tribunal. From what is stated above it follows that the further direction in the award regarding set on cannot be accepted. [111 G] (ii) The Tribunal was justified in disallowing this claim of the union.

Rules for the State and Subordinate Services: "Promotions in a service or class to a selection grade shall be made on grounds of merit and ability, seniority being considered only where merit and suitability are approximately equal." So, what do we have ? There was an adverse entry in a confidential file of the appellant. The basis of the entry 79 was knocked out by the order dated November 29. 1974 of A Government, and the effect thereof was blotted out by promotion of the applicant as Deputy commissioner. After his promotion as Dy Commissioner there had been no entry In the service book to his disbelieve or hinted even remotely, it is still 4l lid possible to sustain the order. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD : The functions which the the Regional Transport Authority is entrusted with are the function which is covered by section 68 C and are also functions which are specified in Ch. IV of the . [353 B] (a)(b) (c) The exclusion of the jurisdiction conferred on the State Legislature under section 68 F(1) merely because that of the Regional 'authority of that area cannot grant permits under Ch. 4 is subject to the unfettered discretion and judg ment of the Corporation where that area can grant permits by reason of section 68F(1). The words "any scheme published under sub section (3) of section68 C should be construed in their widest connotation so as to exclude a policy decision contemplated by s 34. [355 H] Dosa Satyanaraya namurty etc. vs The Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corpora tion, , relied on. (b)(c) While the functions of the State Legislatures are not confined merely to matters mentioned in Chs. The conditions laid down in Ch sections 46 and 48 of the are not satisfied in this case. The appellant was a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. In respect of the accounting year ending with 31st December 1954 the assessee had shown its gross turnover at Rs. 70,99,928 10 0 and claimed exemption thereunder under two heads (i) under section 5(2)(a)(ii) thereof Rs. 6965,65,979 9 6 6 and (ii) under s.5(2) (a)(iii). The Commercial Tax Officer by notice fixed August 4, 1955, for hearing the assessee in respect of its return. On August 8, 1957 he fixed August 10, for hear ing the assessee to produce the necessary documents in order to prove that they had issued the declaration forms to it but the said officer did not issue the requisite summons to the parties concerned. The Commercial tax Officer by his notice dated April 22, 1955 fixed August 9, on which date the assessee produced the necessary information and thereafter on September 23, 1955 passed an order for hearing of the assessee. On November 21, 1957 the Commercial Tax officer made an order of assessment disallowing the assessee 's claim for exemption in respect o the said sales made to the purchasing registered dealers amounting to Rs. 2246,006 0 6 and levied on it additional tax of Rs. 1,49,778 4. The assessee thereafter flied a petition to the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes claiming exemption under two sub heads (ii), (iii) under sections 5(1) (2)(A)(i), (ii). A Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the said application and held that on the construction of section 5 of the Act, the furnishing of the declaration form by the purchasing dealers was a condition for claiming exemption thereunder. The appeal to this Court was filed in this Court after obtaining special leave from this Court it was contended inter alia on behalf of the appellant : (1) By virtue of section 7(2), the expression "on demand" in r. 27A which according to the learned counsel, indicates that the production of the prescribed declaration is not obligatory but only to be made if a demand is made by the authority concerned; and (2) The words "for such sales a declaration form duly filled up and signed by the registered dealer to whom the goods are sold and containing the prescribed particulars on a prescribed form obtainable from the prescribed authority has to be furnished in the prescribed manner by the dealer who sells the goods. HELD: Dismissing the appeal. (1)(a) Though the expression 'on demand ' only fixes the point of time when the declaration formed were to be produced; otherwise, the rule would be inconsistent with the section and if it was substantially compiled with. [627 D] (b) It is well settled that a dealer cannot get the exemption unless he furnishes the declaration in the specified form. It is for the legislature or for the rule making authority to intervene to soften the rigour of the provisions and it is not for this Court to do so where the provisions are clear and unambiguous. [ 631 C D] State of Orissa vs M.A. Tulloch & Co., Ltd., ; referred to. (c) It can be invoked only in a case where the authorityconcerned is empowered to take evidence in respect Of any particular matter; but that does not enable him to ignore a statutory condition to claim exemption. Sub rules (3) and (4) of r.27A are not helpful to the appellant. They provide only safeguards against abuse of the declared forms by the buying dealers; they do not enable the selling dealer to either directly apply or compel the purchasing dealer to apply for duplicate forms. Nor do they enjoin on the appropriate authority to give the selling dealers a duplicate form to replace lost one. [625 E F] (2).
