The appellant was the landlord and the respondent a protected tenant. The respondent gave notice of termination, under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. Subsequently an amendment was made to the Bombay Rent Restriction on residential and Agricultural lands Act by the insertion of sub section (2 A). The Tenancy and Agriculture Lands Act came into force on January 12, 1953. By virtue of this amendment certain restrictions were placed on the right of the landlord to terminate the tenancy of a protectedtenant. The appellant applied for possession of the land under section 29(2) of The Bombay Tenancy Act for obtaining possession of his land to the Mamlatdar. Since the landlord refused the application he moved the High Court for a writ, and contended that he had no right to terminate by one year 's notice under section34(2). Where in an amendment it was provided that a tenant would be liable to ejectment on one year s notice by the landlord. The High Court allowed the application of the appellant relying on its previous Full Bench decision in Durlabbhai Fakirbhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai (I.L.R. LXVII of 1953). On appeal by special leave : Held:(i) The order passed by the High court was correct and sub section(2 A) would apply to all cases where notices might have been given but where the tenancy had not actually terminated before the coming into force of the Amending Act, it could not claim relief from the Court. The fact that in a subsequent amendment a tenant is liable for ejectment on another year ' notice by him will have to be taken into consideration in determining the right to the landlord in the matter of termination of tenancy, for the Amending Acts put certain fetters on this right of termination. In view of the decision of this Court in Durlavabhai Fakir Abdul Kader Chaudhuri (I L.R., LXVII) Cal. 1037 it is clear that the legislature could not have intended that the benefit of this beneficent measure should not be extended to tenants in whose cases the tenancy has not yet terminated, though notices had been given, when the further restrictions were being put on the rights to terminate. (ii) The Amending Act was a piece of beneficent legislation meant for the protection of tenants. Therefore if there is any doubt about the meaning of sub s.(2 A), that doubt should be resolved in favour of the tenant, for whose benefit the Amending act was passed.

The petitioners were evacuees and the houses of one Khadim Ali who had not been declared an evacuee and had died on or about October, 1, 1950. The petitioners contended that they have been wrongly deprived of their rights in the houses by the action of the Custodian. Held, that no property could be declared to be evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under section 7, and his interest in the house was not affected by the order made under section 13(2) Of the Act. In the present case in respect of his rights under the will, if any, and say nothing about them, it was open to the Custodian to declare the entirety of them evacuee property and deprive them of their property which could be impugned under article 31 of the Constitution. The acts of the custodian in so far as they deprives the petitioners of their properties cannot therefore be upheld. Northern India Creser vs Tek Chand Dolwani, , 703 and Ebrahim Aboobaker vs Tekchand Dolani, ; , referred to. Held further, that the acts of N Lines in so much as they deprive the petitioners, of their right in them have no longer any claim to them, and so there had no longer, any claim on them. Under section 12 Of the , the rights, title and interest of any evacuee in the evacuee property specified in the notification shall, on and from the beginning of the date on which the notification is so published, be extinguished and the evacuee properties vest absolutely in the Central Government free from all encumbrances. It was well established that no appeal by him against the order of January 10, 1952, lies within the time prescribed for it, and there was no judicial determination by the Custodian General of any fact affecting his rights in any manner whatsoever affecting his right in the properties concerned.

The assessee company which carried on the operations of spinning of yarn from imported wool tops by raising a loan of Rs. 7 lakhs from the Industrial Finance Corporation, raised a loan from the industrial Finance Corporation and that the plant went into production in September 1952. The assessee Company appointed M/s. Murlidhar Chiranjilal as the sole selling agents for the worsted yarn on payment of 2% commission. Later on on December 15, 1953 the assessee company entered into an agreement with Mis Saligram Premnath under which the latter were appointed as the Producer. The essential conditions of which being that the agents were to finance the assessee Company to the extent of Rs 2,50,000/ and the assessee agreed to pay 6% interest on this advances to be made by the agents and further agreed to paid 2% Commission on the net proceeds of sales of goods in India. Before expiry of this agreement, another agreement was entered into by the assessee firm with Misram Prem Nath under which it was appointed as a sole selling agent on certain specified conditions, the important of which was that the agent were to Finance the assessee by giving him a loan Of Rs. 21 lakhs from industrial Finance Corp. The plant went up in September, 1952 and was working at a constant loss as a result of which in 1952 the assessee assessee Company decided to instal a plant for manufacture of worsted Textile yarn from import wool toises by raising loans of Rs 7 lakhs. On December 15. 1953 the Company entered into agreement with M/S. Murlidhar Kalu Chiranju as its sole selling agency for the products of Milling and that on December 25, 1953, the assessee 's plant went to production in July 1952. By this agreement another agreement dated October 20, 1955 was entered whereunder the agents agreed to a deduction of 50% of the loss incurred by the assesses Company from their remuneration, subject to certain conditions which being: (i) The agents were not only at the beginning of the manufacture of the yarn by the plant to be installed by the assesee company but at every stage in the pro gramme of manufacture. These two agreements were executed on October 20 1955 under which they conferred a right on the agents to finance, (ii) There was a number of other conditions with which we shall deal later. The selling agents M/ s. Murlidhar Moolanjilal agreed to share losses in respect of certain items of sale and purchase proceeds which had come into force on December 13, 1953; and (iii) In order to earn profits, the agents entered into another agreement under which lning the assessee "to get 6% commission" from the gross proceeds of Sales of goods as provided in this agreement a deduction was made in favour of the selling agents. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the deduction claimed but held that the deductions were actually a division of profits after the profits had come to existence and had been ascertained; therefore could not be claimed as a valid deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the 1922 Act, but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner also took an inference in respect thereof. The Tribunal took this view. The High Court on reference held that it was not necessary for the Tribunal to examine the question whether the amount set apart for the purpose of distribution amongst the consumers is not chargeable to tax on the ground that it represents over charge. On appeal by special leave: HELD: (1) In a commercial sense the payments were an expenditure wholly and exclusively laid out for the purposes of the business of the assessee and to disallow it. But when once an individual or a company has in that proper sense ascertained what are the profits of his business or his trade, the destination of those profits or the charge which has been made on these profits by previous agreement or otherwise is perfectly immaterial.

The assessee company maintains an accounts pertaining to him in its books. The accounts showed that as on March 31, 1958 a sum of Rs. 36 lakhs was due to the assessee by the company. In January, 1959 for the first time he became indebted to the company in the sum of RS. 3,757 np. On 23rd April 1959 he becameached to the Company in the terms of Section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 on a total income of Rs 43,407. The Income Tax Officer came to know that the assessee had been withdrawing moneys from the company and in the belief that those amounts were liable to be treated as "dividend" under section 2(7A)(a) of that Act he reopened the assessment by virtue of Section 147 of the Income tax Act, 1961. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal filed by the assessee. The High Court held that the expression "accumulated profits" in Section 2 (6A) which was confined to the connotation it held under the law relating to companies. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the Revenue it was contended that: (1) The definition of "accuxulated profits ' by Explanation 2 to section 2 (22) of Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1939 did not include current profit for the purpose of Section 5(6 A)(e); (2) the expression 'accumured profits" occurring in Section 6(2A) (c) could not be construed as including current profits; and (3) the Tribunal was right in answering the first question in favour of the assessee, and against the Revenue. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Appellate Tribunal was not competent to refer the second question on its merits. [948 G] 2.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan, and he claimed to have been in possession of certain plots of land in the occupation of the respondents or in other alternative for assessment of fair and equitable rent. The trial judge held that the lands were included in Mouza Nala in Thouzi No. 1 and that they had been settled on the plaintiff by the Maharaja of Burdwan, as such to the knowledge of the plaintiff and that on the strength of that entry the respondents were refusing to surrender possession of the land to them. The District Judge however held that both the documents put forward by the defendants as containing assertions by them that they held under a Lakheraj grant were not shown to relate to the suit lands, that the relationship subsisting between the parties was one of landlord and tenant, that as there had been no determination of tenancy, no decree in ejectment could be passed but that the plaintiff was entitled to fair rent therefore. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD : (i) It is well settled that it is beyond the powers of a manager of a religions institution to grant perpetual lease binding the institution for all times to a fixed rent unless there is a compelling necessity or benefit therefor. [1175 F] (ii) When a person was found in possession and enjoyment of land for a considerable period of time under an assertion of title without challenge, Courts in England were inclined to ascribe a legal origin to such possession, and when on the facts a title by prescription could not be sustained it was held that a presumption could be made that the possession was referable to a grant by the owner entitled to the land but that such grant had been lost.

The appellant plaintiff filed a suit for specific performance of a contract dated 15th December 1965 for sale of agricultural land, alleging that the land which was the subject matter of contract was covered by the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act 1948. The defendant contended that the said land which had been the subject subjectmatter of contract had been covered by section 63 of the Tenancy Act, because the intending purchaser, the plaintiff was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Act, section 63, of the said Act prohibited him from purchasing the land and therefore as the agreement was contrary to the provisions contained in section 70(a) read with sections 85 and 85A of the Indian 'Tenancy Act, the same could not be specifically enforced. The trial Court held that the certificate had no evidentiary value and was not valid. On appeal the High Court agreed with the trial court observing that the Civil Court has undoubtedly jurisdiction to entertain a suit on a rival contentions between the parties and that in such a situation the civil suit should be stayed and the parties should be referred to the competent authority under the Tenancy (Tenability Act) for decision, and further held that if an issue arises in a properly constituted civil suit which the Civil court is competent to entertain, an incidental or subsidiary issue which may arise with reference to provisions of The Tenancy Act the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts to settle, decided or deal with any question which is by or under the Bombay 'Telancy Act required to be settled, decided and dealt with by any authority competent to settle.

Respondent assessee company, manufacturing boilers, machinery parts, wagons etc. was a heavy engineer ing concern manufacturing boilers and machinery parts; for the assessment years 1958 59 and 1959 60, it claimed exemption of tax under section 15C of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 in respect of profits and gains derived from its Jute mill Division where the parts made out of raw material supplied by the Vadilal Plant by machining and forging them were given to the Boiler Division of the assessee. The assessee contended that setting up of a separate unit to do something in the course of pre existing manufacturing process would not amount to starting of a new industrial orna ment which took place when there was reconstruction of the old busi ness; that the new undertaking could be said to be not formed out of the reconstruction of its business already in existence, namely the business of heavy engineering; that mere setting up or expansion of the existing business would not attract the exclusion clause in section 15 C(2)(i); and that the two undertakings were set up by reconstruction of their business already 8 years in existence i.e. the business already being carried on; that they were purchased from outside India and since they were sold in the open market, they were not to be treated as forming formed by reconstruction or manufacture from within the assessee 's own business. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the claim of exemption under section '15C being only one part of them, namely, whether the industrial undertakings, Steel Foundry and Jute Mill Division was an indus trial undertaking to which section 15B applied; and that in particu lar with regard to the scope and ambit of the expression therein, namely reconstruction of business already existing and hence the assessee was not entitled to exemption under Section 15C(2) thereof. The Tribunal, however, allowed the appeal of the appellant for exemption under 'section 15C ' on the ground that: (1) on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was right in holding that the steel Foundry Division was a 'industrial undertaking to come within the mischief of the exclusion cl. (i), and therefore, it could not be said that the undertakings formed out Of the existing 'business to come under the mischief 'of section 15A(2). The High Court adopted this view and held that even though the manufactured products of the new industrial undertakings were mostly used in the assessee"s other business of manu facturing boilers, wagons, etc., the element of profit was there and the extent of the same could be ascertained as the asses see was maintaining separate books of account. The High 'Court further held that on the question whether in the factual matrix of the matter, the two industrial undertakings could be called into; (2) the Tribunal had rightly decided the question of assessee 'and accepted the claim for exemption; and (3) that it upheld the demand for exemption. It was contended on behalf of the Revenue that: 1 (1 ) there was no formation of any Industrial undertaking out of: the existing con tended business since that can take place only when the assets of the original business are transferred substantially to the new ac quirement; and, (2). that production of the articles in the steel Spinners and in its jute mill is only ancillary activity to the main business of the asses sees. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1(a) The Tribunal was not right in taking the two new undertakings as formed by the reconstruction.

The inams in the present case were granted to the temple for the performance of services connected therewith. The inam Commission confirmed the grants of the inams in favour of the hereditary officeholders then rendering the service under the direction of the Paisaldars or the trustees of the temple. In 1863, the inam lands and regranted them to the deity. On October 17, 1947 this order was confirmed by the British Government. In 1951, the Arc tive Officer resumed the inam Lands and regin tered them again rendering service under they directions of, the Paiondars or trustees of a temple. The Inam Commission confirmed conditional resumption of the inam on certain grounds as in those cases no alienation thereof made before 1934 could be resumed for failure to perform the conditions of the grant. On appeal by the State, the District Judge held that the inams were personal inams burdened with services and were resumable under section 44 B. In appeals to this Court it was contended : (1) Since neither section 44B(2)(a)(i), nor section 44A(2) (a)(ii) is applicable to a personal inam burdened with a condition of service, the lands did not come within the purview of section 44 D; and (2) in any event, the right of resumption could be extinguished by adverse possession. HELD : (per Desai, J) The inam was not subject to the conditions prescribed by section 44 A(2), or that it was not properly called retrospective 'because a part of the requisites for its action is drawn from a time antecedent to its passing". In essence, the inams are granted to office holders as remuneration for services to be rendered by them in connection with the temple.[549 B D] Further, the title deeds acknowledged their title to Devadayan or pagoda service inam to 1147 acres of land held for the service of Sree Padam Thangi and confirmed the inam to them and their successors tax free to be held without interference so long as the conditions Of the grant were duly fulfilled. Those documents showed that the lands were being enjoyed by the inamdars and were granted as inams. [550 E] The High Court was not right in holding that section 44F(2A)(i) allows resumption of religious and charitable inams on the ground that the land was alienated or otherwise lost to the institution or service to which it once belonged or on the grounds that the terms of the grants were not observed. [549 B C] England vs Crawford, , referred to. Since section 44C(2 (a) (i) is attracted when the holder of the Inam has made an exchange, gift, sale etc., Of the inam or has granted a lease of it for a term exceeding five years. The lands were not personal inams but they were inams granted as. [557 B] Under section 44G(2(a)(iii), however, the Zamindar may on his own motion or on application, resume the whole or any part of an inam and may be resumed under section44B. The words "has failed" in sub section (2)(b)(ii), must necessarily have been absent from the definition of 'rent ' but they are not retrospective in operation. [544 C] In the present cases, there was no period of limitation prescribed for the initiation of proceedings under section 46F(1) or that the right to resume an inam cannot be extinguished By adverse possession of the lands by the alienees for over 60 years.

The appellant was the trustees of a charitable trust. Prior to January 26, 1954, the Indore Municipality was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. By virtue of the power conferred on it by that Act the Municipality used to levy and collect house tax 127 at the rate of 7% of its gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs for repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The difference came to Rs. 1,461 and of this, the trustees claimed refund on the ground that under the 1954 Act the tax could be assessed on the basis of gross annual rental letting value not less 10 percent statutory allowance. The Trial Court decreed the suit and the appeals filed by the Corporation were dismissed. The appellant Company as trustees contended, that the tax imposed on the base of ' gross annual cost ' was saved by section 2(c) and therefore the rate was saved. HELD: (i) Under sections 75 and 76 when the assessment list is prepared in accordance with the provisions of s 73 it has to be published and time has to ance fixed for lodging objections against the entries therein. After such objections are heard and disposed of the assessment lists have to be authenticated as provided by section 76(6). [131 D] (ii) The appellant Corporation was not entitled to demand the tax assessed on its gross monthly rental value. The High Court was right in decreeing the suit. [132 F G]. In order to prevent such a result the legislature has provided by sub section 2 of section 79 that where a municipality adopts a previously prepared list for any subsequent year the provisions 16 of sections 75, 76 and 77 shall be applicable as if a new assessment list had been completed at the commencement of that particular official year. [133 G] In order that it prepares a fresh list oncein every 4 years. But sub sec. 2 of Section 79 provides expressly that when such a previous list is adopted for a particular official Year it can be done subject to the provisions Of sections 75 & 76.

The respondent assessee company carried on its business of manufacturing matches till the account year ending April 30, 1941. In a confidential report made by the appellant under section 25 of the Travancore Income tax Act for the assessment year ending October 30, 1943, to its creditors, the Directors stated that the price obtained had shown a capital appreciation of about six times the cost price, and the sale included chemicals and paper for manufacture which had not been sold in the course of ordinary trading but in a reali sation sale after the company had been wound up. The Income tax Officer assessed the respondent 's profit under section 10(1) of the Income tax. 1922, but the Tribunal reduced the assessable profits to Rs. 1,15,259 and by its order dated October 11, 1937, reduced the partnership to Rs, 1,17,260. Held, that a sale of the chemicals and raw materials for match manufacture was nothing more than a winding up sale. The Revenue could not be said to be in the carrying on of the business, because, it had acquired all the properties of an industrialist within section 25(3) of that Act and hence, the excess obtained by him represented profit. There is no doubt, in this case the assessee company was formed for the purpose of acquiring and reselling mining properties, and though what it had inherited had from the partnership firm was nothing else but a sale in the normal course of business operations which alone would have attracted tax if profit resulted. The fact that the clause in the Memorandum gave power to the appellant company to Bell chemicals cannot be used in this connection because the evidence clearly showed that clause was never used and the two sales also of chemicals through the years were too petty in themselves to afford evidence of a continued or sustained trading business. In this case there was no identifiable price for the chemicals, and raw material except by comparing the two prices offered to be paid by the buyer, that is to say, the price without the chemicals; and raw and materials were sold in a local way as an investment reserve fund. Doughty 's Case (3) did not support the contention, because the agreement clearly indicated that the assessee Company was keeping the factory going, not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf of the buyer till the entire consideration was paid by makes no difference, because ,the agreement clearly mentioned that the appellant Company was maintaining the factory went not on the business in the ordinary course of trade but was merely a trading busi ness. It would be difficult to arrive at the profit in this way if it were the case of a company which involved breeding of sheep for the purposes of selling wool. There was no doubt in this Case that the respondent Company was carrying on a trading business and therefore, the sales could not liable to tax.
